Pratyaksh Grid Technologies: The Meters That Went Quiet

A risk score says 1.4 lakh smart meters will stop communicating before the summer peak. The field data says a third of the ones already replaced had nothing wrong with them. The board meets on Thursday.

1. Bengaluru, Sunday 22 March 2026

Aparna Vaidyanathan had been on the Whitefield office floor since eleven that morning, which on a Sunday meant the air conditioning cycled off every forty minutes and nobody came to fix it. On her second monitor was a map of five electricity distribution circles in western Maharashtra, shaded by a number her own team had invented four months earlier: the Meter Health Score. On the map, 1.42 lakh of Pratyaksh Grid Technologies' installed smart meters sat in the top two risk bands. If the score was right, most of them would stop communicating before the end of May, during the weeks when the discom's billing cycle mattered most and when ambient temperatures in Jalgaon routinely crossed 43°C.

On Thursday, 26 March, Aparna would take a recommendation to the board. She had ₹14 crore of uncommitted capital, a field force that could physically replace about 4,200 meters a week across the five circles, and a contract whose service-level clause began deducting money on the first day billing efficiency fell below 98.5%. She also had, open in another window, an audit her own operations team had completed three weeks earlier: of 1,100 meters replaced during the Nashik pilot on the strength of the score, 418 had come back from the depot marked no fault found.

She had drafted three versions of the recommendation and deleted all three. The version she believed on Friday was not the version she believed on Saturday, and the difference between them was worth about ₹9 crore.

2. How Pratyaksh got here

Pratyaksh was founded in 2016 by Girish Nadkarni and two colleagues from a power-electronics background, building single-phase and three-phase static energy meters under the Drishti brand for state distribution utilities. Its manufacturing sat in Hosur; its firmware and analytics teams in Pune and Bengaluru. For six years it was a component supplier competing on price and BIS certification against established Indian meter manufacturers such as Genus Power, Secure Meters and HPL.

The decision that shapes everything today was taken in September 2022. The Government of India's Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS) had opened a wave of AMISP tenders — advanced metering infrastructure service provider contracts, in which a vendor finances, installs, owns and operates smart meters and is paid a monthly fee per meter over eight to ten years rather than a price per unit. Pratyaksh bid for the Sahyadri Vidyut Vitaran Nigam (SVVN) package: 42 lakh meters across five circles, at ₹1,180 per meter of reimbursable capex and ₹43 per meter per month in service fees. It was the largest contract the company had ever pursued and it won on price, by roughly 6%.

To reach that price, Shreyas Barve's device team made three engineering choices. It selected a lower-cost hybrid communications module from Vaman Microsystems — RF mesh to a local data concentrator, with NB-IoT fallback over a connectivity contract with Meghdhwani Connect. It limited telemetry to four scheduled uplinks a day. And it kept only a seven-day rolling diagnostic log on the device, because retaining more meant a larger flash part. Every one of those choices saved money across 42 lakh units. Every one of them is now a constraint on what Aparna's data scientists can see.

3. The industry

India's smart-metering programme is the largest such rollout anywhere, driven by RDSS and financed through REC and PFC, with the Ministry of Power setting targets and state electricity regulatory commissions approving tariffs and metering regulations. For discoms, the case rests on eliminating provisional bills, reducing aggregate technical and commercial losses, and enabling prepaid recharge — for which Pratyaksh's consumer app supports UPI payments through a Razorpay integration, the single feature with the highest consumer satisfaction in its own surveys.

The commercial structure matters. An AMISP does not sell a meter; it rents an outcome. If a meter stops communicating, no reading is taken, the consumer receives a provisional bill, the discom's billing efficiency falls, consumer grievance forums receive complaints, and the AMISP absorbs both the truck roll and the deduction. Meter replacement itself is not a simple swap: under state metering regulations, seals must be broken and re-applied by authorised personnel, with a discom representative present and a joint inspection note filed for each unit. Pratyaksh cannot simply send a technician.

Pratyaksh also has a second, smaller business: 42,000 commercial sub-meters supplied to Al Tamayuz Utility Systems LLC in Dubai, a facilities-management firm that bills tenants in commercial towers. That fleet uses a different, cellular-only module and sits in an environment of near-constant 24°C plant rooms. It is 4% of installed units and 19% of gross margin, and its renewal is due in June.

Compiled from release notes, the SVVN monthly operations reports and the pilot closure memo of 28 February 2026.

4. The situation in detail

Installations reached 18.6 lakh meters by March 2026, against a contracted 42 lakh. Non-communicating meters — NCM, the contractual term — ran at 1.9% through 2024. In June 2025 the rate rose sharply to 4.4%. The operating assumption at the time was RF mesh coverage degrading in heavy monsoon foliage; Meghdhwani Connect added NB-IoT capacity in two circles and the rate fell back to 2.6% by September. In January 2026 a connectivity audit found that roughly a fifth of that spike had been a SIM-profile provisioning fault on a batch of 90,000 units, corrected silently in August. Nobody re-ran the June analysis afterwards.

In November 2025, firmware v4.2 went out over the air to the whole fleet. Its headline change was faster UPI recharge acknowledgement. Its release notes also record, in the eleventh line, a revised RTC-battery reporting scale and a change to the internal-temperature sampling window from a sixty-second to a five-minute average.

Three things believed in 2025 have since turned out to be at least partly wrong. The monsoon spike was not entirely weather. The fleet was not, as the December analysis assumed, telemetrically homogeneous, because v4.2 reached 99% of Nashik and 91% of Ratnagiri on different weeks. And the pilot, designed to test the score, was executed in a way that destroyed its own evidence.

In December, Yuvraj Sandhu's team in Toronto built the Meter Health Score from the four daily uplinks: communications retry counts, RTC battery voltage, peak internal temperature, and relay operation counts. Backtested against the prior year's NCM events, its top tier showed 68% precision at a three-week horizon (Exhibit 2). In January and February, Sudeshna Roy's field organisation ran a pilot in the Nashik circle: 60,000 meters, 1,900 flagged, 1,100 replaced. The disposition audit that followed (Exhibit 4) is the document that has made this week difficult.

5. The people

Aparna Vaidyanathan — Chief Product Officer, Bengaluru. Owns the recommendation. Believes the score is directionally right and the audit is being read too literally. Has not said that she approved the pilot's replace-everything protocol herself, over Yuvraj's written objection.

Girish Nadkarni — co-founder and CEO, Bengaluru. Wants a decision that protects the SVVN relationship, because ₹96 crore of RDSS-linked receivables are milestone-dependent and a second AMISP tender closes in July. Has not said that he has already described the Meter Health Score to two investors as a live capability.

Shreyas Barve — Head of Firmware and Device Engineering, Pune. Argues the hardware is sound and the problem is network, not meters. Knows that v4.2 changed two telemetry definitions and that his team did not notify analytics; has mentioned it once, in a thread, without emphasis.

Yuvraj Sandhu — Principal Data Scientist, Toronto. Built the score. Says publicly that it needs a randomised holdout before scaling; says privately that his model cannot be evaluated at all now, because every flagged meter in the pilot was replaced. Is also negotiating a DPDP-compliant data-residency arrangement that may restrict what he can process from Canada.

Sudeshna Roy — VP Field Operations, Nashik. Runs 4,200 replacements a week and a technician workforce paid partly per completed job. Wants a large, funded replacement programme. Does not volunteer that "no fault found" is the default depot code when a returned meter powers up normally on the bench, and that bench testing does not reproduce 43°C.

Marianne Köhler — Principal Designer, Berlin. Designed the discom-facing operations console. Reports that SVVN's circle engineers ignore the risk column because it shows a number with no reason code. Wants the score redesigned before it is scaled; her concern is usability, and it is also a delay.

Ashwini Menon — Customer Success Lead, APAC and Gulf, Singapore. Manages both SVVN's programme office and Al Tamayuz. Has been asked by Omar Al Hashimi whether the predictive capability applies to the Dubai fleet, and has not yet answered, because Exhibit 6 says it does not.

Ronald Mathai — SVP Sales, North America, New Jersey. Has built a pipeline pitch around "predictive fleet health" for US municipal utilities. His variable compensation is weighted to new logos. Has already shown Exhibit 2 in three customer meetings.

Prakash Sathe — Nodal Officer, SVVN, Nashik. Not a Pratyaksh employee. Has written twice about provisional billing complaints reaching the consumer grievance forum and has asked, in writing, for a remediation plan by 31 March.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 — Installed fleet and non-communicating rate by circle, February 2026
CircleMeters installedNCM rate, FebNCM rate, Jun 2025Share on v4.2Mean daily max, Feb
Nashik5,20,0003.4%4.9%99%34°C
Jalgaon4,10,0004.1%5.2%99%37°C
Kolhapur3,60,0002.2%4.6%98%32°C
Solapur3,30,0003.8%3.9%97%36°C
Ratnagiri2,40,0001.6%4.4%91%31°C
NCM defined per the SVVN contract as a meter failing to deliver a valid billing read for three consecutive scheduled cycles. Temperature from IMD station data for the circle headquarters, not the meter location. Ratnagiri's lower v4.2 share reflects an incomplete OTA campaign in coastal talukas.

Exhibit 1 is the exhibit most readers reach for and the one most likely to mislead. Ratnagiri is coolest, has the lowest NCM rate, and also has the lowest v4.2 penetration; Kolhapur is cool and heavily on v4.2. The temperature story and the firmware story are entangled in every row, and the contract's own definition of NCM makes no distinction between a failed meter, a failed network and a tampered installation.

Exhibit 2 — Meter Health Score backtest performance, December 2025
BandMeters (fleet-wide, Mar 2026)Predicted NCM within 3 weeksBacktest precisionBacktest recall
A — critical38,000Yes68%31%
B — elevated1,04,000Yes41%29%
C — watch2,90,000Possible17%22%
D — normal13,28,000No——
Backtest window 1 Dec 2024 – 30 Nov 2025, scored on features as reported at the time. Meters that were replaced or repaired during the window were excluded from the denominator. Top three features by gain: RTC battery voltage (0.34), comms retry count (0.22), peak internal temperature (0.19).

Exhibit 2 is the slide that has travelled furthest inside the company; Ronald has used it in New Jersey and Girish in two investor conversations. Its footnote contains two facts that are rarely read aloud. The backtest excludes meters that were repaired — that is, the ones a field team had already identified — and its strongest single feature is a reading whose reporting scale changed in November 2025, four weeks before the model was built.

NCM from SVVN monthly reconciliation files; temperature from IMD, rescaled to share the axis. The June 2025 peak precedes the SIM-provisioning correction of August 2025, which was not retrospectively applied to these figures.

Exhibit 3 is where the case turns uncomfortable. The monsoon peak of June 2025 was explained at the time by weather and has since been partly re-attributed to provisioning. The second, smaller rise begins in December 2025 — after the firmware release, before the hot season, and exactly where the Meter Health Score's training window ends. The April point on the chart is not a measurement at all; it is the model's own forecast, drawn on the same line, a convention nobody in the company has objected to.

Exhibit 4 — Depot disposition of 1,100 meters replaced in the Nashik pilot, Jan–Feb 2026
Disposition codeUnitsShare
No fault found on bench test41838%
Communications module fault24222%
RTC battery / clock fault15414%
Tamper, damage or vandalism777%
Not recorded20919%
Bench testing is conducted at the Nashik depot at ambient temperature, typically 26–30°C. "Not recorded" units were returned during the February inventory migration. No meter flagged by the score was left in the field, so no comparison group exists.

Exhibits 2 and 4 cannot both be read naively. One reports 68% precision in the critical band; the other reports that 38% of replaced meters worked on the bench, with a further 19% unaccounted for. Whether these contradict each other depends entirely on whether a meter that fails at 43°C in a metal enclosure on a Jalgaon wall can be expected to fail at 28°C on a depot table.

Exhibit 5 — Unit economics and capacity, March 2026

Costs from the February management accounts. The SLA deduction is per circle; two circles breaching for one month costs approximately ₹1.67 crore.

Exhibit 5 sets the boundaries of every option. A planned replacement is ₹1,310 cheaper than a reactive one, which makes prevention attractive per unit and unaffordable in aggregate: at 4,200 a week, the entire field organisation working on nothing else clears 54,600 meters before the May peak. The SLA deduction, meanwhile, is levied on the whole circle fleet rather than on failed meters, so a single circle slipping below 98.5% for one month costs more than replacing every Band A meter in it.

Exhibit 6 — Dubai sub-meter fleet, Al Tamayuz Utility Systems

Units42,00018,60,000

Dubai AUC computed on 61 NCM events over fourteen months. Al Tamayuz's contract has no NCM clause; it has an uptime credit tied to monthly billing files.

7. Voices

"I keep hearing that the model found something. It found that meters which report a low clock-battery voltage stop talking. We changed how that voltage is reported in November. I flagged it. I am not going to keep flagging it."Shreyas Barve, engineering review, Pune, 11 March
"Precision of sixty-eight per cent is a statement about a world in which we did not act. We acted on every single one of them. I can no longer tell you what the model's precision is, and I would rather say that than say a number."Yuvraj Sandhu, email to Aparna, 13 March, 02:40 IST
"With respect, my technicians replaced eleven hundred meters in six weeks in Nashik and the circle's NCM rate came down. Nobody in Toronto saw that happen."Sudeshna Roy, operations call, 17 March
"The circle engineers do not use the risk column. I watched six of them in Nashik. They sort by complaint count, because a complaint is a thing they can explain to their superintendent."Marianne Köhler, design research note, 9 March
"Omar has asked twice now whether the health score covers his towers. If the answer is that it does not work there, I need to know before the June renewal, not after."Ashwini Menon, chat thread, 19 March
"Three utilities in the Northeast want to talk about predictive health. I am not going to tell them we have paused it."Ronald Mathai, weekly pipeline note, 20 March
"Ask them what happens to the score if we stop replacing meters for four weeks. If nobody can answer that, we are not running an analytics programme, we are running a replacement programme with a dashboard attached."Girish Nadkarni, executive meeting, 18 March
"Kindly confirm the remediation plan for provisional billing in Nashik and Jalgaon circles by 31 March."Prakash Sathe, SVVN, letter of 16 March

8. The options as Aparna currently sees them

One: scale now. Replace all of Band A and Band B before the peak — 1.42 lakh meters at ₹1,640, roughly ₹23.3 crore, against ₹14 crore available and a field capacity that would need thirty-four weeks. Even a Band A-only campaign, 38,000 meters and ₹6.2 crore, consumes nine weeks of capacity.

Two: pause and rebuild. Retrain with firmware version as a control, hold out a randomised 3% of flagged meters untreated, and re-score in six weeks. This gives Yuvraj what he has asked for and gives Prakash Sathe nothing by 31 March.

Three: fix the instrument. Spend the capital on an OTA firmware release that raises uplink frequency and extends the diagnostic log, reversing the 2022 cost decision. It would take eleven weeks to validate, offers nothing this summer, and would make every model built on the current data stream obsolete — which some would call progress.

Four: renegotiate the definition. Approach SVVN to re-cut the NCM clause so that outages attributable to network provisioning or tamper are excluded. If the January connectivity audit and Exhibit 4 are both right, something between a quarter and a third of the contractual failures are not meter failures at all.

Each option assumes that the thing to predict is a meter that stops communicating. Nobody has yet asked what fraction of the company's actual losses — deductions, truck rolls, grievance-forum complaints, the discom's patience — would disappear if the prediction were about billing gaps rather than about hardware.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets on Thursday 26 March. Prakash Sathe's remediation plan is due 31 March. The hot season begins in the first week of April and peaks in the third week of May. Capital available is ₹14 crore; receivables of ₹96 crore are tied to installation milestones that a diverted field force would slow. Field capacity is 4,200 meters a week and cannot be raised quickly, because each replacement requires a discom representative and a joint inspection note. Vaman Microsystems needs eleven weeks for volumes above 40,000 modules. The Al Tamayuz renewal is due in June. And under the DPDP Act, the arrangement under which consumption-linked data is processed from Toronto is under review by Pratyaksh's own counsel, with an interim recommendation that model training move to an Indian region by the end of the quarter.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What exactly does the Meter Health Score predict, in operational terms, and what would you need to see to believe that it predicts anything about hardware rather than about firmware versions and install cohorts?
  2. Exhibits 2 and 4 appear to contradict each other. Construct the strongest reading under which both are true, and the strongest reading under which the score is worthless. What single piece of evidence would separate them?
  3. The pilot replaced every flagged meter. What did that decision cost Pratyaksh beyond the ₹1,640 per unit, and how should a holdout have been designed given that a discom representative must attend every replacement?
  4. Whose incentives in Section 5 are best served by scaling the programme immediately, and whose by pausing? Where do those incentives distort what each person is willing to say in the Thursday meeting?
  5. The 2022 decision to limit telemetry to four uplinks a day saved money on 42 lakh units. Was it wrong? How should a product leader value diagnostic capability that has no customer-visible benefit at the time of the bid?
  6. What should Aparna do on Monday morning — the first three actions, in order — and what precisely should she tell the board on Thursday about what the company knows, what it does not, and what it is choosing to risk?

At a quarter to nine, Aparna closed the map and opened the Nashik disposition file again. Four hundred and eighteen meters that had come back working. Two hundred and nine that nobody had bothered to code. A model built on a number that had changed meaning in November. A field team that had, by its own account, brought a circle's failure rate down. Outside, the building's generator started its weekly test, and for a moment every light on the floor dimmed and came back.

Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation · Product Analytics & Data Practice

Leading Indicators from Device Data

Which devices will fail next month — and, harder, at what probability is knowing worth what it costs to act?

1. Two decisions, five weeks apart

On Tuesday 4 February 2026, Devika Raghunathan, vice-president of product at Nilaya Medtech, sat in a conference room in Chennai with a single slide on the screen and a decision she had already postponed twice. Nilaya built connected volumetric infusion pumps — the devices that meter fluid into a patient's vein at a controlled rate — and had roughly 62,000 of them installed across 1,400 hospitals in India and South-East Asia. The failure that mattered was not a dead pump — a dead pump is obvious and gets swapped — but calibration drift: a peristaltic mechanism whose delivered flow rate wandered outside the ±5% band the device was certified to hold, silently, while still reporting itself healthy. Drift was confirmed in about 3.1% of pumps a year, and every case was a potential clinical incident and a reportable event.

Devika's engineers had built a model ranking pumps by the probability of drift in the following forty-five days, using signals the pumps had sent for years: motor current per revolution, the shape of the occlusion-pressure curve at each alarm, door-latch cycle counts, and the pass margins on the power-on self-test. The model worked. The question on the slide was what to do with its output. Turning the score into a ward-level alarm meant pulling pumps out of service mid-shift on the word of a statistical model. Burying it in a quarterly maintenance report meant that Nilaya would now be a company that knew, in writing, which of its devices were most likely to drift — and had chosen not to tell anyone urgently. Her regulatory affairs lead had used the word "discoverable" twice.

Five weeks later, on Thursday 12 March, Ritika Bose faced a different version of the same problem in Bengaluru. Ritika ran product at Neerja Water Systems, which rented connected reverse-osmosis water purifiers to 4.1 lakh households across thirty-eight cities at ₹499 a month, competing with Livpure's smart rental plans, Kent's outright sales and the service armies of Urban Company. Neerja's devices reported inlet and outlet TDS, membrane pressure differential, pump run-hours, litres dispensed and UV lamp hours. Her failure was neither clinical nor expensive: a fouled membrane costs a service visit. What it cost was the subscription — Neerja's cohort analysis showed that a household receiving two unscheduled visits in a quarter cancelled at roughly three times the base rate. Ritika did not want to predict failure. She wanted to predict cancellation, and the only instrument she had pointed at the customer was the machine on their kitchen wall.

Both women had a working model. Neither had the harder thing: a defensible answer to at what probability do we act. That question, not the modelling, is the subject of this page.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

A leading indicator from device data is a measurement taken from the device itself that changes, reliably and with usable lead time, before an outcome the business cares about changes. Three words carry the weight. Reliably means the relationship holds out of sample, on devices and in conditions the model has not seen. Usable lead time means the warning arrives far enough ahead for intervention to be physically possible — a signal that turns twelve hours before a failure is a fact, not an indicator, if the nearest technician is a day away. And an outcome the business cares about is where most programmes quietly go wrong, because what the engineers instrument (a hardware fault) is frequently not what costs money (a support call, a return, a cancelled subscription, a breached service level).

The intellectual history runs through reliability engineering, not through software analytics. Waloddi Weibull's 1951 paper gave engineers a distribution flexible enough to describe how the hazard of failure changes with age. The decisive empirical result came in 1968, when Stanley Nowlan and Howard Heap, analysing failures across United Airlines' fleet, found that only about 11% of components showed the age-related wear-out pattern that scheduled overhaul assumes. Most failures were age-independent, which made calendar-based replacement, for the majority of components, expensive theatre. That finding produced Reliability-Centred Maintenance and, downstream of it, condition-based monitoring: if age will not tell you when a part will fail, the part itself must. General Electric and Rolls-Royce industrialised the idea on jet engines in the 1990s, contributing the vocabulary — remaining useful life, prognostics and health management, P-F interval (the span between the point a failure becomes detectable and the point it becomes functional) — that product teams now use without knowing where it came from. What changed by 2026 is only cost: a modem, a microcontroller and a data plan are now defensible inside a ₹9,000 device, not merely a ₹30-crore one.

Beneath that settled history sit three schools that genuinely disagree, and a product manager should be able to tell which one a room is arguing from.

Table 1 — Three schools, and the proposition each will and will not sign
SchoolWill signWill not signStrongest ground
Physics-of-failure (reliability engineers)"A predictor must map to a named degradation mechanism — a swelling cell, a fouling membrane.""A correlated signal is enough if it validates."Mechanism-free models break silently when design, supplier or duty cycle changes.
Statistical learning (survival and ML practitioners)"Learn the hazard from labelled history; mechanism is an aid, not a prerequisite.""No model without a physical story."Real failures are multi-causal; waiting for mechanism means shipping nothing for two years.
Decision-theoretic (operations and economics)"The threshold is set by the cost ratio of intervention to failure, and by service capacity.""Maximise AUC and the business case follows."Excellent models with no capacity plan deliver nothing.
A fourth, smaller position — unsupervised novelty detection — holds that where failure is too rare to label, the only workable target is "this device no longer resembles its own past or its cohort." A fallback the other three respect and none prefers.

The disagreement is not academic. Nilaya's regulatory posture pushed it towards physics-of-failure: a drift predictor that could not name a mechanism would be hard to defend to CDSCO and harder to defend to a hospital. Neerja had every reason to sit with the statisticians — but Ritika's actual problem turned out to be decision-theoretic all the way down.

3. Mechanics, worked through

The first question an expert asks is not "what signals do we have" but "is this failure predictable at all." That is a question about the hazard function — the probability a device fails now, given it has survived until now. Fit a Weibull to a fleet's failure times and the shape parameter β tells you which world you are in. β below 1 means the hazard falls with age: infant mortality, manufacturing defects, the burn-in regime. β near 1 means constant hazard: failures arrive at random, independent of age and, usually, of any slowly-moving telemetry signal. β above 1 means the hazard rises with accumulated use: wear-out, the regime where a physical state is changing and therefore where a sensor has something to see.

Illustrative Weibull hazards at equal scale parameter. Nilaya's pump drift fits β ≈ 2.4; Neerja's control-board failures fit β ≈ 1.05, which is why no feature engineering moved that model above chance.

This single diagnostic saves programmes. Neerja's team spent eleven weeks trying to predict control-board failures before anyone fit the hazard curve and found β near unity. Board failures were random: the right answer was a cheaper board and a faster swap, not a better model. Membrane fouling fit β = 2.9 and was almost embarrassingly predictable.

Defining the label, the horizon and the as-of rule

Three definitional choices determine everything downstream, and teams routinely make all three implicitly. The label is what counts as the event: Nilaya chose "flow-rate error beyond ±5% at a bench calibration," excluding pumps returned for cosmetic damage or battery replacement, which behave nothing like drift. The horizon is the window the prediction applies over: forty-five days, because biomedical teams visit hospitals on a six-week cycle and a prediction that cannot be acted on inside a visit cycle is inert. The as-of rule requires that every feature used to predict a device's state on day D was computable on day D. Violating it is the commonest way a model reaches implausible backtest accuracy and collapses in production.

The threshold is an economics problem

Suppose a device has probability p of the event inside the horizon. Intervening costs Cact; letting it happen costs Cfail. Act when p × Cfail > Cact, giving a break-even probability p* = Cact / Cfail. Everything subtle here lives in how those two numbers are computed.

Table 2 — The same arithmetic, two very different answers
Nilaya Medtech (infusion pumps)Neerja Water Systems (RO purifiers)
Cact — proactive intervention₹3,100 — calibration during a scheduled biomedical round₹640 — filter and membrane swap on a dedicated visit
Cfail — the event, fully loaded₹46,000 — emergency engineer, loaner pump, hospital credit, incident file₹1,668 — ₹1,450 reactive visit plus ₹218 expected margin lost to raised churn
Break-even p*6.7%38.4%
Achieved precision at capacity7.3% (top 930 of 62,000 per 45-day window)31% at the rule's natural threshold
VerdictBarely pays, and only at the top of the rankingDoes not pay as framed
Neerja's churn term: ₹499/month, 26-month mean tenure, 41% contribution margin gives ₹5,315 of gross margin per subscriber; a reactive visit raises quarterly cancellation probability by 4.1 percentage points, so 0.041 × ₹5,315 ≈ ₹218.

Table 2 contains the lesson most predictive-maintenance decks omit. Nilaya's failures are seventy times more expensive than Ritika's, yet Nilaya's programme is the marginal one, because what governs is the ratio of intervention cost to failure cost, not the size of either. A cheap failure with an even cheaper intervention is a better business than an expensive failure you can only prevent expensively.

The second thing Table 2 hides is capacity. Nilaya's biomedical teams can touch about 1.5% of the fleet in a 45-day window — 930 pumps. The base rate of drift over that horizon is roughly 0.38%, about 237 events fleet-wide, and the top 930 contained 68 of them: precision 7.3%, recall 28.7%, lift of nineteen times the base rate. Nineteen-times lift is a strong model. Precision of 7.3% against a break-even of 6.7% clears the hurdle by six-tenths of a percentage point. Both statements describe the same model, and an expert holds them simultaneously.

From Nilaya's 45-day ranking, February 2026 holdout. The crossing point — not the AUC of 0.88 — decides how many pumps get touched.

Now the second-order effects, where the practice separates from the textbook. First, intervention destroys the ground truth. Once Nilaya recalibrates flagged pumps, those pumps never drift, and the next quarter's training data contains no examples of the failures the model prevented. Measured naively, the model appears to get worse every quarter — the prevention paradox, and the reason serious programmes hold out a randomly-selected control fleet of 3–5% receiving no proactive action. That control costs real failures, and is the first line cut by a finance team reading the budget without reading the method. Second, the intervention changes the population. Replace the fouling membranes and the remaining failure modes shift to whatever is now the weakest link. Third, the indicator becomes a target. Once a field team's bonus depends on the count of high-risk devices in its territory, those devices begin to be closed, deferred or re-coded; Goodhart's law arrives in the ticketing system before it arrives in the model.

4. The conditions, stated as testable claims

The practice pays when five claims hold, each checkable before any feature is engineered.

Claim one: the hazard rises with a measurable physical state (β > 1). True for Nilaya's tubing and Neerja's membranes; false for Neerja's control boards. Claim two: the P-F interval exceeds the intervention lead time at the tenth percentile, not the median. Nilaya's median warning was thirty-one days against a six-week service cycle — comfortable on the median, uncomfortable at a p10 of nine days, which is why the top tier was routed to unscheduled visits. Neerja's twenty-one days against a four-day dispatch never bound. Claim three: p* is reachable. Nilaya cleared it by a hair; Neerja, as framed, did not. Claim four: capacity exists to act at the rate flags are generated. A programme producing 4,000 flags a month into a field force that can service 900 is not an analytics programme, it is a queue. Claim five: the telemetry is stable. Firmware releases, sensor recalibrations and modem changes rewrite the meaning of a feature without changing its name.

The idea is actively misleading in three situations. When failures are dominated by external shocks — vandalism, theft, floods, a power event that takes out a street — telemetry predicts nothing and a risk score built on it will confidently blame the device. When the fleet is young, so that observed failures are infant mortality, the model learns a manufacturing lot and is then applied to a lot that no longer exists. And when the true cost driver is customer behaviour rather than device physics — Ritika's real problem — a device-health model answers the wrong question with impressive precision.

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

In regulated products, a prediction creates a duty. Once Nilaya's system records that pump 41-88291 had a 14% probability of drift, the record exists, and regulators and plaintiffs' counsel can both read it. Mature medical-device companies handle this not by refusing to predict but by defining in advance, in writing, the action each risk band triggers, so the record shows a governed process rather than knowledge without response. The cost is that risk bands become quasi-regulatory artefacts, revised slowly, so the model cannot be retrained freely.

In hardware-plus-software fleets, firmware is the hidden adversary. A release changing a temperature sensor's sampling from once a minute to once every five minutes halves the variance of a variance-based feature overnight. The mature answer is a telemetry contract — schema, units, sampling rate and semantics versioned like an API, firmware version carried as a first-class feature, models refitted per version. Few companies do this until a model has failed once.

In two-sided and marketplace settings, a failure has two victims with different economics: when a delivery scooter dies, the operator loses a day of earnings and the platform loses the transactions, so willingness to pay for prevention sits with the platform while the device sits with the operator, and nobody has clean authority over the maintenance schedule. In multi-product fleets the seam is the shared component: one power module across three products means a supplier defect appears in three risk models owned by three teams, each concluding it has a product-specific problem.

In AI-native settings, the temptation is to train a foundation model over raw sensor sequences and skip feature engineering. It does work, and it makes leakage and drift harder to catch, because the model can exploit subtleties — a timestamp pattern, a transmission gap that only occurs after dispatch — that a human reviewing twelve engineered features would have seen.

Each function optimises a metric that moves the threshold in a different direction. With no single owner, it defaults to whatever number the model's author picked — usually 0.5.

6. Nine things an expert sees that a competent practitioner does not

Lead time is a distribution, not a number. The tell is a deck saying "the signal gives us nineteen days of warning." Ask for the tenth percentile. Nilaya's median was thirty-one days and its p10 was nine; a service model built around the median would miss the fastest-degrading pumps, which are precisely the ones whose failures are most severe. The obvious reading — longer average warning means safer programme — inverts when degradation rate correlates with severity, which it usually does.

The cost ratio sets the threshold; the ROC curve does not. The tell is a model review in which AUC, F1 and a confusion matrix appear and no rupee figure does. AUC is invariant to the one thing that matters: how much worse a miss is than a false alarm. Two teams with identical models and different cost structures should operate at different thresholds; if they do not, one has not done the arithmetic.

Rare events make accuracy meaningless and ROC-AUC flattering. At a base rate of 0.38%, a model predicting "no drift" for every pump is 99.6% accurate, and an AUC of 0.88 is compatible with single-digit precision. The expert asks for precision and recall at the operating point service capacity actually permits — lift at k — and treats the rest as diagnostic colour.

The strongest predictor is usually a batch, not a sensor. The tell is a risk map clustering by manufacturing week or serial-number range. The naive reading is that the model found something subtle in the telemetry; the truth is that it found a supplier's process excursion. That is good news operationally — a batch is cheap to act on, because you know exactly which units are affected — and bad news for the model, which loses most of its apparent power once the batch retires.

Many device models are secretly geography models. Water hardness, ambient temperature, voltage stability and dust load vary enormously by pincode, and a model given location will lean on location. Neerja's membrane model took 44% of its gain from inlet TDS, substantially a property of the municipal supply rather than the machine. The tell is that removing location-correlated features collapses performance. Not fatal — a route-level prediction is still actionable — but it moves ownership of the response from product engineering to service operations.

Arrhenius arithmetic explains more variance than most feature engineering. Chemical degradation roughly doubles in rate for each 10°C rise. Nilaya's pumps in hospitals without ICU-grade cooling drifted at 1.7 times the fleet average — an effect no amount of motor-current modelling would have produced, and that one environmental covariate captured immediately. The expert checks whether a physical acceleration law already explains the pattern before building anything.

The marginal cost of a false positive is not the average cost. A wasted inspection performed while the technician is already in the building costs a fraction of a dedicated trip. Neerja's ₹640 intervention became ₹260 folded into an existing route in the same pincode on the same day, moving p* from 38.4% to 15.6% and turning an unprofitable programme profitable without touching the model. The tell is a business case with a single per-visit cost; route density, not accuracy, is often the binding variable.

Failure, ticket and cancellation are three different problems. They share telemetry and nothing else. A hardware fault is physics; a support ticket is physics filtered through a customer's tolerance and their awareness that support exists; a cancellation adds competitive alternatives and billing timing. The tell is a single model whose label was chosen by whoever owned the data rather than whoever owned the P&L.

A prediction nobody can act on becomes a liability rather than an asset. The tell is a risk score on a dashboard with no defined response. In regulated categories that is a compliance exposure; elsewhere it is an organisational one, because field teams learn within a quarter that the score carries no consequence and stop reading it. The obvious reading — visibility is always good — ignores that an unactioned warning is evidence of a decision not to act.

7. How this differs by product type and company stage

Table 3 — Where the differences are real
ContextWhat actually changes
Consumer hardwareThe dominant cost is churn and returns, not repair, so the right label is behavioural; intervention economics turn on route density.
B2B / enterprise fleetsContracts define the event: an SLA's definition of "down" becomes the label whether or not it matches physics, and renegotiating it can be worth more than any model.
Platforms and marketplacesThe device owner and the economic victim differ; prevention has to be sold, subsidised or mandated rather than simply scheduled.
Regulated hardwarePredictions become records; risk bands and their mandated responses must be defined before the model ships.
AI-native productsLittle changes conceptually. Leakage and drift get harder to detect, and interpretability obligations get stricter.
Pure softwareGenuinely different: the fleet updates instantly and centrally, so prediction competes with simply fixing everything, which is usually cheaper.

Stage matters less than people claim, with one exception. Below roughly 20,000 devices and a couple of years of history, a fleet does not contain enough failures to train anything; at 62,000 pumps and 3.1% annual drift, Nilaya had about 1,900 events a year, which is adequate. Early-stage companies should instrument generously and predict nothing. What genuinely changes with scale is the ability to run a control fleet: a company with 4,000 devices cannot afford to withhold service from 200 of them, and therefore cannot measure its own programme.

8. Three worked examples, including one failure

Nilaya, February 2026. AUC 0.88; top 930 of 62,000 pumps per 45-day cycle; 68 of 237 drift events caught, a recall of 28.7%; precision on the 930 flagged pumps was 7.3%; lift 19×. Annualised: about 550 drift events prevented against roughly 7,500 proactive calibrations. Value: 550 × (₹46,000 − ₹3,100) = ₹2.36 crore avoided, less 6,950 unnecessary calibrations × ₹3,100 = ₹2.15 crore. Net ₹21 lakh on a programme costing ₹1.4 crore a year to run. As a financial proposition it fails; as a patient-safety and regulatory proposition it is the only thing on the table.

Neerja, March 2026. The model as built predicted service calls at 31% precision against a 38.4% break-even, and was rejected. Reframed around route density — flagging only devices in pincodes with a technician already scheduled that week — intervention cost fell to ₹260, p* to 15.6%, and the same model's second and third deciles became profitable. Coverage rose from 8% of the flagged population to 34%, with no change to the model.

Bhadra Tower Infra, 2024–25. Bhadra managed power systems — rectifiers, battery banks, diesel backup — at 31,000 telecom tower sites. Its model reached AUC 0.94 in backtest and was celebrated. In production it performed at chance. The cause was label leakage: two features in the training set, a maintenance-status code and a spare-parts-reserved flag, were written to the record after an engineer had already diagnosed the site. The model had learned to predict dispatches that had already happened. Recovery took eleven months and about ₹2.6 crore: an as-of feature store with strict event timestamps, a rebuilt model with an honest AUC of 0.71, and a change of framing from "alarm" to "weekly patrol ranking," which tolerated far lower precision because the patrol was happening anyway. The durable cost was not money but credibility; the reliability team spent two years declining to act on any model output without a manual check.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

Table 4 — What goes wrong, how it shows early, and what it costs late
Failure modeEarly warning signDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late
Label leakageBacktest accuracy implausibly high"Was every feature computable on the prediction date?"Bhadra's eleven months and lost trust
Prevention paradoxMeasured performance decays each quarter after rollout"What happened to the devices we saved?"A working programme cancelled as a failure
Telemetry driftFeature distribution shifts on a release date"Which firmware versions are in this cohort?"Months of silently wrong flags
Capacity mismatchFlag backlog grows week on week"How many devices can we actually touch?"Field teams stop reading the queue
Wrong labelModel accurate, business metric flat"Whose P&L does this event hit?"A quarter of engineering spent on the wrong target
Threshold by defaultOperating point is 0.5 and nobody remembers choosing it"What is Cact / Cfail?"Systematic over- or under-servicing at scale

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether mechanism is required. The physics-of-failure position is that a predictor without a named degradation mechanism is a correlation waiting to break, and that it will break silently and simultaneously across a fleet: a supplier changes an adhesive, every model built on thermal features degrades at once, and no alarm sounds because the models still produce numbers. The statistical position answers that fielded failures are multi-causal, that insisting on mechanism means shipping nothing for years, and that retraining on fresh outcomes catches drift faster than physical reasoning does. The physics camp is wrong if retraining cadence is fast relative to design change; the statistics camp is wrong if fleets change faster than outcomes accumulate, which is exactly the case in high-growth hardware companies.

Whether to run a no-treatment control fleet. One camp holds that without a randomised holdout you cannot measure the programme at all, and that the few failures you allow are the cheapest measurement you will ever buy. The other holds that deliberately withholding a known-beneficial intervention from identified customers is indefensible — clearly so in medical devices — and that quasi-experiments on natural variation in service coverage are adequate. The first camp is wrong if the ethical cost is real and the quasi-experiments unbiased; the second is wrong if service coverage varies with the same geography that drives failure, which it almost always does.

Whether to show the score to the field. One view is that technicians given a raw score and reason codes decide better than any threshold, because they see the site. The other is that human override destroys the calibration the economics depend on, and that the right interface is a work order, not a number. The evidence is mixed, and appears to turn on whether the technician bears any cost of being wrong.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this asks which model to use. Someone who has internalised it asks four questions first: what is the shape parameter, what is the tenth-percentile lead time, what is Cact divided by Cfail, and how many devices can we physically touch in a cycle. They treat the model as the cheap part of the system and the intervention as the expensive part. They are suspicious of good news, and they route their strongest predictors — batches, geographies, environments — to operations rather than data science, because those findings are acted on by changing a route, a supplier or a specification, not by deploying anything. They insist every risk band has a written response before the first score is displayed, and they can say in one sentence, in rupees, what the programme is worth.

12. What they decided

Devika shipped Nilaya's model in March, but not as an alarm. Pumps in the highest band generate a mandatory calibration work order inside seven days; the middle band folds into the next scheduled round; the lowest band is not shown at all, on the reasoning that a displayed score without a defined response is worse than no score. She accepted that the financial case is marginal and argued it to her board as a safety and regulatory investment, which is what it is.

Ritika did the opposite. She abandoned the failure label, retrained against "cancels within ninety days," and found that device features mattered less than the interaction between water hardness and service history. Her programme became a routing change — technicians pre-empting membrane fouling in twelve high-TDS pincodes — rather than a risk dashboard. She has not solved prediction; she has found a cheaper intervention, which moved the break-even far enough that a mediocre model became sufficient.

Discussion questions. (1) Nilaya's programme nets ₹21 lakh against a ₹1.4 crore annual cost. On what grounds, if any, should it continue, and what would you need to believe about unquantified risk for the answer to change? (2) Ritika improved her economics by changing the intervention rather than the model. Where else in a product organisation is the binding constraint mistaken for a modelling problem? (3) Bhadra recovered technically in eleven months and organisationally in two years. What would you have done in month one to protect the team's credibility, and what does that imply about how predictive features should be launched?

13. Going deeper

  • Device telemetry and fleet analytics — the instrumentation layer this depends on; without a versioned telemetry contract, every model here decays silently.
  • Reliability engineering and field failure — Weibull fitting, P-F intervals and failure-mode analysis; the discipline that tells you whether prediction is possible before you attempt it.
  • Constructing a funnel — the same as-of discipline applied to user journeys; why event definitions decide conclusions.
  • Reading drop-off — telling a real break from a measurement artefact: the software analogue of telemetry drift.
  • Defining activation (the aha moment) — the canonical software leading indicator, and the clearest case of choosing a label for predictive power over convenience.
  • Cohort analysis — separates batch effects from device effects; indispensable once you suspect a manufacturing lot.
  • Retention curves and the PMF signal — where leading indicators turn strategic rather than operational.
  • Stickiness and natural frequency — usage intensity is the exposure variable in any hazard model; failures follow use, not calendar time.

Leading Indicators from Device Data

Which devices will fail next month — and can you know that before the failure, not after the complaint?

1. A Thursday in Chennai

On the second Thursday of March, Riya Kannan, head of product for Tijori Payment Systems, opened her laptop at 7:40 a.m. to a message from the field-operations desk in Coimbatore: forty-one card machines had gone dark in Tamil Nadu overnight, all of them belonging to kirana stores and petrol pumps that closed their tills before the failures were reported. Tijori made and leased small card-and-QR payment terminals to roughly 210,000 merchants across nine states, competing for the same countertop space as Pine Labs and BharatPe. Its business model depended on a simple promise: a terminal, once installed, kept working. When it did not, a technician had to travel, a merchant lost a day of digital sales, and Tijori absorbed both a replacement device and a support ticket that cost the company close to ₹1,400 per visit once travel and parts were counted.

Riya's dashboard told her what had happened only after it had already happened: a spike in "device offline" tickets, filed by merchants who had already lost business. What it could not yet tell her was what was about to happen. Somewhere in Tijori's fleet, batteries were degrading, thermal printer heads were overheating, and SIM modules were losing signal lock days before a terminal actually died — and all of that was sitting, unused, inside a telemetry stream the devices had been quietly sending to Tijori's servers every fifteen minutes for two years. Riya's question for the coming quarter was not how to fix broken terminals faster. It was whether Tijori could learn to see a terminal's death coming three weeks out, and act while there was still a device to save.

2. The idea

A leading indicator is a measurement that changes before the outcome you care about changes, and that changes in a way reliable enough to act on. Its counterpart, a lagging indicator, only tells you the outcome after it has already occurred — a support ticket, a returned device, a churn event. Applied to physical devices, "leading indicators from device data" means: instrument the device itself, watch the handful of signals that degrade before the device dies, and treat a bad reading as a forecast rather than as noise to be logged and forgotten.

The problem this idea was invented to solve is old and expensive. Industrial engineers have run physical equipment — jet engines, oil rigs, elevators — on scheduled maintenance for a century: replace the part every N months whether it needs it or not, because unplanned failure is costlier than early replacement. General Electric and Rolls-Royce began fitting jet engines with vibration and temperature sensors in the 1990s specifically to move from scheduled to predictive maintenance, coining much of the vocabulary — "remaining useful life," "condition-based monitoring" — that today's software product teams have inherited wholesale. What changed between an aircraft engine in 1995 and a payment terminal in Coimbatore today is cost: a cellular modem, a small processor and a data plan now make it economical to instrument a ₹9,000 device, not just a ₹30-crore one.

The sentence Riya could say in a meeting without sounding glib: "Our devices already tell us they're dying — we've just been reading the message after they're dead."

3. How it actually works

The mechanics run in five steps, and Tijori's team, guided by data scientist Marcus Chen working out of Toronto, worked through all five in order.

Step one: instrument the right signals

Every Tijori terminal already logged battery voltage, internal temperature, printer motor current, and cellular signal strength (RSSI) every fifteen minutes, because these were needed for basic device management. The team's first task was not to add sensors but to notice which of the existing fields moved differently in the weeks before a failure than in ordinary operation. This is the step teams most often skip: they assume more data means better prediction, when the real work is finding which two or three signals actually separate a dying device from a healthy one.

Step two: define the failure event precisely

"Failure" needed a hard operational definition before anyone could predict it. Tijori settled on: a terminal that generates a hardware-fault error code and is either replaced or requires an on-site repair within the following 30 days. This excluded software crashes fixable by a remote restart, which behaved completely differently and would have muddied any pattern.

Step three: build the labelled history

The team pulled two years of telemetry and matched it against the repair log, tagging every device-day as either "30 days from a hardware failure" or "not." This labelled history — signal readings on one side, known outcomes on the other — is what any prediction, simple or sophisticated, has to be trained or tuned against; without it, a model is just an assumption in code.

Step four: find the threshold that separates the two groups

With the labelled history in hand, the team looked for a simple rule — a threshold on one or two signals — that split failing devices from healthy ones as cleanly as possible, before reaching for anything more elaborate. A threshold is auditable and explainable to a field technician; a black-box model, even a more accurate one, is harder to trust and to debug when it is wrong.

Step five: act on the score before the failure

A prediction that nobody acts on is trivia. Tijori's last step was operational: any device crossing the threshold triggered a proactive service ticket, routed to the nearest technician's existing rounds, days before the merchant would have noticed anything wrong.

4. A worked example

Tijori's fleet in Tamil Nadu held 18,600 terminals. Over the prior twelve months, 930 of them had a hardware failure by the definition above — a base failure rate of 5.0%. Marcus's team tested a simple rule: flag any terminal whose battery voltage fell below 3.55V or whose printer motor current exceeded 640 mA on two consecutive daily readings. Run against the labelled history, the rule performed like this:

Predicted to failPredicted healthyTotal
Actually failed720210930
Actually healthy1,34016,33017,670
Total2,06016,54018,600

Two numbers matter most here. Recall — of the terminals that actually failed, how many the rule caught — was 720 / 930 = 77.4%. Precision — of the terminals the rule flagged, how many actually went on to fail — was 720 / 2,060 = 35.0%. In plain terms: the rule catches three out of four real failures, but two out of three flagged terminals turn out fine. That is not a flaw to be embarrassed about; it is the ordinary shape of an early-warning system, because failure is rare and the leading signal is noisy.

Whether 35% precision is good enough is a business question, not a statistics one. A false alarm costs Tijori a technician's visit that finds nothing wrong — call it ₹550, since it can be folded into an existing round rather than a dedicated trip. A missed failure costs the full ₹1,400 reactive-repair visit, plus a merchant who lost a day of UPI and card revenue and may now be shopping for a competitor's terminal. Under the confusion matrix above: 2,060 proactive visits × ₹550 = ₹11.33 lakh, versus 210 missed failures × ₹1,400 = ₹2.94 lakh in avoidable reactive cost that the rule still fails to prevent, plus whatever the 720 caught failures save relative to letting them go reactive. Net, catching 720 failures before they happened saved roughly ₹8–9 lakh a year on this segment alone, once technician time already on the road is treated as sunk.

Second pass — what changes if the threshold moves. Marcus reran the rule with the voltage threshold loosened to 3.65V, catching problems earlier but on weaker evidence. Recall rose to 88% (818 of 930 failures caught) but precision fell to 24% (818 of 3,410 flags were real), because a higher, earlier threshold sweeps in far more healthy devices whose voltage merely dips normally. This is the leading-indicator trade-off in one pair of numbers: move the threshold earlier and you catch more real problems, but you also pay for more wasted visits — the curve does not let you improve both at once without a better signal, not just a different cutoff.

5. The nuances

A leading indicator is a correlation, not a cause. Battery voltage dropping does not cause the fault; both are downstream of a physical degradation — a swelling cell, a corroded contact — that the voltage reading merely reflects. Treating the indicator as the cause tempts a team to "fix the number" (swap in a better voltage sensor) rather than the underlying part.

Base rate dominates precision. With only 5% of devices failing in a year, even a fairly accurate rule produces more false alarms than true ones in absolute terms, as the worked example showed. Teams new to this repeatedly expect precision to look like recall, and are disappointed by numbers that are, in fact, working as intended.

Leading indicators drift. A threshold tuned on last year's battery chemistry or last year's firmware may quietly stop working when the hardware vendor changes a component — the signal is still there, but its relationship to failure has shifted. A leading-indicator system needs the same maintenance as the machines it watches.

It is easily confused with anomaly detection. Flagging "this reading looks unusual" is not the same as flagging "this reading predicts failure." Many unusual readings are harmless (a store closed for a festival looks like an offline device); many failure-predictive readings are, individually, unremarkable. The distinction matters because anomaly detection and failure prediction are solved with different techniques and validated against different ground truth.

It cannot tell you why, only when. A threshold crossing tells Riya's team that a device is likely to fail soon; it does not diagnose which component, unless the underlying signal is itself component-specific (as voltage is, roughly, for the battery). Teams sometimes oversell a leading-indicator system as a diagnostic tool when it is really a triage tool.

The window between signal and failure is a design constraint, not a fact of nature. Nineteen days of lead time is only useful if the operating model — technician routing, spare-parts stock, merchant scheduling — can act inside that window. A perfectly accurate signal with a two-day lead time may be less useful to a company with weekly technician routes than a noisier signal with three weeks of runway.

Not every degrading signal is actionable. Cellular signal strength dropping might predict failure just as well as battery voltage, but if the cause is a telecom tower outage rather than the device, no technician visit fixes it. A leading indicator is only worth acting on if the intervention available actually addresses what the signal is detecting.

A thoughtful newcomer should ask, before relying on any such system: what exactly counts as a failure, how was the labelled history built, what does the precision-recall trade-off cost in rupees on both sides, and how often does someone re-check that the threshold still holds? A system that answers all four is trustworthy; one that answers none is a plausible-looking guess.

6. Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and early-stage versus scale

In a consumer hardware business like Tijori's merchant terminals, the device fleet is large, homogeneous, and the cost per failure is modest but multiplied across hundreds of thousands of units — so the economics favour simple, cheap, high-recall rules over elaborate models, because the value is in coverage, not precision. In a B2B context — say, an industrial sensor company selling to factories — fleets are smaller, each device sits inside a costlier, more consequential piece of equipment, and customers expect the vendor to explain exactly which reading changed and why, pushing B2B teams toward interpretable, component-specific indicators even at the cost of some coverage. In a marketplace or logistics setting, the "device" of interest might not be owned by the platform at all — a delivery rider's phone or a driver-partner's vehicle — so the leading indicator has to be built from second-hand signals (GPS drop-outs, app-open patterns) rather than clean, vendor-controlled telemetry, and the intervention is a nudge or an incentive rather than a technician dispatch. An early-stage company, without years of labelled failure history, typically starts with a hand-picked threshold based on engineering judgment and a handful of known failure modes; a scaled company like Tijori, with two years of matched telemetry and repair logs, can afford to test and retire thresholds statistically, and eventually train models on dozens of signals at once — but only once the plumbing connecting telemetry to repair outcomes is trustworthy, which is itself the harder, less glamorous half of the work.

7. Common mistakes

Mistake: chasing model sophistication before the labels are trustworthy. Symptom: a very accurate-looking model that performs worse in production than in testing. Underlying error: the repair log used to build "ground truth" was itself incomplete or mislabelled — some hardware faults were logged as software issues by rushed technicians. Cheapest diagnostic: manually audit fifty labelled examples before building anything on top of them.

Mistake: measuring the model, not the outcome. Symptom: the data science team reports a rising accuracy score while the support-ticket volume stays flat. Underlying error: nobody closed the loop from "predicted to fail" to "technician actually visited before failure." Cheapest diagnostic: track the percentage of flagged devices that received a proactive visit within the lead-time window — if it's low, the model is idle, not wrong.

Mistake: setting one threshold for a fleet that is not actually one fleet. Symptom: the rule works well in Chennai and poorly in Coimbatore. Underlying error: different regions run different firmware versions or see different heat and humidity, which shifts the same signal's meaning. Cheapest diagnostic: split the confusion matrix by region or hardware batch before declaring a single threshold fit for the whole fleet.

Mistake: treating a leading indicator as permanent once validated. Symptom: precision quietly erodes over two or three quarters. Underlying error: no one re-ran the validation after a firmware update or a new battery vendor. Cheapest diagnostic: put a calendar reminder — not a dashboard alert, a calendar reminder — to re-check the confusion matrix every quarter.

8. What good looks like

Six months after that Thursday, Tijori's system flagged terminal TX-88213, installed at a fuel station outside Madurai, when its battery voltage dropped below 3.55V and stayed there for two consecutive readings. The flag reached the Coimbatore field team's queue automatically, was folded into a technician's existing Tuesday round eleven days later — well inside the nineteen-day window — and the battery was swapped during a five-minute visit the merchant barely noticed. No ticket was ever filed, because there was no failure to file one about. Multiplied across a quarter, this pattern took Tijori's hardware-fault reactive-ticket rate down by 31%, and freed the same field technicians to cover more ground on planned rounds instead of emergency call-outs. Nothing about the underlying hardware had changed; what changed was that the company started reading a message its devices had been sending all along.

9. What Riya decided

Riya greenlit the threshold-based system for a full state-wide rollout rather than waiting for a more sophisticated model, reasoning that a 77% recall, cheaply achieved and fully explainable to her field team, beat a theoretically better model that would take two more quarters to build and would still need the same repair-log discipline underneath it. She asked Marcus's team to revisit the thresholds quarterly and to track proactive-visit completion, not just flag accuracy, as the metric that mattered to the board. Where she chose to learn more was in reliability engineering itself — understanding why batteries degraded the way they did — because a leading indicator, however well built, only ever bought Tijori time; it did not fix the underlying hardware.

Two questions worth sitting with: if a leading indicator gives you three weeks of warning but your operations can only act within one, is the indicator worth building at all — and what would you change first, the signal or the operating model? And when a leading indicator's precision quietly erodes over time, how would your organisation actually notice, before a customer does?
