Raftaar Electric Mobility: Reading the Warning in the Battery Data

A leading-indicator model has flagged 2,400 scooters in a Dubai delivery fleet as at risk of battery failure. The data scientist wants three more weeks to validate it. The fleet's busiest season starts in three.

1. Pune, 23 September 2026

On the sixth floor of Raftaar Electric Mobility's technology park in Hinjawadi, Ananya Deshpande, VP of Product & Reliability, is looking at a dashboard she had not expected to be reading ten days before Navratri. In two days, on Friday, she has to tell Raftaar's executive committee — and, on a call scheduled for that same afternoon, Rashid Al Naqbi in Dubai — what the company will do about 2,400 electric scooters in Sahl Grocery Express's delivery fleet that an internal model now places at elevated risk of battery failure over the next two to ten weeks. The Sahl account is Raftaar Fleet's largest single contract anywhere: 15,000 leased scooters, roughly ₹42 crore a year in lease and service revenue, and a proof point that Raftaar's model travels beyond India. It is also entering its busiest quarter, as Dubai's dark-store network triples order volumes for the year-end retail season. Whatever Ananya recommends by Friday will commit technician-hours, capital, and Raftaar's credibility with a client whose renewal decision is due in December.

2. Raftaar Electric Mobility

Raftaar was founded in 2018 by two IIT Bombay classmates who wanted to build, in their words, "the Activa of the EV era" — an affordable, service-light electric scooter for India's mass market rather than a premium halo product. Its first model, the Raftaar Vega, launched in 2020; by 2026 roughly 1.9 lakh Raftaar vehicles were on Indian roads across two models, sold through 210 dealerships and, increasingly, through Raftaar Fleet, a leasing arm built for quick-commerce and food-delivery operators. In the domestic EV two-wheeler market Raftaar competes against Ather Energy, Ola Electric, Bajaj's Chetak, and TVS's iQube, and for delivery-fleet contracts against those same rivals' leasing arms and petrol incumbents like the Honda Activa. Margins are thin and volume matters, which is why Raftaar Fleet's 2024 expansion into the Gulf — leasing scooters to quick-commerce operators phasing diesel vehicles out of dense retail zones — was treated as a strategic bet worth protecting. The Sahl Grocery Express account in Dubai, at 15,000 units, is more than a third of Raftaar Fleet's entire leased fleet worldwide. Every Raftaar vehicle carries a battery-management-system telemetry dongle that reports state of charge, pack voltage, per-cell voltage spread, and casing temperature roughly every ninety seconds.

3. What Ananya knows

In March 2026, a batch of battery cells from an outside supplier, PowerCell Dynamics, began failing prematurely in a 2,600-unit rental fleet in Pune. Raftaar's engineers did not spot the pattern until service centres had logged forty-one swelling or capacity-loss complaints over three weeks, including two cells that vented and smoked without catching fire. The episode cost Raftaar roughly ₹1.1 crore in expedited swaps, goodwill vouchers, and a service-level penalty, and briefly froze sales to that rental partner while Raftaar's quality team traced the fault to a manufacturing variance in one PowerCell Dynamics batch. It happened at a moment when Indian regulators and the press remained attentive to EV two-wheeler fires, after a spate of incidents in 2022 had drawn scrutiny from the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. Raftaar's leadership did not want a repeat, anywhere.

Afterward, Ananya asked her Toronto-based data science lead, Elena Voss, to build something Raftaar had never had: a leading indicator rather than a lagging one. Elena's team combined two BMS signals — the spread between a pack's highest and lowest individual cell voltage during fast-charging, and the variance in casing temperature across a charge cycle — into what they call the Thermal Drift Index, or TDI. Backtested against the Pune failures, a rising TDI preceded visible symptoms by four to six weeks in most cases (Exhibit 2). In early September, Karthik Rao, the Bengaluru engineer who runs Raftaar's telemetry pipeline, ran TDI against the live global fleet and found the same signature rising — this time in Dubai, in scooters built from the same PowerCell Dynamics batch. Of Sahl's 15,000 units, 2,400 carry that batch, and TDI now places 380 of them in its highest-risk tier (Exhibit 1).

The complication is that TDI is new and untested outside India. It was validated on Pune's climate, not on Dubai's late-September heat, still touching 38–40°C — a condition that plausibly accelerates the same thermal stress the model is trying to detect, but was not itself in the training data. Elena wants three more weeks of monitoring before Raftaar acts at fleet scale. Karthik, watching the numbers daily, is less patient: to him, the Tier A signature already looks like the one that preceded the Pune failures, and it is worsening — 380 units this week, up from 210 three weeks ago. Meera Pillai in Singapore, who owns the Sahl relationship, has to decide how much of this to tell Rashid Al Naqbi before Friday's call, in a market where Raftaar is still trying to prove itself.

4. The people

Elena Voss — Data Science Lead, Toronto. Built TDI from scratch in six weeks; wants it proven properly before it justifies a multi-crore field campaign, and worries that one wrong call will make Raftaar distrust every model her team ships afterward.

Karthik Rao — Telemetry & Reliability Engineer, Bengaluru. Owns the pipeline that has carried the warning signal since 4 September; has watched Tier A grow every week and does not think the fleet will wait for a textbook validation window.

Meera Pillai — Customer Success Lead, APAC & Gulf, Singapore. Manages the Sahl account and reports into Rajiv Kapoor's global sales organisation in New Jersey; wants Raftaar to look proactive on Friday's call, not caught flat-footed the way it was with the Pune rental partner in March.

Rashid Al Naqbi — Fleet Operations Director, Sahl Grocery Express, Dubai. Runs 15,000 leased scooters against an uptime commitment that keeps his dark stores' delivery promise through the year-end season; wants either fixed scooters or an honest, specific plan — not reassurance.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 — TDI risk tiers, Sahl Dubai fleet, as of 22 September 2026 (2,400 of 15,000 units flagged)
TierUnitsPredicted failure windowBacktest precisionFalse-positive rate
A — high3802–4 weeks71%29%
B — medium8604–6 weeks54%46%
C — watch1,1606–10 weeks (beyond validated horizon)31%69%
Precision is the share of flagged units in each tier that failed within the stated window in Raftaar's backtests on the Pune fleet; the Dubai fleet's hotter climate is not yet reflected in these figures.

Exhibit 1 is the crux of the decision: the three tiers are not equally trustworthy. A Tier A flag is right roughly seven times in ten; a Tier C flag is right fewer than one time in three, and its ten-week horizon runs past anything TDI has actually been tested against. Treating all 2,400 flagged units as equally urgent — or equally ignorable — misreads the exhibit.

Both Pune units that later failed crossed the 0.85 threshold four to five weeks before symptoms appeared; the healthy control never approached it. Dubai's Tier A units average 0.87 today, positioned near where the Pune units sat roughly three weeks before failure.

Exhibit 2 is why Karthik reads urgency into the data: the shape of the Dubai Tier A curve so far resembles the early stage of both Pune failures, not the flat control line. It is also why Elena is cautious — the model has only ever seen this pattern play out twice, in one climate, and a two-case pattern is a thin basis for a multi-crore decision on its own.

Exhibit 3 — Three-week cost and capacity comparison of the options (₹ crore unless noted)
OptionUnits actioned nowDirect costWeeks of Dubai capacity needed1
1. Full proactive swap (Tiers A+B)1,240₹6.85 cr8.3
2. Wait and validate0 (50 manual checks)₹5 lakh<1
3. Tiered rolling service (Tier A only, B/C re-scored weekly)380₹2.1 cr2.5
1. Raftaar's Dubai service partner can complete 150 battery-pack swaps per week without pulling technicians off routine maintenance. A per-unit swap (pack, freight, labour) runs ₹52,000 in Dubai versus ₹38,000 domestically.

Exhibit 3 makes the constraint concrete: at 150 swaps a week, Option 1's 1,240 units take over eight weeks to clear — longer than Tier A's own two-to-four-week failure window, so the "safest-looking" option cannot actually be executed fast enough to prevent the failures it targets. Option 3 fits inside three weeks; Option 1 does not.

6. The options

Option 1 — Proactive swap of Tiers A and B now

Dispatch extra technicians from India to swap all 1,240 flagged units in Tiers A and B before the season peaks. Upside: it addresses every unit with above-50% failure precision in one move and is the clearest message Ananya can send Rashid. Cost: roughly ₹6.85 crore and eight-plus weeks of capacity the Dubai team does not have without pulling technicians off routine maintenance — per Exhibit 3, a rollout that finishes after Tier A's predicted failure window has already passed.

Option 2 — Wait for Elena's three-week validation

Hold fleet-wide action, run 50 manual inspections on the most extreme readings, and let TDI accumulate three more weeks of Dubai-specific data before committing capital. Upside: avoids swapping healthy units — at Tier C's 31% precision, most swaps there would be wasted — and preserves the data science team's credibility for future models. Cost: Exhibit 2 shows failures can begin as little as two weeks after a unit enters Tier A, and the March precedent priced a smaller, comparable cluster at ₹1.1 crore before Raftaar even had a model to see it coming.

Option 3 — Tiered rolling service

Swap Tier A's 380 units now, within existing capacity (2.5 weeks per Exhibit 3); re-score Tiers B and C weekly and escalate any unit that crosses into Tier A; share a live risk dashboard with Rashid instead of a one-time report. Upside: acts fastest where the model is most trustworthy, fits Dubai's real service capacity, and gives Rashid visibility instead of a verdict. Cost: roughly ₹2.1 crore up front, an open question on B and C that Ananya cannot fully answer on Friday, and a dashboard build borrowed from Lukas Richter's Berlin team, mid-way through redesigning the field-technician app.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What does the Thermal Drift Index actually predict, and how much confidence does Exhibit 1 justify in each of the three tiers?
  2. How should the March 2026 Pune incident change how Ananya weighs the cost of waiting against the cost of servicing units that turn out to be false positives?
  3. Whose incentives are aligned and whose are in tension among Elena, Karthik, and Meera — and how should that shape who decides versus who is simply informed?
  4. Given the capacity constraint in Exhibit 3, which option is actually executable in the three weeks available, not just correct in principle?

8. A note for the learner

This case is about what a leading indicator built from device data can and cannot do. Telemetry does not tell Raftaar which scooters will fail — it converts a fleet-wide unknown into a ranked, time-bound forecast, and the value of that forecast lies entirely in how it is used. A well-reasoned answer reads Exhibit 1 correctly: 71%, 54%, and 31% precision are not close enough to treat as interchangeable, and a plan that services all three tiers alike, or none of them, throws away the information the model provides. It also treats the capacity constraint in Exhibit 3 as binding, not incidental — with 150 swaps a week, sequencing is the real decision, and a plan that ignores it cannot be executed inside the failure window it is meant to beat. And it uses the March Pune incident as a base-rate anchor for the cost of waiting, not merely a cautionary story: Raftaar has already paid ₹1.1 crore once for reacting to lagging indicators instead of leading ones.

The defensible path is Option 3. It commits capacity in the order the model has earned trust — Tier A first, where precision is highest and the window shortest — while deferring the lower-confidence tiers to a weekly re-score rather than swapping them blind or ignoring them. It gives Rashid a live dashboard instead of a one-off assurance, protecting the relationship Meera owns without over-promising on units the model is least sure about. And it buys Elena's team the validation window it asked for, applied where being wrong is cheapest. Option 1 spends capacity faster than the fleet can absorb it; Option 2 mistakes a three-week pause for prudence when the data already shows why Raftaar cannot afford one. Option 3 is not the safest-sounding choice — it is the one that matches action to how much the leading indicator actually knows.
case40v1-ana.attribution:
Thikana: Who Sold the Flat?

An unresolved case on attribution, incentives and the limits of measurement in an Indian property marketplace

1. The night before

At 11:40 on the night of Thursday, 12 November 2026, Shalini Deshmukh was still at her kitchen table in Sector 54, Gurugram, with three versions of the same slide open on her laptop. Diwali had fallen on 8 November; the lights were still up along the Golf Course Road. In ten hours she was due to join Thikana's board meeting at Nariman Point, Mumbai, over video, to present a single slide titled Where our growth actually comes from.

Thikana was an online property discovery and transaction platform — flats, plots and new launches across eleven Indian cities, plus a fast-growing non-resident Indian business selling Indian property to buyers in the Gulf. Shalini, thirty-four, had been Senior Director of Product for Demand and Measurement for nineteen months. The slide was, on its face, a reporting task. In practice it would decide whether the ₹19 crore fourth-quarter marketing budget went into performance channels or into things nobody could put a number against, whether forty developer contracts worth ₹163 crore a year were repriced, and whether the growth round that Devika Raghunathan, the chief financial officer, had been negotiating since August closed at the valuation in the term sheet or twenty per cent below it.

The three versions of the slide did not agree. One of them was the number the board had already seen twice. Shalini had come to believe it was wrong. She was not confident that the other two were right.

2. Thikana, and the decision that still binds it

Thikana was founded in Bengaluru in 2017 by Vikram Chandrasekhar, a former Info Edge product manager, and Sunil Kalbag, an engineer who had built search infrastructure at Flipkart. Their thesis was that Indian property portals — 99acres, MagicBricks, Housing.com, NoBroker — competed on listing volume when the actual pain was trust. Thikana verified inventory physically, photographed it itself, and published a RERA registration number against every new-launch project it carried. Developers paid for placement and qualified leads on new launches, two-thirds of the business; brokers and channel partners paid subscriptions; and Thikana took a transaction fee on bookings it originated in its NRI business, where buyers in Dubai, Sharjah and Abu Dhabi bought flats in Bengaluru, Pune, Hyderabad and the Mumbai Metropolitan Region without ever seeing them.

Two earlier decisions shaped everything Shalini could now do. The first was made in 2022: facing weak Android install retention and a spike in cost per install, the team deprecated its consumer app and rebuilt the buyer journey on mobile web plus WhatsApp. It worked — lead volume rose forty per cent in two quarters at lower cost — but it removed the only durable cross-device identifier Thikana had ever owned. A buyer who saw a YouTube pre-roll on a smart TV, searched on a laptop at work, and finally enquired from a phone on WhatsApp arrived as three unrelated strangers.

The second was made in January 2024, and was the one Shalini thought about most. To win the top forty developer accounts from the incumbents, Vikram had offered a structure nobody else would match: a fixed platform fee plus a performance rebate calculated from Thikana's own last-click lead attribution, audited quarterly, the model specified in an annexure. The contracts ran to 31 March 2027. Changing the attribution model was, in the strict legal sense, changing the price.

3. The industry

Indian residential property had spent three years with prices rising, volumes rising, and digital discovery becoming the default even for transactions that still closed across a table with a stamp-paper file. Info Edge's 99acres, Times Internet's MagicBricks, Housing.com and NoBroker fought for the same demand; Square Yards and Anarock worked the transaction side. Developers of the scale of DLF, Godrej Properties, Prestige and Brigade ran their own digital teams, their own Meta and Google accounts and their own CRM instances, and were increasingly unwilling to accept a portal's word for where a booking came from.

Three regulatory forces bore directly on measurement. RERA, administered state by state, governed what could be advertised and when; a project whose registration lapsed had to be pulled from marketing within days, which meant campaign spend in a city could stop for reasons that had nothing to do with demand. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act required granular consent for the processing that ad-tech quietly depends on; Thikana's consent rate for cross-site tracking had settled at around fifty-six per cent on mobile web, and the non-consenting forty-four per cent were invisible to every model in the building. TRAI's DLT regime constrained SMS, and WhatsApp's business messaging pricing had made re-engagement a real cost line.

Outside India, the Gulf mattered out of all proportion to its volume: UAE-based NRIs bought fewer than four per cent of Thikana's units but produced nineteen per cent of transaction revenue, because ticket sizes were larger. That business ran through Al Nakheel Property Partners, a Dubai channel-partner firm led by Nabeel Rahman, which held Thikana's inventory in showrooms in Deira and Business Bay and ran its own WhatsApp groups, mall activations and Friday seminars. Almost none of that was measurable from Gurugram.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Exhibit 1 sets out the sequence. Through FY25 and the first half of FY26, Thikana's growth story was uncontested: performance marketing worked. Aditya Bhatnagar, who ran performance from Pune, reported monthly against a last-click model that credited a lead to whichever paid or organic touch immediately preceded the enquiry form. On that basis Google Search and Performance Max delivered leads at ₹412 apiece, Meta at ₹506, and the brand campaigns — the Hindi-market YouTube films, the cricket-season sponsorship, the two-year outdoor programme in Pune and Hyderabad — delivered almost nothing countable. In April 2026, on the strength of that reporting, brand spend was cut from ₹6.1 crore a quarter to ₹1.8 crore and the money moved into search and social. For one quarter nothing bad happened: lead volume held, cost per lead fell to ₹389, and the April decision was cited in the June board pack as evidence of discipline.

Then three things arrived at once. In July, Dr Ishita Banerjee, the principal data scientist in Toronto, finished a multi-touch model built on the consenting subset of traffic and found that it moved roughly a quarter of all credited revenue away from paid search and towards branded search, direct visits and YouTube (Exhibit 2). In August, Serena Koh in Singapore ran the quarterly reconciliation against developer CRMs for the Bengaluru and Hyderabad accounts and found that the parties claiming credit for the same bookings together claimed 164 per cent of them (Exhibit 4). And in September, the first honest look at the lag data (Exhibit 6) showed a median gap of 5.4 months between a buyer's first recorded touch and a booking, with a long tail past a year. Every quarterly attribution number Thikana had reported was crediting this quarter's channels with last year's demand.

The April brand cut, meanwhile, had begun to show up where nobody was looking. Branded search for "Thikana" was down eleven per cent year on year in the two cities where outdoor had stopped, against a flat national trend. Aditya's dashboard showed this as an improvement: fewer branded clicks bought, lower blended cost per lead. Ishita read the same series as the first visible cost of the cut. Neither reading could be falsified with the data available.

Exhibit 1 — Timeline of decisions and discoveries, January 2024 – November 2026
Compiled from Thikana board packs, the FY26 marketing plan and internal analytics tickets. Dates of "discovery" are the dates results were circulated, not the dates the underlying effects began.
Exhibit 2 — Credited revenue by channel, H1 FY27 (₹ crore), three models

Outdoor receives zero under last-click by construction: a hoarding cannot be clicked. A further ₹54 crore of H1 revenue is excluded entirely, no touch of any kind having been recorded before the enquiry.

Exhibit 2 is the exhibit the board has not seen, and the one Shalini trusts least, for a reason she has struggled to compress into a slide: all three columns are arithmetic performed on the same recorded clicks. If the recording is biased — forty-four per cent unconsented, no app, a WhatsApp channel carrying no referrer at all — then all three columns are biased in the same direction, and their disagreement measures the distance between three sets of assumptions, not the distance of any of them from the truth.

Exhibit 3 — Cost per qualified lead by channel, FY26 Q4 vs FY27 Q1 (₹)

Note: the lead-quality definition was tightened on 1 May 2026 to require a verified phone number, and the attribution lookback window was shortened from 30 days to 7 days on the same date to align with the platform defaults after a Google Ads account migration. Q1 FY27 figures are therefore not directly comparable to Q4 FY26. This footnote did not appear on the version of this table circulated to the leadership team in October.

Exhibit 3 is the table Aditya presents. Read quickly, it says the April reallocation worked. Read with its footnote, a seven-day window mechanically strips credit from every slow channel and hands it to the fast ones, and a tightened quality definition changes the denominator. Shalini had found the footnote herself, in a data-engineering ticket, three weeks ago. Aditya holds that the migration was routine and the direction of travel real regardless; Ishita holds that a measurement change and a budget change landing on the same date make the quarter uninterpretable.

Exhibit 4 — Reconciliation of booking credit, Bengaluru & Hyderabad new launches, Q1 FY27
Claiming partyBookings claimedShare of 412 actual bookings
Thikana (last-click lead tracker)23958%

Compiled by S. Koh (Singapore) from four developer CRM exports and Thikana's own tracker, Q1 FY27. "Actual bookings" is the count of registered sale agreements reported by the developers. Overlap arises because each party records credit under its own rule, and the CRMs let a sales executive tag a source manually at the point of booking. Two of the four developers pay their channel partners a brokerage on any booking the partner tags, which the reconciliation cannot net out.

Exhibit 4 is the one that keeps Shalini awake. Sixty-four per cent of the credit in this market is duplicate. It is not fraud; it is four honest systems each answering a slightly different question, and none of them asking whether the buyer would have bought anyway. The number also matters commercially: the rebate Thikana earns under the 2024 contracts is calculated from its own column, the 239. If a developer ran this reconciliation itself and concluded that Thikana's incremental contribution was 239 minus whatever the channel partner would have delivered regardless, the March 2027 renewal would begin from a very different place. Serena has not shown Exhibit 4 to any client.

Exhibit 5 — Geo-holdout test on YouTube brand spend, six cities, 20 June – 10 September 2026
Design: brand spend held at zero in five test cities while matched controls continued at plan; enquiry volume compared against a synthetic control built from trailing twelve-month city trends. Prepared by I. Banerjee. Notes: (a) the test ran eighty-three days against a median lead-to-booking lag of 5.4 months, so it measures enquiries, not bookings; (b) two large new launches in Ahmedabad were withdrawn from marketing on 2 August after a RERA registration lapse, which the synthetic control does not adjust for; (c) a sixth city, Kochi, was dropped after a pipeline failure corrupted eleven days of session logs. No interval excludes zero.

Exhibit 5 was meant to be the tiebreaker and is not. Three cities point up, two down, every interval crosses zero — the test is underpowered for the effect it is chasing, and the city with the cleanest negative reading is the one where RERA took two projects off the market mid-test. Ishita's summary called the result "directionally consistent with a positive brand effect and formally inconclusive". Vikram read that as support for restoring brand spend; Devika read it as an admission that ₹41 lakh had bought a test that proved nothing.

Exhibit 6 — Lead-to-booking lag and the UAE business, FY26–FY27

Source: Thikana transaction ledger joined to first recorded session, FY26 Q1 – FY27 Q2. "First touch" is the earliest session Thikana can see, which for consenting mobile-web users reaches back at most 90 days and for non-consenting users does not exist; true first touch is therefore earlier than recorded for an unknown share of buyers. For the UAE cohort, 61 per cent of bookings begin in a WhatsApp conversation or an Al Nakheel showroom visit with no preceding tracked session; these are assigned to "direct" in Exhibits 2 and 3.

Exhibit 6 quietly dissolves the premise of the other five. If nineteen per cent of bookings close in the quarter of first touch, then eighty-one per cent of any quarter's reported channel performance is a statement about a quarter that has already ended — and for the UAE business, ninety-six per cent of it is. Rohit Malhotra in New Jersey had argued for two years that NRI demand was created by Al Nakheel's Friday seminars, by cricket-season sponsorship on Gulf television, and by word of mouth in community WhatsApp groups Thikana would never have permission to see. Under every model in Exhibit 2, all of it appeared as "direct".

5. The people

Shalini Deshmukh — Senior Director, Product (Demand & Measurement), Gurugram

Position: the company is optimising against a number that cannot see most of what creates demand. Incentive: her function exists to produce one trusted growth number, and "we cannot know" reads as failure. Not saying: she approved the April brand cut in the room where it was made, and has told nobody she now thinks it was a mistake.

Vikram Chandrasekhar — Co-founder & CEO, Mumbai

Position: restore brand spend before the spring launch season; Exhibit 5 is good enough to act on. Incentive: the round prices on the demand story, and brand-led growth reads better to a strategic investor than paid-search arbitrage. Not saying: he negotiated the 2024 rebate annexure himself, and knows any model change reopens forty contracts before the round closes.

Devika Raghunathan — Chief Financial Officer, Mumbai

Position: she will fund anything with an auditable payback and nothing she cannot reproduce from source data. Incentive: she must sign a representation on marketing efficiency metrics. Not saying: last-click CAC figures are already with the lead investor's diligence team, and a restatement now would look like something worse than a measurement change.

Aditya Bhatnagar — VP Performance Marketing, Pune

Position: last-click is imperfect but it is the only number that updates daily and can be acted on. Incentive: his team's quarterly bonus is set on blended cost per lead, the metric in Exhibit 3. Not saying: he authorised the lookback-window change on 1 May without escalating it, and knows a third of that improvement is mechanical.

Dr Ishita Banerjee — Principal Data Scientist, Toronto

Position: neither last-click nor multi-touch answers the causal question; only holdouts and a properly specified mix model do, and both need six to nine months. Incentive: her reputation rests on methodological caution; her contract renews in April. Not saying: she does not believe her own model's grossing-up assumption survives the non-consenting forty-four per cent, and has said so only in a footnote.

Serena Koh — Customer Success Lead (APAC & Gulf), Singapore

Position: client-facing reporting must change before a developer discovers Exhibit 4 independently. Incentive: her Q4 renewals target covers eleven of the top forty accounts. Not saying: two of those accounts have already asked for a source-level audit and she has been slow-walking it.

Rohit Malhotra — Head of NRI Sales, Edison, New Jersey

Position: the Gulf and US businesses are starved because their demand generation is invisible to the India dashboard. Incentive: he is paid on NRI transaction revenue and wants the cricket sponsorship and Gulf seminars protected. Not saying: much of his pipeline is sourced by Al Nakheel, and precise attribution might show Thikana's own spend contributes little to it.

Jonas Weill — Design Director, Berlin

Position: the channel argument ignores the product; saved searches and price alerts bring buyers back more often than any paid channel and are credited to "direct". Incentive: a regime that values owned surfaces funds his roadmap. Not saying: the instrumentation that would prove it was descoped last year at his own request, to ship a redesign on time.

6. Voices

Vikram Chandrasekhar, leadership call, 28 October 2026

"For two years we have told this board we are a performance company. Now Ishita tells me a quarter of the credit is in the wrong column, Serena tells me our clients count it a third way, and Shalini tells me the whole thing lags five months. Fine. But I am not going to Mumbai to say we don't know. Give me the number that is least wrong."

Aditya Bhatnagar, marketing Slack channel, 3 November

"Genuine question. If we move to Ishita's model tomorrow, what do I tell the Pune team to do differently at 9 a.m.? Multi-touch doesn't tell me which keyword to pause. Last-click is wrong in a way I understand and can correct for. The new thing is wrong in a way nobody can correct for, and it ships once a month."

Dr Ishita Banerjee, reply, four hours later

"You can correct for it? Show me the correction factor and the data you fit it on. The reason last-click feels correctable is that it never disagrees with itself. That is not accuracy, Aditya, that is a closed loop."

Serena Koh, email to Shalini, 5 November

"The Hyderabad account has asked for a source-level audit of the rebate calculation for two quarters. I have been telling them the annexure defines the method and the method was followed, which is true. I would like to stop saying it. If we restate after they audit, we will not be correcting a model, we will be settling a claim."

Rohit Malhotra, voice note transcript, 9 November

"Shalini, please understand the Gulf buyer. He sees the Thikana name on the screen during an India match, his cousin in Sharjah has bought through Nabeel's office, he walks into Business Bay on a Friday, and six months later he signs. Which click do you want me to show you? There is no click. There has never been a click."

Devika Raghunathan, margin note on the board pre-read, 11 November

"Whatever we present must be capable of being presented again in February without a restatement. That constraint binds harder than accuracy."

7. The options as Shalini sees them

Option A — Present last-click, flagged

Take the number the board knows, footnote the lookback-window change, commit to a measurement roadmap next cycle. Protects the contracts, the diligence file and Devika's representation. It also allocates the Q4 ₹19 crore by a rule that Exhibits 4, 5 and 6 each independently suggest is wrong, in the quarter that feeds the spring launch season.

Option B — Present multi-touch as the new standard

Adopt Ishita's model for internal allocation and, from April, for client reporting; roughly ₹14 crore of annualised credit moves from paid search to brand and owned surfaces. But it rests on the consenting 56 per cent grossed up on an untested assumption, cannot be reproduced from source data by Devika or by a developer's auditor, and reopens the rebate annexure eight months early.

Option C — Present the programme instead of a number

Tell the board the growth split is not knowable to the precision being asked for, and fund twelve months of powered geo holdouts, a marketing-mix model on three years of spend, and instrumentation for the owned surfaces Jonas wants measured. Honest, slow, roughly ₹3.4 crore. It asks a board mid-raise to accept uncertainty, and leaves Q4 allocated by the same broken rule anyway.

Option D — Split the question in two

Run last-click unchanged as the settlement currency for developer rebates, and a separate incrementality-based model for Thikana's own budget, never reconciled. Honest that the two uses were always different products. It also means publishing to clients a number the company does not believe, and Shalini does not know what that does to Serena's audits — or to her own position when someone asks which of the two is the truth.

Shalini had written these four on the back of the pre-read, then written a fifth line and struck it out: none of these change what we sell, where, or who we sell it with. The Ahmedabad reading in Exhibit 5, the 164 per cent in Exhibit 4 and the 8.7-month lag in Exhibit 6 might all be symptoms of something the channel frame cannot represent — that where a channel partner, a developer's sales team and a portal all touch the same buyer, the object being attributed may not be a channel, and the unit to be allocated may not be budget.

8. The deadline and the constraints

The board meets at 10:00 on 13 November. The Q4 media plan must reach the agencies by 20 November to hold inventory rates. The developer contracts renew on 31 March 2027; the rebate annexure can be amended only by mutual written consent, and eleven of those accounts sit inside Serena's Q4 renewal target. Confirmatory diligence on the growth round closes in the second week of December, and the metrics already with the lead investor were produced on the last-click basis. Ishita's holdout programme needs approval before she can book test capacity for the January launch calendar. Cash is not the binding constraint — Thikana closed October with ₹210 crore on the balance sheet — credibility is: this is the third consecutive board meeting at which the growth number has moved, and Devika's margin note is a warning that a fourth movement will not be read as rigour.

9. Questions for discussion

  1. Why does every channel in Exhibit 4 over-claim, and what would it take — data, design or contract — for those four claims to sum to a hundred?
  2. Exhibit 2 shows three models disagreeing by as much as ₹37 crore. What, precisely, does the disagreement between them measure? What does their agreement not prove?
  3. Exhibit 3 and Exhibit 5 point in opposite directions about the April brand cut. Which of the two is more load-bearing, and what would you need to see before you let either of them move ₹19 crore?
  4. Given the lag structure in Exhibit 6, is quarterly channel attribution a meaningful management instrument at Thikana at all? If not, what should be reported quarterly instead?
  5. The 2024 rebate annexure turned an analytical convention into a contractual price. Whose job was it to notice, and what should a product leader do when a measurement becomes a commercial commitment?
  6. It is Monday morning, 16 November, and the board has asked for a follow-up note. What does Shalini do — and what exactly does she say about the number she presented in February, in June, and again on Friday?

10. Friday

At 1:15 a.m. Shalini closed the laptop, then opened it again. On the screen was the version with a single headline: Paid search delivers 40 per cent of our growth. It was the number in the diligence file, the number in the rebate annexure, and the number Aditya's team would still be optimising against on Monday whatever she said on Friday. Underneath it she had typed, and not deleted, a second line: We can measure what closes. We cannot yet measure what causes.

She thought about the buyer in Sharjah who had never clicked anything; about Nabeel, who would be in the Business Bay office in six hours and would not care which column he sat in; about eleven per cent of branded search in two cities, which was either an early warning or a rounding artefact. Somewhere in the car park a last Diwali cracker went off, late and alone. The presentation was due at ten. She had not decided which slide to open with.

Indian and international companies, platforms, regulators and institutions named for market context are real and are not portrayed as doing anything improper. All figures are invented for teaching purposes.

Attribution and Its Limits

Credit allocation, causal inference, and the uncomfortable arithmetic of measuring advertising

1. Two decisions, one week apart

On 14 April 2026, Meera Iyengar, VP of growth at Tarang — a subscription audio app with 3.1 million paying users, built on vernacular music and spoken word in nine Indian languages — received a one-line message from her CFO: “Board wants the OTT video line justified or zeroed before the 30th.” That line was ₹1.05 crore a month on connected-television and premium video, roughly 18% of Tarang's paid budget. Tarang's in-app analytics credited that spend with 3,400 of the month's 42,000 new paid subscriptions. Meta and Google, between them, claimed 39,000 of the same 42,000. Meera's problem was not a lack of numbers; she had too many, all internally consistent, none answering the CFO's question, which was causal: if this money stopped, what would Tarang lose?

Nine days later, Priya Natarajan faced a structurally identical question with almost none of the same instruments. Priya ran demand generation at Meridian Logistics Cloud, a transport-management SaaS platform selling six-figure annual contracts to mid-market manufacturers, with engineering in Kraków and sales split between Mumbai and Singapore. Meridian had spent ₹1.1 crore over twelve months on industry conferences and long-form research reports. Its marketing automation system credited that programme with first touch on 66 of the year's 212 opportunities — 31% — while the CRM's last-touch model credited a demo-request form with 68% of the same ones. Meridian closed 48 deals that year at an average contract value of ₹34 lakh. Priya's new CRO, arriving from a consumer company, asked why she did not simply run a holdout; the answer, which took three weeks to make legible to him, is that with 48 wins a year she could not run one that would tell her anything. That asymmetry — Meera can test and must interpret; Priya cannot test and must reason — is the spine of everything below.

2. The idea, and the three schools that disagree about it

Attribution is the assignment of credit for an outcome to the inputs that preceded it. Stated that way it is cooperative game theory, not marketing: a coalition of channels jointly produced 42,000 subscriptions and we want a rule for dividing 42,000 among them. Lloyd Shapley solved the general version in 1953; his is the unique allocation satisfying efficiency, symmetry, the null-player property and additivity. No axiom in that list mentions causation. Shapley's rule is a fairness rule, not a counterfactual.

The counterfactual question has a different lineage: Neyman's potential outcomes of 1923, formalised by Rubin in the 1970s, in which each user has two latent outcomes — what they would do if exposed and if not — of which we observe one. Incrementality is the difference between those averages. The traditions fused into practice recently and imperfectly. Last-click became the default not because anyone defended it but because it was the field web-log analytics could populate unambiguously: a data-availability artefact that acquired the authority of a standard. Multi-touch attribution arrived around 2010 to fix that unfairness, and by 2015 was doing so with Shapley values and absorbing Markov chains. Then came the counter-evidence. Blake, Nosko and Tadelis switched off eBay's paid brand search in randomised US markets in 2013 and found incremental return indistinguishable from zero and plausibly negative, against an attributed return in the hundreds of percent. Lewis and Rao showed in 2015 that even very large advertising experiments are underpowered to resolve commercially interesting return ranges. Gordon and colleagues, inside Facebook in 2019, compared observational estimates against randomised ground truth across fifteen large campaigns and found them wrong by factors of two to three, in an unstable direction.

Three schools argue over that record. An expert states each position in the form its holders would sign.

The path school holds that with complete user-level path data, credit allocation is solved and the axioms are the discipline. It will sign: given a stable identity graph, a Shapley or Markov model produces a defensible, manipulation-resistant division of observed conversions across observed touchpoints. It will not sign that those shares are causal, and its serious practitioners have stopped claiming so. Since Apple's App Tracking Transparency in 2021 and the erosion of third-party cookies, the identity substrate it depends on no longer exists at the coverage its methods assume.

The experimentalist school holds that only a randomised comparison licenses a causal claim. It will sign: a channel's incremental contribution is known only to the extent it has been measured against a randomised counterfactual at the current spend level. It will not sign that experiments are always feasible, nor that a null result means a channel does nothing — a distinction its weaker adherents blur.

The econometric school — marketing-mix modelling, revived by open-source Bayesian implementations from 2021 onward — holds that aggregate time series with priors, adstock and saturation curves recover response functions without any user identity. It will sign: a well-specified hierarchical model, calibrated against experiments where they exist, allocates the whole portfolio better than any user-level method under modern privacy constraints. It will not sign that its coefficients are identified without those experimental priors; media budgets move together, and collinearity is its permanent enemy.

3. Mechanics in depth: what the models actually compute

Take Tarang's three tracked channels over one month, reduced to conversions per 1,000 reached users so coalitions compare. Meera's analyst, Faraz Qureshi, estimated every subset from overlapping-reach cohorts: OTT (A) 20; app-install performance ads (B) 50; CRM (C) 15; A and B 62; A and C 32; B and C 58; all three 70. The subadditivity is the point — 20 plus 50 is 70, but running both yields 62, because the channels reach overlapping people with overlapping intent.

The Shapley value averages each channel's marginal contribution over all 3! = 6 orders the coalition could form in. For OTT the six marginal contributions are 20, 20, 12, 12, 17 and 12, averaging 15.5. For performance ads: 42, 38, 50, 50, 38, 43, averaging 43.5. For CRM: 8, 12, 8, 8, 15, 15, averaging 11.0. They sum to exactly 70, which is efficiency doing its work.

The Markov approach models the journey as an absorbing chain and computes each channel's removal effect: delete its states, re-solve for the probability of reaching conversion. On Tarang's paths the baseline was 0.62; removing performance ads dropped it to 0.25, OTT to 0.50, CRM to 0.58. Those removal effects — 59.7%, 19.4%, 6.5% — normalise to shares of 69.7%, 22.7% and 7.6%.

The same month of Tarang data under four regimes. Shares are of 1,000 conversions; the final column is measured, not allocated.
ChannelLast clickShapleyMarkov removalTested incremental
OTT / premium video8%22.1%22.7%11.8% (±2.3)
App-install performance86%62.1%69.7%not yet tested
CRM push & email6%15.7%7.6%not yet tested

Two things there deserve attention. Shapley and Markov — both principled, both fed identical data — disagree by more than a factor of two on CRM: axiomatic respectability does not produce convergence. And the tested column is not a fourth opinion in the same argument but an answer to a different question; it lands between the allocations, which is common and which people over-read as vindication of the middle model.

The step practitioners leave implicit is the design of the test itself. Meera ran a matched-market geo experiment: 36 cities paired on baseline volume, price mix and language profile, 18 treated and 18 held out, OTT suspended in the holdout for six weeks. After matching, the residual standard deviation of monthly subscriptions across cities was 7% of the mean, so the standard error of the difference between arms of 18 is 7% × √(1/18 + 1/18) = 2.33%, and the minimum detectable effect at 80% power and a two-sided 5% test is about 2.80 × 2.33% = 6.5%.

Now put money against it. Tarang's twelve-month contribution margin per subscription is ₹2,400, so break-even on ₹1.05 crore of monthly spend is 4,375 subscriptions, or 10.4% of the 42,000 national baseline. Since 10.4% exceeds the 6.5% MDE, the design distinguishes break-even from zero — a stronger position than most companies occupy. Observed lift was 11.8%, about 4,956 subscriptions, worth ₹1.19 crore of margin against ₹1.05 crore of spend: ROI 1.13×. But the 2.33% standard error is 979 subscriptions, or ₹23.5 lakh, so the 95% interval on ROI runs from roughly 0.69× to 1.57×. The test resolves “this channel does something”; it does not resolve “this returns 1.5× and so deserves the marginal rupee ahead of performance ads at 1.3×” — the question budget meetings litigate. Halving that interval needs four times the geos or the duration. That is the Lewis–Rao result, derived from Tarang's own numbers rather than cited.

Two second-order effects follow and are routinely missed. First, attribution is not merely a report; it is an input to the bidder. A platform optimises delivery toward the conversions its own model records, so a model over-crediting bottom-of-funnel contact steers targeting toward users already converting, improving measured performance while degrading real performance: changing the model changes the campaign, not just the report of it. Second, reallocations propagate with a lag — cutting an upper-funnel channel raises brand search's measured cost per acquisition six to twelve weeks later, by which time nobody connects the two and the brand-search team is blamed for a decay the video team caused.

4. When the idea applies, stated as testable claims

The conditions under which attribution modelling is worth trusting are checkable rather than assumed, and applied to both protagonists they separate immediately.

Four conditions, each checkable, applied to Tarang and Meridian.
Testable claimTarang (consumer subscription)Meridian (enterprise SaaS)
Conversion volume is sufficient for a randomised design to reach a decision-relevant MDE.Holds: 42,000/month gives a 6.5% MDE against a 10.4% break-even.Fails: 48 wins split 24/24 implies an MDE near 80%.
The unit of conversion is the unit of decision.Holds: one user, one subscription, one payment.Fails: the account converts, five to nine individuals are touched, and the committee shifts mid-cycle.
The measurement horizon exceeds the decision cycle.Partly: six weeks cannot see brand effects maturing over quarters.Fails badly: a nine-month median cycle means any window under a year reads mostly noise.
Identity coverage is high enough that paths are not systematically truncated.Fails on iOS: ~28% of revenue comes from devices with no deterministic path data.Holds well — corporate email as join key gives near-complete tracking within the visible funnel.

Attribution turns actively misleading, rather than merely imprecise, in three situations: any channel targeted on intent — retargeting, brand search, abandoned-cart email — where confounding runs in a known direction and the attributed number must overstate; any category with strong organic demand, where the ad intercepts a purchase that was going to happen anyway; and any period after the model has changed, because the discontinuity will be read as a change in performance by everyone not in the room when the setting was flipped. In all three the number is not noisy but biased, with a sign predictable in advance.

5. Hard edge cases and what mature companies actually do

Multi-product portfolios break the accounting at the top: when one campaign feeds three products with different margins the model must attribute to a channel and a product, and teams resolve this by crediting first product purchased, which undervalues channels bringing users who cross-sell later. Two-sided marketplaces have a sharper problem, because a demand-side incrementality test measures a quantity bounded by supply. If the matching engine is capacity-constrained, switching off buyer acquisition in holdout geos shows a small lift not because the channel is weak but because the marginal buyer was rationed anyway. The honest fix is to test below capacity, or instrument the constraint and report lift conditional on it.

Regulated categories — lending, insurance, pharmaceuticals, anything under a consent regime — often cannot retain the identifiers user-level attribution requires, which is why financial-services teams adopted aggregate modelling earliest. Hardware adds a structural break: conversion happens in a retail channel the manufacturer does not own, so the geo test is the only reliable causal instrument — one reason packaged-goods firms kept matched-market testing through the decades digital marketing abandoned it. AI-native products add a newer difficulty: discovery is migrating to assistants and answer engines that recommend without a referrer, so high-intent arrivals increasingly appear as untraceable direct traffic, while in product-led AI tools the conversion event is diffuse — a user who runs forty free queries over three weeks and upgrades on the forty-first offers no moment to anchor to.

The organisational seams matter as much as the technical ones. Brand and performance teams report through different leaders, hold different measurement systems and are judged on incompatible metrics; the brand team's success mechanically inflates the performance team's numbers, and no accounting rule adjudicates a dispute where both are partly right. Agencies paid on attributed return have a direct interest in the window and model, a conflict almost never written down. What mature companies actually do — as opposed to what their decks say — is keep one model as a fixed operational baseline, run a standing calendar of experiments against it, and reserve causal claims for the few channels tested in the last two quarters. The rest is bookkeeping: useful for detecting breakage, useless for reallocating budget.

6. What separates an expert from a competent practitioner

Incrementality is a property of the margin, not of the channel. The competent practitioner says “OTT tested at 11.8% lift.” The expert asks at what spend, because the same channel at half the spend may return far more per rupee and at double the spend far less. The tell is a lift figure quoted without a spend level; the obvious reading — that a channel “works” or “doesn't” — is wrong because the decision is never whether to have the channel but how much of it to buy.

Public-service-announcement holdouts are contaminated. The standard placebo was long a charity advertisement served to the control group, but those users were still selected by the auction, and serving them any ad changes what else they see. Ghost-ad designs — recording which control users would have won the auction and comparing those to the treated, as Johnson, Lewis and Nubbemeyer set out in 2017 — remove the contamination. The tell is a vendor describing a holdout whose control group sees something rather than nothing.

Analyse by assignment, not by exposure. This is the most expensive error in the field. Once randomised into treatment a user belongs in that arm whether or not they saw the ad; conditioning on exposure re-introduces exactly the selection randomisation removed, because exposure is chosen by an optimiser that selects on intent. The tell is any deck comparing “exposed” to “unexposed” and reporting a lift in the hundreds of percent, as Tarang's earlier retargeting analysis did.

The attribution model is an instruction to the machine. Experts treat a model change as a campaign change, re-baselining with a freeze period in which no channel decisions are made. The tell is measured return improving sharply within two weeks of a settings change with spend unchanged; the naive reading is that performance improved, when the bidder's objective moved.

A null result is not evidence of no effect. Competent practitioners read “not statistically significant” as “does nothing” and cut. Experts report the interval and ask whether it excludes the commercially relevant values; an interval spanning a 60% loss to a 60% gain has established nothing, and cutting on it is a coin toss dressed as rigour. The tell is a decision memo with a p-value and no interval.

Brand search is structurally the most over-credited line in most accounts. A user typing the brand name has already been converted by something else; the ad intercepts the click. eBay's experiment found near-zero incremental return, while later replications found small positive returns where competitors bid on the brand term — which is the real mechanism: defence against interception, not demand creation. The tell is brand-search return that is high and remarkably stable at every spend level, the signature of a metric measuring pre-existing demand rather than responding to investment.

The denominator is usually wrong. Lift measured on orders rather than on new-customer contribution margin flatters any channel reaching existing customers, discounters and low-margin segments. Experts insist the test's outcome variable be the variable in the financial model. The tell is a test whose outcome is “conversions” while the decision is about profit; channels differ systematically in the margin mix of whom they bring.

Effect horizon and test horizon are different quantities. Upper-funnel spend matures over quarters; a six-week window measures the fast component and silently reports it as the whole. Experts extend the window, stagger switch-backs, or state that the estimate is a lower bound. The tell is a two-week test adjudicating a brand channel — a design that guarantees its answer before the data arrives.

Triangulation is not averaging. Methods that disagree resolve not by taking a mean but by asking whose identifying assumption is least violated here; a blended number with no stated uncertainty hides that nobody checked. The tell is a slide showing last-click, MTA and MMM beside a “consensus” column nobody can derive.

7. How this differs by product type and stage

In consumer products with short cycles and single decision-makers the failure mode is halo — upper-funnel channels donating credit to lower-funnel ones — and geo testing is genuinely available as a remedy. In B2B and enterprise the unit problem dominates: credit must be assigned across people as well as channels, samples are too small for randomisation, and the substitutes are opportunity-weighted models validated against sales-conversation evidence and, where the calendar permits, Bayesian structural time series on matched territories. In platforms and marketplaces every attribution exercise runs twice and is read jointly, because a demand campaign's measured performance is partly a statement about supply. In hardware the purchase leaves the measurable system entirely and matched-market testing is a necessity, not a sophistication. For AI products it is too early to claim a distinct discipline: the mechanics are those of consumer subscription or PLG SaaS, with the wrinkle that assistant-mediated discovery erodes the referrer faster than practice adapts.

Stage changes what is worth doing more than product type does. Below roughly 500 conversions a week no holdout reaches a useful MDE, and the right posture is cheap directional tests, weekly switch-backs and a frank acknowledgement that the allocation is judgement. Between 500 and 5,000 a week, geo testing becomes viable for the largest one or two channels. Above that, a standing experiment calendar plus a calibrated mix model is affordable, and its absence is a governance failure rather than a resourcing constraint. Where the difference is not real: the mathematics of selection bias and power is identical at every stage and category, and a smaller budget does not make an exposed-versus-unexposed comparison less wrong.

8. Three worked cases, including one that failed

Tarang's OTT test (success, with a caveat). Six weeks, 36 matched cities, spend suspended in 18: an 11.8% lift, ROI point estimate 1.13×, interval 0.69× to 1.57×. Meera's reading was that the channel clears zero but does not obviously clear the alternative use of the money, and that six weeks captured only the fast component of effects that plausibly accrue over two quarters. The caveat that nearly derailed it: three holdout cities ran a regional festival promotion in week four, which Faraz caught only because he had plotted pre-period parallel trends and saw those three diverge before the intervention. Dropping them widened the interval but preserved the sign.

Meridian's conference programme (no test possible; reasoning instead). Unable to randomise, Priya did three things. She re-cut attribution at the account level with an opportunity-weighted model, moving the programme from 31% of opportunities to 22%. She audited 40 closed-won deal records and first-call transcripts, coding whether the conference was named unprompted as the origin of the relationship: 9 of 40. And she ran a Bayesian structural time-series comparison of demo requests from the four verticals the conferences served against six they did not, finding a 14% differential that was insignificant but consistent in direction across three years. Her conclusion, written as a range with the method named: the programme probably contributes 10–20% of pipeline origin, not 31%, and is not separable from the research reports sharing its budget line.

Tarang's retargeting analysis (failure, and the recovery). Eighteen months before Meera joined, Tarang's agency reported that retargeting delivered a 338% lift, computed by comparing users who saw a retargeting ad (9.2% conversion) to those who did not (2.1%). On that number, retargeting spend was tripled to ₹62 lakh a month and the board's CAC model rebuilt around it. The analysis was not imprecise but structurally invalid: exposure was assigned by an optimiser trained to find users likely to convert, so it measured targeting accuracy, not the ad's effect. Re-run as an intent-to-treat holdout — randomise before the auction, analyse by assignment — treated users converted at 4.02% against control's 3.87%, a 3.9% lift with an interval including zero. The recovery took two quarters and was mostly not analytical: cutting spend to ₹18 lakh was survivable, but unit economics had been restated on the false number, so the CFO had to walk back a blended CAC figure in a shareholder update. The durable change was procedural — any lift claim above 30% must now name its randomisation unit, and analyses conditioning on exposure are rejected at review.

9. Failure modes, their early warnings and the cost of late detection

Five recurring failures. The diagnostic question is the cheapest thing that catches each one.
FailureEarly warning signDiagnostic questionCost if caught late
Selection on exposureReported lift above 100% on an intent-targeted channel“When was randomisation applied, and were non-exposed treated users kept in?”Budget tripled into a channel with no effect; restated unit economics
Platform-claimed conversions exceeding realitySum of platform claims > total conversions“Whose window, whose match logic, how many are modelled not observed?”Systematic over-investment across the portfolio
Underpowered test read as a nullA cut justified by “not significant”, no interval shown“Does the interval exclude break-even?”A profitable channel killed; invisible for two quarters
Model or window change mistaken for performance changeStep change in a metric with no change in spend“What changed in the measurement configuration in 30 days?”Months of decisions anchored to a discontinuity
Stale lift estimate reusedA number quoted with no test date“What spend level and which quarter produced this figure?”Scaling a channel far past the point its curve flattens

Across all five, the early warning costs nothing and is not looked for, while the late cost runs to quarters of misallocated budget and, more damagingly, the credibility of the measurement function: once a growth team has been loudly wrong, its later correct results are discounted.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Position one: experiments are the only admissible evidence. Its strongest form rests on Gordon's 2019 comparison, in which observational methods applied to the same campaigns as randomised tests were off by factors of two to three with no stable direction of error, so the bias cannot be corrected by a rule of thumb. For this to be wrong, modern high-dimensional adjustment would have to close the gap reliably across campaign types — and the 2019 evidence is that rich covariate adjustment helped least exactly where the stakes were highest.

Position two: experiments are too underpowered and too slow to run a business on. Steelmanned, this is Lewis and Rao's point turned against their successors: if resolving a commercially interesting ROI range needs samples an order of magnitude larger than most firms can field, insisting on experiments means deciding with no information rather than imperfect information. A firm running twelve channels can test perhaps three a year; the other nine need budgets on Monday. For this to be wrong, designs would have to become dramatically more efficient — switchbacks, always-on ghost-ad infrastructure and variance reduction on pre-period covariates are the live candidates, and they have narrowed the gap without closing it.

Position three: aggregate modelling, calibrated by the few experiments you can run, dominates both. The Bayesian mix-modelling revival rests on a real argument: privacy changes destroyed the identity substrate MTA needed, mix models require no user identity, they handle offline and untrackable channels, and experimental results enter as informative priors on individual coefficients. The objection is identification — media budgets move together, so the data cannot separate coefficients the priors have not already largely determined. For this to be wrong, the posterior would have to be shown to be driven mainly by the prior; that is testable by prior-sensitivity analysis, which most practitioners do not run.

A fourth, quieter disagreement concerns purpose. One camp holds that the point of measurement is an accurate number; the other, that it is a better decision, and that a crude method which reliably ranks channels beats a precise one arriving after the budget is set. Evidence cannot reconcile them, because they disagree about the objective function.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this names the models and tells you last-click is bad. Someone who has internalised it differs in four visible ways. They ask what decision the number is for before asking how it was computed, because required precision is a function of the decision, not the method. They state estimates as intervals with a method and a date, and notice when others do not. They design measurement before spending, because the cheapest randomisation is built into the campaign at launch and retrofitted causal inference is dearer and less convincing. And they are comfortable saying a channel's contribution is unknown — not unknowable, not zero, but not currently established — while proposing what it would cost to find out. That last is rarest, because organisations reward confident numbers and punish honest ranges, and holding that line is a political skill as much as an analytical one.

12. What each of them decided

Meera did not defend the OTT line on the 11.8% figure alone, knowing the interval straddled the point at which the money would be better spent elsewhere. She proposed holding the line flat for one further quarter while extending the test to a twelve-week switch-back across 48 cities, which she calculated would cut the ROI interval to roughly ±0.22× — enough to rank OTT against performance ads rather than merely against zero — and committed in writing to cut the line if that interval's lower bound failed to clear 1.0×. The board accepted a dated commitment with a stated decision rule over a confident number, which is generally the trade that works.

Priya did something structurally different because she had to. She stopped presenting an attributed pipeline percentage at all, replacing it with a range from three independent methods that disagreed in magnitude but agreed in direction, plus a named list of the four accounts whose origin she could evidence from transcripts. She also changed what Meridian collected, adding a mandatory structured origin field completed by the account executive at first qualified meeting — imperfect, self-reported, and still better than a model with no identifying variation behind it.

Discussion questions.

1. Meera's twelve-week design costs a quarter of delay and roughly ₹40 lakh of foregone optimisation to halve an interval. When is that a good trade, and who should have authority to decide it?

2. Is Priya's three-method triangulation genuinely evidence, or three weak signals agreeing because they share a bias — and what observation would distinguish the two readings?

3. Tarang's retargeting error survived two quarters and a board presentation. What property of the organisation, rather than of the analysis, allowed that, and what single procedural change would most reliably have caught it?

13. Going deeper

  1. Constructing a funnel — attribution assigns credit for the top of the funnel, so poorly defined stages cannot host a coherent attribution argument; the definitions are prerequisite.
  2. Incrementality measurement — the full treatment of design, power and null results that section 3 only opened; unlocks sizing a test before running it rather than regretting it after.
  3. Paid acquisition for PMs — where these estimates become bids and budgets, and the loop from attribution into the optimiser becomes operationally concrete.
  4. Reading drop-off — distinguishing a real behavioural cliff from an instrumentation artefact: the same skill one stage down the funnel.
  5. Defining activation (the aha moment) — changing the conversion event changes every attribution number, and activation is usually a better outcome variable than signup.
  6. Cohort analysis — the next instrument for what attribution cannot answer alone: whether a channel's users are worth having after month three.
  7. Retention curves and the PMF signal — supplies the margin figure that turns a lift percentage into a break-even threshold; without it no ROI statement is possible.
  8. Stickiness and natural frequency — sets the horizon over which an acquisition effect matures, and therefore the correct test window.
  9. Feature adoption analysis — the same credit-allocation logic applied inside the product, where the confounds are different but the selection problem is identical.
