Attribution and Its Limits

Why every channel claims the credit — and what actually caused the purchase

1. A budget meeting in Bengaluru

On the second Tuesday of March 2026, Ananya Rao, head of growth at Cleo Wellness — a four-year-old direct-to-consumer skincare brand selling through its own app and website — opened the quarterly marketing review with a single slide. Cleo had spent ₹1.9 crore in the previous quarter across five channels: Google brand-search ads, Instagram influencer partnerships, email, organic search, and direct traffic from people typing the URL. The company's analytics dashboard, built on standard last-click attribution, credited Google brand search with 62% of the quarter's 10,000 purchases. Instagram, which absorbed 38% of the media budget, was credited with only 9%.

The finance director's question was blunt: why keep funding a channel that last-click data said was barely working? Ananya's instinct said the number was wrong, but she could not yet say why, or by how much. If she defended Instagram on intuition and finance cut it anyway, Cleo might lose the channel that was quietly building the brand awareness that made people search "Cleo" on Google in the first place. If she defended it wrongly and the cut should have happened, she would burn credibility for two quarters. The decision she made next — not to argue the number, but to change what question the company was asking — is the subject of this reading.

2. The idea

Attribution is the set of rules a company uses to assign credit for a conversion — a purchase, a signup, an activation — to the marketing touchpoints that preceded it. It was invented to solve an accounting problem: a customer's path to purchase usually crosses several channels, but a marketing budget can only be allocated once, so someone has to decide how the pie is sliced.

The default slicing rule, last-click attribution, gives 100% of the credit to whichever channel the customer clicked immediately before converting. It became the industry default largely by accident of tooling: when web analytics platforms such as Urchin (later Google Analytics) standardised conversion tracking in the mid-2000s, the last recorded click was the easiest signal to capture reliably, and the convention stuck long after richer data became available. Multi-touch attribution (MTA), which spreads credit across several touchpoints in a customer's path using a chosen weighting rule, was popularised by ad-tech vendors from around 2010 as marketers noticed that last-click was systematically favouring bottom-of-funnel channels. Incrementality measurement — asking what would have happened without a given channel, typically via a randomised holdout — drew on a much older tradition of controlled experimentation and was pushed into mainstream marketing practice by researchers at Google and Facebook publishing geo-experiment studies between roughly 2011 and 2018.

The sentence Ananya needed for the boardroom was this: attribution tells you which channel touched the customer last, or along the way; only an incrementality test tells you which channel actually caused the purchase — and until you have run one, every channel's number is a claim, not a fact.

3. How it actually works

Every attribution model starts from the same raw material: a path, the ordered sequence of tracked touchpoints a single (identified) customer has with a brand before converting. A path might read: Instagram ad seen on day 1, organic Google search on day 3, a click on a Google brand-search ad on day 7, purchase. The model's job is to turn that path into a set of credit weights that sum to one purchase.

Last-click looks only at the final entry in the path and ignores everything before it — the Instagram touch and the organic search touch vanish entirely from the credit ledger, even though they may have introduced the customer to the brand. Linear multi-touch gives equal weight to every touch in the path: in the example above, each of the three channels receives one-third of a purchase. Time-decay weights touches closer to conversion more heavily, on the reasoning that recency signals intent. A step practitioners often skip is deciding the attribution window — how far back in time a touch is allowed to count at all (1 day, 7 days, 28 days) — and window choice alone can flip which channel "wins" without a single number in the underlying data changing.

None of these models, however sophisticated their weighting, answer the question finance actually cares about: if this channel disappeared, how many of these purchases would still have happened through another route? That is a causal question, and correlation-based credit-splitting, however cleverly weighted, cannot answer it. Only a controlled comparison — a holdout in which the channel is switched off for a randomly chosen slice of the market while it runs as normal elsewhere — isolates the channel's true, incremental contribution.

4. Working the numbers

Cleo's analytics held 10,000 tracked purchases for the quarter. Under last-click, Google brand-search took 6,200 (62%), direct traffic 1,400 (14%), email 700 (7%), organic search 800 (8%), and Instagram 900 (9%). Ananya's analyst, Devraj, pulled the full paths instead of just the final click and found that 61% of purchasers had touched at least two channels before buying, with Instagram appearing somewhere in 2,850 of the 10,000 paths — far more than the 900 it was credited with.

Recomputing under a linear multi-touch model, spreading each purchase's credit evenly across every channel in its path, changed the picture sharply: Google brand search fell to about 3,400 purchases (34%), Instagram rose to about 2,850 (28.5%), organic search settled near 2,100 (21%), and email and direct shared the remainder. On this model alone, Instagram looked like Cleo's second-best channel, not its weakest — a swing of nearly twenty percentage points from a single change in accounting rule, with the underlying customer behaviour completely unchanged.

Ananya knew that number was still an accounting artefact, so she ran the second pass: a four-week geo-holdout, pausing all Instagram spend in nine cities chosen to match Cleo's twelve "always-on" cities on size and baseline sales, and comparing total purchases between the two groups. The result: purchases in the paused cities fell by only 3%, not the 28.5% multi-touch credit nor even the 9% last-click credit implied. Most of the people Instagram had "touched" would have found Cleo anyway, through brand search or word of mouth — a pattern called the halo effect, where an assisting channel gets credit for demand it did not create. Instagram's true incremental contribution was closer to ₹6 lakh of the quarter's revenue than the ₹54 lakh the multi-touch model implied.

Same 10,000 purchases, three lenses
ChannelLast-clickLinear MTAIncrementality (holdout)
Google brand search62%34%likely mostly incremental
Instagram ads9%28.5%~3% of total, not 9% or 28.5%
Organic search8%21%not separately tested
Email / Direct21%16.5%not separately tested

5. What a learner must not blur

Attribution is not the same question as incrementality. Attribution answers "who touched this customer," which is descriptive; incrementality answers "what caused this purchase," which is causal. A channel can dominate every attribution model and still add almost nothing incremental, as Instagram did for Cleo.

Every platform's self-reported number is attribution, not incrementality, and it is attribution the platform itself computed. Ad platforms have a structural incentive to claim credit generously, using long look-back windows and liberal cross-device matching; summing what every platform claims will routinely exceed 100% of actual conversions.

The attribution window is a lever, not a neutral setting. Widening it from one day to twenty-eight days mechanically favours channels with slower-building intent, such as content or influencer marketing, and narrowing it favours channels that catch people at the final moment, such as brand search and retargeting.

Multi-touch attribution is still correlational. Spreading credit more evenly than last-click does is an improvement in fairness of accounting, not a step toward causal truth; it can just as easily overstate an assisting channel as understate one.

Incrementality tests answer a local question, not a universal one. A 3% lift measured at the current Instagram spend level says nothing certain about what would happen at double or half that spend; the relationship between spend and incremental return is rarely a straight line.

Attribution cannot see channels it cannot track. Word of mouth, offline conversations, a friend's Instagram story, or a billboard seen on a commute leave no click; last-click and MTA alike silently fold this untracked demand into whichever tracked channel happens to be adjacent to it.

A thoughtful newcomer should ask, before trusting any attribution number: what window was used, who computed it, has anyone tested the channel with a holdout, and does the ranking survive if the window or model changes? If the answer to the last question is no, the ranking was never a fact about the customer — it was a fact about the accounting rule.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace differences

In consumer products like Cleo, purchase cycles are short and a single person makes the decision, so paths are relatively easy to track end to end within one identified user — the main distortion is the halo effect between brand and performance channels. In B2B software, the buying "customer" is usually a committee of several people across weeks or months, so credit has to be assigned not just across channels but across people; companies typically use account-level models (each contact's touches rolled up to one account) and stage-weighted rules such as giving extra credit to the touch that generated the first meeting and the touch that generated the opportunity, rather than a flat linear split. In a marketplace, attribution has to be run twice, once for the demand side (what brought the buyer) and once for the supply side (what brought the seller or driver), and the two interact: a buyer-acquisition campaign that runs when supply is thin can look like it "failed" in the data purely because there was nothing to buy, which has nothing to do with the channel's quality. Early-stage companies, with only a few hundred conversions a week, rarely have enough volume to detect a statistically credible lift in a holdout test and lean on simpler heuristics and directional experiments instead; larger companies with tens of thousands of weekly conversions can run rigorous, regularly repeated geo-experiments and combine them with statistical marketing-mix modelling for the offline channels that cannot be click-tracked at all.

7. Common mistakes

Four failure patterns recur across companies that skip straight from a dashboard number to a budget decision.

What goes wrong, and the cheapest way to catch it
SymptomUnderlying misunderstandingCheap diagnostic
Each ad platform's dashboard claims more conversions than the company's total analytics showsTreating a platform's self-reported number as ground truthSum every platform's claimed conversions and compare to the single neutral source of truth
Retargeting or brand search looks like the best channel by a wide margin, every quarterConfusing "reaches people already about to buy" with "causes them to buy"Run a short suppression or holdout test on that one channel
Channel rankings flip when someone changes the attribution windowTreating the window as a technical default rather than a lever that favours certain channel typesHold the window fixed for a full quarter before comparing channels
A team quotes a lift number from a test run a year ago as still true todayAssuming incrementality is a fixed property of a channel rather than a function of current spend and seasonRe-test after any material change in spend level or competitive activity

8. What good looks like

At a larger Indian consumer company that Devraj had previously worked for, the growth team never made a channel-cut decision from a single attribution model. Every quarter they triangulated three views: last-click as the cheap, always-on baseline; linear multi-touch as a sense check on which channels were being systematically hidden; and a rolling calendar of geo-holdout tests, one or two channels tested at a time, so that every major channel was re-verified roughly twice a year. Budget memos stated a range rather than a point estimate — "Instagram's incremental contribution is between 2% and 6% of quarterly revenue, last tested in February" — and named the model and window behind every number quoted. No channel was ever cut on attribution data alone; a cut followed a holdout result, or an explicit, documented decision to accept the risk of cutting without one.

9. What Ananya decided

Ananya did not defend Instagram on last-click, and she did not let finance cut it on last-click either. She presented the three numbers side by side — 9%, 28.5%, and the holdout's 3% — and recommended holding Instagram spend flat while narrowing it to the two influencer formats that had shown the least halo overlap with brand search in a follow-up path analysis, funding the change from a modest planned increase rather than from existing budget. Finance accepted a decision grounded in a range and a tested method over a single confident-sounding number. Ananya's next study is incrementality measurement in full — how to size a holdout so its result is trustworthy, and how to read a null result honestly rather than as failure. She left the reader with two questions worth sitting with: when your own dashboard shows a channel is "working," have you asked what accounting rule made it look that way; and if a channel disappeared tomorrow, how would you actually find out what you lost?

Attribution and Its Limits: The Diwali Budget Call at Sundara Beauty

A teaching case on marketing measurement and product analytics

1. The scene

On the morning of 16 September 2026, Ananya Rao stood in front of a whiteboard on the fourth floor of Sundara Beauty's office in Indiranagar, Bengaluru, looking at five bars of colour that did not agree with each other. In six days, on 22 September, the leadership committee would lock the marketing budget for the October festive quarter — Navratri, Dussehra and, above all, Dhanteras and Diwali, which together would carry close to forty percent of the brand's annual revenue. Ananya, Vice President of Growth and Analytics, had been asked to bring one number to that meeting: how much of the ₹22 crore festive budget should go to each channel. The trouble was that two perfectly reasonable ways of counting a sale gave two very different answers, and the chief financial officer had already told her which one he preferred.

2. Sundara Beauty

Sundara Beauty was founded in 2019 by two former Myntra category managers who believed Indian skincare needed fewer promises and more disclosed ingredient lists. The brand sold vitamin-C serums, rice-water shampoos and sunscreen sticks priced between ₹399 and ₹899, positioned against Mamaearth, Sugar Cosmetics, Plum, WOW Skin Science and Forest Essentials in the crowded "clean beauty" shelf. It sold directly through sundarabeauty.in and its app, through Nykaa and Amazon, and through fourteen exclusive outlets in Bengaluru, Mumbai, Delhi and Hyderabad. Revenue had grown from ₹18 crore in FY22 to ₹124 crore in FY26, most of it built on a formula common to Indian D2C beauty: seed a product with nano and micro-influencers on Instagram and YouTube, let it surface in Google searches for the brand name, and close the sale with retargeted Meta ads and coupon codes on affiliate sites such as CashKaro and coupon aggregators run through networks like vCommission. The formula had worked well enough that Sundara was now piloting exports to the UAE through a Dubai-based distributor, and testing paid acquisition in Singapore and the United States.

3. The situation

Every month, Rahul Nair, who ran performance marketing from Pune, pulled a report from Meta Ads Manager and Google Analytics 4 that used last-click attribution: whichever channel served the final ad or search result before a purchase got full credit for that sale. By that report, Meta Ads had driven 42% of tracked online revenue in FY26 and Google Search 33%, while affiliate sites earned 12%, influencer-linked traffic 8%, and organic search barely 5%. Karan Mehta, the CFO in Mumbai, read this as a simple story: Meta and Google were carrying the business, and the ₹3.9 crore spent on affiliates and influencers was money that could be redeployed into higher-converting channels. He had asked Ananya to bring a plan that shifted at least ₹1.5 crore of festive budget out of influencer and affiliate spend and into Meta and Google.

Ananya was not convinced the last-click number meant what Karan thought it meant. Priya Sundaram, Sundara's data scientist working out of Toronto, had spent August building a data-driven attribution model inside GA4 and, more persuasively, running a geo-holdout incrementality test around the Independence Day sale: influencer posting was paused in five cities while it continued as usual in five comparable cities, and the results, shown in Exhibit 3, suggested influencer content was doing real work that last-click never saw. In Berlin, Lukas Berger, the creative lead who commissioned the influencer content, argued that cutting the budget would starve the very touchpoint that introduced new customers to the brand in the first place. In Singapore, Mei Ling Tan, who ran customer growth for the Southeast Asia pilot, pointed out that in a market with no brand recognition, last-click on paid search was almost meaningless — someone had to plant the seed before anyone typed "Sundara Beauty" into Google. And Rashid Al Farsi, the Dubai distributor scaling Sundara into UAE malls and Noon.com, told Ananya on a call that in the Gulf, WhatsApp forwards and influencer reels, not search ads, were how his customers found the brand at all.

Exhibit 1 — Last-click credit versus data-driven attribution, FY26 online revenue

Meta Ads7.242%37.830%27.0

MTA = data-driven multi-touch attribution model built by Priya Sundaram inside GA4, distributing credit across every recorded touchpoint in a purchase path rather than only the last one. Both columns are re-splits of the same ₹90 crore of trackable online revenue. Figures rounded to one decimal.

Read as last-click, influencer marketing returned ₹4.00 for every rupee spent (₹7.2 crore ÷ ₹1.8 crore) — the weakest ROAS on the table, and the obvious channel to cut. Read as data-driven attribution, the same channel returned ₹9.00 for every rupee, second only to organic search. Meta's picture reversed just as sharply, from the best-looking channel under last-click to the weakest under MTA. Neither number was fabricated; both were legitimate readings of the same clickstream, built on different assumptions about which touchpoint deserved credit. Exhibit 2 shows why: a real purchase path recorded in Sundara's data warehouse for a customer named Divya in Chennai.

Exhibit 2 — One customer's path to purchase, and where last-click assigns credit
Illustrative path reconstructed from Sundara's app and web analytics for a single order. The pattern — discovery on an unpaid or influencer touchpoint, confirmation on branded search, close on a paid retargeting ad — recurred in a large share of orders Priya sampled for August 2026.

Priya's incrementality test, run over three weeks around the 15 August sale, was designed to settle the argument with evidence rather than a model's assumptions. She paused all influencer posting in five test cities — Pune, Jaipur, Lucknow, Kochi and Bhopal — while five comparable cities continued as usual as a control group.

Exhibit 3 — Geo-holdout incrementality test, 27 July–16 August 2026

Five test and five control cities matched on population, prior-year revenue and category penetration. Forecast built from the trailing twelve-month trend, seasonally adjusted. Branded search volume is Google Trends indexed to each city's own baseline.

When influencer content stopped, branded search for "Sundara Beauty" fell 18% and revenue came in 11% below forecast — a channel that had received only 8% of last-click credit, and looked like the cheapest one to cut, turned out to move a double-digit share of demand when it was actually switched off. It was the clearest evidence Ananya had that last-click was not just imprecise but systematically wrong about where credit belonged, and that every channel operating on last-click logic — including Meta and Google — was likely over-claiming sales that another touchpoint had already earned.

4. The people

Ananya Rao — VP Growth & Analytics, Bengaluru

Owns the recommendation to the leadership committee. Wants a budget the CFO will approve and the data will still support in January.

Karan Mehta — Chief Financial Officer, Mumbai

Wants festive spend concentrated in the channels with the clearest, most auditable ROAS. Distrusts models he cannot see inside.

Priya Sundaram — Data Scientist, Toronto

Wants Sundara to act on the incrementality test, not just the attribution model, and warns that MTA is still an estimate, not ground truth.

Rahul Nair — Performance Marketing Lead, Pune

Owns the Meta and Google accounts and the last-click dashboards leadership already trusts; worried that changing the measurement changes his targets mid-quarter.

Lukas Berger — Creative Lead, Berlin

Commissions the influencer content and wants festive-season budget protected for it, arguing the brand's discovery engine cannot be switched off during its biggest quarter.

5. The options

Option A — Trust last-click and reallocate as the CFO asked

Cut affiliate and influencer spend by ₹1.5 crore and move it into Meta and Google for the festive quarter. Simple to explain, easy to audit, and aligned with the numbers leadership already trusts. The cost: Exhibit 3 suggests this starves the touchpoint that seeds branded search, which could shrink the very channels being expanded, right as competitors run their own festive campaigns.

Option B — Switch fully to the data-driven attribution model

Adopt Priya's MTA weights as the new basis for budgeting: increase influencer to roughly ₹3.2 crore and affiliate to ₹2.7 crore for the quarter, trim Meta and Google accordingly. Better reflects the customer journey in Exhibit 2, but MTA is itself a statistical estimate built on modelling choices Karan cannot independently verify, and Rahul's team loses the last-click targets its incentives are built around mid-quarter.

Option C — Set guardrails from the incrementality test, keep last-click for daily optimisation

Use the Exhibit 3 test as ground truth to fix a floor under influencer and affiliate spend — no less than their current share — while leaving Rahul free to use last-click to tune day-to-day Meta and Google bids inside that floor. Slower to unwind the CFO's original instinct, and requires running further geo tests through the festive quarter to keep the floor honest, but commits no budget on either model's word alone.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. Why does last-click attribution systematically over-claim credit for Meta and Google, and under-claim it for influencer and organic search, given how Sundara's customers actually buy?
  2. What does the geo-holdout test in Exhibit 3 tell Ananya that the attribution models in Exhibit 1 cannot, and what can it not tell her?
  3. Whose incentives are shaped by which measurement — Rahul's, Karan's, Lukas's — and how should that shape how much weight each of their arguments gets?
  4. Which of the three options should Ananya bring to the 22 September meeting, and what would make her change it once October's data starts coming in?

7. A note for the learner

Attribution is the practice of assigning credit for a conversion across the touchpoints that preceded it, and every attribution model — last-click, first-click, linear, or a data-driven multi-touch model like Priya's — is an assumption about causality dressed up as a measurement. Last-click is popular because it is cheap to compute and hard to dispute, but Exhibit 2 shows exactly why it misleads: it rewards whichever channel happens to close the loop, regardless of what opened it. Multi-touch models are a real improvement because they use the whole path, but they remain correlational — they describe which touchpoints tend to appear before a sale, not which ones caused it. That is why incrementality testing matters: a geo-holdout, as Priya ran in Exhibit 3, is the closest thing marketing has to a controlled experiment, because it removes a channel entirely and observes what actually changes, rather than reading credit off a path that already happened. A well-reasoned answer to this case treats none of the three data sources as sufficient on its own, and Option C is the most defensible path for that reason: it uses the one causal evidence Sundara has — the incrementality test — to set a floor that protects the channels last-click was about to defund, without asking Karan to hand budget authority to a model he cannot audit, and without freezing Rahul out of the daily optimisation his last-click dashboards are genuinely good at. It buys Ananya six months to keep running geo tests, at modest cost, before she has to bet the whole festive budget on any single model's story about where a sale really came from.

Sundara Beauty is a fictional company created for classroom discussion. Any resemblance to a real company is coincidental. Brands, regulators and platforms named for market context are real and are not portrayed in any discreditable way.

Kasturi Health: The Engagement Number

A Dubai renewal worth ₹18 crore a year, four honest sources for one contractual metric, an analytics queue nobody can clear, and a strategy review at half past nine on Monday morning.

1. Sunday night, Lower Parel

At twenty past eleven on the night of Sunday, 13 September 2026, Nandita Rane sat at the dining table of her flat in Lower Parel with three laptops' worth of numbers open on one screen. Kasturi Health's quarterly strategy review began at 9:30 the next morning at the office on Senapati Bapat Marg. Item two on the agenda was headed “Care Plus engagement — renewal exposure and data plan.” Nandita, Senior Director of Product, owned both halves of that sentence and could not reconcile them.

The renewal in question was with Al Waseela Insurance Services, a Dubai group-health insurer that had put 28,400 of its corporate covered lives onto Kasturi's chronic-care programme. Al Waseela paid ₹640 per engaged managed member per month. In the year to August 2026 that had come to ₹17.9 crore, a little over nineteen percent of Kasturi's revenue and rather more of its gross margin. The contract's Annexure C defined an engaged member as one who completed “at least two care interactions in a calendar month.” Al Waseela's renewal committee would decide on 31 October. Its head of provider networks had, in August, asked a question Kasturi had not answered: what, precisely, counted as a care interaction, and could Kasturi show that the definition had not changed since the contract was signed?

Nandita had four numbers for August engagement. The product dashboard said 71.2 percent. The data science team's reviewed query said 63.8. Dr Preeti Sundaram's clinical team, working from pharmacy refills and repeat lab tests, said something that did not look like engagement at all: 41 percent of the same population appeared to be following their care plan, and that figure had been drifting down since March. And the number Jaideep Sahni had already quoted to Al Waseela in a June call, taken from a self-serve query he had run himself, was 74 percent. Nobody had lied. She had until the morning to decide what she would say, and rather longer to decide what Kasturi should actually do.

2. The company, and a decision made in January 2023

Kasturi Health had been founded in Mumbai in 2019 as a home-sample-collection business — phlebotomists on two-wheelers, a network of accredited partner laboratories, results in an app. It grew through the pandemic years on the back of home testing, then did what most of its peers did: moved from one-off transactions towards subscriptions, launching Kasturi Care Plus in August 2024, a chronic-care programme for diabetes and hypertension combining quarterly panels, a coach, teleconsultations and medicine reminders. By 2026 it had about 11 lakh registered users, 1.4 lakh paying Care Plus members in India, and the Gulf book with Al Waseela.

One earlier decision shaped everything Nandita could do now. In January 2023, facing a cash-preservation quarter, the leadership team had chosen not to buy a cloud data warehouse and build a governed semantic layer over it. The estimate then had been ₹3.2 crore a year in licences and two additional hires. Instead, Vikram Ghatge's engineering team had extended the existing product event pipeline and built dashboards directly on a read replica of the application database. Clinical and laboratory data stayed where regulation and habit had put it, in the partner-lab information systems and Kasturi's own clinical record, and was joined to product data by a weekly batch process keyed on mobile number, with ABHA identifiers used where members had linked them. The decision was sensible at the time and saved real money. Its consequence, three years later, was that Kasturi had two truths — what a member did in the app and what happened to that member's body — that could only be brought together once a week, imperfectly, by a join that nobody owned.

3. The industry

Kasturi competed on two fronts that shared almost nothing. In Indian diagnostics it faced Dr Lal PathLabs, Metropolis, Thyrocare and Redcliffe Labs on price and turnaround, and Tata 1mg, Apollo 24|7 and PharmEasy on digital reach; its partner laboratories were NABL-accredited and its collection network priced against a market where a lipid panel could be had for a few hundred rupees. In chronic care it was closer to the employer-wellness businesses that insurers and brokers had been buying, where the product was not a test but a behaviour change, and the buyer was a corporate HR head or an insurer's network team rather than a patient.

The Gulf book mattered out of proportion to its size. Indian diagnostics was a volume business with thin margins and a price war that Reliance Retail's and Tata's entries into adjacent consumer health had not made gentler; the Al Waseela contract, by contrast, was recurring, prepaid quarterly, and denominated in a currency that moved in Kasturi's favour. It had also become the reference the company showed to every other Gulf insurer and to the two US brokers Jaideep was courting from New Jersey. A renewal at reduced scope would be survivable financially and difficult reputationally, which was precisely why the question of what the engagement number meant had never been asked out loud in a room containing both Jaideep and Aravind.

Regulation cut across both. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act's purpose-limitation rules meant that health data collected for diagnostic reporting could not simply be copied into a product analytics store for engagement measurement without fresh, specific consent — a constraint Kasturi's legal counsel had raised twice and which had, in practice, slowed every proposal to unify the two data estates. The Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission's ABHA identifier offered a clean join key, but only 31 percent of Kasturi's members had linked one. On the Gulf side, Al Waseela was regulated in the UAE, its corporate clients spread across Dubai and Sharjah, and its members carried international mobile numbers that Kasturi's India-shaped identity matching had never been designed for.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

The Al Waseela relationship began as a 4,000-life pilot in March 2025 and converted to a full contract in November 2025. Annexure C had been drafted by Jaideep Sahni's team in New Jersey in the last fortnight of negotiation; the operative sentence defining a “care interaction” — “a coaching session, a vitals submission, or a teleconsultation logged in the Kasturi application” — had been lifted, near verbatim, from a Slack message Ananya Kshirsagar had written in Pune in answer to a question about how the product dashboard worked. Ananya had not known it would be pasted into a contract. Nobody had asked Aravind Chidambaram, who ran data science from Toronto, to review it.

In February 2026, Lukas Brenner in Berlin shipped an onboarding and home-screen redesign. It moved vitals entry into a persistent card and added a gentle nudge that pre-filled the member's last reading. Engagement, as the product dashboard measured it, rose by nine points over six weeks. The team celebrated. In July, preparing a routine reconciliation, Ananya found two things: the redesign's pre-fill wrote a vitals event even when the member dismissed the card without confirming, and, separately, a client-side retry defect on Android 11 and below had double-logged submissions between 24 February and 30 March. She flagged both in a ticket. The ticket sat in the queue for five weeks.

Meanwhile, in April, Aravind's team had rolled out PoochhO, an internal natural-language query assistant built over the read replica, explicitly to relieve a queue that had reached a median cycle time of nineteen days. Usage was enthusiastic. In June, Jaideep used it to answer Al Waseela's head of provider networks on a call, quoting 74 percent engagement for the Gulf cohort. In August, Dr Preeti Sundaram's clinical team published its first quarterly outcomes review, built from pharmacy refill records and repeat HbA1c tests, and it showed adherence flat to falling since March in exactly the period when app engagement had risen. Dr Preeti's note, circulated on 29 August, used the phrase “a measurement artefact or a clinical failure; we cannot currently tell which.”

Two further facts emerged only in the first week of September. The first was that the Gulf-cohort flag in the product database was written at enrolment and never refreshed, so members who had left a covered employer remained in both the numerator and the denominator until an annual reconciliation removed them — which was the gap Farida Shaikh had been closing by hand since April. The second was that the reviewed query Aravind's team had recomputed in August excluded pre-fill events but had not excluded the February–March duplicate window, because Ananya's ticket was still open. The reviewed series, in other words, was neither the old number nor a corrected one. Nandita learned this on the Friday afternoon before the review, from a footnote.

5. The people

Nandita Rane, Senior Director of Product, Mumbai. Owns Care Plus and, nominally, the metric. Wants a number she can defend to Al Waseela's auditors and to her own board. Not saying: she approved the February redesign's specification without asking what it did to event logging, and she knows it.

Dr Preeti Sundaram, Chief Medical Officer, Chennai. Argues that engagement measured in taps is not care, and that the contract should be keyed to clinical outcomes. Incentive: a paper with a Chennai teaching hospital on chronic-care outcomes, and the January 2027 NABL audit. Not saying: her outcomes review is built on a hand-maintained spreadsheet that one registrar updates, and its Gulf coverage is thin.

Aravind Chidambaram, Head of Data Science, Toronto. Wants an eight-week freeze on ad-hoc requests to build a certified metric layer and a definitions catalogue. Incentive: a team he can retain and a platform he can defend. Not saying: he is two hires short of his approved plan, and Ananya has an offer from a Bengaluru firm at roughly forty percent more.

Ananya Kshirsagar, Lead Analyst, Pune. Does most of the actual pulls, maintains an undocumented library of queries, and has quietly become the arbiter of what PoochhO answers are trustworthy. Not saying: she is the single point of failure, she is tired, and the definition in Annexure C came from her Slack message.

Jaideep “JD” Sahni, VP Enterprise Sales, New Jersey. Covers the Gulf and a nascent US pilot. Position: the engagement question is an internal hygiene matter that must not be allowed to destabilise a renewal. Incentive: 38 percent of his variable compensation rides on the Al Waseela renewal. Not saying: he has already put 74 percent in front of the client, in writing, in a June follow-up email.

Farida Shaikh, Customer Success Lead, Singapore. Sends Al Waseela its monthly engagement report. Position: whatever number is chosen, she needs one number, on the fifth working day, every month. Not saying: since April she has been manually adjusting the report to remove members she knows have left their employer, because the automated feed does not.

Lukas Brenner, Product Designer, Berlin. Position: the redesign worked; members do submit more vitals. Not saying: his design document contained a line noting that the pre-fill would fire the existing event, and nobody commented on it.

Vikram Ghatge, VP Engineering, Bengaluru. Position: the tracking plan is product's responsibility, engineering ships what the spec says. Incentive: his team's delivery commitments for the festive-quarter release. Not saying: the Android retry defect was known internally in March as a crash-rate fix and its data consequence was never traced.

7. Voices

“We are not going to reopen a contractual definition eight weeks before a renewal committee meets. If we tell them the number moved because of a button, they will read it as Kasturi cannot count. That is not a data conversation, that is a trust conversation, and I am the one in the room for it.”

“Forty-one percent of a population we can only see half of is not a finding. I have said this to Preeti's team twice. If we put that number next to the dashboard number in a board pack, we are inviting a comparison that neither series can support.”

By Sunday evening Nandita had written four options on a page, and she was uneasy that all four were about tools and headcount.

A. Freeze and build. Grant Aravind his eight-week freeze on ad-hoc requests, stand up a certified dataset and a definitions catalogue for the twenty metrics that appear in contracts and board packs, and restate the Al Waseela series once. Cost about ₹1.1 crore and three roadmap items, including the festive-quarter medicine-reminder release.

B. Embed. Hire three analysts and place one inside each product pod, so that definitions are argued where decisions are made. Cost ₹1.9 crore annually and a breach of the net-adds cap; also slow, since the first hire would not be productive before December.

C. Harden self-serve. Restrict PoochhO to a small set of certified tables, add a mandatory provenance footer to every answer, and publish a short list of numbers that may be quoted externally. Cost about ₹40 lakh and no headcount, but it leaves the definitional question exactly where it is.

D. Renegotiate the metric. Go to Al Waseela before the renewal committee, propose replacing the interaction count with a clinically-sourced measure, and accept a lower headline number in exchange for a definition that survives audit. Dr Preeti's preferred path; Exhibit 5 suggests Kasturi cannot currently compute it for more than half the Gulf cohort.

What none of the four options addressed was that Annexure C's definition had entered a contract from a Slack message, that no person's name was attached to the phrase “care interaction” anywhere in the company, and that Farida had been silently correcting the monthly file since April.

9. The deadline and the constraints

The strategy review was at 9:30 on Monday. Al Waseela's renewal committee met on 31 October, and its contract gave the client the right to audit Kasturi's engagement methodology on thirty days' notice — a clause never invoked, and now thirty days from being invokable before the committee met. Kasturi had ₹2.4 crore uncommitted in the second half and a board-imposed cap of four net technology hires. The DPDP Act's purpose-limitation position, as Kasturi's counsel read it, meant that unifying clinical and product data for engagement measurement required a consent flow that did not yet exist and would take a quarter to build and roll out. The NABL audit of the partner network was scheduled for January 2027. Ananya's offer letter expired on 30 September. Roshni Mehra, the CFO, had asked Nandita one question on Friday: if the reviewed number is right, have we been over-billing a client for seven months, and does the answer change what we are legally obliged to do next week?

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What exactly is Kasturi measuring in each of Exhibits 2, 3, 4 and 5, and which of those measurements would you be willing to put in front of Al Waseela's auditor?
  2. Exhibit 6 is cited internally as evidence that self-serve analytics worked. What would you need to know before accepting that reading?
  3. Whose fault is the February divergence — and is “fault” the right frame for deciding what Kasturi changes?
  4. Dr Preeti and Aravind both believe they are defending rigour. What is each of them actually optimising for, and where do their interests diverge from Kasturi's?
  5. If Nandita adopts Option A, what does Farida send Al Waseela on the fifth working day of October, and what does Jaideep tell the client about the June email?
  6. What should Nandita do on Monday morning, in what order, and what precisely would she say to the board about the seven months already billed?

At ten past midnight she closed the laptops. The four numbers were still four numbers. On the legal pad beside her she had written, and then circled, a question she did not yet know how to ask in a room: who decided what a care interaction is? She could not find anyone to ask it of. In nine hours she would have to open with something.

Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation · Product Analytics & Data Practice

Working with Analysts and Data Scientists

How a product manager learns to ask good questions, share ownership of definitions, and respect the queue — instead of fighting over whose number is right.

1. A Tuesday in Koramangala, a number nobody can agree on

On the second Tuesday of March, Meera Iyer, the product lead for the tenant-search flow at Basera, a home-rental marketplace, opened a board deck template with one slide left to fill: "Quality of leads, last quarter." She had eleven days before the board met, and the number she needed — the share of tenant enquiries that led to a landlord actually calling back within 48 hours — existed nowhere as a single, agreed figure. Her own spreadsheet, built from a CSV a data analyst had emailed her six weeks earlier, said 34 percent. The company's central dashboard, maintained by the analytics team and last touched by a data scientist named Arjun Rao, said 46 percent. Both numbers were computed correctly, in the narrow sense that no formula contained an error. They answered two different, unstated questions.

Meera's version counted a callback as a "qualified lead" only if the tenant had also viewed at least two additional listings after the enquiry, a proxy for genuine intent she had asked for informally, in a Slack message, four months earlier. Arjun's dashboard counted any enquiry with a logged call event, full stop, because that was the definition on file when the dashboard was built two years prior, before Meera joined. Neither of them had noticed the drift until a board member cross-checked the two documents Meera had sent in successive quarters. The stakes were not abstract: the board was deciding whether to fund a second city launch on the strength of lead quality, and a 12-point gap on that one line item was large enough to change the recommendation. Meera's task, with eleven days on the clock, was not to compute a better number. It was to get Arjun and his queue of nine other open requests to agree with her, in writing, on what the number meant.

2. The idea: a metric is not real until it is written down and owned by both sides

The practice this topic teaches has no single inventor, but it has a lineage. Statistical quality control pioneers such as Walter Shewhart, writing at Bell Labs in the 1930s, insisted on the "operational definition" — a definition precise enough that two different people, given the same raw material, would produce the same measurement. Sixty years later, as software companies built dedicated data science functions in the early 2010s (the Harvard Business Review essay that called data scientist "the sexiest job of the 21st century" appeared in 2012), the same problem resurfaced inside dashboards: a "monthly active user" or a "qualified lead" meant something different in every spreadsheet that used the phrase. The analytics-engineering movement that followed, associated with writers such as Benn Stancil and tools such as dbt from roughly 2016 onward, formalized a response: definitions belong in a shared, versioned "semantic layer," not in any one person's head or personal file.

Stripped of jargon, the idea is this: a request for data is not a query, and a query is not a metric. A metric is a named, documented agreement — population, time window, denominator, and the event that counts as the numerator — that both the person asking and the person answering have signed off on, and that persists after the conversation that created it ends. The single sentence Meera could say in the boardroom without sounding glib is: "A number only means one thing once someone has written down, and both sides have agreed, exactly what counts."

A number only means one thing once someone has written down, and both sides have agreed, exactly what counts.

3. How it actually works: from vague question to shared metric

The mechanics practitioners usually leave implicit have five steps, and skipping any one of them is where Meera and Arjun went wrong. First, the requester translates a business question ("are our leads good?") into an analytical question with a named population, a time window, and a candidate definition of success — not "pull lead quality" but "of enquiries submitted in a given ISO week, what share had a landlord call logged within 48 hours, and separately, within 48 hours and a second listing view." Second, that translation is written down in a short brief, not spoken in a hallway or typed into a Slack DM that scrolls away. Third, the brief enters a shared queue with the rest of the analytics team's work, visible to both sides, so that "urgent" is a claim the requester has to justify against everything else already waiting, not a private escalation. Fourth, the analyst or data scientist runs the query, but critically also runs a sanity check — row counts, a manual spot-check of five or six individual records, a comparison against last quarter's number for continuity — before handing back a result. Fifth, and this is the step almost everyone skips, the agreed definition is written into a durable, versioned place: a wiki page, a dbt model description, a metrics catalog entry, dated and attributed, so the next person who asks the same question in six months inherits the agreement instead of re-litigating it.

Basera had steps one and four. It had no brief, no shared queue, and critically no durable record of the definition, which is exactly how two correct numbers, six months apart, ended up eleven points apart on paper.

Figure 1. The five steps between a vague question and a number the whole company can reuse. Basera had the first and the fourth; skipping the written brief and the durable record is what let two correct numbers disagree by eleven points.

4. A worked example: why the window you choose moves the number

Suppose the cohort in question is the 10,000 tenants who submitted their first enquiry in the week of 3 March. Arjun's dashboard defines a "call-back" as any logged call event within a stated window of the enquiry. The width of that window, on its own, changes the answer substantially, which is precisely why it must be agreed rather than assumed.

Definition of the windowEnquiries with a logged call-backRate
Exactly on day 2 (48 hours, narrowly)2,150 of 10,00021.5%
Within a ±3-day window (days 0–5)2,780 of 10,00027.8%
Within a ±7-day window (days 0–9)3,190 of 10,00031.9%

Each rate is arithmetically simple — divide the count by 10,000 and read off the percentage — and each one is a legitimate way to define "responsive." The trouble is that the difference between 21.5 percent and 31.9 percent, a spread of over ten points on the same cohort, is bigger than most quarter-over-quarter changes a board will ever see. If Meera's brief says "call-back within 48 hours" and Arjun's dashboard was quietly extended to a nine-day window eighteen months ago to smooth out weekend effects, both of them can be telling the truth about a computation and still be reporting materially different realities. The second pass matters as much as the first: before accepting any number, the responsible move is to ask what happens to it if the window, the population, or the denominator changes by a small, reasonable amount, and to be suspicious of a number that turns out to be fragile.

Figure 2. Same 10,000-tenant cohort, same underlying data — three defensible window widths produce a ten-point spread in the headline rate.

5. The nuances a learner must sit with

A request is not yet a question

"Are our leads good?" cannot be queried; it has no population, no window, and no threshold for "good." Translating it is the product manager's job, not the analyst's, because only the requester knows what decision the number will feed. Handing over an untranslated question and expecting the analyst to guess is the single most common source of disagreement.

Ownership of a definition is joint, not unilateral

Once Meera's informal Slack request became her personal definition and Arjun's dashboard definition diverged from it silently, neither side owned the number; each owned a private version. Shared ownership means both names are on the definition, and neither can change it without telling the other.

The queue is a shared, finite resource

Arjun had nine other requests open the week Meera needed her number. A queue made visible — tickets with priority levels everyone can see — lets "this is urgent" be judged against real alternatives, rather than being a private plea that quietly displaces someone else's equally urgent work.

A pulled number answers what happened, not why

Arjun can tell Meera precisely how many enquiries got a call-back. He cannot tell her, from that query alone, whether a redesigned enquiry form caused the change, without a designed comparison — which is a different kind of request, usually an experiment, not a pull.

An ad hoc pull decays; a documented metric persists

The CSV Arjun emailed Meera in November had no home once the conversation around it ended. A metric added to the semantic layer, with a name, an owner, and a change log, survives staff turnover and answers the same question the same way a year later.

Definitions need version history, like code

When the call-back window was extended from two days to nine, nobody recorded when or why. A metric catalog entry with dates lets anyone see that a comparison across quarters straddling that change is not a like-for-like comparison.

Literacy is not the same as expertise

Meera does not need to write the SQL herself, but knowing enough of it — joins, group-by, the idea of a denominator — lets her ask a well-formed question and read a query plan skeptically, rather than either deferring blindly or second-guessing every result.

Bad instrumentation is a shared failure

If the "second listing view" event Meera wanted was never logged cleanly, that is a specification gap from product and engineering, not an analytics failure; blaming the analyst for a hole in the tracking plan misdiagnoses the problem and guarantees it recurs.

6. Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and early-stage versus scaled

In a high-volume consumer product, the population is usually large enough that statistical noise is the main hazard, and analysts push back on requests to slice a metric into segments so small that the "signal" is really sampling error; a marketplace like Basera adds the complication that every metric must specify which side it describes — a "qualified lead" is a tenant-side concept, and a parallel, distinct definition is needed for landlord-side responsiveness, with a third, genuinely two-sided metric such as liquidity (the share of listings that get a completed booking) sitting above both. B2B products invert the volume problem: with a few hundred accounts rather than millions of users, an analyst is often manually joining product-usage logs to a CRM record for a named enterprise customer, and one misclassified account can move a metric by a full percentage point, so requests need more, not less, of the population-definition discipline described above. Company stage matters as much as product type: at a ten-person startup, the product manager frequently writes the SQL directly because there is no dedicated analyst yet, and the discipline is mostly self-imposed; at a company Basera's scale, with a queue, a semantic layer, and a data science function with its own roadmap, the discipline has to be organizational, because informal habits that worked for one PM and one friendly analyst do not survive contact with nine competing requesters.

7. Common mistakes

The "can you just pull this real quick" request. The symptom is a Slack channel full of one-off asks that never appear in any planning document; the underlying misunderstanding is treating a query as free and instantaneous rather than as work that displaces other work; the cheapest diagnostic is simply counting, for one week, how many data requests never touched the ticket queue at all.

Silent redefinition. The symptom is two dashboards, or two people's slide decks, disagreeing on the same-named metric; the underlying misunderstanding is that a definition, once given informally, is stable and universally known; the cheapest diagnostic is to search the company wiki or metrics catalog for how many separate, undated descriptions of "active user" or "qualified lead" already exist.

Treating one query result as ground truth. The symptom is a number restated, embarrassingly, after it has already gone to a board or an investor; the underlying misunderstanding is that correct SQL syntax guarantees a correct answer; the cheapest diagnostic is asking to see the join conditions and a handful of the underlying rows before repeating the number publicly.

Crying wolf on urgency. The symptom is that analysts stop reacting to the word "urgent" at all; the underlying misunderstanding is that urgency is a personal claim rather than a comparison against everything else in the queue; the cheapest diagnostic is tracking what fraction of a requester's tickets are marked urgent over a quarter.

8. What good looks like

Six weeks after the board meeting, Meera and Arjun built a one-page "analysis brief" template together: population, time window, numerator event, denominator, and a named owner on each side. Every request, including Meera's, went into the same queue Arjun's whole team used, visible to the other product managers who competed for his time. When they agreed that "qualified lead" would mean a call-back within a 5-day window plus a second listing view, they wrote it into the metrics catalog with the date and both their names, and the old, undocumented nine-day version was marked deprecated rather than silently abandoned. The following quarter, when a new product manager on the payments team asked an almost identical question about a different funnel, she found the brief template and the catalog entry already there, and needed twenty minutes with Arjun instead of six weeks of quiet drift.

9. What Meera decided, and two questions to sit with

Meera did not pick her number or Arjun's. With four days left, they agreed jointly on the 5-day window plus the second-view condition as the canonical definition of "qualified lead," documented it, and told the board directly that the prior quarter's figures used a narrower, informal definition and were not directly comparable — a harder conversation than presenting a clean trend line, but a defensible one. The natural next thing for Meera to learn is enough of cohort and retention analysis, and enough of how a properly randomized experiment isolates cause from mere correlation, to know when a pulled number is sufficient and when it is not. Two questions worth sitting with: when a metric turns out to have been wrong for two quarters, whose name should be attached to the correction, the requester's or the analyst's, and does your answer change how carefully you would specify the request next time? And how would you design a queue that protects an analyst's focus time from constant interruption without slowing down every product decision that genuinely cannot wait?

Working with Analysts and Data Scientists

A near-expert treatment: the intellectual history of the shared definition, the queueing mathematics of the analytics backlog, the schools of thought that genuinely disagree, and the eight or nine judgements that separate a product manager who has studied this from one who has lived it.

1. Two decisions, two Fridays, one underlying problem

On Friday 7 February, on Baner Road in Pune, Devika Nambiar, Director of Product at Sangati Systems, was asked to stop a renewal from slipping. Sangati sold subscription-billing software to about 340 mid-market Indian companies. The renewal was worth ₹2.4 crore a year, and the customer's finance head had said on a call that the product “did not get used.” Devika's dashboard disagreed: it showed that customer at 71 percent weekly active seats. Farhan Qureshi, the analyst assigned to her pod, found that 71 percent of provisioned seats had logged in, but that four of the customer's five finance users had done nothing except open a scheduled report email. The active-seat definition, written in 2022 when Sangati sold mostly to twenty-person startups, counted an authenticated session as use. For a 900-person company with single sign-on and automated report delivery, an authenticated session meant almost nothing. Devika had six working days. What she needed was not a better dashboard but a written agreement about what “use” meant in an account where the software could log a session without a human reading a screen.

Eleven hundred kilometres away, on the same Friday, Sneha Kulkarni had a different problem. She was head of product at Manjari, a consumer app teaching spoken English and three Indian languages through short speech-recognition drills, with 9.4 million monthly users, most on low-end Android handsets in tier-two cities. Her growth team wanted to ship a redesigned first session before the exam-coaching season. Ritwik Basu, Manjari's staff data scientist, had refused to sign off. The reason was not the effect size; it was that the north-star metric, “learners who complete a speaking drill in week one,” fired its completion event when the audio upload finished rather than when the scoring returned. On the 2G-fallback path used by roughly 18 percent of the base, the upload finished and the scoring frequently did not. For a fifth of the population the metric was measuring bandwidth. Sneha's choice was to ship on a metric she knew was biased, fix the instrumentation and lose six weeks of the season, or find something defensible in between.

Neither problem is an analytics problem in the narrow sense. Both concern a working relationship: what a product manager asks for, how the asking is recorded, who owns the answer afterwards, and what happens to everyone else's questions meanwhile. The two competent practitioners in each story were, in fact, both right.

2. The idea, its history, and the schools that disagree about it

Start with a precise definition. A metric, in the sense that matters here, is a four-part agreement: a population (whose behaviour is counted), a window (over what period), a numerator event (what counts as the thing happening), and an ownership record (who agreed, when, and where a future reader can find it). Remove any one part and you have a query result, which is a fact about a particular execution of particular SQL at a particular moment, not a metric. The distinction sounds pedantic until two query results with the same name reach the same board slide.

The lineage is older than software. Walter Shewhart at Bell Labs in the 1930s, and later W. Edwards Deming, pressed the idea of the operational definition: a definition is adequate only if two competent people, given the same raw material and the definition, produce the same measurement. Deming's example was “clean” — a word that means nothing until you specify the test. Charles Goodhart's 1975 observation, and Donald Campbell's parallel formulation, added the second half: once a measure becomes a target, the behaviour it measures deforms around it. The first idea says a number is meaningless without a written test; the second says a written test attracts gaming, so the writing has to be revisited.

The software history begins with the warehouse arguments of the 1990s — Ralph Kimball's dimensional modelling against Bill Inmon's normalised warehouse — which were, underneath, an argument about who may define a business term. The 2010s added a data-science profession and a characteristic pathology: “active user” instantiated forty times in forty notebooks. The response was the semantic layer — LookML at Looker, Minerva at Airbnb, uMetric at Uber, and the analytics-engineering movement around dbt from roughly 2016 — in which definitions live in versioned code and are the only sanctioned path to a number. Against that, from about 2019, Zhamak Dehghani's data-mesh argument held that central teams become bottlenecks and that domain teams should own and publish their own data products under federated governance. Since 2023, natural-language query tools have made the bottleneck argument sharper and the governance argument more urgent at once, because a confident wrong answer now arrives in three seconds instead of three days.

Three schools, stated as propositions each would actually sign:

SchoolWould signWould not sign
Governance-first (semantic layer, central definitions)“No metric appears in an external document unless it has a versioned definition and a named owner.”“Product managers should be free to publish numbers from their own queries.”
Embedded decision science (analysts inside product pods)“An analyst's output is a changed decision, not an answered question; embed them and judge them on decisions.”“A central data team should arbitrate what a business term means for a domain it does not work in.”
Self-serve / domain ownership (mesh, text-to-SQL, federated)“The queue is the disease; give domains the tools and the accountability and delete the intake form.”“One catalogue, maintained centrally, can serve every domain at acceptable latency.”

These are not points on a spectrum with a sensible midpoint; they disagree about where competence lives. Most large companies run a hybrid and describe it as a choice. It is usually a truce.

3. Mechanics in depth, including the arithmetic nobody writes down

The visible mechanics — brief, queue, query, sanity check, catalogue entry — are easy to recite. The expert work sits in three places the recitation skips: reconciling two numbers additively, treating the queue as a physical system with a nonlinear response, and knowing what measurement noise does to every experiment later run on the metric.

Reconciling by decomposition, not by argument

When Devika's dashboard said 71 percent and Farhan's review said much lower, the unproductive move is to ask whose number is right. The productive move is to walk the definitions from one to the other in ordered steps, attributing the gap to each change, so the disagreement becomes a list rather than a verdict. Sangati's customer had 900 employees, 148 of them with provisioned seats.

Step (applied in order)NumeratorDenominatorRateDelta
Dashboard as built: any authenticated session / provisioned seats10514870.9%—
Exclude sessions opened only by the report-email deep link7114848.0%−22.9 pts
Require at least one screen interaction, not just a page load5214835.1%−12.9 pts
Require an action that writes data (edit, approve, export)2914819.6%−15.5 pts
Restrict denominator to seats billed as “full” (exclude 41 viewer seats)2910727.1%+7.5 pts

Each row changes exactly one clause. The last step moves the rate up while tightening the definition, because it narrows the denominator; a decomposition that mixes numerator and denominator changes in one step hides this, and that is where most reconciliations go wrong.

The queue is a physical system

Product managers treat analyst capacity as a scheduling problem — five days of work, five days before the deadline, it fits. It does not, because arrivals are random and service times variable. Treat the team as a single server receiving requests at rate λ and completing them at rate μ, with utilisation ρ = λ/μ. Expected time in the system is W = 1/(μ − λ), which behaves violently as ρ approaches one. Ritwik's four-person team at Manjari closed about twenty substantive requests a week.
