180.902.50 weeks+0.83 weeks
190.955.00 weeks+3.33 weeks

Service rate μ = 20/week. Turnaround W = 1/(μ−λ). The final column is the marginal delay your “quick pull” imposes on everyone else, which is the number a requester should be shown and almost never is.

Two second-order effects follow. First, the right response to a chronically slow queue is often to reduce arrivals rather than add servers, because arrivals are elastic: when turnaround is three weeks, people ask for everything at once as insurance, raising λ further. Second, reserving 15 to 20 percent of analyst time as unallocated is not slack; it is the purchase of a fast lane, and it is cheaper than the hiring a 95-percent-utilised team will eventually demand.

What measurement noise does to the next experiment

A definition is not only a reporting object; it is the outcome variable of every future test. For a two-arm test on a proportion, required sample size per arm scales as n ≈ 16p(1−p)/δ² for 80 percent power at the conventional threshold. Manjari's drill-completion metric, as instrumented, misclassified some share of the 2G-path population. Misclassification that is independent of the treatment does not usually bias the direction of an effect, but it dilutes it: if a fraction m of events are misclassified symmetrically, the observed lift shrinks roughly by a factor (1 − 2m), and required sample grows by 1/(1−2m)².

Misclassification rate mObserved lift on a true 3.0 pt effectRequired n per armWeeks at 120k/arm/week
0% (clean instrumentation)3.00 ptsapprox. 178,0001.5
5%2.70 ptsapprox. 220,0001.8
12%2.28 ptsapprox. 308,0002.6
18% (Manjari's 2G path, if wholly affected)1.92 ptsapprox. 435,0003.6

Baseline p = 0.40. The shape matters more than the arithmetic: bad instrumentation is not a reporting inconvenience but a tax on every future decision, levied in weeks of calendar time. This is the argument that persuades a growth team to pay for a fix.

The harder effect is that misclassification is rarely symmetric. At Manjari it correlated with network quality, which correlates with device tier, which correlates with the segment the redesign targeted. When error correlates with the treatment's target population, dilution becomes bias and the sign of the estimate is no longer safe.

4. When the discipline applies, and when it misleads

State the conditions as claims that can be tested against a specific situation rather than as maxims.

Claim one: the number will be quoted by someone who was not in the room. If so, the definition must be durable and written. Sangati's renewal number would be read aloud by an account executive to a customer's CFO — durability required. Manjari's readout would be seen only by the growth pod for one week before being superseded — durability optional, correctness not.

Claim two: the decision flips within the plausible definitional range. Run the ladder. At Sangati, the renewal argument flips between 70.9 and 27.1 percent; the definitional work is the decision. At Manjari, if the redesign wins under every reasonable completion definition, the instrumentation debate can be deferred and the ship decision made now — and an expert says so out loud rather than performing rigour.

Claim three: the same question will recur. Recurring questions deserve catalogue entries; genuinely one-off questions deserve a fast, cheap, explicitly disposable answer. Treating every ad-hoc question as a semantic-layer candidate is how governance programmes die of their own weight.

Claim four: instrumentation error is uncorrelated with what you are changing. If it is correlated, as at Manjari, no definitional agreement fixes it; the fix is in the event pipeline, and the honest statement is that the metric cannot arbitrate this question at all.

The discipline is actively misleading in three situations. In an outage, insisting on definitional process before looking at raw logs costs revenue by the minute. In early discovery, where the signal is that eleven of fourteen interviewed users could not find a button, converting the observation into a metric destroys the information it carried. And in an unfamiliar market a carefully governed metric inherited from the home market can be precisely wrong: Manjari's engagement definitions, tuned on urban users with home wi-fi, were a poor instrument for a Bhojpuri-speaking user on an intermittent connection, however well documented.

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

In multi-product companies, the seam is the shared user: “active customer” must specify at what grain identity is resolved, and identity resolution is owned by neither product team. The mature answer is a single identity service with a published match rate; the common actual answer is three join keys and a quarterly argument. In two-sided marketplaces a metric is meaningless without a side, and the genuinely two-sided metric — liquidity, match rate, time to fill — belongs to neither side's product manager, which is why it decays fastest.

Regulated products introduce a competing definitional authority. A lending product's “delinquency,” a broking product's “active client,” a health product's “adherence” already have regulatory or clinical definitions the company does not control, and the failure mode is a product metric that quietly diverges from the reported one until an auditor notices. Under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, purpose limitation adds a wrinkle: a definition requiring a join across datasets collected for different stated purposes may be undefinable in practice though trivial in SQL.

Hardware-plus-software breaks the assumption that absence of an event means absence of behaviour. A connected device silent for six days may be unused, unpowered, out of coverage or bricked, and the four cases have opposite commercial meanings. Expert practice adds a heartbeat channel so that silence is itself measured.

AI-native products break something deeper. When output is probabilistic, “success” is a judgement rather than an event, and the population of judgements is itself a dataset with its own definitional questions: who labelled, against what rubric, with what agreement rate. At Manjari, scoring a drill as “correct” involved a model threshold the machine-learning team retuned twice in a quarter, and each retune silently redefined the north-star metric. The seam is severe: the model team's objective function and the product team's metric are the same number, owned by different people, changed on different cadences, almost never versioned together. Mature companies pin a frozen evaluation set and report the metric on both the current and the previous threshold for a quarter after any change. What most companies actually do is discover the shift six weeks later in a cohort chart nobody can explain.

6. The judgements that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Translation is the requester's job, and delegating it is a status move disguised as trust. The tell is a ticket reading “can you look into retention for the new flow?” The analyst must now invent a population, a window and a success event, and will do so plausibly and invisibly. The obvious reading — that a vague brief gives creative latitude — is wrong, because the analyst is not free to know what decision the number feeds.

The right first question is what will change, not what to measure. Experts open with “if the number comes back at 20 percent, what do we do; and at 40?” The tell is a requester who cannot answer for either value, meaning the number is decorative and should be declined. Declining looks uncooperative, and it is the highest-leverage thing a PM can do for an over-subscribed team.

Speed of disagreement matters more than accuracy of the first number. An expert prefers a rough number in two hours with a stated error bar to a precise one in nine days, because the rough number surfaces the definitional argument while there is time to resolve it. The competent-but-not-expert practitioner waits for the “proper” analysis and discovers on the deadline that it answered a different question.

A catalogue entry is a liability as well as an asset. Every documented metric must be maintained, and an abandoned catalogue is worse than none because it lends false authority. Experts keep the catalogue small — a few dozen entries, each with an owner who would be embarrassed if it were wrong — and delete freely. The tell is a catalogue with 400 entries and no deletions in a year.

Analysts have a roadmap, and it is mostly invisible. Pipeline reliability, backfills and data-quality monitors are the work that makes the next hundred answers cheap, and ad-hoc requests displace it first because it has no complaining customer. The tell is an analytics team whose velocity has been flat for a year while headcount doubled: the new capacity went to interruptions, and the platform debt compounded.

Escalation is a currency with a fixed supply. When everything is urgent, nothing can be expedited, including the thing that genuinely matters. Experts spend the word two or three times a quarter. The obvious reading — that flagging urgency is free and helps the analyst prioritise — is wrong, because the flag's value comes entirely from its scarcity across all requesters.

Aggregate movements are often composition, not behaviour. Simpson's paradox is not an exotic curiosity in product analytics; it is the default hazard whenever mix shifts. If Manjari's Android-low-tier segment holds at 22 percent completion and its Android-high-tier segment holds at 51 percent, but the low-tier share of new users rises from 40 to 62 percent in a festive-season acquisition push, the blended rate falls from 39.4 to 33.0 percent with no user behaving differently. The tell-tale sign is a metric that moves in the opposite direction from every one of its segments, and an expert's reflex is to ask for the segment mix before asking for the explanation.

Instrumentation gaps are a product specification failure, not an analytics failure. If the event Devika needed to distinguish a human read from an automated session was never emitted, no query can recover it, and treating the analyst as the responsible party guarantees the gap recurs next quarter. The tell is a tracking plan that lives in a spreadsheet nobody has edited since the last reorganisation, while the product has shipped forty releases.

Sharing ownership means giving up the right to change a definition unilaterally — including when the change is an improvement. Experts treat a definitional change as a release: announced, dated, with the old and the new reported side by side for one period. The tell-tale sign of the amateur is an improved definition deployed quietly on a Tuesday, which is how a genuine improvement becomes an unexplained step change in a year-on-year chart.

Enough SQL to read a query, not enough to own one. A product manager's SQL literacy exists to make the brief well-formed and to read a join condition sceptically, not to produce numbers that bypass review. The tell is a PM whose personal queries reach slides: literacy has become a second, unowned source of truth — the harm it was meant to prevent.

7. How this differs by product type and company stage

In high-volume consumer products the hazard is spurious precision: with nine million users every segment is statistically significant and almost none is decisive, so the analyst's most valuable contribution is refusing to slice. In B2B the arithmetic inverts. Sangati had 340 customers; one misclassified account moves a percentage by three tenths of a point, and the account manager will notice. The B2B discipline is therefore account taxonomy — what counts as one customer when a group has four subsidiaries on three contracts — and the work is closer to careful accounting than to statistics. Platforms add a further problem: sellers and developers observe the platform's own metrics and optimise against them, so Goodhart's law operates from outside the company, where documentation cannot reach it. Hardware and physical goods face a latency problem — returns, damages and cash reconciliation arrive weeks late, so fresh numbers are provisional and expert teams publish a restatement policy alongside them.

Stage changes the constraint rather than the principle. Below roughly twenty people there is no analyst, the product manager writes the SQL, and the discipline reduces to one habit: write the definition in the same document as the decision. Between twenty and two hundred, the first analyst arrives and becomes a query service for six requesters with no intake; this is when a visible queue pays for itself, and it is almost always installed a year late. Above a few hundred the arguments become organisational, and the things that determine quality are unglamorous: whether definitional changes are announced, whether the tracking plan is reviewed at spec time, and whether anyone is accountable for a metric's truth after its requester has changed jobs. Where the difference is not real, say so plainly: the four-part definition, the written brief, the visible queue and the announced change are identical at every stage and in every product type. Only the enforcement mechanism differs.

8. Three worked examples, including one failure

Sangati Systems, B2B, successful. Devika and Farhan ran the ladder in Figure 1 and took it to the customer rather than around the customer. Instead of arguing about whether the software was used, both sides looked at 29 users performing write actions against 107 billed full seats and agreed that Sangati had oversold by roughly forty seats. Sangati cut the contract by ₹61 lakh, extended it two years, and catalogued “active seat = at least one data-writing action in a rolling 28 days” with both names on it. The benefit was that sales forecasts became, for the first time, comparable with product usage data.

Manjari, consumer AI, partially successful. Sneha did not fix the instrumentation before the season. She and Ritwik defined a temporary secondary metric — drills with a scoring response received — unbiased but undercounting everywhere, ran the test on both, and shipped because the redesign won on both, by 2.6 and 2.2 points. The fix landed eleven weeks later. The judgement is worth naming: the metric was not fit to report, but it was fit to compare, because both arms carried the same bias. The compromise was defensible only because the decision was a comparison.

Chirag Power Tools, hardware plus software, failed. Chirag sold connected drilling and cutting tools to construction contractors, with a subscription service tracking tool utilisation across sites. In 2024 it built a “fleet utilisation” metric — share of tools used on at least ten days in a month — and built a customer-facing dashboard and a sales incentive on it. The failure had three layers. Devices that lost connectivity on basement sites reported nothing and were counted as unused, understating utilisation for exactly the customers with the largest fleets; a firmware release in month five changed reporting cadence from hourly to six-hourly, reducing the chance that any given day registered an event; and because the metric sat in customer contracts, nobody could correct it without renegotiating twenty-eight agreements. Two contractors used the understated numbers to demand concessions worth ₹3.1 crore. The recovery took nine months and was not a data project: Chirag added a heartbeat signal so unreachable devices formed a third category, restated fourteen months of history with a published methodology note, honoured the concessions rather than clawing them back, and moved the contractual metric to tools with activity against tools known to be reachable. The lesson drawn internally was not “we needed better analysts.” It was that a metric had entered a contract without anyone asking what its silence meant.

9. Failure modes, with their early warnings

Failure modeEarly warning signDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late
Shadow definitionsTwo decks, same metric name, different values“How many undated descriptions of this term exist in our wiki?”Restatement in front of a board or a customer
Queue bypassMost requests arrive as direct messages“What share of last month's analyses had a ticket?”Invisible work; the team's roadmap silently disappears
Urgency inflationAnalysts stop reacting to “urgent”“What fraction of my tickets did I mark urgent?”No fast lane exists when one is genuinely needed
Silent redefinitionA clean step change in a long series“What changed in the pipeline that week?”A year of trend analysis becomes uninterpretable
Instrumentation driftEvent volume moves without a product change“When was the tracking plan last reviewed at spec?”Experiments underpowered or biased for months
Analyst as order-takerRequests specify SQL, not questions“When did an analyst last change our plan?”Attrition of the best analysts, then of institutional memory
Contractualised metricsA metric appears in a signed agreement“What does silence in this data mean?”Renegotiating every contract to fix a definition

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Should product managers write production-facing SQL? Governance, steelmanned: every unreviewed query is a potential second source of truth, written by someone who does not know which of four order tables is authoritative, and restatement incidents reliably cluster around numbers produced outside the reviewed path. Self-serve, steelmanned: the alternative to a PM's own query is not a reviewed query but a decision made with no data at all, because the queue is three weeks long; organisations that invested in access and literacy show faster decision cycles without measurable increases in error, provided external reporting stays gated. For the first to be wrong, gating external reporting alone would have to capture most of the risk. For the second to be wrong, informal numbers would have to leak into external documents regardless of policy — which, anecdotally, they do.

Centralised or embedded analysts? Centralists argue that consistency, career development and defensible methodology require a professional home, and that embedded analysts drift into being spreadsheet staff. Embedders argue that context is the scarce resource, that an analyst outside the pod's arguments answers the stated question rather than the real one, and that the best analytical work is indistinguishable from product work. Both cite analyst retention data; both are selective. Most large companies oscillate between the poles every three years or so, which is itself evidence that neither dominates.

One north star or a portfolio? The single-metric school argues that alignment is the scarce good and a portfolio lets everyone select the flattering number. The portfolio school argues that any single metric is Goodhart-vulnerable and that a small set with guardrails is more robust. The evidence is confounded: companies with a strong single metric tend also to have strong leadership, and it is unclear which caused the focus.

Will natural-language querying dissolve the problem or sharpen it? One camp holds that a semantic layer plus a language model finally delivers self-serve, because the model queries governed definitions rather than raw tables. The other holds that models will be pointed at raw tables anyway, that a confident well-formatted wrong answer is more dangerous than a slow one, and that ungoverned numbers are multiplying faster than any catalogue can cover. This is genuinely open; incident data over the next few years will settle more of it than argument.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this writes better tickets. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in four visible ways. They arrive with a decision and a threshold rather than a question, so the analyst can propose a cheaper analysis that answers it. When two numbers conflict they ask for the ladder rather than the verdict, and present it publicly, which removes the incentive to defend a number rather than examine it. They protect the analytics roadmap in planning as if it were their own, having learned that platform debt is repaid by them in six-week delays. And they are visibly willing to be told that a number cannot be produced honestly, and to decide anyway, saying so — which is what makes analysts trust them, and trust is what converts a service relationship into a partnership.

12. What Devika and Sneha decided

Devika took the decomposition into the renewal call and lost ₹61 lakh of annual contract value to gain a two-year term and a definition both companies could quote. Her reasoning was that the credibility of every future number Sangati showed that customer outweighed one year's revenue on unused seats, and that defending 71 percent would have cost the relationship anyway once the customer examined its own IT logs. Sneha shipped on a biased metric, having established that the bias was common to both arms and that the redesign won under every definition she could construct; she wrote the bias into the readout in two sentences, committed publicly to the fix, and accepted that Manjari's absolute completion numbers for that quarter were not comparable with the next.

Three questions. First: Devika's ladder made Sangati look worse to a customer — when is it right to publish a decomposition that damages your own position, and who should make that call? Second: Sneha separated a metric fit for comparison from one fit for reporting — where does that distinction break down, and what would have to be true of Manjari's 2G population for her to have been wrong? Third: what process would have caught Chirag's contractual metric before signature, and what would it have cost in the two years before it was needed?

13. Going deeper

  1. Querying data (SQL basics) — the literacy that makes a brief well-formed; it unlocks the ability to read a join condition sceptically rather than deferring to or second-guessing every result.
  2. Constructing a funnel — where definitional disagreements first become visible, since every step needs a population and a window.
  3. Reading drop-off — distinguishes a step that loses users from one that filters them, the distinction most misread dashboards blur.
  4. Defining activation (the aha moment) — the canonical case of a definition that must be agreed jointly and revisited; it unlocks onboarding work that can actually be evaluated.
  5. Cohort analysis — the antidote to the composition effects in section six; it unlocks telling a mix shift from a behaviour change.
  6. Retention curves and the PMF signal — where definitional choices have the largest leverage on strategic conclusions, because the shape of the tail decides whether a product is working.
  7. Stickiness and natural frequency — supplies the prior that tells you whether a window is right for your product at all, the question underneath most window disputes.

Poonji's Active-Investor Number

Three teams, three honest counts, one board deck — and a Dubai placement deal riding on which number Rohan Malhotra chooses to call the truth.

1. Bengaluru, Monday, 11 August 2025

Rohan Malhotra, Vice President of Product at Poonji, a direct mutual-fund and stock investing app headquartered off Sarjapur Road in Bengaluru, read the Thursday board agenda for the third time that morning. Item four read simply: "Monthly active investors — trend and Series C data room figure." He had four days. Poonji's Series C term sheet, being negotiated with a Mumbai-based growth fund, used active-investor count as one input into a comparables-based valuation line, and separately, a placement agreement Poonji's institutional sales head had been closing in Dubai carried a preferred-tier threshold keyed to the same number. Rohan had, at that moment, three different counts on his laptop, produced by three people he trusted, none of them wrong, and a gap between the smallest and the largest of roughly seven times.

2. Company background

Poonji had launched in 2019 as a direct-plan mutual fund app, expanding by 2022 into stocks and exchange-traded funds once it secured its stockbroking licence, putting it in the same arena as Groww, Zerodha's Coin, Paytm Money, and Kuvera. It cleared know-your-customer checks through PAN, Aadhaar-based e-KYC and CKYC, settled payments over UPI through NPCI's rails, and reported fund flows in line with AMFI norms, with SEBI as its ultimate regulator for both the broking and advisory sides of the business. By July 2025 it had 42 lakh registered accounts and 7.2 lakh accounts that were fully KYC-complete and bank-linked — "funded," in the company's internal language — a base large enough to be a credible fourth or fifth player nationally, and one the growth fund wanted to underwrite for a $60 million Series C ahead of the festive quarter, when brokerage apps traditionally see a surge in new SIP starts around Dhanteras and Diwali.

3. The situation

Poonji's product organisation was, by design, distributed. Engineers sat in Bengaluru and Pune; a product designer, Meret Baumann, worked out of Berlin on the onboarding and KYC flows; the lead data scientist, Daniel Osei, worked from Toronto on a nine-hour offset from Bengaluru; customer success was run out of Singapore by Su-Lin Tan, close to Poonji's growing base of NRI investors in South-East Asia; and institutional sales, including the Gulf distribution channel, was led by Karan Bhatia from New Jersey. Each of them saw the active-investor question from a different vantage point. Daniel's team maintained the canonical data warehouse and, for two years, had defined a monthly active investor conservatively: a funded account that executed at least one buy, sell, or SIP instalment in the trailing thirty days. By that count, July's figure was 2.15 lakh. The product dashboard that Rohan's own team watched daily used a looser, older definition dating to 2023 — a funded account that opened the app and viewed its holdings screen, transaction not required — and showed 4.32 lakh. Karan, negotiating the Gulf placement tier with Faisal Al Mansoori, a Dubai-based distributor whose preferred-tier terms required Poonji to show at least 10 lakh active investors, had asked one of Daniel's junior analysts, Ananya Deshpande in Pune, for "whatever number is highest and still defensible," and received a count of any registered account with any login event in thirty days, including passive app opens triggered by push notifications: 14.7 lakh. Nobody had lied. Nobody had agreed, in writing, what "active" meant, and the request had gone through three different informal channels rather than one shared one.

Exhibit 1. Poonji's distributed team, and the definition of "active investor" each location was working from before Rohan intervened.

4. The people

Rohan Malhotra — VP Product, Bengaluru. Owns the board deck due Thursday and the metrics catalog; wants a number he can defend to the board, to the fund's diligence team, and to Karan's Dubai counterpart without contradicting himself next quarter.
Daniel Osei — Lead Data Scientist, Toronto. Built the transacting-investor definition two years ago as the SEBI-adjacent, audit-safe number; worried that a looser figure in a fundraising data room invites exactly the kind of restatement scandal that has embarrassed other Indian startups during due diligence.
Karan Bhatia — Head of Institutional Sales, New Jersey. Needs Poonji to clear the 10-lakh threshold in Faisal Al Mansoori's placement agreement this quarter or lose the preferred referral tier for another two quarters; sees the dispute as pedantry standing between Poonji and a real distribution deal.
Su-Lin Tan — Customer Success Lead, Singapore. Fields tickets from NRI investors whom the dashboard calls "active" but who have not invested a rupee in months; worried that whichever number goes external, support will be the first to hear when it does not match customers' lived experience.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 2. Three definitions of "monthly active investor," same July 2025 data.
DefinitionBase populationCountRate
Transacting (Daniel) — buy/sell/SIP in last 30 days7.2 lakh funded accounts2.15 lakh29.9%
Engaged (product dashboard) — app open + holdings viewed7.2 lakh funded accounts4.32 lakh60.0%
Any login (Karan's request) — any open, incl. push-triggered42 lakh registered accounts14.70 lakh35.0%

Exhibit 2 shows why the three numbers cannot be reconciled by better arithmetic: they divide by different populations as well as counting different events. Daniel and the product dashboard both use the 7.2-lakh funded base but disagree on the numerator; the "any login" figure looks smaller as a percentage than "engaged" only because it is measured against the much larger 42-lakh registered base — a reminder that a rate is only comparable to another rate when both the numerator's event and the denominator's population are held fixed.

Exhibit 3. What each number is worth, in the two live negotiations.
Which count is reportedSeries C data-room line (₹14,000/active investor, illustrative)Dubai preferred-tier threshold (10 lakh)
2.15 lakh (transacting)₹301 croreMissed
4.32 lakh (engaged)₹605 croreMissed
14.70 lakh (any login)₹2,058 croreCleared

Exhibit 3 is why the question could not wait for a leisurely definitional debate: the growth fund's term sheet treated active-investor count as one line among several comparables inputs, at a stylised ₹14,000 per active investor, so the gap between 2.15 lakh and 14.70 lakh is worth over ₹1,750 crore on that single line, and only the "any login" figure clears Faisal Al Mansoori's 10-lakh threshold for Poonji's preferred referral tier in the Gulf.

6. The options

Option A — Report the "any login" figure, 14.70 lakh

This is the number Karan wants and the one that clears the Dubai threshold immediately and strengthens the valuation line for Thursday's board meeting. The cost is that it includes accounts that opened the app only because a push notification asked them to, a definition Daniel considers indefensible if the fund's diligence team or, later, a SEBI-adjacent disclosure asks how "active" was defined, and one Su-Lin already fields complaints about internally.

Option B — Report the transacting figure, 2.15 lakh, and only that

This is Daniel's conservative, audit-safe number, defensible against any later scrutiny. The cost is immediate and specific: Poonji misses the 10-lakh Dubai threshold this quarter, Karan loses the preferred tier he has spent two months negotiating, and the Series C comparables line shrinks by roughly ₹1,750 crore relative to Option A, a number the board will ask Rohan to explain.

Option C — One documented primary metric, a labelled secondary metric, and a renegotiated Dubai threshold

Rohan adopts the transacting definition as Poonji's single, catalogued "monthly active investor" figure for the board and the data room, reports the engaged-user figure separately and explicitly as a funnel metric rather than a headline number, and asks Karan to go back to Faisal Al Mansoori to reset the placement tier's threshold against assets under management growth, a number Poonji is not disputing internally, instead of investor headcount. The upside is a number that will not need restating; the cost is a harder, slower conversation with Karan and a real risk the Dubai renegotiation fails.

7. Questions for discussion

1. What decision does Thursday's board number actually feed, and what happens to Poonji if the figure presented does not survive due diligence three months later?

2. Why do Daniel's, the product dashboard's, and Karan's numbers all differ, given that all three are drawn from the same underlying database?

3. How should Rohan weigh Karan's near-term commercial pressure against Daniel's longer-term credibility argument, and whose call should this be?

4. Of Options A, B and C, which would you choose, and what exactly would you tell Faisal Al Mansoori and the board about why the number is what it is?

8. A note for the learner

This case turns on the discipline the topic teaches: a metric is not a fact waiting to be pulled, it is an agreement that has to be written down and owned jointly before it can be trusted under pressure. Poonji did not have a bad data team; it had three good, honestly computed numbers and no shared queue or documented definition to reconcile them before a commercial deadline forced the question. A well-reasoned answer treats Option A as tempting but fragile — it solves this week's problem by creating next quarter's restatement risk — and Option B as principled but incomplete, since it treats a genuine commercial negotiation as if it did not exist. The defensible path is Option C: Rohan asks Daniel to make the transacting definition Poonji's one official "monthly active investor" figure, written into a shared metrics catalog with both their names on it, so the board, the fund, and any future analyst inherit the same answer; he lets the engaged-user number live on, clearly labelled, as a funnel metric useful to the product team without ever appearing unlabelled in an external document; and he asks Karan to renegotiate the Dubai tier against AUM growth, a metric that is not in dispute, rather than letting a commercial deadline quietly redefine what "active" means. It costs Rohan a harder conversation this week. It buys Poonji a number that means the same thing in November as it does in August.

Anomaly Detection and Alerting

Will I know a metric moved before someone in leadership asks?

1. The Tuesday morning Kartik almost missed

At 9:40 a.m. on a Tuesday in March, Kartik Mehra, VP of Product at Verve, a five-year-old direct-to-consumer fashion app with 2.1 million monthly active users, opened his dashboard out of habit before a leadership sync. Daily new-user signups, usually a steady 5,000 to 5,600, showed 3,650 for the previous day. Nobody had flagged it. Nobody had paged him. The number simply sat there, quietly 30 percent below where it should have been, discovered only because Kartik happened to scroll before a 10 a.m. meeting where the CEO would ask about growth. He had ninety minutes to find out whether this was a payment-gateway outage, a botched app-store update, a marketing spend that lapsed overnight, or nothing at all — ordinary noise that would correct itself by Thursday. Verve's board deck was due in six days, and if signups had genuinely fallen off a cliff, the company needed to know today, not when the monthly review surfaced it. Kartik's problem was not that the number moved. Numbers move constantly. His problem was that Verve had no system that reliably told him when a movement was worth ninety minutes of his morning, and it had cost him the ninety minutes he did not have. This is the exact gap that anomaly detection and alerting exists to close.

2. The idea

Anomaly detection is the practice of comparing a metric's current value against the range of values it would plausibly take if nothing unusual were happening, and flagging the cases where the gap is too large to be ordinary variation. Alerting is the delivery mechanism: the rules and routing that take a flagged anomaly and put it in front of a specific human, on a specific channel, with enough context to act, before the delay itself becomes the damage. The two are usually discussed as one because neither is useful alone — a detector nobody sees is a diary entry, and an alert with no statistical basis is just noise with a siren attached.

The statistical backbone is old. Walter Shewhart, an engineer at Bell Labs, developed control charts in 1924 to help factory floors distinguish a process that had genuinely drifted out of tolerance from one that was merely exhibiting the random scatter every process has. His insight — that you need an explicit model of "normal" before you can recognize "abnormal" — travelled from manufacturing into software operations in the 2000s and 2010s, as companies like Google, Etsy, and Amazon built systems to watch server error rates and latency in real time, then into product analytics as tools such as Amplitude and Mixpanel added anomaly alerts on business metrics like signups, checkout completion, and retention in the years after 2015. The line Kartik could say in a meeting without sounding glib: an anomaly detector separates a metric's normal noise from a real shift, and alerting is the plumbing that gets that distinction to a human before it becomes a crisis.

3. How it actually works

The mechanics run in five steps, and the first is the one practitioners most often skip. Step one is establishing a baseline: not "yesterday's number" but a model of what a normal day looks like, built from enough history to capture the metric's natural rhythms — day-of-week effects, month-end effects, festival-season spikes. A baseline built from a raw seven-day average will misfire constantly if Mondays are structurally lower than Fridays, because it treats a predictable pattern as an anomaly. Step two is computing the expected range for the period being checked — typically a mean and a measure of spread (standard deviation, or a percentile band for skewed metrics) specific to that day-of-week or segment. Step three is measuring the deviation: how far the actual value sits from the expected value, usually expressed as a standardized score (a z-score) or a percentage deviation, so that metrics of very different scale can be compared on one footing. Step four is the threshold decision — a rule, set deliberately rather than left at a tool's default, for how large a deviation must be before it counts as worth a human's attention. Step five, the one most often left implicit, is routing and suppression: deciding who gets the alert, on what channel, and whether it should be held back because a known event (a deploy, a planned outage, a flash sale) already explains it. Skipping step five is how alerting systems earn a reputation for crying wolf.

4. A worked example, twice

Take Kartik's Tuesday with real arithmetic. Verve's trailing eight-week average for daily signups is 5,000, with a standard deviation of 400, computed without adjusting for weekday. Tuesday's actual figure was 3,650. The z-score is (3,650 − 5,000) ÷ 400 = −3.38. Under a common threshold of ±3 standard deviations, that trips the alarm loudly: this looks like a 1-in-3,000-day event, not routine noise.

Now run the second pass, changing one input: build the baseline from Tuesdays only, since Verve's data shows Tuesdays running lower than the weekly average because of a Monday-night email campaign that pulls signups forward. The Tuesday-specific mean is 4,200, with a standard deviation of 350 (Tuesdays are also less variable, since the campaign effect is consistent). The same 3,650 now scores (3,650 − 4,200) ÷ 350 = −1.57 — inside the normal range, not an alert.

Baseline usedMeanStd. dev.Actualz-scoreFlagged?
All-week average5,0004003,650−3.38Yes, at ±3
Tuesday-only average4,2003503,650−1.57No, at ±3

The number did not change. The verdict flipped entirely because the baseline changed. This is the single most consequential design choice in anomaly detection, and it is exactly the choice a dashboard's default settings will make for you, silently, unless someone decides it on purpose.

5. The nuances a learner must sit with

Statistical significance is not business significance. A z-score of −3.5 says the deviation is unlikely to be random noise; it says nothing about whether losing 1,350 signups matters to the quarter. A metric can be statistically anomalous and commercially irrelevant, or move only 5 percent and be commercially catastrophic if it is revenue on a thin-margin day.

Seasonality is not anomaly, and confusing the two is the most common failure mode. Any detector that does not decompose day-of-week, month-end, and festival-calendar effects will flag the same predictable pattern week after week until the team mutes it — at which point it will also miss the real event hiding behind that week's normal seasonal dip.

Point anomalies, level shifts, and contextual anomalies are different animals. A single bad day is a point anomaly and often self-corrects. A permanent step down — say, after a pricing change — is a level shift, and a detector tuned only for single-day spikes will alert once and then quietly re-baseline itself to the new, worse normal. A contextual anomaly is a value that is normal in isolation but wrong given the surrounding conditions, such as flat signups on the one day a major marketing push should have doubled them.

Sensitivity and alert fatigue trade off directly against each other. A tight threshold catches real problems earlier but also fires on more false positives; each false positive spends a little of the team's trust, and trust, once spent, means real alerts get ignored too.

Low-volume metrics behave badly under the same math that works for high-volume ones. A metric with 40 events a day has a standard deviation that swings wildly from week to week, and z-score thresholds built for a metric with 40,000 events a day will either flag constantly or never at all when applied naively to the smaller one.

An alert tells you a metric moved, not why it moved. Detection and diagnosis are separate skills; a well-built alerting system hands the responder a starting point — a link to a segmented dashboard, a note on recent deploys — but the causal work is still a human investigation.

Detection has an inherent lag that depends on window size. A detector built on rolling seven-day windows will not confirm a level shift until it has absorbed enough days to move the average, which means the alert that would have been most valuable arrives late by design; tightening the window to catch shifts faster also makes the detector twitchier on ordinary noise.

An alert with no owner is not an alert, it is a broadcast. Systems that page a shared channel rather than naming a specific accountable person routinely see the same unresolved anomaly re-fire for days, because everyone assumes someone else is on it.

6. How this differs by business shape

In a high-volume consumer product like Verve, metrics have enough daily observations that statistical methods work cleanly and can largely run unattended, with humans reviewing only what crosses threshold. In B2B products, volumes are lower and lumpier — a metric like "enterprise logo churned this week" might be a count of zero or one on most days, which breaks z-score math entirely and pushes teams toward rule-based alerts (a named account went silent for ten days) and human judgment over statistics. Marketplace products add a second axis: supply and demand must be watched both separately and as a ratio, because a demand-side anomaly can be a lagging symptom of a supply-side problem three days earlier, and alerting only on the customer-facing metric misses the earlier, more actionable signal. Company stage matters as much as business model. An early-stage team with a handful of metrics and a founder who checks the dashboard daily needs little more than simple threshold alerts on the two or three numbers that matter. A large organization with hundreds of tracked metrics needs alert governance — deduplication so one root cause does not generate forty pages, tiered severity so a minor dip does not wake anyone at 2 a.m., and an on-call rotation so an alert always has a first responder, not just a channel.

7. Common mistakes

Static thresholds with no seasonality adjustment. Symptom: alerts fire reliably every Monday morning and get muted within a month. Underlying error: treating a predictable weekly pattern as noise around a flat mean. Cheapest diagnostic: plot alert timestamps by day of week — a strong cluster on one weekday is the tell.

Alerting on every metric available rather than the few that matter. Symptom: a Slack channel with dozens of daily pings that nobody opens. Underlying error: mistaking comprehensiveness for rigor. Cheapest diagnostic: track the ratio of alerts that led to any action; below roughly one in five, the system is manufacturing noise, not insight.

No named owner or routing logic. Symptom: the same anomaly appears in the weekly review three weeks running, unresolved. Underlying error: assuming visibility equals accountability. Cheapest diagnostic: ask who closed the last five alerts, by name, within 24 hours — a shrug is the diagnosis.

Treating instrumentation breakage as a genuine metric movement. Symptom: every metric on the dashboard drops or spikes at once, at the exact minute of a deploy. Underlying error: not distinguishing "the world changed" from "our measurement of the world broke." Cheapest diagnostic: check the deploy log before opening an investigation into the business.

8. What good looks like

Six months later, Verve's version of that Tuesday looks different. The baseline for signups is now built from eight trailing weeks, decomposed by weekday and flagged for known campaign days, refreshed weekly. When Tuesday's number comes in at 3,650 against a Tuesday-specific expectation of 4,200 with a tight band, the deviation is real this time — a payment-gateway partner had an outage between 11 p.m. and 4 a.m. The alert fires within twenty minutes of the daily rollup, tagged medium severity, routed by name to the on-call growth engineer with a link to a dashboard pre-segmented by payment provider and a note flagging no deploys in the prior twelve hours. The engineer confirms the outage from the provider's status page by 8:15 a.m., a fix ships by 9 a.m., and Kartik walks into his leadership sync already able to say what happened, why, and that it is resolved — instead of discovering the dip live in the room.

9. What Kartik decided, and what comes next

Kartik's actual Tuesday resolved the mundane way: a coupon-code bug in the previous night's release had silently broken signup for one browser segment, and the number recovered by Wednesday. But the near-miss was the real finding. He commissioned a weekday-adjusted baseline for Verve's ten core metrics, tiered severity levels, and named on-call ownership by the following sprint — the system sketched in Section 8 is now Verve's actual setup. What Kartik still needs to learn is root-cause diagnosis: once an alert correctly says a metric moved, the harder discipline is a structured way of asking which segment, which channel, which cohort moved, so that detection converts into an explanation fast enough to matter. He is also aware this topic has a ceiling: no alerting system, however well tuned, will tell him whether a real movement is worth caring about — that judgment about business significance stays irreducibly human. Two questions worth sitting with: if your team currently discovers metric movements by someone happening to look, what is that costing you in delayed decisions that you have never tried to price? And for the metrics you already alert on, do you know — specifically, not generally — what baseline each threshold is measured against, and who would tell you if that baseline quietly went stale?

case20v1-ana.anomaly:
Fatafat Mart: The Pune Number

Bengaluru, 14–17 September 2026

1. The Wednesday deadline

On the morning of Monday, 14 September 2026, Ananya Rao, Senior Product Manager for Growth & Analytics at Fatafat Mart, opened the metrics dashboard she would present to the board in three days and found a red flag she had not put there. Checkout conversion in the Pune dark-store cluster had fallen from a steady 78–80 per cent to 74 per cent over the weekend, and stayed there. The board call on Wednesday at 11 a.m. was not an ordinary review. It was the closing session for Fatafat Mart's Series C, and the lead investor, Faisal Al-Mansoori of Dunes Capital in Dubai, had asked specifically to see the checkout funnel before wiring the final tranche of ₹550 crore. Ananya had forty-eight hours to find out whether the Pune number was a real problem, a measurement artefact, or noise — and to decide what to tell the room either way.

2. Ten minutes, eighteen cities

Fatafat Mart delivers groceries in under fifteen minutes from a network of 210 dark stores across eighteen Indian cities, competing directly with Zepto, Blinkit and Swiggy Instamart, with BigBasket and JioMart fighting for the same slower, larger basket. Founded in 2021 by two former Flipkart supply-chain managers, the company had grown its monthly active users to 6.1 million and its annualised GMV run-rate to roughly ₹1,800 crore, on an average order value of ₹310. It had raised ₹340 crore in a Series B in 2024 and was now, a year later, closing a Series C of ₹550 crore led by Dunes Capital, with two existing investors following on. Growth had been real, but the quick-commerce sector in India was under close watch for cash burn, and Dunes Capital's term sheet included a covenant that the company's core funnel metrics be reviewed quarterly against board-approved definitions. A clean, well-instrumented growth story was not a nicety for this round; it was close to a condition of the wire.

3. What happened, and what nobody was sure of

On Friday night, 11 September, Fatafat Mart's engineering team in Pune shipped a routine change to the checkout service, altering how the app retried a payment call to the gateway when the first attempt timed out, in order to cut failed transactions during the upcoming Navratri rush. The release passed staging tests and went out to all eighteen cities. By Sunday, conversion in most cities had held steady, but Pune's had not recovered from its usual weekend dip.

Fatafat Mart ran an automated anomaly-alerting layer over its core metrics, built the previous year by Vikram Desai, the company's data scientist, who works out of Toronto. The system used an exponentially weighted moving average with control bands to flag when a city-level metric moved outside its expected range. It should have caught the Pune drop by Saturday morning. It did not, because in July the on-call engineers, exhausted by pages triggered by ordinary monsoon delivery-slot volatility, had widened the alert bands city by city and muted several as "noisy." Pune's checkout-conversion alert was one of the muted ones. Vikram found the drop himself on Sunday evening, almost by accident, while pulling a cohort chart for the board deck, and flagged it in the team's channel at 11 p.m. Toronto time — 8:30 a.m. Monday in Bengaluru, just as Ananya was starting her day.

By Monday afternoon two explanations were on the table. The retry-logic change might be silently failing a subset of Pune's transactions on a specific payment method, which would be a real, fixable defect. Alternatively, the drop might be a logging artefact: the new retry code could be double-counting checkout attempts as fresh sessions, deflating the conversion ratio without any user actually failing to buy groceries. Meera Joshi in Pune, the engineer who had shipped the release, believed the second explanation was more likely but could not rule out the first without a deeper log audit, which would take at least two full days.

4. The people around the table

Vikram Desai
Data Scientist, Toronto		Built the anomaly-detection layer and found the Pune drop. Wants the alerting redesigned with tiered severity so a real signal is never muted again — and wants that fix documented before the board call, as proof the metric is now trustworthy.
Meera Joshi
Backend Engineer, Pune		Shipped the retry-logic change and is closest to the code. Wants time to audit the logs properly rather than issue a rushed rollback that could reintroduce the payment timeouts the change was meant to fix.
Priya Subramaniam
Customer Success Lead, Singapore		Has fielded a rising number of complaints from Pune dark-store franchise partners about the app "hanging" at payment. Wants the issue acknowledged and fixed fast, whatever the metric turns out to say.
Rajeev Malhotra
Head of Investor Relations, New Jersey		Owns the board deck and the relationship with Dunes Capital. Wants a number he can defend on the call without caveats that spook a Gulf-based investor already weighing quick-commerce burn rates against the term sheet.

5. Exhibits
