6. The options

  • A. Present the deck as scheduled, with a footnote. Keep Wednesday's call. Show the Pune number as reported, with a one-line note that it is under investigation. Upside: no delay to a Series C close that the whole company is counting on, and no admission of an unresolved defect. Cost: if the funnel keeps slipping, or if Faisal Al-Mansoori's own diligence team notices the drop first, Fatafat Mart looks either unaware of its own metrics or unwilling to say so — a bad way to open a covenant relationship built on quarterly metric reviews.
  • B. Delay the call two to three days. Ask Rajeev to push the board call until Meera's log audit is complete and the root cause is confirmed one way or the other. Upside: whatever number is presented on the rescheduled call will be true and defensible. Cost: a late board call on a signed term sheet reads, to a growth-stage investor, as a company that found a problem it is not ready to explain — a costly signal in a quarter when quick-commerce funding is already being scrutinised, even if the real cause turns out to be harmless.
  • C. Present on time, with the anomaly disclosed and the fix in motion. Keep Wednesday's call. Show the Pune drop explicitly, explain what is known (retry-logic release, likely a logging double-count, confirmed fix shipping that day), and present the redesigned tiered alerting — city-level severity bands instead of blanket muting — as evidence the team now catches this class of issue itself. Upside: turns a data-quality incident into a demonstration of measurement discipline, which is exactly what a covenant on metric reviews is meant to test for. Cost: requires Ananya to walk into the room with an open item rather than a closed one, and depends on Meera's team actually shipping the fix and the new tiering before the call.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What, precisely, made the Pune anomaly invisible to the system that was built to catch it? Separate the technical cause from the organisational one.
  2. Using Exhibit 1, would you have expected the existing alert to fire before Vikram found the drop manually? What does that imply about the trade-off the team made in July?
  3. Of the three stakeholders other than Ananya, whose objection is hardest to satisfy under a 48-hour deadline, and why?
  4. Which option would you choose for Wednesday's call, and what would have to be true by Tuesday night for you to switch to a different one?

8. A note for the learner

This topic is not about building a cleverer statistical model. It is about a much plainer question, asked under a deadline: will you know a metric has moved before someone in leadership asks you about it? Fatafat Mart had the model — Vikram's control-band system was reasonably sophisticated. What it lacked was an alerting policy matched to the cost of being wrong in each direction. Widening every threshold to stop the pager going off during monsoon volatility solved the team's fatigue problem and created a blind spot exactly where it could least be afforded: a metric a board-closing investor had asked to see.

A well-reasoned answer starts by separating two different failures that are easy to conflate: a detection failure (the alert did not fire) and a data or product failure (something about checkout genuinely changed). Exhibit 1 shows the second is real — the line moved and stayed moved after a specific release, which is a pattern noise does not usually produce. Exhibit 2 shows the first is also real, and traces it to a specific trade-off made in July, not to bad luck. Once both are established, the choice among the three options stops being about optimism versus caution and becomes a question of what each option asks the audience to trust.

Option A asks Dunes Capital to trust an unexplained caveat. Option B asks them to trust a delay. Option C asks them to trust a team that can find its own blind spots and close them in public — which is closer to what a metrics covenant is actually testing. The defensible path here is Option C: disclose the anomaly with its likely cause, ship the fix, and show the redesigned tiered alerting live on the call, so that the incident itself becomes the evidence of the discipline being purchased. It is not the most comfortable path for Ananya, since it requires walking into the room before the story is fully closed. But it is the one that treats the anomaly-alerting system as what it is: not a dashboard feature, but the mechanism by which a product team keeps its promises about knowing its own numbers.
exp40v2-ana.anomaly:
Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation · Product Analytics & Data Practice

Anomaly Detection and Alerting

Depth reading. The companion page established the baseline-and-threshold mechanic. This one takes up what happens when the baseline is contaminated, when thresholds are set across hundreds of series at once, and when the organisation rather than the statistics is the binding constraint.

1. Two mornings

At 8:20 on 4 February, Nandita Rau, Director of Product at Cadence, a Bengaluru-headquartered workflow-automation company selling to global enterprises, was building a renewal forecast when a colleague forwarded her a cohort chart she had not requested. Cadence's headline engagement metric — workflows executed per active account per week — had been flat to rising for eight weeks, 41.2 to 41.9. The cohort chart said something else. Among the 214 mid-market accounts onboarded the previous July to September, the same metric had fallen from 33.4 to 24.1 over five weeks, a 28 per cent decline. The aggregate held because one large customer, a bank running 8,900 seats, had ramped over the same period and filled the hole. Cadence's alerting system, watching forty-one company-level metrics at a three-sigma band, had fired nothing, and had been right not to: at the company level nothing anomalous had occurred. Renewals for those accounts, worth $9.1 million, opened on 1 March. Nandita had twenty-four days and a signal her detection system was structurally incapable of producing.

At 23:10 on 11 March, in Pune, Sameer Bhatt, principal product manager at Lumen Draft, an AI writing assistant with 910,000 weekly active users on a ₹499 monthly plan, was reading a support cluster: twenty-two users in four days complaining the assistant had become verbose and was ignoring instructions. Lumen Draft's quality proxy was its regeneration rate — the share of drafts discarded and re-run within thirty seconds. The trailing benchmark was 11.4 per cent; the seven-day figure was 13.9 per cent, twenty-two per cent higher in relative terms and, on the company's own elasticity estimates, roughly ₹40 lakh of annualised churn risk. The detector had not fired, because it compared the last seven days against a rolling twenty-eight-day baseline and nine of those days already contained the regression. The provider had shipped a model point release on 2 March without a version bump. By 09:00 Sameer had to choose between pinning back to the prior version, delaying a launch six weeks in the making, and waiting six more days for a hastily started A/B test to reach power.

Both are detection failures, and neither is a threshold problem. Nandita's system watched the wrong unit of analysis; Sameer's was trained on the incident it was meant to catch. The argument of this page is that once a team is past static thresholds and weekday seasonality, nearly every remaining failure takes one of those two forms. By that point the statistics are the easy part.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Stated precisely: anomaly detection is the estimation of a conditional predictive distribution for a metric — what values it would take given everything routinely known about the period — followed by a decision rule on where the realised value falls in it. Alerting is the separate discipline of converting that decision into a routed, owned, actionable interruption of a named human, with the interruption budget treated as the scarce resource it is. The word "conditional" carries the weight. Conditioning on day of week is the beginner's version; conditioning on release state, marketing calendar, cohort mix and upstream data freshness is the practitioner's, and each variable added shrinks residual variance, which is what makes a detector sensitive without making it noisy.

Three traditions feed the practice and have never fully merged. Walter Shewhart's control charts at Bell Labs in 1924 supplied the founding distinction between common-cause variation, which is the process being itself, and special-cause variation, which is something interfering with it. W. Edwards Deming pressed the point Shewhart's users kept missing: reacting to common-cause variation — tampering — reliably makes a process worse. That tradition is conservative about alerting. The second is site reliability engineering, codified in Google's practice and Rob Ewaschuk's alerting philosophy: page on user-visible symptoms rather than causes, tie thresholds to an explicit objective and its error budget, and hold every page to the standard that it is urgent, actionable and novel. The third is the machine-learning tradition that arrived as metric counts exploded — Twitter's Seasonal Hybrid ESD, Facebook's Prophet, the detectors inside Amplitude, Anodot and Datadog — which decompose a series into trend, seasonalities and holiday effects and flag on the robust residual.

They sign different propositions. Shewhart–Deming will sign "most metric movements are noise and most responses to them destroy value" and will not sign "a more sensitive detector is a better detector." SRE will sign "an alert that does not demand action tonight should be a report instead" and will not sign "activation rate belongs in a paging rotation." The machine-learning school will sign "nobody can hand-tune thresholds across four thousand series" and will not sign "a flagged residual is an explanation." A fourth position, common among analytics leads, holds that the binding constraint is neither model nor coverage but attention: it will sign "the real question is how many alerts a week your organisation can metabolise" and will not sign "detection quality and response quality are separable." Refereeing two competent practitioners usually means refereeing between two of these four, and it does not resolve until someone says which they hold.

3. Mechanics in depth

Expert practice begins by refusing the mean and the standard deviation. Both are non-robust: a single incident inside the training window inflates the standard deviation, widens the band, and makes the next incident harder to detect. The robust substitutes are the median and the median absolute deviation. Cadence's mid-market cohort had fourteen weekly values before the decline — thirteen ordinary weeks around 33, and one week of 28.9 depressed by a holiday cluster. The mean is 32.82 with a standard deviation of 1.44; the median is 33.30 with a median absolute deviation of 0.50, which converts to a robust scale of 0.50 ÷ 0.6745 = 0.74. One contaminated week nearly doubled the classical estimate. A value of 31.0 is 1.26 classical deviations below the mean, unremarkable, and 3.1 robust deviations below the median, a clear flag. The estimator, not the threshold, decided the outcome.

The second move is to stop treating observations independently, because a single-point rule is superb at catching spikes and poor at catching the drifts that do most commercial damage. The formal tool is the cumulative sum: Sₜ = max(0, Sₜ₋₁ + (xₜ − μ − k)), with k conventionally half the shift you care about and a decision interval h of four or five sigma. The exponentially weighted moving average is the smoother cousin, zₜ = λxₜ + (1 − λ)zₜ₋₁, with limits at ±Lσ√(λ ÷ (2 − λ)) — which at λ = 0.2 and L = 3 sits at almost exactly one raw standard deviation. The quantity making these comparable is average run length: ARL₀ is how many periods pass before a false alarm, larger being better, and ARL₁ how many pass before a real shift is caught, smaller being better. Cadence's decline was about a 1.25-sigma shift against the robust scale.

Read rows one and four together. The three-sigma point rule and the CUSUM at h = 5 have nearly identical false-alarm rates — one spurious signal every four hundred periods — yet the CUSUM detects the drift three times faster. This is the most underused technique in product analytics: teams argue about moving from three sigma to two, trading sensitivity for noise, when the available move is to change the statistic and buy sensitivity at no cost in noise. It is rarely made because the output is harder to explain, and explainability is part of an alert's value.

The third move concerns scope: detection across a portfolio is a multiple-comparisons problem, and the arithmetic is unforgiving. Suppose an organisation monitors 400 series daily and 1.2 of them per day contain a genuinely actionable event. At a two-tailed three-sigma threshold the per-series false-alarm probability is 0.0027, so expected false alarms are 398.8 × 0.0027 = 1.08 a day. If the detector catches 72 per cent of real events, expected true positives are 0.86 and precision is 44 per cent. Nearly three alerts in five are wrong, and that is the well-behaved case.

Two conclusions follow, both routinely resisted. Alert fatigue is not a cultural failing that discipline will fix; it is arithmetic, and a team adding series faster than it tightens thresholds arrives at an ignored channel with mathematical certainty. And no threshold is simply correct: moving from three sigma to two costs seventeen extra false alarms a day to recover 0.7 missed events a week, while four sigma buys a clean queue at the price of six misses a week. The answer depends on the asymmetry of the loss, which makes the threshold a business decision in statistical clothing, belonging to whoever owns the consequence rather than the tool.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

Four conditions can be put as testable claims. The metric has a stable generative process between events. Cadence passes at cohort level, where account behaviour is stationary over months; Lumen Draft fails, because its metric's process includes a third-party model that changes without notice, so there is no normal, only a normal-since-the-last-change. The metric has enough events per period that sampling noise is smaller than the effect worth catching. For counts the Poisson approximation gives σ = √λ, so a metric averaging 40 events a day has σ = 6.3 and a three-sigma band from 21 to 59; a genuine 30 per cent drop to 28 sits at −1.9σ and never fires. Cadence's account-level metrics fail this constantly; Lumen Draft passes easily. A movement is actionable within the time detection buys. Sameer's is: a rollback takes twenty minutes. Nandita's barely is, since a five-week decline cannot be reversed in twenty-four days, which is why the lag mattered more than the detection. Measurement integrity is independently verified. Neither company monitored its own telemetry pipeline, the most common silent violation.

The idea turns actively misleading in three situations. During a deliberate change — a pricing migration, a redesign rollout — every detector reports anomalies that are the intended consequence of the decision, and teams that do not suppress deliberately end up suppressing by habit, which is how the unintended consequence of the same change goes unseen. In heavy-tailed metrics such as revenue concentrated in a few accounts, Gaussian bands are simply the wrong model. And where a metric is itself a target under management pressure, the detector becomes a compliance instrument: flags stop describing the world and start describing how well the team keeps the number inside the band.

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

In multi-product companies the seam is the shared metric with no owner. When Cadence's sign-in success rate dips, the identity team sees a platform metric within tolerance while three product teams see activation fall, and each waits for another to own it. Mature organisations say they solve this with a single accountable team per alerting metric; the honest version is that they keep a handful of composite customer-visible alerts owned by one rotation while hundreds of component metrics feed reports nobody pages on.

Two-sided marketplaces have a structural problem: the sides have different response latencies, so the fast side's anomaly is the slow side's leading indicator, and alerting on the ratio hides both. A drop in supply availability appears in demand-side conversion three to seven days later, attenuated. What works is monitoring each side separately plus a third detector on the relationship between them — a regression of conversion on availability, alerting when that residual shifts — which catches the case where both levels look normal but the coupling has broken.

Regulated contexts invert the economics: in payments, lending and health a missed anomaly can become a reportable incident, so thresholds move toward sensitivity and a 15 per cent alert precision is tolerated where a consumer app would not tolerate it. Hardware adds the connectivity confound — a fleet that stops reporting looks identical to a fleet that stopped being used — and the only defence is a heartbeat whose denominator is devices expected to report. AI-native products add the deepest problem: the quality metric is a proxy with no ground truth, and when the model changes the proxy's relationship to quality changes too. The answer is a frozen evaluation set scored on a schedule, so at least one series has a fixed instrument.

6. What separates an expert from a competent practitioner

The denominator is unmonitored more often than the numerator. Ratio metrics are alerted on constantly and their denominators almost never are. The tell is a ratio alert firing while the numerator sits inside its own band, meaning the denominator moved: fewer sessions, not worse sessions. The obvious reading is that the product got worse; the right one is usually that traffic mix changed and the product behaves identically for everyone who arrives. An expert's first click on a ratio alert is the denominator.

Threshold choice is a queue-design decision, not a per-metric one. Competent practitioners tune each detector to its own noise. Experts fix total alert volume — say twelve a week, because that is what the rotation can genuinely investigate — and allocate that budget by consequence, so an unimportant metric gets a wide band precisely because a more important one needs a narrow one. The tell is a team that can state its weekly alert budget as a number.

Detectors that learn from their own monitoring window erase the incident they exist to catch. A rolling baseline absorbs a sustained shift at a rate set by its window. With twenty-eight days and a step of 2.6σ, the apparent gap shrinks in proportion to the contaminated fraction, so by day seven it is 2.0σ, and by day ten the empirical standard deviation has inflated enough to close the window entirely. Detection is six to nine days wide and then shuts forever. The tell is a metric visibly worse than last quarter with every detector reporting normal.

Dispersion moves before level does. A degrading payment provider, an inconsistent model, an onboarding flow broken for one browser: each raises a metric's variance before moving its mean, because each affects a subset first. Experts run a second detector on rolling standard deviation. The tell is a series whose band keeps widening while its centre holds; the obvious reading is that the metric got noisier, the correct one that a subpopulation has separated from the rest.

Suppression windows are where real incidents hide. Every mature system suppresses alerts during deploys, sales and migrations, and has therefore missed a genuine incident that began inside one. The tell is a suppression rule with no expiry and no post-window reconciliation. Expert practice is to suppress paging but not detection, and to review what the suppressed detector flagged once the window closes.

The most informative signal is often the metric that did not move. If checkout conversion drops while authorisation rate, latency and traffic all sit inside their bands, the space of explanations has narrowed more than any firing alert narrows it. Competent practitioners investigate the alert; experts read the whole panel including the silence, treating non-firing correlated metrics as evidence.

A detector that stops firing looks exactly like a healthy week. Pipelines break, credentials expire, a metric is renamed and the query silently returns zero rows. Because absence of alerts is the desired state, the failure is invisible by construction. Experts monitor the monitor with a synthetic anomaly injected on a schedule, or an alert that fires when nothing has fired for an unusually long stretch. The tell is a team that cannot say when its system last fired correctly.

The unit of analysis, not the threshold, decides what is detectable. This is Nandita's lesson and the deepest of the ten. An anomaly confined to a segment is diluted in the aggregate roughly by the segment's share, so a 28 per cent drop in a cohort holding 19 per cent of volume appears as 5.3 per cent at the top, inside any sensible band. Detectors on every segment are not the answer either, since that multiplies Table 2's arithmetic by the number of segments. The expert compromise is a few deliberately chosen cuts — cohort, plan, platform, region — each with a widened threshold, trading per-segment sensitivity for the ability to see anything at all below the aggregate.

7. How this differs by product type and company stage

Across consumer, B2B and enterprise the difference is real and it is about volume, not sophistication. Consumer products have the observation counts for statistical detection to run unattended. Enterprise products, where a metric may be two or three events a week per account, do not, and their working systems are rule-based and account-level — usage below half an account's own trailing median for three straight weeks — plus human review of a watchlist. Cadence's most valuable detector is not statistical at all. Marketplaces differ because of the coupling problem above; hardware because the physical return path is slow, so a firmware-induced regression caught three weeks late means three weeks of shipped units; AI products because the baseline is non-stationary by construction.

Where the difference is overstated is stage. Early-stage companies are said not to need anomaly detection because the founders watch the numbers. Half right: they do not need infrastructure, but they need the conditioning discipline just as much, and their characteristic failure is not a missed alert but a small-sample movement misread as signal and steered on — Deming's tampering, with the roadmap as the funnel. Past roughly a hundred people the change is organisational: the person who notices is no longer the person who can act, so routing, ownership and severity tiering become the hard part.

8. Three worked examples

Cadence: finding the signal by changing the unit

After February, Nandita rebuilt detection around cohort-level CUSUMs on eleven metrics with the alert budget fixed at fifteen a week. On the mid-market cohort, using the robust scale of 0.74 computed earlier, the 1.25σ decline would have crossed the decision interval in week 11 rather than surfacing by accident in week 14 — in renewal terms, the difference between a save motion and a post-mortem. The cause was a September release that moved a bulk-import function behind a plan gate; mid-market accounts, its heaviest users, had quietly stopped running their Monday batch jobs. Thirty-nine of the 214 churned; Cadence estimated week-11 detection would have saved twelve to eighteen, roughly $600,000 in recurring revenue.

Lumen Draft: where the approach failed

Sameer's detector did not merely miss the regression; it certified it as normal. By 11 March the twenty-eight-day baseline held nine contaminated days, so its mean had risen from 11.4 to 12.2 per cent and its standard deviation from 0.41 to 0.68. The realised 13.9 per cent scored (13.9 − 12.2) ÷ 0.68 = 2.5σ, inside a three-sigma rule; by 18 March, with sixteen contaminated days, it scored 1.4σ and was indistinguishable from normal. A self-referential baseline cannot detect a sustained shift for longer than a fraction of its own window. Recovery took three changes: a 600-prompt evaluation set scored nightly against pinned model versions, giving one series a fixed instrument; a CUSUM alongside the point rule, which on the same data crossed its decision interval on 7 March, four days before the support cluster; and the provider's version identifier as a required dimension on every event. The four-day delay cost roughly ₹11 lakh in refunds and involuntary churn.

Hearth: the anomaly that was the instrument

Hearth, a connected water-purifier manufacturer with 340,000 installed units, saw daily active devices fall 21 per cent over nine days. Three detectors fired and the growth team opened a churn investigation. The cause was a firmware release that changed the telemetry heartbeat from five minutes to fifteen, so devices sending fewer than four beacons an hour fell out of the active definition. Usage had not changed at all. The recovery was a denominator monitor — devices expected to report, from shipment and registration records — and a rule that any alert where the expected-to-observed ratio moves is a measurement incident routed to data engineering, not a product incident routed to growth. Eleven analyst-days had gone into a metric that never moved.

9. Failure modes and their early warning signs

Each announces itself first as an absence — of alerts, of contradiction, of acknowledgement — and absences are the hardest thing for an organisation to notice on a schedule. That is why the practices distinguishing serious programmes are review rituals rather than technical controls: a monthly precision recount, a quarterly baseline refresh with a contamination check, and a standing agenda item asking what the system failed to tell anyone.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Should product metrics ever page a human outside working hours? The SRE position reserves paging for conditions where delay compounds damage and a human can act tonight, and holds that activation and retention anomalies fail that test and belong in a morning report. The opposing position, common among consumer growth leaders, is that a marketing misconfiguration or a broken signup flow burns money hourly and that the infrastructure-versus-product line is an artefact of org charts. The evidence differs in kind: the SRE case rests on measured degradation of response quality under sleep disruption, the growth case on incidents with quantified overnight losses. For the SRE position to be wrong, the expected overnight loss from product anomalies would have to exceed the expected loss from a degraded rotation — a comparison almost nobody has made.

Learned detectors or hand-set rules? The machine-learning case is that coverage is the real gap, that hand-tuning does not scale past a few dozen series, and that decomposition handles seasonality better than any human will. The rules case is that a learned detector's flags are uninterpretable at the moment of highest stress, that its failures correlate with the events you most care about because it was trained on contaminated history, and that such teams end with more alerts and fewer actions. This is empirically resolvable and largely unresolved, because almost nobody publishes precision against a labelled incident log. For the ML case to be wrong, marginal alerts beyond the first twenty or so series would have to contribute negative value once queue effects are counted — which Table 2 suggests is possible.

Should level shifts alert at all? One school holds that a permanent step change is a strategic fact best handled in a weekly review with full context, and that alerting on it produces panic without analysis. The other holds that the gap between a level shift and its review is exactly the window in which the change is still cheaply reversible. The disagreement is about reversibility, and each side is right about different products: a pricing change is not reversible in a week; a release that breaks a flow is reversible in an hour.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this configures detectors. Someone who has internalised it designs the response first and works backwards: how many investigations a week the team can complete, what one costs in hours, what a miss costs in each direction — and only then chooses statistics that fit the budget. They state their queue's precision as a measured number. They distrust any baseline not checked for contamination since the last incident. They reach for the segment and the denominator before the dashboard. They treat a quiet week as a claim requiring verification. And they will say in a leadership meeting that a movement is statistically real and commercially irrelevant, or too small to detect and large enough to matter — the two sentences separating someone who understands the instrument from someone operated by it.

12. What each protagonist decided

Nandita escalated on 6 February without waiting for a detector to confirm anything, reasoning that the cohort evidence was already stronger than any alert would be and that the renewal calendar made a false alarm trivially cheap against delay. She then rebuilt detection at cohort level and — the harder decision — cut Cadence's monitored series from forty-one to nineteen, holding the alert budget fixed while adding segmentation. Sameer pinned the model version at 06:40 on 12 March and delayed his launch nine days, accepting a known cost against an unbounded one; the frozen evaluation set later showed the release had degraded instruction-following on long prompts by 9 per cent, confirming a decision already made on judgement.

  1. Cadence's aggregate metric was correct and its detector was correctly configured, and the company still nearly lost $9.1 million of renewals. If neither was wrong, what exactly failed, and whose job was it?
  2. Lumen Draft's baseline absorbed the incident within nine days. What is the longest sustained regression your own most important metric's baseline would absorb before the flag disappeared — and how would you find out without waiting for one?
  3. Given Table 2, a team can have a clean alert queue or a low miss rate, not both. Whose decision is that trade-off in your organisation, and on what evidence about the cost of a miss is it currently being made?

13. Going deeper

Signal vs noise; product vs measurement is the prerequisite assumed throughout: the Hearth example is unreadable without it. Constructing a funnel matters next because the segment-versus-aggregate problem is solved by having a structure to alert on rather than a list of metrics; it unlocks stage-level detection, which localises an anomaly before the investigation starts. Reading drop-off converts a fired alert into a diagnosis, the gap this page names and does not fill. Defining activation identifies the metric where detection latency pays most, since activation failures are fast-moving and cheaply reversible. Cohort analysis is the direct remedy for Nandita's failure. Retention curves and the PMF signal supply the slow-moving baselines where drift detection earns its keep. Stickiness and natural frequency gives a metric's natural period, the input every windowing decision depends on: alert daily on a weekly-frequency product and you will detect nothing but noise.

Milaan Systems: Nine Days of Silence

Bengaluru, Sunday 8 November 2026

1. The night before

At a quarter past eleven on Sunday night, Nandita Iyer sat at her dining table in Indiranagar with two printouts in front of her: a one-page incident summary for Hiranya Finserv, and the 2027 investment plan for Pulse, the alerting product she had owned for three years. Open on her laptop was a third document she had not printed — the disposition log of every alert Milaan Systems had generated in ninety days, 41,882 rows she had been reading since Friday evening and did not yet know how to describe in a sentence.

At nine the next morning, on Old Airport Road, the executive team would decide how to spend ₹6.2 crore and fourteen engineers, and Nandita was expected to bring a recommendation. Prakash Nair, the chief executive, had asked for it in four words on Thursday: "Tell us what broke." She had spent the weekend discovering that the honest answer had at least three parts, that they pointed in different directions, and that the exhibit her own team had prepared to support the recommendation was, on the fourth reading, not quite true.

The last of the Diwali lights were still up on the building opposite. Hiranya's chief financial officer had asked for a written root-cause statement by Friday, addressed to his statutory auditors and his board's risk committee. Gautam Bhalla, in New Jersey, had asked whether he could quote a ten-minute detection guarantee to a processor in Newark. Both requests sat in the same inbox, and Nandita could not see a version of Monday morning in which she said yes to one without making the other false.

2. How Milaan came to be built this way

Milaan Systems was founded in Bengaluru in 2019 by Prakash Nair and Sridhar Venkataraman, who had spent eleven years between them inside the reconciliation functions of Indian payment companies and shared one conviction: in Indian digital payments money rarely disappears, but it very often goes to the wrong ledger and stays there quietly. Milaan sold what it called settlement assurance: it ingested gateway feeds, switch files, bank statements, virtual-account postings and the customer's own ledger, matched them against one another, and raised an alert when a rupee that should have arrived somewhere had not. By late 2026 it had 310 customers, ₹96 crore of annual recurring revenue, 240 employees across Bengaluru, Pune, Singapore, Toronto, Berlin and New Jersey, and coverage over roughly ₹1.9 lakh crore of annualised payment volume.

One decision, in March 2023, shaped everything after it. To win its first large enterprise contract Milaan agreed to a service-level clause it has since copied into 140 agreements: material settlement anomalies will be surfaced to the customer within thirty minutes of detection, at a documented false-alert rate below five per cent, with service credits for breach capped at fifteen per cent of annual fees. Sridhar had argued that the clause was survivable because its two halves pulled against each other and Milaan could choose which to honour. In practice the company honoured the second. A false-alert rate above five per cent was contractually visible; a missed anomaly was not, because nobody outside the company could count the things Milaan had failed to say.

To hold the line, the solutions team began hand-tuning thresholds customer by customer: every implementation produced bands, seasonal exclusions and suppression rules written during onboarding. By November 2026 there were 640 such rule sets in production, and a triage desk of nine analysts in Bengaluru sat between the detection engine and the customer, reviewing every candidate alert before it went out. The desk was the company's quality mechanism, its cost centre, and, as Nandita had come to suspect over the weekend, its blind spot.

3. The market Milaan sells into

India's payments stack had become, by 2026, enormous and structurally unforgiving. UPI cleared well over 20 billion transactions a month; NPCI's mandate rails carried recurring collections for lenders, insurers and subscription businesses; the RBI's payment aggregator regime had made escrow discipline a supervisory matter rather than housekeeping; ONDC had added settlement complexity for sellers whose orders, logistics and payments moved through different participants. For a mid-sized lender, money now passed through four or five hands before it landed, and reconciliation was no longer a month-end activity.

Milaan competed on three fronts. Aggregators such as Razorpay, Cashfree and PhonePe gave their own merchants reconciliation dashboards free, capping what Milaan could charge the small end of the market. Global observability vendors bundled generic anomaly detection into platforms finance teams already paid for, which made "we detect unusual patterns" hard to sell as a line item. And Infosys, TCS and their peers would build a bespoke reconciliation engine for any bank willing to fund it. Milaan's defence was domain depth: it knew what a broken escrow leg looked like in a way a general-purpose tool did not.

The exposure was no longer purely Indian. Fourteen per cent of ARR came from the Gulf, anchored by Al Khatib Retail Group in Dubai, a 190-store grocery and general-merchandise chain signed in March 2026, whose settlement rails, instant-payment behaviour and weekend cycle bore no resemblance to India's. The DPDP Act had meanwhile forced a review of what payer-level data Milaan could hold and for how long; the company had settled on a seven-day window for hashed payer identifiers, a decision taken in 2024 as much for storage cost as for principle, and one that now sat in the middle of a product argument.

4. What happened, in the order it was believed

On 24 August 2026 the sponsor bank for Hiranya Finserv — a Pune-headquartered NBFC with roughly ₹180 crore a month of UPI Autopay collections across 11.4 lakh active mandates — began a planned core-banking migration. Hiranya was informed; Milaan was not, because nothing in the contract required it to be.

From 28 August, borrower accounts were debited exactly as before and the money reached the bank. But postings for one of Hiranya's two escrow legs were written against a virtual-account prefix the migration had retired, so the funds sat in an unallocated suspense pool instead of flowing into Hiranya's loan management system. Over nine days ₹41.6 crore accumulated there; roughly 62,000 borrowers were marked as having missed an instalment, and about 9,400 received dunning messages for money they had already paid.

Pulse fired once. At 03:14 IST on 29 August, an alert was raised on Hiranya's "unallocated settlement ratio" — severity low, notify-only, routed to the Bengaluru triage queue rather than to the customer. At 10:20 the same morning a triage analyst closed it with the disposition code SEASONAL and the free-text note: "Ganesh Chaturthi week, collections timing shifts every year, matches Sep-2025 pattern, monitor." He was not being careless. His screen showed a green seasonal-context badge, a design Ira Mehta's team had shipped in 2024 precisely to damp festival-period false alerts, and the year-ago comparison it drew on did show a similar-shaped bump.

Nothing else fired for nine days. Hiranya's total inbound settlement value stayed inside its control band throughout, because the money did arrive at the bank; only its allocation across legs was wrong. Milaan monitored value, count, success rate and unallocated ratio at customer level. The quantity that had actually broken — postings per virtual-account prefix — was not, on 28 August, a metric anyone had defined.

On 7 September Hiranya's finance team noticed the gap at month-close and telephoned their customer-success manager. The incident was reopened, root-caused within eleven hours, and the funds re-allocated by 12 September. Milaan's post-incident review, circulated on 18 September, concluded that "detection coverage was adequate; the failure was in triage disposition." Nandita had signed it. On Friday 6 November, pulling the ninety-day log, she found that of 2,314 alerts closed as SEASONAL since July, 197 had later been reopened by someone else, and that the Hiranya alert had been the fourth SEASONAL closure of a Saturday shift staffed by two analysts instead of the usual five.

That was the first thing she had been wrong about. The second surfaced on Saturday, when Dev Rathore in Toronto sent her the arithmetic behind the contractual false-alert rate. The 2.8 per cent Milaan reported to customers was computed over alerts that had reached customers — the output of the triage desk, after 68 per cent of candidates had been suppressed. Computed over everything the engine generated, the figure was 31 per cent. Neither was false. They answered different questions, and the contract did not say which it meant.

7. Voices

— Mohan Kulkarni, CFO, Hiranya Finserv, in a call with Prakash Nair, 29 October 2026

8. The options as Nandita sees them

  • A. Rebuild the detection layer. Replace the 640 rule sets with a hierarchical model that scans segments automatically, so a series like Exhibit 4's escrow leg is watched without anyone having thought to name it. Sridhar wants it, Prakash can sell it to Sahyog and Gautam can turn it into a claim. It costs ₹6.2 crore, needs fourteen engineers Anjali cannot release, and depends on a retention change Ritu has refused. It also assumes the binding constraint was that the anomaly was not found — which Exhibit 1 does not obviously support.
  • B. Fix the human layer. Severity routing that cannot be set to notify-only without a named owner, a follow-the-sun triage rota across Bengaluru, Singapore and Toronto, mandatory audit of closed alerts, and no one-click bulk close. Cheap, fast, and the only option that touches the 197 reopenings in Exhibit 2 — a number Nandita suspects is a fraction of the truth. It gives a salesperson nothing to say and a board deck nothing to show, and it worsens Shalini's queue before it improves it.
  • C. Productise the judgement. Expose detection settings to customers, publish a confidence score with every alert, and renegotiate the SLA from a detection guarantee to an obligation to surface and explain. It makes Milaan honest about what it can promise and pushes the decision to whoever owns the money. It also invites 140 customers to reopen commercial terms in the quarter Milaan is raising, and Mohan Kulkarni's remark suggests the customer may not want the judgement handed back.

Nandita had put these three on one slide and stared at it long enough to notice what it presumed. All three treated the question as how well Milaan detects. None asked what Exhibit 3 makes plain — that the company had spent three years measuring detection from a clock that starts when Milaan is already sure — and none addressed the fact that the quantity which broke at Hiranya had never been a metric at all. A fourth framing had occurred to her around ten that night, and she had not written it down, because she could not tell whether it was an insight or an excuse.

9. The deadline and the constraints

The decision is due at nine on Monday 9 November: the 2027 plan goes to the board on 20 November and Sahyog's investment committee meets on 27 November. Hiranya's written root-cause statement is due Friday 13 November; Mohan Kulkarni has not said whether Hiranya renews its ₹4.8 crore contract in February, and his auditors will read whatever Milaan writes. Al Khatib renews in April 2027 at ₹6.3 crore, and its auditors have already asked Ritu Kaul what payer data Milaan holds. Gautam's Newark deal, roughly ₹11 crore ARR, closes or dies in January, and its lawyers want the false-alert methodology in writing — a request nobody has answered.

Money is the smallest constraint: ₹52 crore in the bank, eighteen months of runway. People bind. Anjali has eight engineers where she had eleven; Dev is one person in Toronto at a band equal to four in Pune; Ira has asked twice for a researcher. Any option consuming fourteen engineers consumes the Gulf ingestion work Al Khatib's renewal rests on. And the 2023 clause sits in 140 signed agreements: Milaan cannot quietly redefine "detection" in an assurance pack without either telling customers or hoping none of them reads Exhibit 3 the way Nandita finally read it on Friday night.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 1 and 4 together, state precisely what failed at Hiranya Finserv. How many distinct failures are there, and which is an alerting failure?
  2. Exhibit 3 reports full SLA compliance for a quarter containing a nine-day miss. Is that report wrong? What would you have to change to make it both accurate and useful?
  3. Exhibit 2 gives two false-alert rates, 2.8 per cent and 31 per cent. Which one should Milaan manage against, and what does each choice do to the behaviour of the triage desk?
  4. Shalini Menon's bulk-close practice produces the Gulf CSAT of 4.6 and the pattern in Exhibit 5. Is she managing a queue or concealing a defect, and how would Milaan tell the difference?
  5. Dev Rathore's prototype claims it would have caught the break on day one, on 34 self-labelled incidents. What would you need to see before funding Option A on that claim — and what would you do if the retention window needed to test it cannot lawfully be opened?
  6. What should Nandita say at nine on Monday morning, and what should she write to the board on 20 November? If those two statements differ, say why, and say which one she should be willing to defend in front of Mohan Kulkarni.

11. Sunday, continued

By half past one Nandita had reduced Monday's slide to a single line and then deleted it. The trouble was not that she lacked an answer; she had four, and each required her to believe something about her own company that the others contradicted. If Sridhar was right, three years of hand-tuning were a debt and the money should retire it. If Ira was right, the debt was in the interface, and the money would buy a more sophisticated way of not noticing. If Anjali was right, both were arguing about the last mile of a road that ended two hours earlier. And if Mohan Kulkarni was right, the thing Milaan sold — the promise that someone would know — had always depended on a person at the other end who was awake, empowered and looking, and nobody at Milaan had ever asked whether such a person existed.

She closed the disposition log without saving her filters. Behind the spreadsheet the green seasonal badge was still on her screen, a small, well-designed rectangle that had once seemed an obvious improvement. She turned off the lamp and left the two printouts where they were.
