Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation · Product Analytics & Data Practice

Device Telemetry and Fleet Analytics

What does the data streaming back from thousands of devices in the field actually tell you about the health of the fleet — and where does that story stop being true?

1. A Tuesday in March, Bengaluru

On the morning of 12 March 2024, Devika Rao, VP of Product at Urja Swap Networks, opened a dashboard she had been staring at for three weeks and still could not fully trust. Urja ran 410 battery-swap stations across Bengaluru, Pune and Jaipur, circulating 38,000 lithium-ion packs through a fleet of electric two-wheelers used mostly by food-delivery and quick-commerce riders. A rider pulled into a station, docked a depleted pack, and fifteen seconds later rode off with a charged one. The business existed because riders could not afford to wait forty minutes to charge a battery themselves; Urja's whole value proposition was that a pack was always ready.

Each pack carried a battery-management system, or BMS, that measured voltage, current, internal temperature and cycle count, and reported them over a mix of cellular and LPWAN radio links every time it was docked, plus an hourly heartbeat while idle. Devika's engineering team had built a "Fleet Health Score" meant to flag packs likely to fail before they did — important because two packs in Jaipur had overheated in January, and although neither had caused an injury, the news cycle around electric-scooter battery fires elsewhere in the country made the board unwilling to tolerate a repeat. Summer was six weeks away, ambient temperatures in Jaipur would cross 42°C by May, and thermal stress on lithium-ion cells rises sharply with heat. Devika had to decide, by 1 April, whether to ship the health score to station operators fleet-wide, delay it, or ship a narrower version. Getting this wrong in either direction was expensive: false alarms would have operators pulling thousands of perfectly good packs out of rotation during peak delivery season, at a replacement cost of roughly ₹9,000 per pack pulled unnecessarily; missed warnings risked exactly the failure the board feared.

2. The idea: what telemetry and fleet analytics actually are

Device telemetry is the automated, remote transmission of measurements from a device to a system that can store and act on them — the device instrumenting itself and reporting back without a human present to read a gauge. Fleet analytics is the discipline of aggregating that telemetry across every device in a population to answer questions no single device's data can answer alone: how healthy is the fleet, how is it being used, and which devices are drifting toward failure.

The word "telemetry" is older than computing — it comes from the Greek for "distant measure" and was used for remote instrument readings as early as the 1900s in weather balloons and, more famously, in the Soviet and American space programmes of the 1950s and 60s, where an engineer on the ground needed to know a rocket's fuel pressure and skin temperature without being aboard it. Industrial equipment makers borrowed the idea decades later: GE Aviation began pulling engine-performance data off aircraft in the 1990s to plan maintenance before a part failed rather than after, and elevator companies such as Otis followed with similar programmes for lifts. What changed telemetry from a specialist aerospace practice into a mainstream product-management skill was the arrival of cheap connectivity — the BLE, Wi-Fi, cellular and LPWAN radios that let even a ₹3,000 sensor phone home affordably. Once transmission became cheap, the constraint moved from "can we get the data" to "what do we do with it once we have millions of readings a day," and that second question is fleet analytics.

The sentence Devika could say in a board meeting without sounding glib: "Telemetry turns every device in the field into a sensor for the whole fleet, and fleet analytics turns that stream of sensor readings into a running, fleet-wide estimate of health, usage and risk that no single device's data could give us."

3. How it actually works, step by step

Walking through Urja's pipeline exposes the steps most people skip when they describe telemetry as if data simply "arrives." First, instrumentation: someone decided which signals the BMS firmware would capture at all — voltage, current, temperature, cycle count, station ID, GPS fix. Anything not instrumented at this stage cannot be recovered later, however good the analytics team is; Urja's first-generation packs, for instance, never logged the exact charge rate at each station, which later turned out to matter.

Second, transport. A docked pack talks to the station over BLE and the station backhauls to the cloud over cellular; an idle pack in a rider's scooter reports over LPWAN, a low-power wide-area radio built for infrequent, small messages rather than continuous streaming. This matters because LPWAN devices deliberately sleep between transmissions to conserve battery, so "the pack didn't report" can mean the pack is fine and asleep, or the pack is in trouble — telemetry absence is ambiguous by design, not a bug.

Third, ingestion: messages arrive out of order, duplicated by retries, occasionally days late from a pack that was in a connectivity dead zone. A pipeline that assumes clean, ordered arrival will quietly corrupt every downstream number. Fourth, identity resolution: a raw message must be matched to a specific pack in an asset registry, and packs get swapped between scooters, reassigned between cities, and occasionally have their identifiers reused after decommissioning — a step teams routinely under-invest in until a "phantom failure spike" turns out to be one physical pack's history wrongly split across two IDs.

Fifth, enrichment: joining the raw reading with context — which station, which city, what was the ambient temperature that day, which firmware version. Sixth, aggregation into events and funnels: a swap is a small funnel — pack docked, authenticated, diagnostics passed, charge completed, pack released — and fleet analytics runs funnel and cohort analysis over these device-level events rather than over human user sessions. Seventh, computing indices such as uptime, mean time between failures (MTBF) and a composite health score. Eighth, surfacing the result to someone who can act — an operator, a planner, a firmware engineer. A dashboard nobody consults is not fleet analytics; it is a chart.

4. A worked example: uptime and MTBF, and what changes when a definition changes

Devika's team pulled a slice of 500 packs and tracked them for 30 days. Over that window, the packs together accumulated 500 × 30 = 15,000 pack-days in service. Field logs showed the average pack was in active duty — docked, discharging or charging — for about 14 hours a day, giving 15,000 × 14 = 210,000 pack-hours of operation. During those 30 days, 18 packs were pulled from service for a genuine fault (a cell imbalance or thermal-cutoff event, not a routine swap). Mean time between failures is total operating time divided by number of failures:

QuantityValue
Packs tracked500
Days tracked30
Avg. active hours/pack/day14
Operating hours (packs × days × hrs/day)210,000
Genuine faults logged18
MTBF210,000 / 18 ≈ 11,667 hrs (≈ 486 days)

That single number — a pack fails, on average, roughly every 486 days of active use — sounds reassuring until Devika's data scientist, based in Toronto and working the overnight-for-Bengaluru shift, asked the obvious next question: how much of the fleet did this 18 even see? The team also computed telemetry coverage, defined as the share of the 500 packs that sent at least one heartbeat within every rolling 24-hour window across the month: 460 of 500, or 92%. That looked healthy, and it was the number in the first draft of the board slide.

Then came the second pass. Because January's near-miss fires had both occurred after a pack went quiet for several hours before failing, Devika's engineers tightened the definition of "actively monitored" from a 24-hour heartbeat window to a 6-hour one — the interval within which they wanted to guarantee they could catch a developing thermal event. Recomputing coverage under this stricter definition, only 340 of 500 packs met it: 68%, not 92%. Nothing about the fleet's actual health had changed between the two calculations; only the yardstick had. The gap was explained by LPWAN duty-cycling — idle packs deliberately slept for up to eight hours to save their own charge, which is exactly why the network chosen for a use case matters, and exactly why one input (the coverage window) can turn a green metric into an amber one without a single pack getting worse.

5. The nuances a learner must sit with

Telemetry is not ground truth. A sensor reads what it reads, not what is physically true; a thermistor near the terminal, not the cell core, can under-read a hot cell by several degrees. Treating a dashboard as reality rather than a noisy proxy for it is the root of most overconfidence in fleet data.
Silence is not a health signal, it is a missing observation. A pack that stops reporting has left the sample, not proven it is fine. Averages computed only over packs still reporting will always look better than the true fleet, because the ones in the worst trouble are disproportionately the ones that go dark.
"In the fleet," "active," and "reporting" are three different denominators. Urja owned 38,000 packs; perhaps 34,000 were deployed rather than in warehouse stock; of those, only the ones meeting a coverage threshold were "monitored." Every fleet metric should state which of these three counts it divides by, because switching denominators silently is the single most common way a number is made to look better than it is.
Sampling cadence is a design choice, not a fact of nature. As Section 4 showed, tightening a window from 24 hours to 6 changes conclusions without changing the fleet, because the radio technology itself trades battery life for reporting frequency.
Correlation across the fleet can hide a confound. Packs in Jaipur ran hotter and failed more often than packs in Bengaluru; before concluding heat causes failure, note that Jaipur's stations also had the oldest firmware, because that region was onboarded first. Cohort and city were confounded, and disentangling them required deliberately comparing same-firmware packs across cities.
A usage funnel and a health funnel are different instruments. The swap funnel (docked → authenticated → charged → released) measures process friction and throughput; a health score measures physical degradation. A station with a smooth funnel can still be circulating packs that are quietly wearing out, because funnel completion says nothing about what happens to the pack after release.
Firmware and hardware cohorts must be kept separate. Pooling first-generation and third-generation packs into one fleet-wide average produces a number that describes no real pack, because the two cohorts fail for different reasons at different rates.
Telemetry cannot explain why, only that. It told Urja a pack's internal resistance was rising; it could not say whether that was a manufacturing defect, a bad charge cycle, or ordinary end-of-life wear, without a technician physically inspecting a sample of flagged units.

6. Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and early versus large

In consumer IoT — a fitness band or a smart thermostat — telemetry is constrained by privacy and battery life as much as by radio range; users can revoke consent, and firmware must assume long gaps between connections. In B2B and industrial settings, such as commercial refrigeration or elevators, telemetry is typically written into the contract itself: an annual maintenance agreement may promise 99% uptime, and telemetry exists partly to prove compliance, which changes who is incentivised to interpret a reading generously. Urja sits in a third pattern, the operated marketplace fleet: the platform owns the devices but does not control how hard any individual rider uses them on a given day, so usage variance is enormous and must be normalised before health comparisons mean anything.

Stage matters as much as category. An early-stage company with 500 devices can get away with a spreadsheet and a founder personally reading fault logs; past a few thousand devices that approach breaks, and dedicated data engineering, automated cohorting and alerting thresholds become necessary. Urja, at 38,000 packs, was well past that point, which was precisely why getting the score's assumptions right, rather than merely shipping it fast, was the actual decision in front of Devika.

7. Common mistakes

Mistake: treating the average health score as the fleet's risk. Symptom: leadership sees one number trending up and relaxes. Underlying error: an average hides a long tail of a few genuinely dangerous devices inside a large population of fine ones. Cheapest diagnostic: look at the score's distribution, not its mean, and track the count of devices in the worst decile.

Mistake: excluding non-reporting devices from calculations rather than flagging them. Symptom: fleet metrics that always look better than field complaints suggest. Underlying error: silence is quietly treated as "no data, so don't count it" instead of "unknown, possibly bad." Diagnostic: recompute every headline metric twice, once excluding silent devices and once assuming the worst case for them; a wide gap between the two is itself the finding.

Mistake: skipping identity resolution. Symptom: a device's health history shows an impossible jump, as if it aged five years overnight. Underlying error: two physical units were merged under one ID, or one unit's history was split across two IDs after reassignment. Diagnostic: audit for duplicate first-seen timestamps and for IDs whose reported location teleports.

Mistake: reaching for a machine-learning failure-prediction model before basic definitions are agreed. Symptom: a sophisticated model that different teams do not trust and quietly override with their own spreadsheets. Underlying error: nobody agreed what "active," "failure," or "in the fleet" meant before modelling began, so the model was trained on an inconsistent label. Diagnostic: ask three people on the team to independently compute this month's uptime by hand; if they disagree, the model has no chance.

8. What good looks like

A large elevator-services operator that does this well publishes a weekly fleet report segmented by installation cohort and firmware version, states its coverage denominator on every slide, and treats any unit that has gone silent for longer than its expected reporting window as "unknown, investigate" rather than "assumed fine." Its health score is deliberately conservative: it flags more units than technicians can inspect in a day, and the operations team, not the data team, decides the cut line, because they carry the cost of both false alarms and missed failures. The result is not a perfect score; it is an organisation that trusts the number enough to act on it, and that knows exactly what it does not yet know.

9. What Devika decided

Devika shipped the Fleet Health Score on 1 April, but only for the two firmware cohorts with more than 90 days of stable telemetry history and at least 85% six-hour coverage — about 22,000 of the 38,000 packs. For the remaining, mostly older, packs she published coverage honestly as "insufficiently monitored" rather than silently omitting them from the fleet-wide number, and she asked station operators in Jaipur to physically spot-check a sample of those older packs weekly until better telemetry could be retrofitted. The reasoning traced directly back to the nuances above: shipping one blended score across cohorts of different firmware and different coverage would have produced a number nobody could act on responsibly, and a false sense of coverage was more dangerous, going into a hot summer, than an honest gap. The natural next topic for her team to study was leading indicators from device data — how to move from describing a pack's current health to forecasting, days in advance, which pack is likely to need attention next. Two questions worth sitting with: when your dashboard shows a metric improving, have you checked which denominator moved rather than which devices got healthier? And what would your fleet's silence be hiding if the worst 5% of devices were exactly the ones most likely to stop reporting?
case40v1-ana.hw.telemetry:
Case · Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation

Jalanidhi Water Systems: The Green Badge

Eleven thousand connected water systems, one colour-coded promise, and a board meeting in nine hours.

1. Baner, Pune — 23 June 2026, 11.40 p.m.

The monsoon had arrived four days early and Aparna Bhide's window rattled every time a gust came off the Mula. On her laptop were two tabs. The first was a signature packet from Al Sidrah Facilities Management LLC in Dubai: 2,400 units across hospital and school campuses, ₹14 crore over three years, the largest contract Jalanidhi Water Systems had ever been offered, with a signature window that closed on 30 June. Clause 7.3 of that packet wrote Jalanidhi's “Jal Assure” monitoring badge into the service level agreement by name.

The second tab was a letter, dated 18 June, from the group procurement head at Vasantika Hospitals. It gave Jalanidhi thirty days to produce an independent verification plan, failing which the hospital chain would terminate a ₹4.6 crore annual contract covering 640 units across nine facilities in Maharashtra and Gujarat. The letter attached a NABL-accredited laboratory report from the group's Rajkot hospital showing total coliform in water dispensed from a Jalanidhi unit on 11 March. Jalanidhi's dashboard had shown that unit green, continuously, for 187 days.

Aparna had spent the evening rereading the audit her team had finished that afternoon. It did not say the fleet was unsafe. It did not say the fleet was safe either. What it said, in a sentence she had read perhaps twenty times, was that for 1,340 units the badge on the dashboard reflected the last reading received rather than the current state of the device, and that the system had no way of telling the two apart. At 9.15 a.m. the board would want to know whether to sign Dubai.

2. How Jalanidhi got here

Devang Marathe founded Jalanidhi in 2019 after eleven years in industrial filtration, with a thesis that the Indian market for institutional drinking water was stuck between two bad options: cheap point-of-use purifiers from the consumer brands — Eureka Forbes' Aquaguard, HUL's Pureit, Kent, Livpure — that nobody maintained on schedule, and expensive bottled-water contracts that generated plastic and invoices in equal measure. Jalanidhi's answer was a wall-mounted reverse-osmosis-plus-ultraviolet system with a cellular SIM in it, sold not as a product but as a per-litre service: the customer paid ₹0.42 a litre dispensed, and Jalanidhi owned the box, the filters and the maintenance.

The connectivity was the pitch. Every unit reported flow, inlet and permeate total dissolved solids, membrane differential pressure, ultraviolet lamp power-on hours and door-open events over a Jio or Airtel M2M SIM. In 2023 the company wrapped that stream in a customer-facing badge — green, amber, red — called Jal Assure, and the marketing line, approved by Devang personally, was “continuously monitored water safety.” Facility managers loved it. It turned an invisible service into a number they could show their own bosses.

One earlier decision constrains everything available to Aparna tonight. In August 2022, bidding for a Maharashtra school-programme tender funded partly through CSR budgets, Jalanidhi had to reach a unit price the tender could accept. The team took ₹2,100 out of the bill of materials, and the two items removed were the inline ultraviolet-intensity sensor and the second pressure transducer. UV lamp health would instead be inferred from a power-on-hours counter and a lamp-life constant. The reasoning at the time was documented and, on its own terms, sound: lamps degrade predictably with hours, and a counter is cheaper than a photodiode. Jalanidhi won the tender, 4,100 school units, and then used the same cost-reduced board in every unit it built until late 2024, because carrying two hardware variants was expensive.

The consequence, which nobody wrote down as a consequence, is that 6,800 of the 11,600 units in the field today cannot measure whether their ultraviolet lamp is actually emitting. They can only measure that it has been switched on. The Rajkot lamp had failed on 29 January. Its ballast continued to draw current. The counter continued to count.

3. The industry

Institutional water in India sits between several authorities and is owned outright by none of them. Drinking-water quality is specified by BIS in IS 10500. Packaged drinking water is licensed by FSSAI, which does not apply to a point-of-use dispenser. Laboratories are accredited by NABL, and a hospital's infection-control committee typically runs its own quarterly microbiological tests regardless of what a vendor promises. Public programmes such as the Jal Jeevan Mission have made water quality a boardroom word in a way it was not a decade ago; CSR committees fund school installations and then want dashboards; and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act has made even site-level consumption data something Jalanidhi's contracts now have to speak to explicitly.

The competitive field is crowded at both ends. Eureka Forbes and Kent have brand and service density Jalanidhi cannot match. Tata Chemicals and a dozen regional integrators compete on institutional tenders. Newer entrants bundle service through platforms in the way Urban Company organised home services. What Jalanidhi has that they do not, or did not until recently, is the telemetry story — which is precisely the asset now in question.

Abroad, the Gulf is Jalanidhi's first real export market. Al Sidrah manages facilities for hospital and school campuses across Dubai and Sharjah, and Dubai Municipality requires third-party laboratory verification of dispensed water on a quarterly cycle regardless of any vendor's monitoring. Joanne Tay, who covers the account from Singapore, has pointed out more than once that this makes the Gulf contract both easier and harder: the badge is not load-bearing there in the way it has become in India, but Al Sidrah's procurement team has nonetheless written it into clause 7.3 because it is what the sales deck promised.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Through 2024 the fleet grew and the dashboards stayed green. Coverage, reported monthly to the board, ran at 97–98 per cent, computed as the share of units that had sent at least one message in the preceding thirty days. Nobody asked what a thirty-day window meant for a promise described as continuous.

In September 2025, after a monsoon in which patchy cellular coverage in Konkan and northern Gujarat produced a wave of amber badges on units that were, on inspection, working perfectly, Kaustubh Deshmukh's firmware team shipped version 3.2. Its release note described a “badge stability improvement”: where a reading was missing, the badge would retain its last known value rather than falling to amber. Complaints stopped. Customer satisfaction on the quarterly survey rose four points. In November, Vikrant Menon posted in the analytics channel that the change meant a unit which stopped reporting entirely would remain green forever. The thread got two emoji reactions and no replies.

On 11 March 2026, Vasantika Hospitals' Rajkot infection-control team ran a routine quarterly test and found total coliform. Jalanidhi's technician found a dead ultraviolet lamp whose ballast was still drawing power. On investigation, the unit had also stopped sending messages on 17 February, after a SIM provisioning lapse; the last state received had been green, and green it had stayed. Two independent failures — a silent lamp and a silent radio — had aligned, and the badge had no vocabulary for either.

The June audit found 1,340 units whose badge had been held at a last known value for more than seven days. It also found that Jalanidhi's service ERP and its telemetry store disagreed about how many units had failed in each of the last six quarters, and that the gap was widening.

5. The people

Aparna Bhide, VP Product, Pune. Believes the company must restate what the badge means before it sells another unit. Her incentive is a product organisation whose credibility is the asset in question. What she is not saying: her team owned the 3.2 requirement review and signed it off in a batch of eleven tickets on a Friday.

Devang Marathe, co-founder and CEO, Pune. Wants Dubai signed on schedule and believes the Rajkot event was a hardware failure, not an analytics failure. What he is not saying: a bridge term sheet from Chandrabhaga Capital is conditional on Jalanidhi showing a ₹40 crore annualised run rate by September, and the Al Sidrah contract is most of the gap.

Suchitra Rane, head of service operations, Ahmedabad. Manages 240 technicians and says the field has known for two years that lamps fail silently. Her incentive is a service cost line already 8 per cent over budget. What she is not saying: since early 2025 her regional leads have quietly been swapping lamps on a fixed nine-month cycle regardless of badge state, which has both suppressed the problem and destroyed the evidence of its true scale.

Kaustubh Deshmukh, firmware lead, Bengaluru. Argues that 3.2 did exactly what was asked and that the real defect is a fleet with no staleness model. What he is not saying: he raised staleness in the 3.2 design note and dropped it when the ticket was re-scoped as a user-interface fix.

Vikrant Menon, data scientist, Toronto, working the overnight shift for Pune. Wants every fleet number published as a range with its coverage stated. His incentive is a methodology he has been arguing for since 2024. What he is not saying: his own coverage metric used the thirty-day window for two years because it was the number that made the board deck work.

Lena Brandt, design lead, Berlin. Argues that a three-colour badge on a water dispenser is read by every human being as a safety guarantee, and that no sensor set Jalanidhi can afford will support that reading. What she is not saying: in the 2024 visual refresh she removed the “last updated” timestamp from the badge tile because it cluttered the card.

Joanne Tay, customer success lead, Singapore. Wants a Gulf-specific version of the badge that references Dubai Municipality's quarterly laboratory verification rather than making a standalone claim. Her incentive is a renewal book, not a signature. What she is not saying: Al Sidrah's facilities director has already asked her, informally, what happens if the badge is wrong.

Douglas Reiner, head of international sales, New Jersey. Points out that the Gulf regulator already mandates independent testing, so the badge is decorative there, and that delaying the signature past 30 June means waiting for Al Sidrah's next procurement cycle in January. His commission is 40 per cent weighted to new logos.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

“We did not make the water less safe. The lamp failed. A lamp can fail in a Kent unit in a hospital in Nagpur tomorrow and nobody will write us a letter about analytics.”Devang Marathe, leadership call, 19 June
“With respect — nobody told their customers that a Kent unit was continuously monitored. We did. That is the difference and it is the whole difference.”Lena Brandt, same call, from Berlin, 3.45 p.m. her time
“I need to know what I am telling my leads on Thursday. They have been swapping lamps on a calendar for a year because they stopped believing the colours. If we now tell them the colours are authoritative again, I will have two systems running and neither will be trusted.”Suchitra Rane, email to Aparna, 20 June
“Reposting from November. If a unit stops transmitting, the badge does not change. It is not a bug in 3.2. It is the specified behaviour. We should publish coverage at 72 hours and stop quoting 30 days.”Vikrant Menon, analytics channel, 21 June, 02.14 IST
“Their municipality already requires quarterly lab tests. We are arguing about a badge that in Dubai is a nice-to-have. If we go back to Al Sidrah in January the incumbent will have locked the campuses.”Douglas Reiner, to Devang, 22 June
“Their facilities director asked me last Tuesday what happens if the badge is wrong. I said I would find out. I have not gone back to him.”Joanne Tay, direct message to Aparna, 23 June

8. The options as Aparna sees them

Option A: retrofit. Fit ultraviolet-intensity sensors to all 6,800 Gen 2 units at roughly ₹1.97 crore, keep Jal Assure as it stands, and tell Vasantika that the physical gap is being closed. It is the answer that makes the promise true. It also takes nine to eleven months, which is seven months past Vasantika's deadline, and it does nothing about the 1,340 units whose badge is green because nobody has heard from them.

Option B: restate the badge. Rename Jal Assure as a service-status indicator, strip the safety language, add a visible last-updated timestamp and a staleness rule, and sell quarterly NABL laboratory testing as a paid add-on at roughly ₹1.1 crore a year. Honest, fast and cheap. It also concedes, in writing, that the claim on three years of marketing material was broader than the sensors supported — a concession that Vasantika's lawyers will read, that the school programme's service-parity clause may not survive, and that Al Sidrah's procurement will see before 30 June.

Option C: two tiers. Keep the full badge on the 4,800 units with intensity sensors, including the Gulf fleet, and give Gen 2 an explicitly narrower “monitored for service” tier with a retrofit roadmap. Sign Dubai on Gen 3 hardware only. It is the option Aparna currently favours and the one Suchitra calls “telling four thousand schools they got the cheap one.”

Aparna wrote all three on a page and then, at half past eleven, wrote a fourth line underneath and did not know what to do with it: all three of these assume the badge is per device. Vasantika does not buy a device; it buys drinking water at nine facilities, each of which already runs its own quarterly test. Al Sidrah manages campuses. The school programme is audited by district. Nothing in Jalanidhi's data model corresponds to a site, and nothing in any of the three options changes that. There was also the matter of 3.2 itself: not one of the options prevents a future release from redefining what green means without anyone noticing, which is the only thing that had actually gone wrong twice.

9. The deadline and the constraints

The Al Sidrah signature window closes on 30 June; their next procurement cycle opens in January. Vasantika's notice expires on 18 July. Achala Electronics' retrofit quote expires on 22 July and its tooling lead time is fourteen weeks, so a decision after mid-July pushes delivery past the following summer. The school-programme contract contains a service-parity clause whose interpretation Jalanidhi's counsel describes as “arguable in both directions.” Cash runway is about eleven months, and the Chandrabhaga bridge is conditional on a run rate that Dubai substantially supplies. Jalanidhi has two firmware engineers who understand the badge pipeline, one of whom is on leave until 6 July. And whatever Jalanidhi does in India, Dubai Municipality will keep testing the water itself every quarter.

10. Questions for discussion

1. Exhibit 3 shows coverage of 97.8 per cent under one definition and 71.4 per cent under another. Which number should have been in the board deck since 2023, and who at Jalanidhi should have decided that?

2. Exhibit 2 reports that 11.3 per cent of green units had a degraded lamp, and its footnote says the sample was not random. What would you need to know before using that figure in a letter to Vasantika — and what would you say if you could not get it before 18 July?

3. Exhibit 4's gap has widened from 12.7 to 38.2 per cent. Is that evidence that telemetry is missing failures, evidence that the two systems count different things, or evidence of Suchitra Rane's off-book lamp swaps? How would you tell the three apart?

4. Firmware 3.2 was reviewed and approved as a user-interface change. What process would have caught that it was a change to the meaning of a safety-adjacent metric, and what would that process cost a company of Jalanidhi's size?

5. Douglas Reiner argues the badge is decorative in Dubai because the municipality mandates independent testing. If that is true, what exactly is Jalanidhi selling to Al Sidrah — and does signing clause 7.3 unchanged create an exposure that the Indian contracts do not?

6. It is Monday morning, 29 June. What does Aparna do first, what does she say to the board about the Dubai signature, and what does she commit to Vasantika in writing before 18 July?

At 12.20 a.m. Aparna opened the audit spreadsheet one more time and filtered to the 1,340 held badges. Four hundred and ninety were school units, almost certainly switched off for the summer vacation and perfectly fine. Eleven were at Vasantika facilities. She could not tell, from anything in front of her, which of the eleven were fine. The rain had settled into a steady sound against the glass. She still had not decided what to open the meeting with.

Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation · Product Analytics & Data Practice

Device Telemetry and Fleet Analytics

A fleet does not report its health. It reports what its firmware was told to measure, when its radio was awake, from the devices that were still willing and able to speak. Everything a product manager believes about the fleet is an inference across that gap.

1. Two decisions, two weeks apart

On the evening of 14 April 2026, Anuradha Kelkar sat in Sinchan Agri Systems' office in Nashik with two documents in front of her and sixteen days before a board meeting. Sinchan made solar pump controllers — the box that sits between a farmer's solar array and a submersible pump, managing the motor, logging run hours, and reporting over LPWAN with a 2G fallback. There were 20,400 of them in the field across Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh and northern Karnataka, most sold under state subsidy schemes through farmer producer organisations, all carrying a service commitment: a dead pump restored within forty-eight hours during the irrigation season.

The first document proposed a predictive pump-health programme — data engineering, a failure model, alerting into the service app — at ₹2.6 crore over eighteen months. The second, from the service head, proposed spending the same money on eleven more vans and twenty-two technicians. Both were defensible. Sinchan's failure rate had drifted upward for three quarters, and nobody could agree whether that was ageing hardware, a firmware regression, or the fact that newer installations sat in hotter, dustier districts. Anuradha's problem was not a lack of data; she had 340 million telemetry rows from the previous season. It was that she could not say what fraction of the fleet those rows described.

Eight hundred kilometres south, on 9 March 2026, Ishaan Varma had faced the mirror image. Nidra Labs had shipped 1.6 million sleep-tracking bands, mostly in India, with a growing export line. The band has no radio of its own beyond Bluetooth Low Energy; it talks to a phone, and the phone talks to Nidra. Between January and March, the company's headline engagement metric — nightly wear rate, the share of active bands worn at least five nights in the last thirty — had fallen from 62 per cent to 51 per cent. Finance wanted to know whether to raise warranty accruals. Marketing wanted to know whether to delay the next launch. The board wanted to know what had broken. Ishaan's honest first answer, which he did not say out loud in that meeting, was that he did not know whether anything about customer behaviour had changed at all.

Both are fleet-analytics problems, seen from two ends. Anuradha must decide how far to trust a health signal she wants to act on; Ishaan must decide whether a signal he already acts on measured what he thought. The argument of this page is that the two questions collapse into one: fleet analytics is the discipline of quantifying, and then bounding, the distance between what the fleet is doing and what the fleet reports. Teams that treat that distance as a nuisance to be cleaned away build dashboards that fail precisely when they matter. Teams that treat it as the primary object of study build numbers they can defend to a board, a regulator, or a technician standing in a field at 6 a.m.

2. The idea and the schools that disagree about it

Device telemetry is the automated remote transmission of measurements from a device; fleet analytics is the aggregation and interpretation of those measurements across a device population to estimate health, usage and risk. That much is uncontroversial. The disagreements begin one level down, and they are inherited from four different intellectual traditions that arrived at the same data from different directions.

The oldest is reliability engineering, which came out of aerospace and military logistics in the 1950s and 60s and was formalised in reliability-centred maintenance in the airline industry. Its core commitment is that a device fails through a physical mechanism — bearing wear, insulation breakdown, thermal cycling — and that a health index which is not grounded in a named mechanism is numerology. The second is the product-analytics tradition, which arrived from consumer software in the 2000s with funnels, cohorts and retention curves, and which treats each device as an entity moving through states: shipped, activated, connected, active, dormant, dead. The third is observability and site-reliability engineering, whose instinct is that you cannot know in advance which signal will matter, so you instrument widely, sample deliberately, and alert on user-visible symptoms rather than on internal causes. The fourth is machine-learning predictive maintenance, which holds that failure precursors exist in the data whether or not anyone can name the physics, and that a sufficiently rich model will find them.

Anuradha's engineering lead was a reliability engineer by training and her data scientist in Toronto a machine-learning person, and for four months they had been having the argument in Table 1 while both believing it concerned roadmap sequencing. Naming the traditions does not resolve the dispute; it locates it. The reliability school is right that an unexplained model cannot be defended after a mass warranty claim, and the ML school is right that Sinchan's dominant failure mode — dry running, where a pump runs with insufficient water and cooks its own bearings — has precursors in current waveform that no human was going to codify into a threshold.

3. Mechanics in depth: the arithmetic experts actually do

Three calculations separate practitioners who can run a fleet programme from those who can draw one. Each is elementary; each is skipped routinely.

3.1 Detection probability is bounded by duty cycle

Sinchan's controllers report a full sample every fifteen minutes while pumping and a heartbeat every six hours while idle. Dry-running events, in the logs Sinchan had physically confirmed, lasted a median of four minutes before the motor's thermal cutout tripped. If sampling phase is independent of event onset, the probability that a fifteen-minute sampler observes a four-minute event is roughly 4/15, or 27 per cent. This is not a data-quality problem that better analysis can fix; it is an instrument limit, the fleet-analytics analogue of a sampling theorem. Sinchan could not detect most dry-run events with the firmware it had shipped, and no model trained on the 27 per cent it did see would be unbiased, because the events long enough to be caught were systematically the ones where the cutout failed to trip promptly.

The corollary matters more than the calculation. Expected detection latency for a persistent fault is roughly half the sampling interval plus backhaul delay — about three hours for an idle Sinchan controller. Whether that is acceptable depends entirely on the lead time of the failure and the logistics time of the response. A precursor with a four-day lead time tolerates a three-hour detection latency easily; one with a two-hour lead time does not, and no amount of model sophistication repairs it.

3.2 MTBF describes an exponential world; hardware usually lives in a Weibull one

Sinchan's board slide said the controller's mean time between failures was about 975 days, comfortably beyond the thirty-six-month warranty. The number was arithmetically correct and strategically misleading. Mean time between failures is a sufficient summary only when the hazard rate — the instantaneous probability of failing given survival so far — is constant. Wear-out mechanisms are not constant; they accelerate. Fitting a two-parameter Weibull distribution to the same field data gave a shape parameter β of 2.4 and a characteristic life η of 1,100 days. A β above one means the hazard rises with age.

Under that fit, the tenth-percentile life — B10, the age by which one device in ten has failed — is η × (−ln 0.9)1/β = 1,100 × 0.391 ≈ 431 days. And the cumulative failure probability at 1,095 days, the end of the warranty, is 1 − exp(−(1095/1100)2.4) ≈ 0.63. In other words, a fleet whose MTBF exceeds the warranty period by more than a year would still see roughly sixty-three per cent of units fail inside warranty. Anuradha's finance team had accrued against the MTBF. This single substitution — distribution for mean — moved the warranty provision by more than the entire ₹2.6 crore she was asking for.

3.3 The threshold is an economic choice, not a statistical one

Suppose Sinchan builds the model. At a monthly base rate of 0.9 per cent, its 20,400 controllers generate about 184 genuine failures a month. A preventive dispatch costs ₹1,450. A failure that reaches the farmer costs Sinchan an estimated ₹38,000 — emergency parts, an SLA credit, and the share of churn attributable to a lost irrigation cycle. Three candidate thresholds:

Two second-order effects hide inside that flat curve, and both are more consequential than the optimisation. First, the aggressive point is infeasible: 2,100 flags against 930 dispatch slots means technicians will triage, and they will triage by proximity and convenience, which means the fleet's prevented failures become geographically biased — and next year's training data inherits that bias, because the failures that were prevented never appear as failures. Second, precision below about one in seven destroys operator trust faster than any deck can rebuild it; the practical floor on precision is set by human psychology, not by expected value. Experts choose the operating point by asking what the service organisation can absorb and still believe, then check that the economics are not absurd — not the other way round.

4. When the idea applies, stated as testable claims

Fleet analytics earns its cost when five claims hold. Each is checkable in an afternoon, and each fails differently.

Telemetry becomes actively misleading in three situations. When the act of measuring changes the behaviour measured — technicians who learn that an alert closes when a counter is reset will reset counters. When sensors saturate, so that the extremes you most want are clipped into invisibility and the fleet looks calmer the worse conditions get. And when the population reporting is a survivor set: a fleet average computed over devices still transmitting will always flatter the fleet, because the units in worst trouble are disproportionately the ones that have gone quiet. That third case is not an edge case. It is the normal condition of every fleet, and the whole practice is organised around it.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

In multi-product households and sites, the unit of analysis stops being the device. A Nidra customer with a band, a bedside hub and a partner's band produces three telemetry streams for one behaviour, and any per-device retention number double-counts. In two-sided and channel structures, the device's data rights are split: Sinchan's controllers are installed by FPO-appointed technicians and partly financed by state subsidy, so three parties can claim the run-hour data, and Sinchan's own standard contract — signed years earlier by a sales team optimising for close rate — forbids pooling one distributor's data with another's. That single clause makes cross-cohort baselines legally impossible for about a third of the fleet, and nobody discovered it until the data team tried to build them.

In regulated settings the constraint is sharper still. India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act obliged Nidra to obtain fresh, granular consent for analytics use of sleep data, and sleep data is close enough to health inference that Ishaan's team treats it conservatively. The result is a telemetry population that is not a random sample of customers — it is the subset who said yes, and who said yes under a notice whose wording changed in July. In hardware-plus-software fleets, every over-the-air update is a potential redefinition of the instrument; staged rollouts create cohorts that are simultaneously firmware cohorts and self-selected early-adopter cohorts, confounded by construction. In AI-native devices that run inference on the edge, the telemetry is itself a model output: when on-device classification changes version, the fleet appears to change behaviour, and distinguishing model drift from fleet drift requires a held-back population still running the old model.

The seams are organisational as much as technical. Warranty finance counts RMAs; product counts telemetry-detected failures; support counts tickets; the three never agree, because each has a different denominator and a different device identifier. Mature companies do not reconcile them perfectly. They publish the gap as a tracked metric and treat its widening as an early warning in its own right.

6. Nine nuances that separate expert from competent

Missingness is informative, and it can be bounded rather than argued about. The competent practitioner excludes non-reporting devices and notes the caveat. The expert computes the metric twice — once over reporters, once assuming the worst for the silent — and reports the band. The tell: a team that can state its metric as a range, and whose range width is itself trending, has internalised this; a team that quotes a point estimate for a fleet with 30 per cent silence has not.

Event time is not ingest time, and device clocks lie. Controllers with a depleted real-time-clock battery reboot to epoch zero or to a boot-relative counter. The tell: an implausible cluster of events at exactly midnight UTC, or a thin permanent line of events dated 1 January 1970, or a seasonal pattern that shifts by hours when a region changes its network provider.

A mean hides the hazard shape. Quoting MTBF is not wrong; treating it as a survival statement is. The tell: a deck in which MTBF comfortably exceeds the warranty while the RMA rate rises monotonically with install cohort age. Those two facts are only compatible if the hazard is increasing, which means the MTBF was never the relevant number.

Edge aggregation destroys exactly the tail you need. Firmware that transmits a five-minute mean to save bandwidth makes a forty-second current spike arithmetically invisible. The tell: post-mortems that repeatedly conclude “telemetry showed nothing unusual” for failures technicians can explain at a glance in the field.

The instrument changes more often than the thing it measures. Firmware ships weekly; human behaviour moves over quarters. The tell: a metric step-change whose date aligns to a release train rather than to a season, a festival, a price change or a competitor launch. Expert teams keep a release calendar overlaid on every fleet chart as a default, not as a debugging step.

Pooled fleet trends can invert every segment trend. Sinchan's firmware 4.3 looked worse than 4.1 fleet-wide because it was deployed first into the harshest districts. The tell: a fleet-level conclusion that contradicts the direction of every cohort within it. The obvious reading — that the new firmware is bad — is wrong, and the correct instinct is to look for what determined the rollout order.

Capacity, not accuracy, usually binds. A model that flags more than the service organisation can visit does not deliver its recall; it delivers whatever triage the technicians invent. The tell: a dispatch backlog that grows while the model's offline metrics improve.

Successful prevention censors the data that trained the model. Once alerts are acted on, the prevented failures never occur, so next year's training set contains only the failures the model missed. The tell: a model whose measured performance quietly degrades after its best year. The standard remedy — a small holdout where alerts are logged but suppressed — is ethically awkward and, in safety-relevant fleets, sometimes indefensible; that tension is real and is discussed below.

Telemetry rights are product decisions disguised as contract clauses. Data-pooling permissions, retention periods and consent granularity determine which analyses are possible years later. The tell: a data team that discovers, mid-project, that a third of the fleet cannot legally be compared with the rest.

7. How the practice differs, and where it does not

8. Three worked examples

8.1 Sinchan finds Simpson's paradox in its firmware

Anuradha's first instinct had been to halt the 4.3 rollout. Fleet-wide, 4.3 showed a seasonal failure rate of 6.2 per cent against 4.1's 2.9 per cent. Segmenting by agro-climatic zone reversed it.

8.2 Nidra's eleven-point drop that may not exist

Ishaan's team rebuilt the wear-rate metric as a device funnel with explicit denominators and computed the bounds described in nuance one.

Ishaan's team resolved part of it empirically: 40,000 devices had been held back from the February firmware for unrelated release-engineering reasons. Among that frozen cohort, wear rate moved from 61.4 to 59.8 per cent — a real but small decline. The accidental control group answered in a week a question the full fleet could not answer at all.

8.3 Where it failed: Pavan Air Systems

Pavan Air Systems, a Coimbatore maker of industrial screw compressors, ran the cautionary version. It trained a failure model on eighteen months of telemetry from 4,100 machines, launched it in 2023, and reported a 34 per cent drop in unplanned downtime in the first year. In year two, precision fell from 0.29 to 0.11 and the service organisation stopped acting on alerts. Two causes compounded. Successful interventions had removed precisely the failures the model was trained to predict, so the retraining set was progressively enriched with the model's own blind spots. Separately, a vibration-sensor supplier change in mid-2023 shifted the noise floor on newer machines by a factor the model read as a precursor. Recovery took seven months and was not clever: Pavan reverted to physics-grounded per-cohort thresholds, froze a 400-machine holdout where alerts were logged but not dispatched, added sensor part number as a first-class cohort dimension, and rebuilt trust by publishing weekly precision to the service team before asking them to act again. The lesson Pavan's head of service repeats is that the model did not fail; the measurement system around it did, and nobody owned that system.

9. Failure modes and their diagnostics

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Physics-grounded thresholds versus learned models. The reliability camp argues that an alert you cannot explain cannot be defended to a regulator, a court or a technician, and that explainability is not a nicety but the condition of operational trust; their evidence is a long record of learned models degrading silently, as at Pavan. The machine-learning camp replies that the dominant failure modes in modern fleets are multivariate and interaction-heavy, that human-authored thresholds miss them entirely, and that Sinchan's dry-run precursor is a real example nobody codified in a decade of trying. The first camp would be wrong if learned models could be made to degrade loudly — if drift detection were reliable enough that silent decay stopped being the norm. The second would be wrong if, on audit, most of the value in deployed models turned out to come from two or three features a domain engineer would have named in an afternoon.

Raw retention versus edge summarisation. One camp keeps the full-rate stream because the analysis that matters in 2028 cannot be specified in 2026, and because summarising at the edge destroys the tail where failures live. The other points at the bill: a controller reporting at full rate over cellular costs real money per device-year, and on an ₹18,000 product with a thin margin, telemetry cost is a product decision. The resolution most large fleets converge on — summarise by default, burst to full rate on a trigger — is genuinely a compromise, not a synthesis, because the trigger is defined by today's understanding of failure and therefore cannot catch tomorrow's.

Whether holdouts are legitimate in safety-relevant fleets. Pavan's 400-machine suppressed-alert holdout is methodologically correct and ethically uncomfortable. Practitioners who defend it argue that without it the programme's effect is unmeasurable and will eventually be cancelled or, worse, trusted blindly. Those who refuse it argue that knowingly withholding a warning from a customer who paid for monitoring is indefensible whatever the statistics say, and that the correct alternative is staged geographic rollout, which is weaker but honest. There is no settled answer; the position a company takes tends to follow its regulatory exposure rather than its analytics maturity.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this produces a fleet dashboard with a health score, an uptime figure and a trend line. Someone who has internalised it produces the same dashboard with three habits visible in it. Every number carries its denominator in the label, not in a footnote. Every chart carries a release-and-rollout overlay, so the first question about any step change is answered before it is asked. And every headline metric carries its worst-case bound, so the width of the band — not the point estimate — is watched as a measure of how much the organisation currently knows. Behaviourally it shows up as a reflex: when a fleet number moves, the expert's first hypothesis is that the measurement changed, and only the second that the fleet did. When that reflex is wrong it has cost an hour; the reverse mistake costs a quarter.

12. What they decided

Anuradha went to the board on 30 April and asked for neither proposal as written. She requested ₹95 lakh for twelve months: firmware to raise sampling rate on a trigger rather than continuously, sensor part number and rollout wave added as first-class cohort dimensions, a Weibull-based warranty re-accrual, and a 600-controller instrumented sub-fleet in Marathwada to establish a ground-truth failure rate against physical inspection. The predictive model was deferred by two quarters, and four vans were approved instead of eleven. Her argument to the board was that Sinchan could not yet detect most of the events it wanted to predict, and that buying a model before fixing a 27 per cent detection probability would be paying for inference over an instrument that was not looking.

Ishaan told the board on 19 March that the eleven-point drop was somewhere between one and eleven points, that the frozen 40,000-device cohort put the real decline at roughly 1.6 points, and that he would not recommend a warranty-accrual change on the current evidence. He shipped a sync-health metric alongside wear rate, made consent status a reported dimension, and made one durable organisational change: no fleet metric at Nidra may be presented without its denominator and its coverage percentage on the same slide.

Discussion questions.

1. Sinchan's cost curve is flat between 700 and 2,100 flags a month. If expected value cannot choose the operating point, what should — and who in the organisation has the standing to decide?

2. Nidra's accidental frozen cohort answered the question. Should a consumer hardware company deliberately maintain a permanently un-updated control fleet, and what does it owe those customers?

3. Both protagonists concluded that their instrument, not their fleet, was the thing that had changed. Under what conditions would that reflex become its own failure mode?

13. Going deeper

  1. Constructing a funnel — the device lifecycle is a funnel; get the stage definitions right and most fleet metrics fall out of them.
  2. Connectivity: BLE, Wi-Fi, cellular, LPWAN — the radio sets your sampling rate, and sampling rate sets what you can ever detect.
  3. Device telemetry and fleet health — turns raw readings into a defensible composite index with a stated coverage claim.
  4. Fleet and device-lifetime metrics — where hazard functions, warranty accrual and unit economics meet.
  5. Leading indicators from device data — the move from describing current health to forecasting, and the lead-time arithmetic that governs it.
  6. Reading drop-off — the same diagnostic discipline applied to the stage where devices leave the funnel.
  7. Defining activation (the aha moment) — for hardware, activation is the first stage where your denominator becomes trustworthy.
  8. Cohort analysis — the antidote to pooled fleet trends and the only defence against Simpson's paradox by build.
  9. Retention curves and the PMF signal — device retention has a floor set by hardware life, which changes how the curve is read.
  10. Stickiness and natural frequency — how often a device should report is a product claim before it is an engineering setting.
  11. Feature adoption analysis — on connected hardware, adoption is inseparable from firmware version, so cohorting by build comes first.
case20v1-ana.hw.telemetry:
Case · Device Telemetry and Fleet Analytics

Sheetal Cold Chain Systems: The Alert Nobody Trusted

A vice-president of product in Ahmedabad has three weeks to decide how much of her cold-chain sensor fleet gets a smarter warning system before the hottest month of the year.

1. Ahmedabad, 2 February 2026

Meher Chawla, VP of Product at Sheetal Cold Chain Systems, closed her laptop after a call with an angry distributor in Rajkot and looked again at the calendar pinned above her desk. Two dates were circled: 20 February, when the Vadilal-linked distributor network would decide whether to renew its ₹1.8 crore annual contract with Sheetal before the summer ice-cream season, and the same date, coincidentally, when Sheetal's first serious international prospect — a Dubai retail chain called Al Waha Fresh Markets — expected a live demonstration of the company's analytics before signing a three-year, ₹3.2 crore deal. Both dates sat before the real deadline that mattered more than either contract: by mid-March, ambient temperatures across Gujarat and Rajasthan would begin climbing past 38°C, ice-cream sales would triple, and every deep freezer and reefer truck Sheetal monitored would be worked harder than at any other time of year. Whatever Meher decided in the next eighteen days would run, unattended, through the season that made or lost the company's money.

2. Company background

Founded in 2019 in Ahmedabad, Sheetal Cold Chain Systems made a small, LPWAN-and-cellular-connected temperature-and-door sensor that clipped onto deep freezers and reefer trucks, paired with a subscription dashboard sold as an annual maintenance contract. Its customers were not ice-cream companies themselves but the distributors who trucked and stored their stock: the network of local distributors that moved Vadilal and Amul ice cream from factory to shop, and increasingly the dark-store operators supplying quick-commerce platforms such as Zepto and Swiggy Instamart, for whom a single warm freezer overnight could mean a full night's frozen-category inventory written off. Sheetal's pitch was simple — know a freezer is failing before the ice cream melts — and it competed against both larger international cold-chain telemetry vendors and against distributors simply doing nothing and hoping. By early 2026, Sheetal had roughly 4,000 telemetry units live across fourteen states and annual recurring revenue near ₹14 crore, most of it from the Vadilal- and Amul-linked distributor networks.

3. The situation

Every Sheetal unit fired an alert whenever its sensor read a temperature above a fixed threshold for more than ten minutes — a rule written into the product in 2020 and never substantially revised. Through the 2025 season, distributors on the Vadilal network received an average of several dozen such alerts a month per unit, the overwhelming majority triggered not by a failing compressor but by a shopkeeper opening a freezer door repeatedly during a busy afternoon, which spikes the internal temperature briefly and harmlessly. Field technicians, buried in false alarms, had begun ignoring the alert queue altogether by mid-season. In July, a reefer truck serving a Rajkot distributor genuinely lost cooling for six hours; its alert arrived, unremarkable, as the fortieth message of that week, and nobody acted until a driver noticed melted stock at the next stop. The distributor wrote off roughly ₹38 lakh of ice cream and told Sheetal, bluntly, that its system was noise.

Meher's data scientist, Daniela Cruz, working from Toronto, had already prototyped a fix: instead of a single temperature threshold, a composite "Cold Chain Risk Score" that combined the rate of temperature change, the frequency of door-open events, and the compressor's duty cycle, distinguishing a freezer being used normally from one that was actually losing its ability to cool. Early tests on Sheetal's newest hardware generation, installed over the past year, cut false positives sharply. The complication was that roughly 1,200 of Sheetal's 4,000 units were older, 2019–2020-vintage devices with coarser sensors and thinner historical data, for which Daniela's model had not been calibrated and might behave unpredictably. Calibrating it properly, cohort by cohort, was a six-to-eight-week job for an engineering team that, from Bengaluru and Pune, had eighteen days before the season began in earnest.

4. The people

Arjun Deshpande, engineering lead, Bengaluru. Wants a phased rollout; worried that pushing the risk score to uncalibrated legacy units under deadline pressure creates a second, harder-to-diagnose failure mode right when trust is already low.

Daniela Cruz, data scientist, Toronto. Built the risk-score prototype and believes it is genuinely ready for the newer hardware cohort, but is explicit that she cannot vouch for its behaviour on the 1,200 older units without more data.

Mei Lin Goh, customer-success lead, Singapore. Fields the distributor complaints directly and wants a visible, fleet-wide fix announced before 20 February, arguing that a partial fix will read as Sheetal favouring its newer, pricier hardware over existing customers.

Brian Kessler, sales head for international accounts, New Jersey. Is pushing hard for a polished live demo for Al Waha Fresh Markets on 20 February, and sees the Dubai contract as bigger upside than smoothing over one Gujarat distributor's complaint.

5. Exhibits

6. The options

  1. Ship the risk score fleet-wide by 20 February. Every unit, including the 1,200 uncalibrated legacy devices, gets the new scoring in time for both the Vadilal renewal and the Dubai demo. Upside: one consistent story for every customer, and the strongest possible demo for Al Waha. Cost: Daniela's model has not been validated on the legacy cohort's coarser sensors, and a wrong all-clear or a fresh wave of misfires on exactly the customers already angriest could cost Sheetal the Vadilal renewal outright rather than saving it.
  2. Phase the rollout by cohort. Ship the risk score only on the roughly 2,800 units with a year or more of clean telemetry, including the Dubai pilot units, and recalibrate the old fixed-threshold rule for the remaining 1,200 legacy devices to be less trigger-happy around door-opening, without claiming it is the new system. Upside: an honest, working demo for Al Waha and a real improvement for most of the Vadilal network at manageable engineering cost. Cost: Sheetal must tell the Vadilal-linked distributors running older hardware that their fix is a smaller, interim one, which Mei Lin fears reads as second-class treatment right before a renewal decision.
  3. Delay the risk score past the season. Keep the existing threshold system everywhere, spend the eighteen days recalibrating thresholds modestly rather than shipping anything new, offer the Rajkot distributor a service credit and extra manual monitoring staff through peak season, and show Al Waha a smaller, non-analytics pilot. Upside: no risk of a rushed model failing in the field. Cost: it does not address the alert-fatigue problem distributors are already angry about, and Brian believes it likely costs Sheetal the Dubai contract to a competitor with a more current-looking product.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What does Exhibit 2 reveal about why the false-positive rate is so much worse on the Vadilal reefer-truck cohort than on the Dubai pilot units — and is that a hardware problem, a usage problem, or a data problem?
  2. Whose complaint is really about telemetry quality, and whose is really about something else — a contract renewal, a sales deadline, a support burden? How should that change how much weight each voice gets in Meher's decision?
  3. If Meher chooses Option 2, what should she tell the Vadilal-linked distributors on legacy hardware about what they are and are not getting, and by when should she promise the full recalibration?
  4. What would have to be true about the 1,200 uncalibrated units for Option 1 to be the right call despite Daniela's warning?

8. A note for the learner

This case is a decision about fleet analytics maturity, not about sensors. Sheetal already had telemetry: every freezer reported temperature reliably. What it lacked was a fleet-analytics layer that told the difference between a device behaving normally under heavy, legitimate use and one genuinely failing — exactly the distinction between raw telemetry and a derived health signal that this topic exists to teach. The static threshold treated every unit identically regardless of usage pattern or hardware cohort, which is why it generated so much noise that technicians stopped trusting it — the same alert-fatigue failure mode that has caused real hospital and industrial monitoring systems to miss genuine emergencies.

A well-reasoned answer does three things. First, it segments the fleet by cohort before promising a fleet-wide number: the 2,800 well-instrumented units and the 1,200 legacy units are not the same population, and pretending otherwise, in either direction, produces a claim nobody can stand behind. Second, it is honest with customers about what is proven and what is provisional, rather than promising more than the data supports to save a renewal conversation or win a demo. Third, it treats the Dubai opportunity and the domestic renewal as different products of the same fleet-analytics discipline rather than as competing priorities to be traded off in a hurry.

On that reasoning, Option 2 is the most defensible path. It gives Al Waha Fresh Markets an honest, working demonstration on Sheetal's best-instrumented units, which is the customer segment the new system was actually built and tested for. It gives the Vadilal network a real, if smaller, improvement immediately, paired with a credible, dated commitment to bring the same score to legacy hardware once it has been properly calibrated — addressing the alert-fatigue complaint without gambling the renewal on an unvalidated model. It costs less to ship on deadline than Option 1 and does more than Option 3. The lesson worth carrying forward is that a fleet's health signal is only as trustworthy as the honesty of its coverage claims, and that segmenting by what you actually know, cohort by cohort, is usually cheaper than the alternative of promising one number for everyone and hoping it holds.
