Payas Daily: What Is a Milk Subscriber Worth?

A subscription fresh-delivery company must certify a lifetime-value number before its board meets — and every honest way of computing it gives a different answer.

1. Hyderabad, Thursday night, 12 November 2026

The eleventh-floor office in Gachibowli had emptied by nine. Devika Iyer, Senior Vice-President of Product and Growth at Payas Daily, had three windows open on one screen and a printed deck on the desk beside her. The deck was the board pre-read for Friday morning. Page fourteen carried a single figure in 48-point type: LTV per subscriber: ₹5,930. LTV:CAC 9.3×. It was the number Payas Daily had published in its 2023 investor letter, repeated in 2024 and 2025, and it was the number on which the Dubai licensing royalty, the Series D term sheet and — Devika suspected — a fair amount of the company's self-belief now rested.

On the second window was Ishaan Grewal's refit, mailed from Toronto at 4.20 that afternoon with the subject line "please read before you send anything". On the same cohorts, defining an active subscriber by deliveries rather than billing events, and using contribution margin rather than revenue, the number came out at ₹1,920. On the third window was a spreadsheet Devika had built herself over two evenings, in which the same underlying curves produced any value between ₹1,760 and ₹7,250 depending on five choices nobody at Payas Daily had ever formally made: what counts as active, what counts as revenue, over what horizon, at what discount rate, and whether a returning customer is a new customer or an old one.

The board would ask her, at some point before lunch on Friday, to stand behind one figure. Tejomay Capital's ₹520 crore term sheet carried a gate: management certification that trailing-twelve-month cohorts delivered a contribution LTV to CAC ratio of at least 3.0×. The ₹42 crore expansion into Indore, Kochi, Nagpur and Chandigarh, already halfway committed in cold-chain leases, assumed the old number. And Rajat Khosla would be dialling in from New Jersey at 8 a.m. India time to remind everyone that the royalty schedule in the Al Ghadeer contract stepped down if the published lifetime value fell below ₹3,000.

Devika wrote one line in her notebook and underlined it twice: the curve is the same in all five versions. Then she sat looking at it, unsure whether that was reassuring or the whole problem.

2. The company, and the decision that still binds it

Payas Daily began in 2019 as a two-SKU milk subscription in Hyderabad: full-cream and toned, delivered before 6.30 a.m., billed from a prepaid wallet. Shantanu Barve, its founder, had run supply chain at a packaged-foods company and believed that the defensible thing in Indian grocery was not assortment but habit — a household that finds milk at the door every morning does not shop for milk. By 2021 it had opened Bengaluru and Pune, added bread, eggs, curd, fruit and atta, and grown the average subscribed basket from ₹62 a day to ₹146.

The decision that constrains everything today was made in March 2022. To secure farm-level sourcing and a fourth city, Payas Daily acquired Nitya Farms Collective, a producer company with two chilling centres near Nalgonda and roughly 1.1 lakh legacy home-delivery customers in Hyderabad and Warangal. The acquisition agreement carried a clause the founders accepted in a week: every migrated Nitya household would keep a fifteen per cent lifetime discount on dairy, non-revocable, non-repriceable, transferable within the household. It bought the deal. It also created a population of about 94,000 accounts that are, four years later, the only cohorts old enough to show what a mature retention curve looks like — and whose pricing and pre-quick-commerce habits cannot be generalised to anybody acquired since, nor changed by management even if it wished to.

Payas Daily today serves roughly 4.2 lakh active subscribers across eight cities, billing about ₹1,380 per active subscriber per month on FY2026 revenue of ₹624 crore. Blended contribution margin after goods, last-mile delivery, wallet and payment costs and city overhead is reported at fourteen per cent. The company lost ₹58 crore at the EBITDA line in FY2026 and has fourteen months of runway.

3. The industry

The subscription fresh-delivery market in India sits in an uncomfortable middle. Above it are the dairy incumbents — Amul, Nandini, Heritage, Dodla — whose distribution through neighbourhood retailers costs a fraction of app-based delivery. Beside it are the direct competitors: Country Delight, Milkbasket, Akshayakalpa, each with its own version of the morning-delivery promise. Below and increasingly through it runs quick commerce. Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart do not sell subscriptions; they sell the elimination of the need for one. Internal research since 2024 shows the commonest reason a household cuts its standing order is not dissatisfaction but the discovery that milk arrives in eleven minutes whenever it is wanted.

The regulatory frame matters more than once. The prepaid wallet Payas Daily bills through is a closed-loop instrument, and compliance has tightened its handling of dormant balances under the Reserve Bank of India's prepaid payment instrument norms; ₹38 crore sits in customer wallets, of which ₹4.7 crore belongs to accounts that have taken no delivery in twelve months. UPI autopay mandates through NPCI, adopted in January 2026 for wallet top-ups, removed the recharge friction that had been the largest cause of involuntary churn. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act's retention obligations, and the company's own privacy notice, commit it to purging personal data for accounts inactive beyond twenty-four months — a purge scheduled for January 2027 that will, unless something is done first, delete the order-level history of the 2022 and early-2023 cohorts. FSSAI licensing governs the cold chain, and ONDC has begun making hyperlocal grocery discovery cheaper for entrants.

Internationally, the exposure is a licensing one. In July 2025 Payas Daily licensed its subscription and route-optimisation stack to Al Ghadeer Foods Trading LLC in Dubai, which now runs morning delivery across Dubai and Sharjah. The royalty schedule is tiered, and the tiers are indexed — through a clause drafted quickly at the end of a long negotiation — to "subscriber lifetime value as published in the Licensor's annual investor letter".

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

The published LTV of ₹5,930 was first computed in April 2023 by Ishaan Grewal, then a contractor. He took the Hyderabad and Bengaluru cohorts of 2021 and 2022, observed for between eleven and twenty-two months, fitted the decay, assumed the curve flattened where it appeared to be heading, integrated to thirty-six months, and multiplied the resulting 19.5 expected active months by ₹304. Against a marketing-only CAC of ₹640, the ratio was 9.3×. Nobody disputed it. It was, at the time, defensible: the curves did flatten, and margin genuinely was twenty-two per cent in two dense, mature cities.

Three things have since changed, each invisible at the time it happened.

First, in March 2025 the company migrated its data warehouse. Order-level records before April 2023 were not carried across; what survives for the oldest cohorts is a monthly aggregate table of billing events per account. Every retention curve older than three and a half years is therefore now reconstructed from billing, not from deliveries.

Second, in January 2026 two features shipped in the same release. Katharina Vogel's team in Berlin rebuilt the pause flow, removing the seven-day cap on pausing a subscription and the requirement to state a reason — a change that lifted satisfaction scores materially and was one of the year's clearest product wins. In the same release, UPI autopay wallet recharge went live. The combination had an arithmetic consequence nobody modelled: a household can now pause deliveries indefinitely while its wallet continues to top up automatically, and it will appear in the billing table as an account with activity. Retention measured on billing events flattened beautifully from February 2026 onwards. Deliveries per subscriber did not.

Third, the April 2026 expansion into Lucknow, Jaipur and Coimbatore added subscribers at densities well below the Hyderabad and Bengaluru baseline. Nandita Pillai's operations team reports contribution margin by density band; in the lowest band, the figure is negative. The blended fourteen per cent that the company uses in every LTV calculation is an average across cities whose economics differ by a factor of three.

On 6 November, Cheryl Ong sent a two-line message from Singapore noting that win-back subscribers — households her team reactivates through a ₹500 wallet credit — enter the acquisition dashboard as month-zero cohort members while simultaneously remaining in their original cohort's denominator. Depending on which dashboard a person opens, the same household is a new customer acquired at a cost booked to retention budget, or a retained customer who never left. Roughly 11 per cent of FY2026 "new" subscribers are win-backs. Nobody has yet worked out which of the two numbers on page fourteen the double count inflates.

Figure A — The sequence that produced the number, and the sequence that undermined it.

5. The people

Devika Iyer, SVP Product & Growth, Hyderabad. Owns the metric definitions and will be asked to certify the figure. Position: the published number cannot be repeated without a footnote. Incentive: her credibility with the board rests on having caught this rather than on the level of the number. What she is not saying: she approved the January 2026 release note that described the pause redesign as "retention-positive", and she wrote the sentence herself.

Shantanu Barve, Founder & CEO, Hyderabad. Position: the business is fundamentally sound, the cities that are mature are profitable, and a definitional argument three days before a term sheet closes is an act of self-harm. Incentive: the Series D at the indicated valuation is the difference between building the next three years and selling the company. Not saying: he has told two existing investors informally that the round is "effectively done".

Farida Qureshi, Chief Financial Officer, Mumbai. Position: any number that goes into a data room must be reproducible from the general ledger, and contribution margin is the only honest multiplicand. Incentive: she joined nine months ago and is building an audit trail she can defend to a future diligence team. Not saying: she has never reconciled the ₹38 crore of wallet balances against recognised revenue and does not yet know which way the error runs.

Ishaan Grewal, Head of Data Science, Toronto. Position: the refit is right; the old curve was fitted on unrepresentative cohorts and the tail assumption was never tested. Incentive: professional — he authored the original number as a contractor and would rather correct it himself than have a diligence team find it. Not saying: his refit changes the definition of an active subscriber mid-series, so the drop from ₹5,930 to ₹1,920 is partly a real deterioration and partly a measurement change, and he has not decomposed the two.

Nandita Pillai, VP Operations, Bengaluru. Position: stop the expansion; new cities destroy contribution, and every subscriber added in a low-density pincode makes the average worse. Incentive: her cost-per-delivery target is blended across cities and she is judged on it. Not saying: two of the four new cities were her proposal in 2025, when she modelled density improving faster than it has.

Katharina Vogel, Principal Designer, Berlin. Position: the pause redesign is one of the best things the company shipped; households that can pause come back, and punishing them with a seven-day cap only pushed them to cancel outright. Incentive: her team's roadmap for FY2027 is built on the flexibility thesis. Not saying: her own research diary from March 2026 records that a third of interviewed pausers described the product as "something we've stopped using" while still technically subscribed.

Cheryl Ong, Customer Success & Retention Lead, Singapore. Position: win-back is the cheapest acquisition the company has and should be scaled; a household reactivated for ₹500 is worth more than a stranger acquired for ₹1,120. Incentive: her budget and headcount grow if win-back is treated as a channel. Not saying: her reactivation cohorts churn again within four months at roughly twice the rate of first-time subscribers, a figure she has computed but not circulated.

Rajat Khosla, President, International Sales, New Jersey. Position: whatever is published must not go below ₹3,000, and the company should publish a range rather than a point. Incentive: his multi-year earnout is tied to Al Ghadeer royalty receipts. Not saying: he has quoted the ₹5,930 figure in three prospect conversations in Riyadh and Doha as evidence of the model's durability.

Yusuf Rahman, Managing Director, Al Ghadeer Foods Trading LLC, Dubai. Position: the licence is performing and he would like the relationship deepened, with exclusivity across the GCC. Incentive: a restated Indian LTV gives him grounds to reopen the royalty tiers at a lower level. Not saying: his own Dubai cohorts retain substantially better than the Indian ones, and he has not shared the data.

7. Voices

"I want to be careful about the word 'wrong'. The 2023 model was a reasonable model of the business we had in 2023. The business changed underneath it and nobody re-fitted. That is a process failure, not a fraud, and I would like us to say so in exactly those words before someone else says it differently."

Farida Qureshi, CFO, on a call with Devika Iyer, 10 November

"Every single one of you was in the room when we agreed the pause redesign was a win. It was a win. Households that pause in November for Diwali travel come back in December. Katharina Vogel, Berlin, in the #retention-defs channel, 9 November

Rajat Khosla, New Jersey, voice note to Shantanu Barve, 11 November

8. The options as Devika sees them

By Thursday night Devika had written four options on the whiteboard behind her desk, in the order they had occurred to her, which was not the order of their merits.

Option one: certify the refit. Publish ₹1,920, tell Tejomay that the trailing-twelve-month gate is not met at 1.7×, and ask them to re-cut the round on the strength of the mature cities alone. This is the version Ishaan and, in a different register, Farida are pressing for. It ends the ambiguity in a single move. It also accepts a number that mixes a genuine deterioration with a definitional change nobody has decomposed, on cohorts too young to have a tail, in cities the company opened six months ago.

Option two: certify the published number with disclosure. Keep ₹5,930 as the historical figure, footnote the basis, and commit to a re-baselining in the FY2027 letter after twelve more months of delivery-based data. This preserves the royalty tier and the round. It also means the company's central number remains one computed on the Nitya cohorts — households with a permanent fifteen per cent discount, acquired before quick commerce existed, in the two densest cities it operates — and every reader of the letter will continue to treat that as the business.

Option three: publish a segmented set. Report LTV separately for mature high-density cities, for newer cities, and for win-back cohorts, on a single stated basis, with no company-wide figure at all. Devika believes this is the most honest thing available. It is also the option that requires the board to accept that the company cannot answer, in one number, the question every investor asks first, and it hands Yusuf Rahman a menu from which to pick the lowest tier.

Option four: defer. Certify nothing on Friday, ask Tejomay for a four-week extension, run the decomposition Ishaan has not run, specify the pre-purge aggregation before January, and bring a settled basis to the December board. Four weeks of runway costs roughly ₹4.6 crore at current burn, the expansion leases are already signed, and Shantanu believes an extension request will be read in the market as a diligence problem.

Nandita's exhibit suggests a different reading — that a business whose lowest-density fifteen per cent of subscribers contributes negative margin does not have a lifetime-value problem at all, but a mix problem, and that no integral of any curve will fix it. Cheryl's unshared finding suggests a third reading: that the company has been buying back the same households repeatedly and calling it growth, in which case the unit of analysis is wrong before the arithmetic begins.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board convenes at 10 a.m. on Friday 13 November in Hyderabad, with Rajat dialling from New Jersey and Tejomay's partner joining from Mumbai. The term sheet's exclusivity expires on 30 November. The certification language — "contribution LTV to CAC of not less than 3.0× on trailing-twelve-month cohorts" — does not define contribution, does not define the horizon, does not specify a discount rate and does not say whether win-backs are new cohorts; Farida's view is that a sloppy definition binds management more tightly, not less, because the ambiguity will be resolved against the party that drafted around it.

Cash gives fourteen months at present burn, less if the new cities continue at their October contribution. Cold-chain leases in Indore and Kochi carry ₹11 crore of committed spend with a nine-month exit clause. The Nitya discount cannot be repriced. The DPDP purge runs in January and the aggregation specification must be frozen before it. The Al Ghadeer tier resets on a published figure below ₹3,000, worth about ₹6.4 crore a year, and Yusuf has asked for a GCC exclusivity conversation in the same quarter. Eleven people across four countries know the number is contested; none has yet put it in writing to the board.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Reconstruct the ₹5,930 figure from Exhibits 1, 4 and 5. Which of its inputs are measurements, which are assumptions, and which are choices? What would have to be true for it to still be correct in November 2026?
  2. Exhibits 1 and 2 describe the same cohorts and disagree. Which one is measuring the thing that lifetime value is supposed to capture, and what does your answer imply about how a pause feature should be treated in a retention curve?
  3. The blended line in Exhibit 3 is flatter than every cohort curve drawn beside it. Explain how that can be arithmetically true, and identify which decisions at Payas Daily may have been made on the strength of that line.
  4. Exhibit 5 shows contribution rising with tenure and falling with newness of city. How should a lifetime-value model handle a multiplicand that is not constant over a customer's life, and what does that do to the comparison between rows A and D of Exhibit 4?
  5. Cheryl Ong's win-back cohorts cost ₹500 and churn at twice the first-time rate. Are they acquisition or retention? Construct the case for each treatment, and show what each does to CAC, to the curve, and to the ratio Tejomay is gating on.
  6. It is Monday morning, 16 November. Devika Iyer has to send one email and hold one meeting. What does she do, what number — if any — does she certify, and what exactly does she say to the board about the four years in which the company reported a figure it can no longer reproduce?

11. Gachibowli, 11.40 p.m.

Devika closed the laptop and then opened it again. The security guard had begun switching off the corridor lights. On the whiteboard, someone — Ishaan, on his last visit — had drawn a retention curve in green marker months ago and never wiped it off, and under it written the words area under the curve × value per period, which was, Devika thought, the whole of the theory and none of the difficulty.

She thought about the Nitya households in Warangal, paying fifteen per cent less for milk four years on, holding up the only part of the curve anyone had seen flatten. She thought about the pause screen, a better product and a worse measurement, and about the ₹4.7 crore in the wallets of people who had stopped opening the app. She opened a blank mail to Shantanu, typed "on tomorrow —", and stopped.

Outside, the 5.30 a.m. route vans were already being loaded at the Kondapur hub for the morning delivery, to households that had not been asked what they were worth.

Modelling LTV from Retention: the depth treatment

1. Two decisions, one November

On 4 November 2026, Devasena Iyer, Chief Product Officer of Anaaj Intelligence, a Hyderabad company selling an AI underwriting copilot to non-bank lenders, took a paper to her board asking for ₹12 crore to build a fourteen-person enterprise sales team. It turned on one claim: that an enterprise account was worth enough to justify a fully loaded acquisition cost of ₹22 lakh. Anaaj had nineteen months of account-level billing across ninety-six lenders. Gross revenue retention over the last twelve months was 84 per cent; net revenue retention, which counts expansion among survivors, was 131 per cent. Her head of analytics had produced three LTV figures from those same nineteen months, by three defensible methods, ranging from ₹18.7 lakh to unbounded.

On 12 November, Revathi Balasubramanian, Head of Product at Kharif Devices in Coimbatore, was deciding whether to stop making money on hardware. Kharif sold a solar pump controller with soil-moisture telemetry to farmer producer organisations and, increasingly, to two state agriculture departments; it shipped at ₹9,400 against a landed cost of ₹7,330 and carried a ₹180-a-month telemetry subscription. Sales wanted it at ₹7,900 — roughly cost — arguing that every controller in the field is an annuity. Revathi's objection was not that this was wrong but that nobody could say how long the annuity ran. Devices had shipped for twenty-one months, and the subsidy-funded cohort, now over half of new volume, had its subscription paid by a state department for exactly twenty-four. The most important number in the model was one Kharif had never observed.

Both are the same decision: convert a retention curve into a present value when the curve stops well short of the horizon the money is committed against. What separates a competent answer from an expert one is not arithmetic — the arithmetic is a weighted sum — but knowing which part is data and which part is a modelling choice wearing data's clothes.

2. The idea, and the traditions that disagree about it

Lifetime value is the discounted sum, over a horizon, of contribution margin expected each period, weighted by the probability the customer is still active then:

LTV = Σt=0..H   S(t) · m(t) / (1 + d)t

where S(t) is the survivor function, m(t) is contribution margin per active customer in period t, d is the periodic discount rate and H the horizon. Every serious disagreement is about one of those four symbols, and the first thing an expert asks of someone else's LTV is which were varied and which frozen.

The idea has three parents still arguing. The customer-equity tradition came out of direct marketing: Blattberg and Deighton's 1996 Harvard Business Review article on customer equity, Rust, Zeithaml and Lemon's 2000 book, Gupta, Lehmann and Stuart's 2004 paper valuing firms by summing their customer bases. Its motivating problem was accountability: catalogue marketers had to defend spend as investment rather than expense. It signs that a discounted aggregate of customer margins is a legitimate proxy for enterprise value; it will not sign an undiscounted LTV, nor one that ignores cost to serve.

The probabilistic tradition is sharper. Schmittlein, Morrison and Colombo's Pareto/NBD model of 1987, and later Fader and Hardie's beta-geometric work, treat churn as a stochastic process whose parameter varies across customers. Its central claim is the biggest single gap between a competent practitioner and an expert: an aggregate retention curve flattens mainly because of sorting, not loyalty. If every customer has a fixed monthly probability of leaving but those probabilities differ, the high-risk customers leave first and the surviving pool is progressively enriched in low-risk ones. This school signs that a two-parameter model fitted to twelve months of a contractual cohort out-predicts any hand-drawn geometric tail on months thirteen to thirty-six. It will not sign that a company has an LTV; it insists on a distribution, and where possible a per-customer score.

The operator tradition — the SaaS-metrics lineage most product managers learned from — prizes a number recomputable on the fifth of every month. It signs that a crude LTV recomputed monthly beside a payback control beats a precise one computed annually, and will not sign a projection beyond two or three years.

Against all three stands a sceptical camp, stated most clearly in Bill Gurley's 2012 essay on the LTV formula. Its proposition: LTV is an average while every spending decision is made at the margin, and the marginal customer from a saturating channel retains worse than the cohort average — so LTV/CAC flatters most exactly when spend is scaling fastest and the error is most expensive. It signs payback period, which uses only observed months, as the more honest control, and will not sign a single LTV figure in a board deck.

3. Mechanics: what the curve is made of

Start with the sorting claim, because if it holds the standard method is biased in a knowable direction. Beejmantra Learning, a Jaipur exam-preparation app charging ₹399 a month, tracked a January 2025 cohort of 42,000 sign-ups for twelve months. The right-hand column is what almost nobody computes.

Exhibit 1 — Beejmantra Learning, January 2025 cohort. A shifted-beta-geometric with α = 1.6, β = 3.0, fitted to these twelve months, agrees with them within half a point throughout.

The implied rate rises monotonically and keeps rising: there is no month at which the curve becomes flat, only months at which it becomes flatter. The standard operator method — declare the curve flat, read the rate, sum a geometric series — assumes the rate stops improving at whatever month the analyst chose. Do that at month twelve with r = 0.897: the observed months contribute 3.87 customer-months, and the tail contributes S(12) × r / (1 − r) = 0.085 × 8.75 = 0.75, for 4.62 months in total. The fitted shifted-beta-geometric, whose expected lifetime has the closed form (α + β − 1) / (α − 1) when α > 1, gives 6.00. At ₹255 contribution per active month that is ₹1,178 against ₹1,530 — against a CAC of ₹640, an LTV/CAC of 1.84 against 2.39. The geometric tail is not merely imprecise; it is biased low by construction, and the bias grows with the heterogeneity of the base.

Three further mechanics are usually left implicit. First, m(t) is a function, not a constant. Support cost per account falls with tenure; renewal discounts accumulate; and in AI-native products the heaviest users, disproportionately the survivors, consume the most inference. At Anaaj, blended gross margin rose from 44 to 71 per cent in nineteen months through model substitution, so an LTV on historical margin understates badly and one on current margin assumes a cost curve that has already flattened.

Second, the horizon is not a technicality. With churn and no expansion the sum converges and H can be infinity; add expansion and it may not converge at all. If survivors grow spend at monthly rate g while the cohort decays at monthly rate r, each term is proportional to [r(1+g)/(1+d)]t, finite only when r(1+g) < 1+d. Anaaj fails. Its 84 per cent annual gross revenue retention is a monthly r of 0.9857; net revenue retention of 131 per cent implies survivors expand 1.31/0.84 = 1.56× a year, a monthly g of 3.77 per cent; at an 18 per cent cost of capital d is 1.39 per cent monthly. The product is 1.0089 and the sum diverges. Anaaj does not have a large LTV; it has no LTV, and any figure quoted is a horizon choice presented as a measurement.

Third, censoring. A pooled curve has a different number of cohorts behind each point: month one has all of them, month eighteen only those old enough to reach it, which are the earliest and most self-selected. Plot the contributing sample size beneath the curve, and refuse to extrapolate from a point supported by a handful of cohorts.

4. When the model applies, stated as tests

C1 — the setting is contractual. Can you say, for any customer on any day, whether they are a customer, without inference? Anaaj passes: every lender sits on a platform floor with a contract end date. Kharif passes for telemetry and fails for hardware, since an organisation that does not buy a second controller has not churned. Marketplaces fail outright; they draw an activity curve, which is not a survivor function.

C2 — you have observed a material fraction of the horizon you intend to underwrite. A workable rule is a third. Anaaj has nineteen months and wants thirty-six: marginal, defensible with a stated assumption. Kharif has nothing past the month-24 cliff and fails absolutely for most of its current volume.

C3 — the acquisition process is stationary. Will next quarter's customers resemble the cohort you measured? Anaaj fails: its nineteen months were inbound and founder-led, and field sales will reach slower, more price-sensitive lenders. Kharif fails too, if volume comes from the subsidy channel.

C4 — margin per active customer is stable or explicitly modelled. Anaaj fails and must model. Kharif passes: SIM data, cloud and field-support costs per device are predictable.

C5 — value is separable per customer. No network effects, no cross-subsidy between sides. Both protagonists pass; the marketplace in section 8 does not, and that is where a per-customer LTV becomes actively misleading rather than imprecise.

The model points the wrong way in three situations: when channel mix shifts fast, because the blended curve describes a population you no longer buy; when expansion is strong, because the arithmetic does not converge and the figure reported is the horizon; and when the binding constraint is cash rather than return, because a company can be right that a customer is worth ₹62 lakh over three years and still die in month eleven.

5. Hard edges and organisational seams

Multi-product companies find LTV is not additive. An account buying two modules is not worth two single-module LTVs, because cross-purchase is itself the strongest retention signal available, and attributing the lift to either module double-counts. Mature vendors model at account level and treat module attach as a covariate; the product-line P&Ls sum anyway.

On two-sided platforms, a supply-side participant's value is partly the retention it confers on the demand side. Compute each side separately and the network effect vanishes from both models, undervaluing whichever side is scarce. The workaround — treating liquidity as a market-level state variable and running cohort value conditional on it — is expensive and rarely done well, which is why marketplace CAC ceilings are judgement dressed as arithmetic.

Regulation changes the curve's meaning. Kharif collects under UPI AutoPay mandates, and about 3.1 per cent of active mandates fail monthly — expiry, insufficient balance, re-authentication — of which dunning recovers 62 per cent within a fortnight, leaving net involuntary churn near 1.2 per cent against steady-state voluntary churn of 1.6. Nearly half the tail decay is a payments problem no roadmap item will fix.

Hardware plus software has a ceiling software lacks. Kharif's controller has a median field life of 58 months in Tamil Nadu conditions; beyond that the subscription cannot continue without a new device sale, itself a new acquisition with its own cost. An infinite geometric tail on a device subscription is not conservative or aggressive; it is a category error.

AI-native products break the assumption that margin is a company-level constant. When cost of goods is inference, the customers who stay are the ones who use most: Anaaj's top volume decile ran at 52 per cent gross margin against a book average of 71. Against that, model costs fall as cloud costs never did, so a cohort's margin can improve twenty points with no commercial action.

The organisational seam is where most of this goes wrong. Rabi Systems, a twenty-year-old Pune manufacturing-execution vendor, runs two LTV models: finance owns a contract-cohort NPV for revenue guidance, on booked contract value, conservative renewal rates and a three-year cap; growth owns a cohort LTV for channel budgets, on net revenue retention over five years. They differ by 1.9×. Rabi's honest practice, visible only in the planning cycle and never in any public statement, is that spend above ₹2 crore must be defensible under both. What mature companies say is that they have a single source of truth; what they have is two models and a negotiated boundary.

6. Nine things experts see that competent practitioners miss

Flattening is sorting, not loyalty. The tell is that implied monthly retention rises monotonically in every cohort of every product at every company, including cohorts that received no product change. The obvious reading — that onboarding improvements are working — would predict the effect only where those improvements landed. Because it is composition rather than conversion, changing who you acquire moves the curve more than changing the product does, and the two look identical on a dashboard.

Right-censoring masquerades as fact. The tell is "our twelve-month retention is 31 per cent" quoted for a product with meaningful volume for fourteen months. Two cohorts have reached month twelve, both from the earliest, most self-selected period. The obvious reading treats it as an average; it is a statement about the founders' friends.

Survivorship inflates ARPU. The tell is cohort ARPU rising smoothly with tenure while nobody can name a price increase. Decompose it into a within-customer term and a mix term; if the within-customer term is near zero there is no expansion, only the cheap plan churning faster — and stacked on a survivor curve, the same selection is counted twice.

Average LTV is not marginal LTV. The tell is an LTV that stays stable while CAC climbs. If it holds while spend triples, either the channel has unusual depth or the figure is blended across vintages. Recompute on the latest fifth of spend; the gap is the honest measure of saturation.

Involuntary churn wears the same clothes as product failure. The tell is churn clustering on particular days of the month, or differing by payment instrument — in India, mandate expiry, tokenisation breakage, re-authentication thresholds. The obvious reading is that users stopped valuing the product. The diagnostic is cheap and never run: split the curve by payment method.

The tail's start month is a free parameter doing more work than the data. The tell is two competent analysts producing LTVs 40 per cent apart from identical data, differing only in whether the tail begins at month six or nine. Under sorting there is no true flat point, only flatter regions, so the choice is never data-determined. Report LTV as a function of horizon, not a scalar.

Negative churn breaks the arithmetic, not merely the estimate. The tell is ARPA × gross margin / (1 − NRR) producing a negative or gigantic number, quoted with enthusiasm. The obvious reading is that the business is extraordinary; the correct one is that it has a growth rate and no lifetime value, and someone must choose a horizon and a decay assumption in public.

Contribution margin usually falls with tenure. The tell is flat company-level gross margin alongside falling cohort-level margin. Renewal discounts compound, survivors are support-heavy by selection, and in usage-priced products the loyal heavy user can be margin-negative. That long-lived customers are the best customers is true of revenue and often false of profit.

Tenure time is contaminated by calendar time. The tell is cohorts acquired in different quarters showing different retention at the same tenure. A pooled curve attributes to tenure what belongs to a price change or a rival's promotion; if cohorts do not overlay, extrapolating tenure-time is forecasting the past.

7. How the practice differs, and where it does not

In consumer subscription, cohorts are large and the statistics are kind: a two-parameter probabilistic model is feasible, and the main risk is heterogeneity across channels rather than sampling error. In B2B and enterprise, cohorts are small enough that a fitted survivor curve is mostly noise — Anaaj's ninety-six accounts cannot support a beta-geometric — so practice shifts to dollar-weighted retention, segment renewal rates and explicit expansion modelling. The real difference is the unit: enterprise LTV is a revenue-retention object and consumer LTV a logo-retention object, and applying either method to the other is the commonest cross-domain mistake.

For platforms the difference is structural: the setting is non-contractual, churn is latent, resurrection common. For hardware it is the finite device life and the month-zero margin lump, which makes payback trivially short and lifetime value genuinely capped. For AI products it is that m(t) moves on a technology curve rather than a commercial one.

Stage changes what the number is for more than how it is computed. Pre-product-market-fit, LTV is close to meaningless and the honest artefact is the curve's shape. At Series A and B its job is to set a CAC ceiling, as a range with a horizon, revised monthly. At scale it shifts to segment-level capital allocation, and the horizon lengthens because there is data to support it. What stage never changes is the requirement to use contribution margin rather than revenue and to state the horizon: a seed-stage company has every reason to be approximate and no excuse for either omission.

8. Three worked examples

Anaaj Intelligence: the horizon is the model

Contribution margin per surviving account is ₹1.48 lakh a month after inference, support and customer success. With r = 0.9857, g = 3.77 per cent and d = 1.39 per cent, the per-period factor is 1.0089 and the sum grows without bound.

Under the last row, 58 per cent of the value sits beyond month thirty-six — longer than the tenure of Anaaj's own head of sales.

Kharif Devices: two cohorts, one LTV, different risk

Hardware contributes ₹2,070 at month zero against a ₹430 warranty reserve; telemetry contributes ₹117 a month after SIM data, cloud and amortised field support. The self-pay curve loses 28 per cent in six months, then decays at 1.6 per cent voluntary plus 1.2 per cent involuntary, capped by the 58-month device life: 34.6 expected subscription-months.

The subsidy cohort is the interesting one. It retains at 99.6 per cent monthly for twenty-four months because a department pays, then meets a cliff at month twenty-five where, on the evidence of a comparable scheme in a neighbouring state, about 41 per cent convert to self-pay: 23.7 months before the cliff and 10.8 after, 34.5 in total, within a whisker of the self-pay cohort's 34.6. The expected LTVs are identical and the cohorts must be managed completely differently. The subsidy cohort's value is front-loaded and contractually certain for two years, then binary; the self-pay cohort's is back-loaded and continuously uncertain. Discounting catches part of this — the subsidy cohort is worth 9 per cent more in present value — but the decision-relevant difference is that its LTV turns on a scheme renewal taken in a state secretariat, which is neither a product risk nor one Kharif can hedge. Cutting hardware to ₹7,900 drops month-zero contribution from ₹2,070 to ₹570 and pushes two-thirds of value past month twenty-four, in a business with eleven months of cash.

Khalihan Exchange: the model that failed

Khalihan Exchange, a Ludhiana business-to-business marketplace for industrial surplus — metal offcuts, polymer regrind — built an LTV model in 2024 on what it called a buyer retention curve: the fraction of a buyer cohort transacting in each subsequent month. It fell to 22 per cent by month twelve and looked reassuringly like a subscription curve. The standard method gave ₹41,000 per buyer against a blended CAC of ₹26,000. Trade-show buyers had the worst curve and paid search the best, so Khalihan cut trade-show spend 70 per cent and doubled paid search.

The model failed for two connected reasons. Monthly activity is not survival in a non-contractual setting: a fabricator buys when a job comes in, and a quiet month is not a departure. The curve measured purchase frequency, rewarding buyers who bought small and often over those who bought rarely and large. Second, resurrection was invisible to it. Rebuilding in late 2025 with a latent-churn model of the Pareto/NBD family, on spend-weighted rather than count-weighted cohorts, Khalihan found that 38 per cent of buyers counted as churned at month six transacted again by month fourteen, and that trade-show contribution per acquired buyer over eighteen months was 2.3 times paid search. Restated trade-show LTV was ₹1.18 lakh. The error cost some ₹3.2 crore of misdirected spend over fourteen months, plus something harder to quantify: those relationships ran through a handful of scrap aggregators and had to be rebuilt cold. The recovery was not a better formula but the recognition that the company had been drawing a survivor function for a process in which nobody dies.

9. Failure modes and their early warning signs

Extrapolating a tail from too few post-shakeout months. Sign: LTV swings more than a fifth between board decks with no business change. Diagnostic: how many cohorts contribute to the last point you fitted on? Cost late: a CAC ceiling 40 per cent too high for two quarters — at scale, the round.

Revenue in place of contribution margin. Sign: the LTV slide implies profitability the cash-flow statement contradicts. Diagnostic: what share of ARPU goes to payment fees, support, delivery and inference? Cost late: it surfaces in diligence and destroys management credibility on every other number.

Blending a bimodal cohort. Sign: a channel with a healthy blended LTV persistently misses payback. Diagnostic: split the curve by channel and by first-week activation and see how widely the sub-curves bracket the blend. Cost late: months of spend into a channel that looked average only because good and bad customers cancelled out.

Treating an unobserved parameter as data. Sign: a critical input has no corresponding column in any table — Kharif's month-25 conversion rate is the archetype. Diagnostic: for every input, name the query that produced it. Cost late: the assumption is discovered at the moment it fails, which is the moment the money is spent.

Confusing realised cohort revenue with forecast LTV. Sign: a mature cohort's cumulative revenue quoted as validating a projection for a new one. Diagnostic: same channel, same price? Cost late: a growth plan underwritten by customers the company no longer acquires.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Model-based projection versus horizon-capped conservatism. The probabilistic camp argues that a beta-geometric fitted to twelve months predicts months thirteen to thirty-six with low single-digit errors across dozens of published holdout tests, and that refusing it prefers known bias to measured error. The conservative camp answers that this accuracy was shown on stationary populations, and no venture-stage company has one: mix, price and product change faster than the parameters are identified. The probabilistic position is wrong only if out-of-sample error is dominated by non-stationarity rather than curve shape — which the sparse evidence on fast-changing products suggests and the abundant evidence on mature subscription businesses contradicts.

Average versus marginal. The sceptics hold that LTV/CAC pairs an average numerator with a marginal denominator, and that the real question is what the next rupee buys. Defenders answer that marginal LTV is unmeasurable — you cannot observe the retention of customers not yet acquired — and that a blended figure recomputed monthly beside a payback control catches deterioration soon enough. The sceptics are wrong if saturation shows in payback as fast as in retention; the evidence is that retention degrades first and payback follows by one to two quarters, which is long enough to matter.

Whether LTV belongs in capital allocation at all. One camp, increasingly loud among Indian growth-stage boards since 2022, holds that LTV should be an internal diagnostic and never a budgeting input, and that allocation should run on contribution-margin payback, which is composed entirely of observed months. The opposing view is that payback-only allocation underfunds products with long, valuable tails — enterprise software, insurance, anything with a durable annuity — and hands those categories to rivals willing to underwrite them. Both are held by serious people, and the answer depends on the cost of capital, so it moves with the funding cycle rather than the mathematics.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this produces an LTV. Someone who has internalised it produces a function and a sensitivity: value against horizon, with the observed region shaded and the assumed region marked, and a statement of which single assumption the decision turns on. They quote LTV per acquired customer, not per activated one, because they have been burned by the unit mismatch. They read the implied monthly retention series before the curve, because that is where sorting, seasonality and payment failures announce themselves. They know a point of tail retention is worth more than a point of ARPU, which makes retention claims worth auditing harder than revenue claims. They can tell a CFO, "we do not have an LTV for this segment," and then say what they propose to decide with instead, and they treat a projected retention improvement as a hypothesis with a measurement date, never as value banked the day the feature shipped.

12. What they decided

Devasena did not take the ₹12 crore. She took ₹4.2 crore for five field sellers on a nine-month pilot, on condition that the full build-out's LTV be recomputed on the pilot's own cohort rather than the inbound one, and that the board paper carry a horizon-explicit range — ₹39 lakh at twenty-four months, ₹46 lakh at thirty-six under decaying expansion. Her reasoning: the divergence was information. A business whose value calculation does not converge is one whose value rests entirely on a behavioural assumption, and the cheapest way to test it was to buy nine months of it.

Revathi held hardware at ₹9,400 for self-pay and offered ₹7,900 only on subsidy orders where the department pre-paid twenty-four months of telemetry, turning the discount into a receivable rather than a bet. She moved two engineers onto mandate recovery, on the arithmetic that halving the 1.2 per cent involuntary churn would add more subscription-months than any feature on the roadmap.

Three questions. First: Anaaj's LTV diverges under its own reported net revenue retention — cap the horizon, model expansion decay, or abandon LTV here and manage to payback, and what does each cost? Second: Kharif's two cohorts have identical expected LTV and entirely different risk; what would have to appear in a single metric for it to distinguish them, and is that metric worth building? Third: if flattening curves are mostly sorting rather than loyalty, what does that imply about retention features relative to acquisition targeting, and how would you design an experiment separating the two?

13. Going deeper

  • Retention curves and the PMF signal — the input to everything here; no flattening means no tail to value.
  • CAC, LTV and payback — where this number is consumed, and the control that survives when LTV does not converge.
  • Cohort analysis — separates tenure-time from calendar-time and makes censoring visible rather than silent.
  • Defining activation (the aha moment) — the cleanest way to split a bimodal cohort before fitting.
  • Stickiness and natural frequency — decides whether a survivor function is the right object at all.
  • Reading drop-off — locates the shakeout, which sets the whole level of the curve.
  • Constructing a funnel — supplies the denominators that keep LTV and CAC in the same units.
  • Feature adoption analysis — the route from "the tail improved" to a causal claim.

Modelling LTV from Retention

On the second Tuesday of September 2026, Meher Anand, VP of Growth at Arunoday Health, a Bengaluru subscription fitness and coaching app, sat across from her board with a single slide open: a request to raise the paid-acquisition CAC ceiling from ₹1,200 to ₹1,800 per subscriber. The company was closing a Series B, growth had plateaued at the old ceiling, and performance-marketing channels were telling her they could deliver volume at ₹1,650 if she would just say yes. Her CFO wanted one number before he would sign off: lifetime value. Not a guess, not a benchmark borrowed from a SaaS blog, but a number built from Arunoday's own nine months of cohort data. Get it right and the company could safely spend up to three times its LTV per customer and still hit its return targets. Get it wrong — treat six months of early, volatile churn as if it were the company's steady state — and Arunoday would either starve a channel that was actually profitable or bankroll one that was quietly burning the new round. Meher's task that week was to derive LTV properly from the shape of the retention curve, not from the ARPU figure alone.

The idea

Lifetime value, in the sense this page treats it, is the total contribution margin a company expects to collect from a customer over the whole span of the relationship, computed by adding up, month by month, the fraction of the original cohort still paying multiplied by what each of them contributes in that month. It is not a fixed number you look up; it is an output of a model, and the model's honesty depends entirely on the retention curve you feed it. The idea has two intellectual parents. Direct-marketing statisticians in the 1980s and 1990s built customer-lifetime-value models to justify catalogue and database-marketing spend — Robert Blattberg and John Deighton's 1996 Harvard Business Review piece on "customer equity" is the clearest academic statement of treating a customer relationship as a stream of future margin to be valued today. Two decades later, subscription-software operators — David Skok's widely circulated SaaS metrics writing around 2010 is the best-known example — popularized a shortcut formula, ARPU times gross margin divided by monthly churn, that lets a founder estimate LTV from three inputs instead of a full curve. Both traditions agree on the underlying logic even though the shortcut hides the curve inside a single churn rate. The sentence Meher could say in the boardroom without sounding glib was this: "LTV is what the retention curve says a customer is worth, not what we hope the average customer is worth."

How it actually works

The mechanics start with the retention curve itself: the percentage of an acquisition cohort still active at the start of each month after signup. Arunoday tracks this from its billing system — a customer counts as retained in month t if their subscription is still live at the start of that month. The next step, often skipped, is converting ARPU into contribution margin per active customer per month: revenue minus the variable costs of serving that customer — payment-processing fees, trainer time, cloud costs, customer support. Skipping this step and using raw revenue is the single most common way an LTV model flatters a business that isn't actually profitable per customer.

With margin per active customer in hand, the model multiplies each month's retention fraction by that margin and sums across all future months. This sum is the expected number of "margin-months" a single acquired customer generates, and multiplying it by the margin figure gives LTV. The step practitioners most often leave implicit is recognising that most retention curves have two regimes: an early shakeout phase, in which users decide within weeks whether the product fits their life and a large fraction quit, and a later, flatter core phase, in which the survivors who remain churn slowly and fairly predictably. Treating the whole curve as one process — or worse, extrapolating the early steep drop forward — understates LTV badly. The disciplined approach fits a steady monthly retention rate only to the flat, later part of the curve, then sums that tail using the geometric-series formula: if the tail begins at a retained fraction a and decays at a constant monthly retention rate r, the tail's contribution is a/(1−r). A further step some models add and many skip: discounting future months to present value at a monthly rate, which matters more the longer the tail and the higher the company's true cost of capital. And a step nearly everyone leaves out until it costs them: distinguishing logo retention (is the customer still paying anything at all) from revenue retention (how much they're paying), because a model that holds ARPU constant misses customers who upgrade, downgrade, or churn on price alone.

A worked example

Arunoday charges ₹499 a month and runs a 70% gross margin after payment fees and coaching costs, so contribution margin per active customer per month is ₹349. Nine months of billing data on a 1,000-person acquisition cohort show retained fractions of 100%, 64%, 54%, 49% and 46% for months one through five, after which the curve settles into a steady monthly retention rate of about 97% (3% monthly churn) from month six onward. The first five months, summed as fractions of the original cohort, contribute 1.00 + 0.64 + 0.54 + 0.49 + 0.46 = 3.13 "customer-months." The tail, starting at month six's 0.44 and decaying at 0.97 per month, contributes 0.44 / (1 − 0.97) = 14.67 customer-months. Total expected lifetime: 3.13 + 14.67 = 17.80 months. LTV is then 17.80 × ₹349 = ₹6,212.

The second pass changes one input: Arunoday's product team is about to ship a streak-and-community feature meant to shave a single point off the steady-state monthly churn rate, moving tail retention from 97% to 98%. Rerunning only the tail: 0.44 / (1 − 0.98) = 22.00 customer-months, total lifetime 25.13 months, LTV = 25.13 × ₹349 = ₹8,770 — a 41% jump in LTV from a change that, described in a product update, sounds almost too small to mention. This is the central mechanical lesson of curve-based LTV: because the tail is summed as a geometric series, small changes in steady-state retention compound into large changes in value, far larger than an equivalent change in ARPU would produce. It also means the CAC ceiling Meher is deciding on this month is only "safe" at ₹1,800 if the 98% assumption — not yet observed, only hoped for — actually materialises.

Nuances a learner must sit with

Logo retention is not revenue retention

A curve built on whether a customer still has an active subscription tells you nothing about whether they upgraded, downgraded, or stayed at the same price. B2B and marketplace businesses in particular need a revenue-weighted curve, because a shrinking logo count can coexist with growing revenue if the survivors are spending more — and vice versa.

The tail is an extrapolation, not an observation

Arunoday has only three months of data past the point where the curve looks flat. A 97% figure estimated from three months carries real sampling noise; treating it as settled fact, the way the CFO's spreadsheet implicitly does, is the most dangerous nuance in this whole exercise.

Margin, not revenue, is the multiplier

Running the model on ARPU instead of contribution margin overstates LTV by whatever fraction of revenue variable costs consume — for Arunoday, a 30% overstatement, enough on its own to justify a CAC ceiling the unit economics cannot actually support.

An average curve can hide two populations

If a channel recruits both highly engaged and drive-by users, the blended curve looks moderate while masking a bimodal reality: a durable core and a fast-churning majority. Acting on the blended number misallocates spend toward channels that only look average because good and bad customers cancel out in the mean.

Discounting matters more than most models admit

A twenty-five-month expected lifetime, undiscounted, overstates present value relative to a company's actual cost of capital, especially for an early-stage business raising expensive equity. Many practitioners skip this for speed; it is defensible for short-tail products and indefensible for long ones.

LTV is easily confused with realized lifetime revenue

A backward-looking number — how much a cohort has actually paid so far — is a fact. A forward-looking LTV built from an extrapolated tail is a forecast wearing the same name. Boardrooms routinely conflate the two, quoting realized revenue from mature cohorts as if it validated a forecast for a brand-new one.

What the model cannot tell you

LTV tells you what a customer is worth if the curve holds; it cannot tell you why the curve looks the way it does, which acquisition channels bring customers who sit on the good side of the curve, or what cash constraint might force Arunoday to slow spending long before any three-year payback period completes.

Questions worth asking before trusting the number

How many months of actual post-shakeout data underlie the tail rate? Is the curve computed on logos or revenue? Is the margin figure gross or fully loaded with support and processing costs? Does ARPU reflect list price or the discounted price most customers actually pay?

Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and scale

Arunoday's consumer subscription model relies on a large cohort and a statistically fitted curve, because no single customer's behaviour is individually predictable, only the aggregate is. A B2B counterpart such as Prabhat Cloud, a Chennai-based workflow-software vendor, sells to a few hundred accounts rather than hundreds of thousands of individuals, so its meaningful curve is a net-revenue-retention curve at the account level, not a logo curve — an account that expands seats and modules can push net retention above 100%, meaning the surviving accounts are worth more each year even as some accounts on the margin churn, a phenomenon SaaS operators call negative churn. A two-sided marketplace such as Kiranpath Mandi, which connects grain traders to mill buyers, has to run two separate curves — one for buyers, one for suppliers — because their retention dynamics differ, and neither curve alone captures the network effect by which a thicker market on one side improves retention on the other, a value the standard per-side LTV formula understates. Scale changes the exercise as much as business model does: an early-stage company like Arunoday has too few months of data to observe a stable tail directly and must lean on proxy cohorts, analogous companies, or conservative assumptions revisited monthly; a mature company has years of segment-level curves and can extrapolate with real confidence, but has to watch for curve drift whenever the product, price, or competitive landscape shifts under a curve that was fitted to an earlier era.

Common mistakes

The first mistake is extrapolating a tail rate from too few months of post-shakeout data. The symptom is an LTV figure that swings by 30% or more between successive board decks with no change in the underlying business; the misunderstanding is treating an early, noisy estimate as settled; the cheapest diagnostic is recomputing LTV using only data through month three and again through month nine and checking whether the two answers differ by more than roughly a fifth — if they do, the number is not yet stable enough to anchor a large CAC decision. The second is using revenue instead of contribution margin, which shows up as a business that looks profitable on an LTV slide while burning cash in the actual P&L; the fix is to ask what fraction of ARPU is consumed by processing, support, and delivery costs and rerun the model on what remains. The third is averaging across a bimodal cohort, visible when a channel with a plausible blended LTV keeps failing to hit payback in practice; the diagnostic is splitting the retention curve by acquisition channel or by an early activation event and comparing the resulting curves rather than trusting one blended line. The fourth, common in B2B, is ignoring expansion revenue and modelling on a flat per-seat price, which understates the value of accounts that grow; the fix is to build the curve on dollars retained per account, not logos retained.

What good looks like

A comparable Bengaluru operator, further along than Arunoday, splits its retention curve by acquisition channel and by whether a new user completed a specific first-week activation action before fitting any tail. It computes LTV on contribution margin, states its tail assumption with an explicit confidence range rather than a single number, and revisits that range every quarter as fresh cohort months arrive, adjusting the CAC ceiling incrementally rather than in one large jump. When a product change is expected to move retention, it treats the improvement as a hypothesis to be confirmed in the data before it is baked into next quarter's spending plan — never as a number banked the day the feature ships.

Closing

Meher did not approve the full move to ₹1,800. She proposed, and the board accepted, a staged ceiling of ₹1,500 now, with a commitment to revisit ₹1,800 once month-nine data from the cohort exposed to the new retention feature confirms whether the tail has actually moved from 97% to 98%, and she asked her team to rebuild the curve split by acquisition channel before any further increase. The reasoning she gave was simple: the arithmetic behind ₹1,800 was correct, but it depended on an assumption nobody had yet observed. The next topic worth her team's attention is payback period against cash constraints — because an LTV-justified CAC ceiling can still be the wrong number for a company that runs out of runway before the eighteen-month lifetime pays it back. Two questions worth sitting with: how many months of your own retention curve would you need to see before trusting a tail extrapolation for a decision this size, and is the ARPU figure in your model gross of the discounts and coupons your actual customers are paying — and would your ceiling survive if it weren't?

What Is a Vyayam Cloud Subscriber Worth?

A festive-season budget decision at a Bengaluru fitness-subscription app, and the retention math behind it.

1. Bengaluru, 17 September 2026

Ananya Deshpande, VP of Growth & Analytics at Vyayam Cloud, printed the two retention curves again before her 6 p.m. call with the founder. The festive-quarter marketing budget — ₹1.6 crore for October through December, the richest acquisition window of the year thanks to Navratri and Diwali gym-resolution traffic — had to be locked by Friday, 25 September. Rohan Kapoor, the CEO, wanted to move ₹40 lakh out of the company's established Google and Meta performance-ads spend and into an influencer-affiliate channel that had, in an August test, brought in subscribers at less than half the cost per acquisition. The number looked irresistible on a CAC slide. Ananya's job before Friday was to tell him whether it looked as good on an LTV slide — and the answer depended entirely on the shape of two retention curves that had only five months of real data behind them.

2. Vyayam Cloud

Founded in 2019 and headquartered in Bengaluru with an engineering pod in Pune, Vyayam Cloud sold subscription access to live and on-demand fitness classes, a habit-tracking app, and a growing line of connected home equipment, competing directly with cult.fit, HealthifyMe and Fittr in a market that Reliance Retail and Decathlon India had also begun courting through their own fitness ecosystems. The company had roughly 4.5 lakh paying subscribers across monthly (₹899) and annual (₹7,499) plans, blending to a net average revenue per user, after payment-gateway fees, of about ₹750 a month. Consumer subscriptions funded the bulk of revenue, but a smaller corporate-wellness line — bulk annual licences sold to employers — had become an important, stickier complement, anchored by a large three-year contract with Zarafa Logistics LLC, a Dubai-based freight and warehousing conglomerate that had enrolled 6,000 employees across its Gulf operations in 2025.

3. The situation

Every festive quarter, Vyayam Cloud ran a paid-acquisition surge on Google Search and Meta ads — its oldest, best-understood channel — supplemented by smaller experiments. In August 2026 the marketing team had trialled a new channel: partnerships with regional fitness influencers on Instagram and YouTube, who ran 21-day challenge campaigns and routed sign-ups through affiliate codes. The channel's cost per paying acquisition came in at ₹950, against ₹1,850 for the performance-ads channel — a gap large enough that Rohan had already floated the reallocation in the last board pre-read. But Marcus Tan, Vyayam Cloud's lead data scientist in Toronto, flagged a complication when he pulled the five-month cohort data: subscribers who arrived through the influencer challenges churned far faster than the performance-ads cohort once the 21-day challenge ended. The question was not which channel was cheaper to acquire from — it plainly was the influencer channel — but which channel produced customers worth more than they cost, once the full shape of their retention curve, not just the CAC, was priced in. Lukas Hoffmann, the product designer in Berlin who owned onboarding, suspected the drop was fixable — challenge-cohort users landed on a generic home screen with no continuation path — but any redesign was at least six weeks from shipping, past the festive window.

The people

Rohan Kapoor, Founder & CEO, Bengaluru — wants the cheaper channel scaled immediately; the board has pushed him hard on efficient growth, and a lower blended CAC this quarter helps the next funding conversation.

Marcus Tan, Lead Data Scientist, Toronto — built the retention-curve model; is wary of extrapolating a steep five-month curve into a twelve-month LTV number, having been burned by an overstated channel forecast in a previous job.

Priya Menon, Head of Sales & Partnerships, New Jersey — manages the Zarafa Logistics relationship and other overseas corporate accounts; worried that a visible consumer-growth stumble could unsettle enterprise renewal conversations, and wants budget certainty more than upside.

Wei Ling Tan, Customer Success Lead, Singapore — owns onboarding health metrics across regions; has raised, independently of this budget debate, that challenge-cohort users rarely reach the habit-forming third week that other cohorts do.

5. What the data showed

Ananya's team tracked two cohorts acquired between March and July 2026 and observed monthly, expressed as the share of the original cohort still paying (Exhibit 1). Both curves start at 100% and decay, but at visibly different rates and toward different floors.

Exhibit 1 — Cohort retention by acquisition channel (% of original paying cohort still active)
Month since acquisition012345 (actual)12 (proj.)
Performance ads (Google + Meta)100%64%54%48%44%42%34%
Influencer-affiliate100%46%30%22%18%16%10%

Months 6–12 are Marcus's projection, fitted from the observed decay shape toward an assumed long-run floor. Months 0–5 are actuals from cohorts billed through August 2026.

Exhibit 1a — same data, plotted. The influencer curve falls faster and settles lower.

To turn a curve into a lifetime value, Marcus summed expected active months per subscriber — the area under each curve — and multiplied by the ₹750 monthly ARPU. Because only five months were observed, the months 6–24 contribution rests on an assumed floor: 30% for performance ads, where the curve was already flattening by month 5, and 10% for influencer-affiliate, where it was still falling. Exhibit 2 lays out the resulting LTV and the CAC:LTV ratio the board uses as its efficiency gate, benchmarked at 3:1 or better.

Exhibit 2 — LTV and CAC:LTV by channel, base case
ChannelCACExpected active monthsARPU/monthLTVLTV:CAC
Performance ads₹1,8509.3₹750₹6,9603.8×
Influencer-affiliate₹9504.3₹750₹3,2253.4×

If the influencer-channel floor is 6% rather than 10% — plausible given the curve had not levelled by month 5 — expected active months fall to about 3.6 and LTV to roughly ₹2,700, taking LTV:CAC to 2.8×, below the board's gate.

6. The options

  1. Shift the full ₹40 lakh to the influencer-affiliate channel now, as Rohan proposed. Upside: roughly double the festive sign-up volume for the same spend at the base-case LTV:CAC of 3.4×, and a marketing story the board will like. Cost: the ratio is thin and rests on an unproven floor assumption; a small shift in that floor pushes the channel below the efficiency gate, and the festive cohort is large enough that a wrong bet is expensive to unwind.
  2. Hold the budget on performance ads, the proven channel at 3.8× LTV:CAC on much more mature data. Upside: predictable economics, no dependence on an extrapolated tail, and no disruption to the enterprise sales narrative Priya is managing with Zarafa Logistics and other overseas accounts. Cost: forgoes the cheaper acquisition cost entirely, and cedes the fast-growing influencer-driven segment of the market to cult.fit and HealthifyMe, both of which were already running comparable campaigns.
  3. Stage the bet: commit ₹10 lakh, not ₹40 lakh, to the influencer channel this quarter, keep the rest on performance ads, and use the extra ten weeks of data this buys — reaching month 8–9 retention — to re-fit the curve before committing further budget in the January cycle. Pair it with Lukas's onboarding fix for challenge-cohort users, which, if it lifts the floor even modestly, changes the channel's economics materially. Upside: bounds the downside while the curve is still uncertain, and creates real data instead of an assumption. Cost: slower to capture the cheap-CAC opportunity, and a smaller festive result to show the board this quarter.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Why is comparing CAC alone across the two channels misleading, and what does the shape of each retention curve add that a single CAC number cannot?
  2. How sensitive is the influencer-affiliate channel's LTV:CAC ratio to the assumed long-run retention floor, and what does that sensitivity say about how much weight the number should carry in this decision?
  3. What would Ananya need to see in the data — and how soon — to be confident recommending the full ₹40 lakh shift rather than a staged one?
  4. How should the interests of Marcus, Priya and Wei Ling — none of whom control the budget decision — shape what Ananya recommends to Rohan?

8. A note for the learner

This topic asks what a customer is worth, given how long they stay — and the honest answer is that lifetime value is only as trustworthy as the retention curve it is built on. A curve observed for five months and projected for twelve is not a fact; it is a forecast with an assumption embedded in its tail, and the influencer-affiliate channel's attractive CAC survives only if that assumption holds. The performance-ads channel's LTV rests on a curve that has already begun to flatten, so its forecast risk is lower even though its acquisition cost is higher.

A well-reasoned answer does three things: it computes LTV from the curve shape rather than from CAC alone; it stress-tests the result against the least favourable plausible assumption, not just the base case; and it treats the size of the bet as proportional to the confidence in the number. On all three counts, Option 3 is the defensible path here. The full reallocation Rohan wants is attractive only under an optimistic floor assumption that the data does not yet support, and holding the budget entirely on the known channel forfeits a real opportunity the August test surfaced. Staging the bet — a bounded ₹10 lakh commitment, paired with the onboarding fix that might genuinely improve the curve's floor — buys the extra months of retention data needed to price the channel properly before the next, larger commitment. It is slower than Rohan would like, but it prices what the topic is actually about: not what a subscriber costs, but what the shape of their loyalty says they are worth.
exp40v2-ana.data.storytelling:
Data Storytelling for Decisions

Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation — Product Analytics & Data Practice — advanced treatment

1. Two rooms, two weeks apart

On Tuesday, 17 November 2026, Nandita Salve, Vice President of Product at Vaachak Cloud, had ninety minutes of her chief executive's time and one number she could not explain. Vaachak Cloud sells conversation intelligence — call transcription, quality scoring and compliance flagging — to banks, insurers and outsourced contact-centre operators. It ends FY26 with ₹94 crore of annual recurring revenue across 212 enterprise accounts, engineering split between Pune and Bengaluru. Net revenue retention, the ratio of this year's recurring revenue from last year's customers to what those customers paid last year, had fallen from 118% to 105%. Arvind Rege, the chief executive, had already formed a view: the company had drifted downmarket into low-quality outsourcing accounts, and the fix was to stop selling to them. Nandita's own engineers wanted ₹6 crore and two quarters to rebuild the scoring model, which they believed was the real cause of unhappiness. Both proposals were plausible, both were expensive, and both would be decided in that room.

Seventeen days later and 840 kilometres south, Kabir Anand faced a structurally similar problem in an entirely different medium. Kabir is Head of Product at Aavega Mobility, which leases electric two-wheelers with swappable batteries to gig delivery riders in nine Indian cities and runs the rider app, the swap-station network and the telematics stack behind them. Thirty-one thousand scooters were in the field. Thirty-day rider churn — the share of riders who stop paying lease instalments within a month of onboarding — had risen from 18.0% in September to 25.3% in November. On 4 December Aavega had a diligence session with the lead investor in a Series C round, and three explanations were live inside the company: a swap-pricing change made nationally on 1 October, a suspected cell-quality problem in scooters built in August under batch code B-114, and a cut in per-order payouts by the delivery platforms Aavega's riders work for. The first was cheap to reverse, the second cost roughly ₹4 crore to remedy, and the third was outside Aavega's control entirely.

Neither Nandita nor Kabir lacked data; both had a warehouse, a dashboard and an analyst. What both needed was the discipline this page is about: an argument in which a claim is stated, evidence is assembled that could have come out otherwise, rival explanations are actively attacked rather than listed, and a recommendation carries its own conditions of defeat. That sequence — claim, evidence, alternatives, recommendation — is easy to recite. What separates an expert is knowing which cut of the data is worth pulling, how much a given piece of evidence is worth, and when the apparatus should be abandoned in favour of an experiment.

2. The idea, and the schools that disagree about it

A precise definition: data storytelling for decisions is the construction of a minimal argument, from quantitative evidence, that changes the posterior probability a decision-maker assigns to competing explanations enough to change the action they take. Three clauses in that sentence do real work. Minimal means that evidence which does not discriminate between the live explanations is deleted regardless of how interesting it is. Competing explanations means that the unit of analysis is not the metric but the set of hypotheses about why the metric moved. Change the action means that an analysis which cannot, under any outcome, alter what the organisation does is not a weak analysis but a wasted one.

The problem the practice was invented to solve is older than product management. Barbara Minto, working at McKinsey from the late 1960s, observed that consultants presented findings in the order they had discovered them, which is almost never the order a reader needs; the Pyramid Principle inverted this into answer-first prose. Edward Tufte's The Visual Display of Quantitative Information (1983) established that graphical integrity is separable from numerical accuracy — a chart in which every number is true can still be a lie of emphasis. Richards Heuer, writing for the United States intelligence community and published openly in 1999 as Psychology of Intelligence Analysis, supplied the piece product managers most often miss: Analysis of Competing Hypotheses, in which the analyst lists hypotheses first, then scores each piece of evidence by how inconsistent it is with each hypothesis, and treats evidence consistent with everything as worthless. Ronald Howard and Howard Raiffa's decision analysis, from the same era, supplied the economics: the value of information is zero unless some possible result would change the choice. Amazon's replacement of slide decks with six-page narrative memos, from the early 2000s, is the organisational enforcement mechanism — prose cannot hide a missing causal claim the way a bullet can.

These lineages do not agree, and the disagreement is not cosmetic. Five positions are worth being able to name, because experienced practitioners argue past each other when they do not realise which one they are standing on.

The pyramid school would sign the proposition that a decision-maker should know the recommendation within the first thirty seconds and that everything below it exists to support it. It would not sign the proposition that a presentation should leave the decision genuinely open; for this school, ambiguity in the deliverable is a failure of the analyst's nerve. The inquiry school, descended from Heuer, would sign the proposition that the analyst's job is disconfirmation and that the strongest evidence is the evidence that would have looked different under the rival hypothesis. It would not sign the proposition that the same person should both assess the evidence and recommend the action, because commitment to a recommendation reliably degrades the assessment. The graphical-integrity school, descended from Tufte and from William Cleveland's work on graphical perception, would sign the proposition that small multiples and high data density beat a single summary statistic, and that the reader should be able to reach their own conclusion. It would not sign "cut everything that does not serve the recommendation," which it reads as editorialising with a spreadsheet. The narrative-memo school would sign the proposition that forcing the argument into prose exposes causal claims that charts conceal. It would not sign the premise behind the phrase "the one chart that makes the decision obvious"; in its view, no single chart ever makes a non-trivial decision obvious, and the belief that one can is precisely the failure mode memos exist to prevent.
