Three Numbers, One Board Meeting

Gaadi Ghar Technologies, Gurugram — September 2026

1. Sunday night, 27 September 2026

The Gurugram office was empty except for the security desk and the third floor, where Ira Bhatnagar, Vice-President of Product at Gaadi Ghar Technologies, had three browser windows open on the same question and three different answers in front of her. Certified inspection-to-sale conversion for the quarter ending 30 September was 22.1 percent, or 26.8 percent, or 29.4 percent, depending on whose query she ran. The board pre-read was due to circulate at eight the next morning. The Series D term sheet, ₹720 crore at a valuation the founders had fought for, carried an expiry of 15 October and a condition that the operating metrics presented in July be "confirmed without material restatement."

In July, on the strength of the 29.4 percent figure, Gaadi Ghar had moved ₹40 crore of its ₹96 crore annual marketing budget out of Hyderabad and Ahmedabad and into Delhi NCR and Bengaluru. Since then, units sold had not moved. Ira had spent Saturday reading three queries line by line. None of them was wrong. Each answered a slightly different question, and no one in the company had noticed that the questions had drifted apart.

2. The company, and a decision made in 2022

Gaadi Ghar was founded in Gurugram in 2018 by Harsh Vardhan Sethi, a former operations manager at a large logistics firm, and Damini Kapoor, an engineer who had built pricing tools for a two-wheeler manufacturer. It began as a classifieds board for used cars and pivoted in 2021 to the full-stack model that now defines the category: buy the car, inspect and refurbish it at a company-run centre, certify it, and sell it with a warranty. By FY26 it operated thirty-one inspection centres across Delhi NCR, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, Ahmedabad and Jaipur, sold roughly 3,900 certified cars a month, and booked ₹2,840 crore of gross revenue, on which margins were thin because the car itself sits on the books.

The decision that constrains everything today was made in August 2022, six weeks before a Series B close. The data team, then two people, needed event tracking and had no time to model it. They shipped a single wide table, transaction_event, with a free-text stage column into which every service wrote whatever string it liked: inspection_done, INSPECTION_COMPLETE, insp_complete_v2, and eventually forty-one distinct values. It worked. It was never replaced, because replacing it was never the most urgent thing in any quarter, and because by 2024 four teams had built dashboards on top of it, each filtering the stage column with its own list of strings.

3. The industry

India's organised used-car market is a war of inventory and trust. Cars24 and Spinny compete on the same full-stack model; CarDekho, Droom and OLX Autos approach it from the marketplace side; Maruti Suzuki True Value and Mahindra First Choice Wheels bring manufacturer distribution and a dealer network that no startup can match. Roughly four used cars now change hands for every new one sold. Certification is the differentiator, which makes the inspection the product and the inspection report the moment of truth.

The regulatory surround is unusually heavy. Ownership transfer runs through the state RTOs and the VAHAN system, and the lag between physical delivery and registered transfer varies from four days in Pune to as much as five weeks in parts of NCR. GST on used cars is levied on the dealer's margin, which means finance recognises a sale on a different trigger than operations does. The Reserve Bank of India's digital lending rules govern how Gaadi Ghar can pass a buyer to Chetana Finance, its captive lending partner, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act restricts which buyer attributes may be joined to marketing tables at all. Two of Ira's analysts had been told in March that they could no longer join phone-number-level tables without a documented purpose.

Gaadi Ghar's exposure is not only domestic. Since 2024 it has exported right-hand-drive certified stock in lots to Firdaus Motors Trading LLC in Dubai, a contract worth roughly ₹180 crore annualised, carrying a certification SLA: every car in a lot must carry a valid inspection record. And a small team led from New Jersey licenses Gaadi Ghar's inspection-scoring software to independent dealers in North America, a business of ₹31 crore that sells almost entirely on the credibility of the company's own conversion numbers.

Two macro currents complicate the reading of any trend. The shift to electric vehicles has made three- and four-year-old petrol hatchbacks cheaper to source and slower to sell in metros, while the government's vehicle scrappage policy has thinned supply at the older end. Both effects are strongest in NCR, where the ten-year diesel rule already removes a cohort of cars from circulation each year. A conversion rate that moved in NCR between April and September was therefore moving in a market that was itself moving, and nobody at Gaadi Ghar had attempted to separate the two.

4. What happened, in order

In January the board set a target: raise certified inspection-to-sale conversion from 22 percent to 28 percent by the September quarter. Nobody at the meeting wrote down the definition; it was understood to mean the share of completed inspections that ended in a sale.

In March, growth shipped Doorstep Inspection in NCR and Bengaluru — an inspector visits the seller's home rather than the seller driving to a centre. It was expected to raise inspection volume and, perhaps, to lower conversion slightly, since a doorstep inspection is easier to start and easier to abandon.

In May, the design team in Berlin shipped a rebuilt inspection report. In the old flow the inspection_completed event fired when a supervisor signed off the physical inspection at the centre, typically two to six hours after the car arrived. In the new flow the report is generated the moment the inspector submits the checklist on the tablet, and the engineer implementing it moved the event there, because that was where the report existed. Nobody thought of it as a metric change. It was a rendering change.

In June, the platform team in Pune migrated the warehouse, normalising the forty-one stage strings into eleven modelled values. The backfill ran to 1 January 2026 and stopped, because scanning 2024 and 2025 would have cost an estimated ₹9 lakh in compute and the team had ₹4 lakh left in its quarter. The migration note said so, in the fourth paragraph.

In July, Kabir Anand, Head of Growth in Bengaluru, ran his own query against the new tables and found NCR conversion at 29.4 percent — above target, three months early. The reallocation of ₹40 crore followed within a fortnight. In August, finance closed the month and units sold were flat: 3,880 against 3,910 in June. In September, Dr. Aparna Menon in Toronto ran an audit and found that three teams were computing the same metric from three different filters, and that none of the three could be compared to any month before January 2026.

What was believed at each point looks reasonable in isolation. In March, everyone believed Doorstep Inspection would raise volume and might dilute quality; that belief was never tested, because the two cohorts were never separated in the data. In May, the design and engineering teams believed they had changed a screen. In June, the platform team believed a migration that preserved eleven modelled values was a like-for-like improvement, and it was, forward of 1 January. In July, Kabir believed he was reading a cleaner version of a metric he had tracked for two years. What has turned out to be wrong is narrower than any of them fears and broader than any of them admits: the metric's denominator changed twice in eight weeks, in two different ways, for two unrelated reasons, and no artefact in the company records that it did.

5. The people

Ira Bhatnagar, VP Product, Gurugram. Owns the metric as far as the board is concerned. Her position is that the company cannot present a number it cannot reproduce. Her incentive is a leadership role after the Series D. What she is not saying is that she approved the Berlin redesign without asking what it did to instrumentation, and that she signed off Kabir's July memo after reading the summary and not the query.

Harsh Vardhan Sethi, co-founder and CEO, Gurugram. Wants one number, defensible, in the pre-read. His incentive is the term sheet and the no-material-restatement condition. What he is not saying is that he has already told two of the incoming investors, informally, that conversion crossed 29 percent.

Kabir Anand, Head of Growth, Bengaluru. Believes his number is the truest of the three because it counts only inspections that reached a priced offer. His variable pay is tied to blended customer acquisition cost, which the reallocation improved on paper. What he is not saying is that in mid-July he added two of the new stage values to his filter and removed one, and told nobody, because it looked like a routine fix.

Nandita Rege, Data Platform Lead, Pune. Believes the migration was overdue and correct. Her incentive is a platform roadmap that has been deferred twice. What she is not saying is that the 1 January backfill boundary makes every year-on-year comparison in the board deck unsupportable, and that she raised it once, in a note nobody acknowledged.

Dr. Aparna Menon, Senior Data Scientist, Toronto. Wants warehouse write-access narrowed to a modelled semantic layer, with product managers querying certified marts only. Her incentive is the credibility of her own team. What she is not saying is that her audit's own reconstruction of pre-2026 conversion relies on an assumption about abandoned doorstep inspections that she has not tested.

Rohit Thakkar, Financial Controller, Gurugram. Computes conversion from the ledger: certified cars invoiced divided by inspections logged. His incentive is a clean audit before the round. What he is not saying is that his denominator comes from a monthly operations spreadsheet maintained by regional managers, not from the warehouse at all.

Lena Hoffmann, Principal Designer, Berlin. Believes the redesign was a clear improvement and has the usability data to show it. Her incentive is to defend a launch that is being retroactively blamed. What she is not saying is that she left a comment on the handoff file in April asking whether the completion event should move, and that nobody replied.

Vikram Salvi, Head of Dealer Suite Sales, New Jersey. Uses Indian conversion figures in every North American pitch. His incentive is a ₹31 crore business with a Q4 quota. What he is not saying is that two prospects have already been sent a deck citing 29.4 percent.

Tariq Al Suwaidi, procurement head at Firdaus Motors Trading LLC, Dubai. Has flagged that two export lots in August contained cars whose inspection records his team could not locate in the shared portal. His incentive is leverage in a renewal negotiation due in November. What he is not saying is how many cars are actually affected.

7. Voices

"The query is four lines. Inspections that reached a priced offer, divided into sales. That is the funnel we actually manage. If finance wants to divide by a number typed into a spreadsheet in Indore, that is finance's business."— Kabir Anand, growth review, 22 September
"I am not saying the redesign was wrong. I am saying that on 4 May the event moved four hours earlier in the process, and from that day the denominator in two of the three definitions includes cars that in April would not have been counted at all. Whether that is an improvement depends entirely on what you think the metric is for."— Aparna Menon, recorded audit call, Toronto, 23 September
"I asked about this in April. It is in the handoff file. I can send the link."— Lena Hoffmann, Slack, 24 September, 06:12 CEST

"Restating an operating metric three weeks before signing is not a data problem, Ira. It is a governance problem, and they will read it as one."— Harsh Vardhan Sethi, corridor, Friday evening

8. The options as Ira sees them

The first is to adopt the finance definition as the single board metric, present 22.1 percent, explain the drift, and announce that self-serve querying will be routed through a modelled semantic layer under Aparna's team by January. It is honest and it is legible to auditors. It also concedes that the company missed the board's target by six points, invites the material-restatement question, and takes away from every product manager the tool that let them find anything, in exchange for a layer that will take a quarter to build and will encode a definition Kabir does not accept.

The second is to keep the growth definition and present a bridge: 22.1 percent on the ledger basis, plus the effect of the event-timing change, plus the priced-offer filter, arriving at 29.4 percent, with each adjustment quantified. This preserves the July narrative and is the only option that does not require Harsh to revise what he has already told investors. It depends on being able to quantify the May event shift, which nobody currently can, because the redesign and Doorstep Inspection landed in the same cities in the same quarter.

The third is to tell the board that the number is under audit, present ranges rather than a point estimate, and ask for two weeks. It is the most defensible position intellectually and the most dangerous commercially, with the term sheet expiring on 15 October.

A fourth possibility had occurred to her and she had not written it down, because she could not see how to present it: that the board should be given all three numbers, with the filters attached, and asked to choose the one it wants managed against. Harsh would call it an abdication. Aparna would call it the only intellectually honest option. Kabir would treat it as a rebuke.

Ira had written all three on a whiteboard and then, around eleven, noticed what none of them addressed. Every option was a question about which number to report. None was a question about whether the ₹40 crore had been moved to the right cities — Hyderabad and Ahmedabad had lost 660 units between them while NCR gained seventy — or about who, after Monday, would own the definition of a metric that four teams compute and nobody maintains. Nor did any of them explain Exhibit 5.

9. Deadline and hard constraints

The pre-read circulates at 08:00 on Monday, 28 September; the board meets on Thursday, 1 October. The term sheet expires 15 October and carries the no-material-restatement condition. The marketing commitment for the festive period — ₹11 crore across Navratri, Dussehra and the run-up to Diwali — is contracted and non-refundable. Headcount is frozen until the round closes, so Aparna's semantic layer would be built by the four people she already has, two of whom are committed to a DPDP consent-tracking project that cannot slip because it carries a legal deadline. The Firdaus Motors renewal negotiation opens in November, and the contract's certification SLA allows the buyer to reject a lot in which any car lacks a valid inspection record. And the analyst who owns the export portal query returns on 6 October.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. State precisely what each of the three definitions in Exhibit 1 measures. Which of them, if any, answers the question the board asked in January?
  2. Exhibits 1 and 2 cannot both be describing a healthy NCR business. What would you need to see to decide which is misleading, and could you get it before Monday?
  3. The May redesign changed when an event fires. Who, in a company organised like this one, should have caught that — and what would have had to be true for them to catch it?
  4. Kabir's query is correct SQL answering a question he chose. Is the problem his query, his filter change in July, the absence of a definition owner, or the 2022 decision to ship a free-text stage column? Defend your ranking.
  5. Aparna proposes narrowing warehouse access to a certified semantic layer. Argue the strongest case against her proposal, using evidence from the case rather than principle.
  6. What should Ira do on Monday morning — what goes in the pre-read, in what words — and what would she say to the board on Thursday if a director asks whether the company knows its own conversion rate?

At a quarter past midnight Ira pulled up Kabir's query one more time and read the fourth line, the one that listed the stage values. She counted them. There were nine. Aparna's had seven. She could not remember whether the difference mattered, and she no longer trusted her own sense of which of the two lists was the right one to defend at eight o'clock.

Querying Data: SQL at Depth

Pulling your own numbers is easy. Pulling the right ones, and knowing when the number you pulled cannot mean what you want it to mean, is the skill.

1. Two product managers, two weeks apart

On the evening of 14 September 2026, Meera Joshi sat in the Pune office of Ghumakkad, a bus and rail ticketing app with 9.4 million monthly active users across twenty-one states, looking at a number she did not believe. In July her team had shipped Seat Map Preview, an interactive coach layout letting a traveller choose a seat before paying rather than after. The growth dashboard reported that search-to-booking conversion for the treated half of traffic had moved from 6.3 percent to 6.7 percent. Four-tenths of a point was not nothing; it was also not enough for the marketing director to commit the ₹18 crore Diwali campaign to a message built around seat choice, which was the decision on the table for 19 September.

Meera's suspicion was specific. Seat choice should matter most to a family booking a long journey three weeks before Diwali, and almost not at all to someone booking a Pune–Mumbai bus for the following morning, where any seat will do. If that were true, the blended lift was an average concealing a weak effect on a large group and a strong effect on a small one — and the Diwali campaign targets exactly the advance-booking traveller. The dashboard had no advance-purchase cut; it had been specified in 2024 around city pairs and payment method. The tables underneath it carried a journey_date and a booked_at timestamp, and the difference between them was the cut she needed.

Eight days later and eight hundred kilometres south, Arjun Sabharwal, director of product at Hastakshar Systems, an enterprise contract-workflow platform in Bengaluru with 240 accounts and ₹96 crore of ARR, was preparing a Q4 roadmap argument. Customer success ran an account health score built from signature events per account per week, and by that score the three largest accounts were the healthiest in the book. Arjun did not believe it. All three had integrated Hastakshar through the API eighteen months earlier, and he suspected the events being counted were now generated by scheduled jobs rather than by people — in which case the score measured the robustness of a cron schedule. The question he needed — how many licensed human seats in each account had opened and completed a document in the last seven days — had never been asked of the warehouse in that form.

Both decisions turn on the same capability and, more importantly, on the same discipline. Neither manager is blocked by syntax. Both are blocked by the harder question of what, precisely, a row in the answer should represent.

2. The idea, and the three camps that disagree about it

SQL is a declarative language for relational data: the analyst states the properties of the desired result and the query planner decides how to obtain it. When Edgar Codd published his relational model at IBM in 1970, the prevailing systems required a programmer to navigate explicit pointers between records; Codd proposed instead that data be represented as mathematical relations — tables of tuples — manipulated by a closed algebra of selection, projection, join and union whose outputs are themselves relations. Chamberlin and Boyce built a readable surface for that algebra in 1974; it became an ANSI standard in 1986. The property that made it durable is closure: every query returns a table, so queries compose and a question can be built in layers.

The more instructive history is recent. Between roughly 2004 and 2012 the industry decided SQL was a poor fit for web-scale data and moved to procedural distributed computation — MapReduce, then Hadoop — and within a few years moved back, because the procedural approach put the cost of every analysis on an engineer. Hive put SQL over Hadoop in 2008; Dremel, BigQuery, Redshift and Snowflake put it over columnar cloud storage. The consequence for a product manager in 2026 is that the marginal cost of one more question is a few rupees of scanned bytes rather than a sprint of engineering time.

What people now disagree about is not the language but who should write it and against what. Three camps matter, because a product manager will be managed by one of them.

The modelling school, descended from Ralph Kimball's dimensional design and alive in today's semantic layers, holds that the important work happens before anyone opens a query editor: facts and dimensions modelled once, "active account" defined in one place, everyone querying curated marts. It would sign the proposition that a metric with two definitions in circulation is worse than a metric nobody can compute. It would not sign the proposition that product managers be kept from the raw tables; only that numbers leaving the building come from the modelled layer.

The self-serve school, associated with ELT tooling and transformation logic versioned alongside application code, holds that curation is too slow to be the only path: raw events land in the warehouse, anyone may query them, and correctness is maintained by review and automated tests rather than by restricting who asks. It would sign the proposition that a product manager who cannot get a cut within a day will decide without data. It would not sign the proposition that a query result is fit to quote externally without reconciliation.

The gatekeeping school is less written about and more widely practised than either. It holds that analysis is a profession, that the failure mode of self-serve is a proliferation of confidently wrong numbers, and that any figure crossing an organisational boundary should pass an analyst. It would sign the proposition that most self-serve queries contain a defect that changes the answer materially. It would not sign the proposition that product managers should not learn SQL — it wants them fluent enough to argue with a query and disciplined enough not to publish their own.

Meera works in a self-serve shop; Arjun works in a modelling shop with a semantic layer that does not contain the concept he needs. Their problems are therefore mirror images.

3. Mechanics: grain, population, and the two things that are usually left implicit

An expert's first move on a new question is not to write a SELECT. It is to write two sentences. The first fixes the grain: one row in my answer is one ____. The second fixes the population: the set of ____ that satisfied ____ during ____. Almost every wrong number that survives review violates one of those two sentences rather than a rule of syntax.

Consider Meera's warm-up question: how many users opened the seat map in the week of 1–7 September 2026? The warehouse can answer it five ways, all correct, all different.

Table 1. One question, five grains — Ghumakkad, week of 1–7 September 2026.
Grain (one row is one…)CountRatio to users
Seat-map open event4,812,0003.18×

Device1,740,0001.15×

Source: Ghumakkad event warehouse, evt_seat_map_opened joined to dim_user. Device count exceeds user count because travellers book on a phone and a shared desktop; booking count is lower because most opens do not convert.

The gap between 4.81 million and 1.51 million is a factor of 3.18, large enough that a conversion rate built with the event count in the denominator would understate reality by roughly two-thirds. This is the commonest defect in product-manager SQL, and it is invisible in the output: the query runs, the number is plausible, and nothing flags it.

The second implicit step is fan-out. A join multiplies rows whenever the right-hand table has more than one match per key, and any SUM computed afterwards is multiplied with it. If Meera joins bookings to payments and 11 percent of bookings settle in two instalments, a naive SUM(booking_amount) counts those twice — on 611,000 bookings at a ₹640 average ticket, some ₹4.3 crore of imaginary weekly revenue. The defence is mechanical: before trusting an aggregate after a join, check that COUNT(*) equals COUNT(DISTINCT booking_id).

The formal treatment that matters most is the window function, which computes a value across related rows without collapsing them — exactly what cohort and funnel work requires. To find each traveller's first booking and measure behaviour relative to it, an expert writes ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY booked_at) and filters to rank one, in a single pass. The self-join alternative gives the same answer but scans twice and silently duplicates any user with two bookings at an identical timestamp, which retry logic produces more often than intuition suggests.

Now Meera's real cut. She sets the grain at one user-experiment assignment, the population at users assigned between 21 July and 10 September who ran at least one search, and the dimension at days between search and journey date, bucketed.

In relative terms the 10+ day segment improved by 21 percent and the same-week segment by about one percent. The blended figure is arithmetically correct and strategically useless: it answers a question nobody asked, namely what happens to an average traveller who does not exist. Randomisation holds within each bucket, so the comparison is valid; but concluding that pushing everyone to book earlier would raise conversion mistakes a segment effect for a causal lever.

4. When the capability applies, stated as testable claims

Three conditions determine whether writing your own query is the right move, and each can be checked in under an hour.

Claim one: the fact you need was instrumented. SQL retrieves; it does not create. Meera's cut exists only because journey_date was captured at search time, for an unrelated reason, in 2023. Arjun's question fails this test at first: Hastakshar logs an account ID and an actor ID, but until March 2026 service accounts were not flagged, so his answer is available for six months, not eighteen, and any trend he draws must start in March.

Claim two: the decision is worth the error bar you will carry. A self-written query carries an unknown defect probability. For a reversible internal choice the bar is low. If the number will be quoted to a board, a regulator or a customer, it must be reconciled against a source of record before it leaves the room. Meera's number is going into a planning meeting; Arjun's will appear in a deck the CEO shows the board, which puts it on the far side of that line.

Claim three: the question is descriptive, not causal. SQL answers what happened to whom, never because of what. Where a randomised assignment already exists in the data, as in Meera's case, the query inherits the experiment's causal validity. Where it does not, it produces a correlation that will be read aloud as a cause by the third person who repeats it.

The capability is actively misleading against a mutable dimension table. Most warehouses keep dim_account as a current-state snapshot, overwriting plan tier and region when they change, so a query joining six months of usage to it attributes all historical usage to today's plan. Arjun's predecessor produced exactly this artefact in 2025 — an apparent usage advantage for the Enterprise tier that was really the signature of heavy users being upgraded. The fix is a type-2 dimension with validity dates; the tell is that history changes every time the query is rerun.

5. Hard edges: multi-product, two-sided, regulated, hardware and AI-native

The clean two-table world survives only in small companies. Four situations break it.

Multi-product. Once a company sells more than one thing the identity key fractures. Ghumakkad has a user_id for a signed-in traveller, a device_id for anonymous browsing and, since the hotel add-on, a traveller_profile_id covering several passengers under one booker. Retention differs by 15 to 30 percent depending on which is chosen. Mature companies resolve this with an identity-resolution model; what they say is that they have one user table, and what is true is that the mapping is probabilistic and revised quarterly.

Two-sided. Haldhar Agri Networks, a marketplace matching farmer producer organisations in Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh to institutional buyers, has two populations with different natural frequencies: buyers transact weekly, sellers seasonally. A blended monthly-active metric is an average of two unrelated distributions and moves mostly with the harvest calendar. Expert practice is to refuse to build it, carry two grains permanently, and add a match-rate metric whose grain is the listing rather than either party.

Regulated. Under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, and under Reserve Bank of India rules for anything touching payments, the warehouse a product manager can reach is usually not the warehouse. Identifying columns are masked or tokenised, row-level policies restrict which accounts are visible, and consent state is itself a column that must be joined into any query producing a marketing list. The correct first question is not "can I write this join" but "am I permitted to."

Hardware plus software. Deeya Devices, which sells connected water purifiers with a subscription service layer, receives telemetry from units that are offline for days. About 6 percent of events arrive more than 48 hours late and the tail runs to nine days, so any query over the last week is computed on an incomplete table and the most recent three days are provisional. Figure 3 shows what this does to a retention curve computed too early.

AI-native. Bodhini AI, whose assistant drafts replies inside customer-support desks, has a grain problem of a new kind: one user request produces on average 3.4 model calls, because the system retries, reranks and classifies. Logging every model call means "requests per user" overstates usage by 3.4× and moves whenever the retry policy changes. The commercially meaningful unit — a resolved conversation, at a blended inference cost of ₹1.9 — must be built in SQL by grouping calls under a conversation key the application has to be instructed to emit. The query cannot be written until the taxonomy is amended.

At every seam the same organisational pattern appears: finance and product disagree about a number, both are right within their own grain, and the disagreement surfaces in a meeting rather than in a model. What mature companies actually do, as distinct from what their data-strategy documents claim, is designate a handful of figures as reconciled and treat everything else as exploratory by default.

6. Nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The denominator is usually the finding. Arguments about metrics are nearly always arguments about population disguised as arguments about definition. When two people produce different activation rates, the expert asks not "how did you define activated" but "how many rows are in your denominator" — the numerators usually agree and the population filters usually do not. The tell is two numbers with the same numerator and different totals.

Ratios of averages are not averages of ratios. Compute conversion per city and then average the city figures, and a town in Vidarbha counts as much as Mumbai. Meera's blended 6.68 percent is a ratio of sums; the unweighted mean of her three buckets is 6.73 percent, trivial here and severe when segment sizes differ by an order of magnitude. The tell is a metric that moves when a tiny segment does.

Approximate distinct counts are approximate. Warehouses implement COUNT(DISTINCT) over large columns with sketch algorithms carrying one to two percent relative error, and some tools substitute the approximation silently. On 1.51 million users that is a band of roughly fifteen thousand. The tell is a number that changes in the third digit when rerun on unchanged data.

NOT IN with a nullable column returns nothing. Three-valued logic means a comparison against NULL is unknown, not false, so WHERE user_id NOT IN (SELECT user_id FROM churned) returns an empty set if a single row in churned has a null user ID. The result is not an error; it is zero rows, which a hurried reader interprets as "no such users exist." The tell is an empty result where a small one was expected.

The blessed table is itself somebody's query. A curated mart feels like ground truth because it has a tidy name, but it is a transformation written by a person with assumptions, and reading its source is often the fastest way to settle a discrepancy. Arjun found that fct_account_activity excluded sandbox accounts by a name pattern that also excluded three real customers whose legal names contained the word "Test". The tell is a mart whose counts sit consistently just below the raw tables.

Cost is a design constraint. A query without a predicate on the partitioning column scans the full history — at Ghumakkad's volume, several terabytes and a few thousand rupees per run, trivial once and material when a scheduled dashboard runs it hourly. The expert writes the date filter before the logic and checks the estimated scan before executing. The tell is a warehouse bill rising faster than usage.

The event log records instrumentation, not behaviour. A drop in seat_map_opened on 3 August 2026 traced to an app release that renamed the event, not to any change in traveller behaviour. Experts check release timelines against any discontinuity before building a narrative on it. The tell is a step change rather than a slope, landing on a deploy date.

Self-serve creates a shadow canon. The second-order effect of teaching everyone SQL is not better decisions but a drawer of half-documented queries that get pasted into decks and cited by people who cannot rerun them. The expert response is not to restrict access but to promote anything quoted more than twice into a modelled, tested object. The tell is a number in a deck that nobody present can reproduce.

7. How the practice varies by product type and company stage

In consumer products the binding constraints are volume and identity: tables run to billions of rows, so partitioning discipline matters, and the same human appears under several keys. In B2B and enterprise the constraint is the opposite. Two hundred and forty accounts means one customer can move a metric several points, tests over accounts are underpowered, and the right instinct is to read the account list rather than the aggregate. Arjun can literally read all 240 rows; Meera cannot read any of her 9.4 million.

Platforms and marketplaces carry two grains permanently, as Haldhar does, and the interesting metrics live at the match. Hardware businesses have a denominator problem: the installed base is known from manufacturing rather than from events, so numerator and denominator come from different systems and disagree by the units sitting unsold in a warehouse. AI products carry the model-call grain, non-deterministic outputs that defeat exact-match evaluation in SQL, and a unit cost per interaction that makes every usage metric also a cost metric.

By stage, the difference is mostly about what is being queried. At seed stage there is no warehouse and the PM queries a production read replica, which is fast, dangerous and entirely reasonable. Between Series A and C the first modelled marts appear and practice bifurcates into raw exploration and mart-based reporting. At enterprise scale the PM mostly queries the semantic layer, and the valuable skill shifts to reading someone else's model and knowing which of its assumptions the current question violates. What does not change is the discipline of grain and population — the same at nine employees and at nine thousand, which is why this topic is taught before funnels, cohorts and retention rather than after.

8. Three worked examples, one of them a failure

Ghumakkad. Meera's segmented cut changed the shape of the decision rather than its direction. Applying the 0.9-point lift to the roughly 2.8 million advance-booking searches expected in the Diwali window, at a ₹640 average ticket and an 11 percent take rate, yields about ₹1.8 crore of incremental revenue — enough to justify a campaign built around seat choice for long-distance travel, and nothing at all for the next-day commuter, where the effect was a tenth of a point and indistinguishable from noise.

Hastakshar. Arjun's account-grain query produced the reversal he suspected. The three API-heavy accounts generated 61 percent of all events and had the lowest human seat utilisation in the book.

The three accounts, collectively ₹21 crore of ARR, had become invisible to their own users: the software ran, the people had stopped opening it, and a renewal conversation would be held with a procurement team that had heard from nobody internally who valued the product. That is a retention risk the event dashboard was actively concealing.

Haldhar, and how it went wrong. In April 2026 a product manager at Haldhar Agri Networks was asked for half-year gross merchandise value for an investor update. He joined orders to payments to pick up the settlement date, grouped by month and summed order value. Because institutional buyers settle in instalments, roughly a third of orders had two payment rows and the join duplicated them. He reported ₹412 crore; the figure later reconciled to the finance ledger was ₹307 crore, an overstatement of 34 percent. Nothing in the output looked wrong — the monthly shape was right and only the level was inflated.

The error surfaced six weeks later when the finance controller in Pune closed the quarter and could not tie out. The recovery had three parts: a correction memo to the four investors who had seen the figure; a modelled fct_order_payments table with an explicit uniqueness test on order_id, so that any future join fans out visibly rather than silently; and a rule that any number leaving the company be reconciled against a source of record by a second person. The rule costs perhaps two hours per external number. The incident cost considerably more in credibility — and the failure was not one of SQL knowledge, since the query was valid and readable, but of never asking whether one row in the result was one order.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Table 4. Six recurring failures, the sign that precedes them, and the diagnostic that catches them.
FailureEarly warning signDiagnostic question
Grain confusionRate implausibly low or above 100%What is one row in my output?
Join fan-outTotal rises after adding a tableDoes COUNT(*) equal COUNT(DISTINCT key)?
Mutable dimensionHistory changes on rerunIs this dimension type-1 or type-2?
Late-arriving dataLast three days always weakWhat is the p99 event arrival lag?
Silent filter in a martMart count slightly below rawHave I read the model's source?
Shadow number in a deckNobody can rerun the queryWhere is this figure's SQL stored?

The cost of catching each late scales with how far the number travelled. A grain error caught in the query editor costs ten minutes; the same error caught by a controller after an investor update costs a correction memo and a year of extra scrutiny on every figure the product team produces. That asymmetry is the argument for the two sentences at the start of section three.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The first live disagreement is whether broad query access improves decisions on net. The self-serve position rests on latency: most product decisions run on a horizon of days, an analyst queue runs to weeks, and a decision made on a flawed number beats one made on no number because the flaw is usually in the third decimal while the direction is right. Its evidence is the observed collapse in time-to-answer where warehouses were opened. It would be wrong if the errors were directional rather than random — and Haldhar is the case the other side cites, since a fan-out error always inflates.

The gatekeeping position, steelmanned, is not about protecting analysts' jobs. It is that the cost function is asymmetric: the benefit of a fast correct number is bounded by the value of one decision, while the cost of a confident wrong number compounds through every downstream artefact that cites it. It would be wrong if organisations proved able to retract numbers cleanly, which in practice they are not.

The second disagreement concerns the semantic layer. One camp holds that a governed metric definition is the only durable answer to the shadow-canon problem. The other holds that semantic layers ossify: "active" is contested for good reasons, the layer freezes one answer, teams route around it, and the fragmentation returns with an extra system to maintain. Both effects are real, the balance depends on how fast the product's underlying concepts are changing, and nobody has produced evidence that settles it.

The third and newest disagreement is whether a product manager in 2026 needs to write SQL at all, given assistants that generate competent queries from natural language. The affirmative case is that generated SQL is syntactically excellent and semantically naive: it will cheerfully join orders to payments, because nothing in the question said not to, and it does not know that Haldhar's buyers pay in instalments. On that view the skill has shifted from writing to reading — the PM must still ask what one row represents. The negative case is that this is transitional: assistants are increasingly given schema metadata, uniqueness tests and lineage, and the grain question will soon be answered by tooling. What would settle it is error-rate evidence on genuinely novel questions, which does not yet exist in public.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this writes a query and reads the answer. Someone who has internalised it writes the two sentences first, predicts the order of magnitude before running anything, and treats a result that matches the prediction too closely with as much suspicion as one that misses. They reconcile any externally bound number against a second source without being asked. They read the source of a mart before arguing with it. They know the arrival-lag profile of their own event stream and refuse to comment on the last three days. And when a colleague brings a surprising figure, their first question is about the denominator, not the definition — which usually ends the argument in ninety seconds.

12. Closing: what each of them decided

Meera took both numbers to the 19 September meeting: the blended 0.38-point lift, and the segmented table showing that virtually all of it sat in the 10+ day bucket. She recommended that the ₹18 crore Diwali campaign lead with seat choice for long-distance travel, that the same-day commuter creative drop the feature entirely, and — explicitly — that the segment effect did not license a push to make travellers book earlier. The decision in the room was about creative targeting, and the cut she pulled was the one that matched it.

Arjun did not put his account-grain table in the board deck. He took it to the analytics team first, had the service-account exclusion rebuilt as a modelled column with a test, and accepted a two-week delay. He then used the reconciled version to argue that Q4 should fund in-product adoption tooling rather than the compliance module, on the grounds that ₹21 crore of ARR was renewing against a customer base that had quietly stopped using the software. He stated the six-month history limit in the deck rather than letting it be discovered.

Discussion questions.

  1. Meera's blended and segmented numbers are both correct. On what principle should a product manager decide which one is the number, and who in the organisation should own that principle?
  2. Arjun accepted a two-week delay to have his figure modelled and tested. Under what conditions is that the wrong trade, and what would you need to know about the decision to tell?
  3. Haldhar's failure was a valid query answering an unasked question. Would a policy of analyst review have caught it, and if so, what does that imply about how far self-serve querying should extend?

13. Going deeper

  • Designing an event taxonomy — the query can only ask what the taxonomy captured; Bodhini's conversation key is a taxonomy fix, not a SQL fix.
  • Data pipelines and warehouses — arrival lag and partitioning determine which queries are honest.
  • Working with analysts and data scientists — fluency turns requesting numbers into arguing about them.
  • Analytics when anyone can query the data — the governance problem behind this page's first disagreement.
  • Constructing a funnel — the first structured application of grain and population.
  • Reading drop-off — separates a real step loss from an instrumentation gap.
  • Defining activation (the aha moment) — a definition fight that is usually a denominator fight.
  • Cohort analysis — the canonical use of window functions, and the cure for calendar-window artefacts.
  • Retention curves and the PMF signal — where the flattening tail matters more than the level.
  • Stickiness and natural frequency — why Haldhar's two sides cannot share a metric.

Querying Data: SQL Basics

Can I pull my own numbers when the dashboard doesn't have the cut I need?

1. A dashboard that stops one filter short

It is the morning of 11 August 2026, and Rohan Kulkarni, senior product manager for the reorder experience at Dabba Mart, a fifteen-minute grocery delivery company running forty-two dark stores across Bengaluru, Pune and Hyderabad, has four days before a retention review with the leadership team. Two months earlier his team shipped Smart Reorder, a home-screen nudge that resurfaces a customer's usual basket the moment historical ordering data suggests they are due to run out. The dashboard built by the growth analytics team shows a clean, shallow number: seven-day retention across the whole nudge cohort moved from 41 percent to 44 percent, a three-point lift that is respectable but not the story Rohan suspects is underneath it. He believes the lift is concentrated among customers whose very first Dabba Mart basket contained a dairy item, a category with an unusually short reorder cycle, and that averaging that spike across everyone who saw the nudge is hiding a sharper, more useful pattern. The dashboard has no filter for "first basket category." It was built to answer questions the growth team asked eighteen months ago, not the one Rohan is asking now.

If he walks into the review with only the blended three-point number, Smart Reorder is likely to be rated a mild success and left alone. If he can show, with real numbers pulled from the underlying event tables, that the effect concentrates in one segment and roughly why, he can argue for a second, sharper version instead of a shrug. The dashboard cannot get him there. The tables underneath it can, if he can write the question himself.

2. The idea

Structured Query Language, SQL, is a language for asking precise questions of data organised into tables: named collections of rows, each row a record and each column an attribute of that record. It lets someone state what they want — "the number of users whose first order contained a dairy item" — without writing a program that says how to fetch it row by row; the database works out its own retrieval plan. The idea traces to a 1970 paper by Edgar F. Codd at IBM proposing that data be stored as tables linked by shared keys rather than as rigid, hand-coded files. Two of Codd's IBM colleagues, Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce, turned that theory into a usable query language in 1974, first called SEQUEL; renamed SQL after a trademark dispute, it became an ANSI standard in 1986. Every modern analytics warehouse — Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, or the Postgres instance behind a smaller startup's dashboard — speaks a dialect of it.

The sentence Rohan could say in the leadership review without sounding glib is this: "SQL lets me ask the warehouse a question nobody built a dashboard for, in the language the tables are already stored in." That is the whole promise of the skill, and also its whole limit: it multiplies what a PM can find out, but it does not manufacture data that was never captured, and it does not replace the judgment needed to interpret what comes back.

3. How it actually works

Every query answering a question like Rohan's rests on a small set of building blocks, applied in a fixed logical order even though they are typed in a different one. Three tables matter here: users (one row per signed-up customer, with a signup date), orders (one row per completed order, with a user id, an order id, a timestamp, and a basket_first_category flag the data team already computes), and events (one row per app interaction, such as nudge_shown). A query is executed by first deciding which tables to read (FROM, plus any JOIN that stitches a second table's rows onto the first using a shared key such as user_id), then discarding rows that fail a condition (WHERE), then collapsing the surviving rows into groups sharing a value (GROUP BY, here one group per basket category), then discarding whole groups on a condition over an aggregate (HAVING), then choosing which columns or computed values to display (SELECT, typed first but run almost last), and finally ordering the output (ORDER BY).

Two steps practitioners who already know the syntax tend to leave unspoken are exactly the ones a newcomer must ask explicitly. First, the grain: is one row in the final output one user, one order, or one event? Second, the population: every customer ever, or only those who saw the nudge during the review window? Deciding both before writing a clause is what separates a query that answers the intended question from one that is merely syntactically correct.

4. A worked example, twice

Rohan's query joins orders to users, filters to customers whose first order fell between 3 and 9 August 2026 — the week Smart Reorder went live for a random half of new signups — groups by whether that first basket's category equals dairy, and computes, for each group, the share who placed a second order within fourteen days. The counts are small enough to check by hand, which is exactly what a careful PM does before repeating a headline number in a room.

GroupFirst-basket cohortReturned within 14 days14-day retention
Dairy first basket2,1501,26558.8%
Non-dairy first basket6,2502,87546.0%
Gap8,400 total—12.8 pts

1,265 divided by 2,150 is 0.5884, or 58.8 percent; 2,875 divided by 6,250 is exactly 0.46, or 46.0 percent. The gap, 12.8 percentage points, is nearly triple the three-point lift the dashboard showed for the blended cohort, because that blended figure averages a strong effect on 2,150 people with a much weaker one on 6,250. Before treating 12.8 points as the finding, Rohan reruns the identical query with the retention window changed from fourteen days to thirty, because dairy is simply a faster-repeat category on its own, nudge or no nudge, and a longer window gives slower-repeating non-dairy customers time to catch up. At thirty days, 1,527 of the 2,150 dairy-first customers have returned (71.0 percent) against 4,000 of the 6,250 non-dairy customers (64.0 percent) — a gap of 7.0 points, roughly half of what fourteen days showed. Changing one input, the length of the window, cut the apparent effect nearly in half without altering a single underlying row. That is not a flaw in SQL; it is SQL faithfully answering two different questions, and the discipline it demands is deciding, before looking at results, which window the business decision actually turns on.

5. What a learner must become aware of

Grain confusion

The most common source of a defensible-looking wrong number is mixing grains inside one query: counting events when the question is about users, or counting orders when the question is about accounts. A customer who placed four orders in the window will be counted four times in an event-grain query and once in a user-grain query, and both answers can be "correct" for different questions.

GROUP BY does not forgive ambiguity

Every column named in SELECT that is not wrapped in an aggregate function must appear in GROUP BY. Stricter engines such as Postgres and BigQuery refuse to run an ambiguous query at all; older MySQL configurations will silently pick an arbitrary row's value for the ungrouped column, producing a number that looks fine and is wrong.

The join type decides who survives

An INNER JOIN keeps only rows with a match on both sides; a LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the first table regardless. Joining users to orders with an inner join silently drops every customer who has never ordered, which is invisible until someone asks why the "total customers" count in a query is smaller than the number in the users table.

Time zones and date boundaries move the answer

Event timestamps are typically stored in UTC; a "day" measured in UTC and a "day" measured in India Standard Time disagree for roughly five and a half hours out of every twenty-four, which is enough to move a handful of midnight orders across a boundary and change a day-level metric by a percentage point or two.

Duplicate events inflate everything downstream

Mobile clients retry failed network calls, and pipelines occasionally reprocess a batch; both can insert the same logical event twice. A query that uses COUNT(*) where it needed COUNT(DISTINCT event_id) will report a rate that can exceed 100 percent, or one that shifts slightly on every rerun with no new data.

A number from SQL is not evidence of cause

Rohan's query shows that dairy-first customers retain better; it cannot show that the nudge caused it. Dairy-first customers may simply be more habitual grocery shoppers to begin with, a selection effect the query cannot distinguish from a treatment effect no matter how carefully it is written.

Every query has a blast radius

A query without a filter on the table's partitioning column can scan years of events, taking minutes and consuming warehouse compute that a finance team eventually notices on an invoice. Testing on a narrow date range with a row limit before widening scope is not caution for its own sake; it is what keeps a curious PM from becoming the subject of a data-platform incident report.

6. Where the pattern changes

In a consumer product like Dabba Mart, the natural grain is the individual event or order, tables run to hundreds of millions of rows, and the useful cuts are typically cohort, geography and category. In a B2B product the natural grain is often the account rather than the individual user, so a PM must remember to aggregate up to account_id before comparing companies, and tables are far smaller, which makes a clumsy query merely annoying rather than expensive. In a marketplace, the same completed transaction lives in both a buyer's history and a seller's, and a query that reads only one side gives an answer that is honest and half true. At an early-stage company the PM is often the only person who can write the query at all, tables are thinly documented, and the skill is close to a survival requirement; at a large company the same skill is used less to produce a first answer and more to sanity-check, quickly and independently, whether an analyst's dashboard number is even plausible before it is repeated in a room.

7. Common mistakes

The query's number does not match the dashboard's. Symptom: two numbers for the same-sounding metric disagree by a few points. Underlying cause: the dashboard defines a "day" as a rolling twenty-four hours from signup while the query used calendar-day boundaries. Cheapest diagnostic: recompute one well-known day or user by hand and compare the two definitions side by side.

A rate above 100 percent, or one that keeps drifting on rerun. Underlying cause: duplicate rows in the events table from client retries. Cheapest diagnostic: compare COUNT(*) against COUNT(DISTINCT event_id) on the identical filter.

The cohort is smaller than everyone expected. Underlying cause: an inner join silently dropped every user with no matching row on the other side. Cheapest diagnostic: rerun with a left join and count how many rows come back with nulls in the joined table's columns.

The query is killed after forty minutes and a cost alert fires. Underlying cause: no date filter was applied to a table the warehouse must otherwise scan in full. Cheapest diagnostic: check, before submitting, whether the WHERE clause references the column the table is partitioned by.

8. What good looks like

Before writing a line, Rohan states on paper what one output row will represent and which population it covers. He runs the fourteen-day version, then deliberately reruns it at thirty days rather than presenting the first number that arrives. He asks Dabba Mart's data engineer, Kavya Iyer, to confirm the events feeding the join are deduplicated, a five-minute question that would have been an embarrassing correction after the fact. He brings both retention windows to the review rather than the more dramatic one, states plainly that the gap is correlational, and proposes a specific next step rather than a verdict. That combination — a number he checked, a caveat he did not hide, and a next step he can defend — is what makes a self-served query trustworthy in a room full of people who cannot see his screen.

9. What Rohan decides

Rohan takes the thirty-day, 7.0-point version to the review, not the more dramatic fourteen-day figure, because he judges it the more durable read of a real effect. He recommends against declaring Smart Reorder finished: instead of rolling out one nudge to everyone, he proposes a small, randomised follow-up that varies the nudge's wording specifically for dairy-first customers, so the team can tell whether the gap is something the product caused or something the product merely revealed. He also asks the analytics team to add basket_first_category to the permanent dashboard so the next PM does not need to write this query from scratch. What he should learn next is how to design that follow-up properly — the topic of experimentation and working alongside analysts and data scientists who can catch a subtler flaw in his logic than a fourteen-versus-thirty-day check ever could.

Two questions worth sitting with: whose number would you have trusted more in that review, the dashboard's blended three points or the query's twelve-point gap, and why might a careful person defend either one? And before you next run an untested query against a live production warehouse, what would you check first to make sure you are not the person who sets off a cost alert at two in the morning?

Indrayani Motors: The Eighty-Six Crore Question

Pune, November 2026. A used-car marketplace has measured its own advertising and cannot decide what the measurement means.

1. The night before

At a quarter past eleven on Thursday, 12 November 2026, Rukmini Sathe was still at the office in Baner, Pune, with three versions of the same slide open on her laptop. The board met at ten the next morning. Her recommendation on the FY28 marketing plan — ₹210 crore of proposed annual spend, of which ₹86 crore was brand — was the second item on the agenda, ahead of the update on the draft red herring prospectus that the company hoped to file with SEBI in the first quarter of FY28.

The first version of the slide recommended cutting ₹52 crore, almost all of it from brand, on the strength of a city-level holdout her team had run in August and September. The second recommended cutting nothing and re-running the test properly, which would take until March. The third recommended a proportional cut across everything, which she privately thought was the coward's option and which she suspected the board would like best. Diwali had been four days earlier. The festive quarter had gone well — 19,400 cars retailed in October and the first half of November, a record — and nobody in the building agreed on why.

2. Indrayani Motors

Indrayani Motors was founded in Pune in 2019 by two former automotive-component executives who had watched the organised used-car market grow around unorganised dealers who could not offer a warranty, a clean RC transfer or finance. By FY27 the company operated in 22 cities, retailed roughly 96,000 cars a year at an average selling price of ₹6.4 lakh, and employed 4,100 people. It competed with Cars24, Spinny, CarDekho and OLX Autos in the organised segment, and with Maruti Suzuki True Value and Mahindra First Choice Wheels, whose franchised networks had the advantage of manufacturer trust.

The decision that constrained everything else had been taken in 2023. Offered a choice between an asset-light listings model and a full-stack one — buy the car, refurbish it at a company-owned hub, warranty it, sell it — the founders chose full-stack, on the reasoning that Indian buyers would pay a premium for certainty about a used car's history. They were right about the premium and did not fully price the consequence: each city required a refurbishment hub costing ₹9 to ₹14 crore to establish, working capital locked in inventory, and a minimum viable stock of retail-ready cars before demand generation made any sense at all. Supply, not demand, had been the binding constraint in eleven of the twenty-two cities for most of FY27. Nobody's marketing dashboard had a field for that.

A second decision, smaller and more irritating, had been taken in July 2024: a three-year media contract with Prakhar Media Partners carrying a guaranteed annual minimum of ₹19 crore, with fourteen months still to run. It had been signed to lock in television inventory rates ahead of a cricket season, at a time when the company's volumes were growing 60 per cent a year and a floor on spending looked like a floor nobody would ever stand on. Volumes now grew at 11 per cent.

3. The industry around it

India's used-car market moved roughly 1.4 cars for every new one sold, and the organised share had been climbing for a decade without anyone's marketing budget obviously explaining it. Three forces bore directly on Indrayani. First, financing: about 62 per cent of its retail sales were financed through partner NBFCs regulated by the Reserve Bank of India, and a tightening of risk weights on unsecured and vehicle lending in 2024 had made approval rates, not advertising, the swing factor on conversion in several cities. Second, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act: Indrayani's consent architecture was rebuilt in June 2026, and device-level match rates on its advertising platforms fell from 78 per cent to 41 per cent within a month. Third, GST on the dealer's margin rather than the vehicle value, which made the arithmetic of each transaction sensitive to refurbishment cost in a way that made marketing look like the easiest line to cut.

Indrayani's exposure to global markets ran through an unexpected door. The inspection and dealer-management software built for its own hubs had been licensed since 2024 as Indrayani DMS to dealer groups abroad — sixteen customers, ₹41 crore of annual recurring revenue, the largest of them Al Hudaib Motors LLC of Dubai, whose contract came up for renewal in January 2027. The DMS business had better margins than the marketplace and was the part of the equity story that investment bankers kept returning to. It also meant that a decision about Indian television spending was, by a route nobody had designed, connected to a renewal negotiation in Dubai and to a pipeline of North American dealer groups who had never seen an Indrayani advertisement in their lives.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

The sequence is worth laying out in the order the company experienced it, because at each point the team believed something that later evidence complicated rather than cleanly refuted.

In April 2026, with the contribution margin per car at ₹31,000 and blended customer acquisition cost at ₹19,600, the leadership team accepted a plan that raised brand spend by 40 per cent for FY27 on the argument that Indrayani's unaided awareness, at 22 per cent, trailed Cars24 and Spinny badly. The IPL flight ran through May. Attributed return on ad spend, as reported by the agency and the platforms, stayed comfortably above 4.

In June the consent rebuild landed. Aparna Rege's engineering team in Pune replaced the old tracking stack in nine days, as the compliance deadline required. Nobody in marketing was told that the attributed-conversion series in the dashboards would not be comparable across that boundary; the charts continued in an unbroken line, and the line went down, and the performance team read the drop as fatigue in the channels.

In July, Ira Menon, the data scientist in Toronto, proposed a geo holdout: switch off all brand and upper-funnel spend in a matched set of cities for six weeks and compare retail sales per lakh of population. It ran from 4 August to 14 September across the 22 cities, eight of them held out. The headline result was a lift of 3.1 per cent with a 95 per cent confidence interval running from −4.2 per cent to +10.4 per cent. Menon's memo said, in its second paragraph, that the test could not distinguish a strongly profitable brand programme from a worthless one. By the time the deck reached the executive committee, the second paragraph had become a footnote and the 3.1 per cent had become the number people said out loud.

In October the agency delivered a media-mix model of its own, unprompted, which put brand's contribution at 31 per cent of FY27 sales and its return at 2.6. Bhatnagar circulated it the same afternoon with the subject line "for balance". Menon's reply, sent at two in the morning Toronto time, ran to four hundred words on adstock assumptions and was read by three people. Sathe read it twice and could not decide whether she was reading a methodological objection or a territorial one.

And in November the festive quarter closed at a record. Brand spend during it had been ₹18.4 crore, roughly flat; the finance partners' approval rates had risen four points after a policy change at one NBFC; three new hubs had come online in September; and Vogel's revised finance-eligibility screen had shipped to half the traffic on 6 October without anyone designating it an experiment. Every one of those could account for some of the record, and the company had no way to apportion it among them.

Three things have since turned out to be wrong. The eight holdout cities carried 22 per cent fewer retail-ready cars during the window than the treated cities, because two hub expansions had slipped — so the control group was handicapped on supply, which would inflate the measured lift. Menon had dropped four cities from the analysis after the test began, on the grounds of "supply anomalies", a decision she made alone and documented in a comment in her notebook. And the window closed on 14 September, three days before Navratri began, against a median consideration period — first site visit to purchase — of 38 days.

5. The people

Rukmini Sathe, Chief Growth Officer, Pune, owns the recommendation. She believes the brand spend is probably overstated by a factor of two but is unwilling to say so without a number she trusts. What she is not saying is that she championed the FY27 brand increase in April and that reversing it publicly costs her something.

Devashish Ranade, Chief Financial Officer, Mumbai, wants ₹52 crore out of the plan and the money redirected to two new hubs and the DMS roadmap. His incentive is the DRHP: a marketplace that can show falling CAC alongside rising volume prices differently from one that cannot. He is not saying that he has already shared an indicative FY28 marketing number with two prospective anchor investors.

Ira Menon, Senior Data Scientist, Toronto, designed the holdout and wants it re-run over sixteen weeks with supply-matched cities. Her incentive is her own credibility, and she is not saying how uncomfortable she is about the four excluded cities.

Harish Bhatnagar, Vice President of Performance Marketing, Gurugram, argues that brand is unmeasurable by construction and that the cut, if there must be one, should come from the untested affiliate and dealer-referral lines. He negotiated the Prakhar contract and its guaranteed minimum. He is not saying that his team of 40 shrinks to 26 under any version of the cut he is publicly proposing.

Aparna Rege, Director of Engineering, Pune, knows precisely what the consent rebuild did to the data and has said so twice in writing. She is not saying that restoring any richer form of measurement would require a fresh consent flow whose legal review has not started.

Gopal Sundaram, Head of City Operations, Bengaluru, insists the company is demand-rich and supply-poor, and that every rupee argued over in this meeting is second-order to hub throughput. His incentive is capital for hubs. He is not saying that his own inventory feed failed for nine days in two holdout cities during the test window.

Jaideep Khanna, Head of Enterprise Sales, New Jersey, sells Indrayani DMS to North American dealer groups and argues that visible brand strength in India underwrites the software's credibility abroad. He is not saying that Al Hudaib's renewal is already wobbling for product reasons unrelated to any of this.

Annika Vogel, Product Designer, Berlin, has spent six weeks on the listing and finance-eligibility flow and believes the company is buying traffic to a page that converts at 2.4 per cent when comparable flows convert at 4. Her position is that the entire meeting is about the wrong number. Serena Koh, customer success lead in Singapore, has stayed out of it except to point out that the APAC DMS clients read Indian trade press.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

"The interval includes zero and it includes ten. That is not a finding, it is a request for a bigger test."

— Ira Menon, memo to the executive committee, 22 September 2026

"Ira's own chart says plus three point one. If we are going to ignore the number when it is inconvenient and quote it when it is not, let us at least agree which of those we are doing today."

— Harish Bhatnagar, executive committee, 29 September

"I want to be careful here. The six weeks after June are a different measurement system. Comparing them to May is comparing a thermometer to a different thermometer."

— Aparna Rege, engineering review, 7 July

"We sold every retail-ready car we had in Coimbatore and Indore in the third week of August. What exactly was the advertising supposed to add there?"

— Gopal Sundaram, chat thread, 11 September

"If the India brand goes quiet, the first question in my January renewal call with Al Hudaib will be whether we are in trouble. I cannot prove that costs us the contract. I also cannot prove it does not."

— Jaideep Khanna, email to Sathe, 4 November

"Two point four per cent. We are arguing about how to fill a bucket that leaks."

— Annika Vogel, design review, 28 October

8. The options as Sathe currently frames them

Option A — cut ₹52 crore from brand. The holdout's point estimate, applied to the brand budget, implies a return below the contribution margin. Ranade gets his number for the DRHP, the hubs get funded, and the measurement programme is vindicated as a decision tool. The risks are that the estimate is confounded by Exhibit 4's supply gap in precisely the direction that inflates the measured lift, that a third of buyers convert outside the measured window, and that an unaided-awareness decline is slow and unrecoverable.

Option B — protect brand, cut performance. Exhibit 3 says brand is the better-returning line. But the exhibit comes from the agency whose fee scales with brand billings, is fitted on a period spanning the June measurement break, and rests on an adstock assumption nobody at Indrayani has interrogated.

Option C — hold the plan and re-run the test properly. Sixteen weeks, supply-matched cities, a pre-registered analysis and no post-hoc exclusions. It is the answer Menon wants and it lands in March, two board meetings and one DRHP draft too late.

Option D — cut 25 per cent across every line. Politically survivable, defensible as prudence, and guaranteed to cut whichever rupees were working alongside whichever were not. It also has the property, which Sathe noted and did not write down, that if volumes fall nobody will be able to attribute the fall to any particular decision, including hers.

Each option carries a second-order consequence the slide does not have room for. Option A frees capital for hubs, which addresses the constraint Sundaram argues is real, but it does so by acting on an estimate that Sundaram's own inventory shortfall may have manufactured. Option B keeps Khanna's Dubai conversation comfortable and hands the company's allocation logic to a vendor with a stake in the answer. Option C is the only route to a number anyone would defend in a prospectus, and it asks the board to accept four more months of spending at a level the CFO has already indicated to outside investors will fall.

Sathe had written a fifth line on her notepad at some point in the evening and then drawn a box around it without expanding it: what if the question is not which channel. Exhibit 4 shows holdout cities out of stock on 17 of 42 days. Exhibit 5 shows a third of the effect landing after the window shut. Vogel's conversion rate implies that a 1.6-point improvement in the listing flow would add more retailed cars than the entire brand budget plausibly does. None of those sit in the column of the slide the board expects to see.

9. Deadline and constraints

The board meets at ten on 13 November and the FY28 plan must be approved at that meeting, because city hiring and the hub capital plan key off it. The Prakhar contract carries ₹22.2 crore of guaranteed minimum over its remaining fourteen months, and early termination triggers the full balance. Any new device-level measurement requires a fresh DPDP consent flow that legal has not begun to review, and the compliance head has said informally that she would want six weeks. The performance-marketing team of 40 sits inside any cut Sathe proposes. The DMS renewal with Al Hudaib Motors LLC falls in January, and Khanna will be in Dubai for it. And the bankers advising on the listing had asked, twice, for a marketing plan that "shows leverage" — a phrase Sathe had not asked either of them to define.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What exactly did the August–September holdout measure, and what would have had to be true about the eight holdout cities for its estimate to mean what the executive committee took it to mean?
  2. Exhibits 2 and 3 disagree. Reconstruct the strongest case for each being the more trustworthy, and identify what evidence would distinguish them.
  3. Menon excluded four cities after assignment. How much does that decision change the standing of the result, and what should a company's rule about such decisions be?
  4. Given Exhibits 4 and 5, is Indrayani's binding constraint demand, supply, or conversion — and how would you design an inexpensive test, runnable before March, that would tell you?
  5. Who in this company is structurally incapable of producing an unwelcome measurement, and what change to reporting lines or incentives would fix that without creating a new version of the same problem?
  6. What should Sathe do on Monday morning, and what precisely should she say to the board on Friday about a number she does not believe, in a room that has already been told what it means?

At twenty to one, Sathe closed the third version of the slide without saving it. On the whiteboard behind her, someone had written the October retail figure in green marker and circled it twice. The number was real. Nobody could tell her what had caused it, and at ten in the morning she would be asked to spend ₹210 crore on the assumption that somebody knew.
