The WhatsApp Renewal Nudge

1. Mumbai, the second week of August 2026

Priya Nair, Vice President of Growth at Ambar Finserv, had eleven days before the quarterly board meeting to recommend one of three things: renew the company's WhatsApp engagement contract at its current tier, upgrade it to a costlier personalised tier the vendor was pushing, or cancel it and move the budget elsewhere. The contract funded the automated messages sent to small retailers fifteen days before their working-capital loan matured, reminding them to renew. The marketing team's dashboard credited those messages with lifting renewals by twelve percentage points. The finance team, squeezed by a rising cost of funds, wanted the number re-checked before anyone signed a cheque for more of it.

2. Ambar Finserv

Ambar Finserv was a five-year-old, Mumbai-headquartered non-banking financial company that lent small amounts of working capital, typically ₹25,000 to ₹5 lakh, to kirana stores and small retailers across India, disbursed and repaid through a mobile app in partnership with UPI rails. It competed directly with Lendingkart, FlexiLoans and Kissht for the same merchant segment, and indirectly with the working-capital products that PhonePe and Paytm were increasingly bundling into their merchant apps. Ambar operated under an RBI NBFC licence and reported roughly 4.2 lakh active borrowing merchants, with about 40,000 loans maturing and eligible for renewal in an average month. A second, smaller line of business licensed Ambar's underwriting API to partners who wanted to embed working-capital lending into their own platforms; one such partner was Zafraan Trading LLC, a Dubai-based distributor that offered short-term credit to the small retailers in its supply network using Ambar's engine under the hood.

Renewal was the single most important number in Ambar's unit economics: a renewed loan cost almost nothing to originate a second time, while a lapsed merchant had to be re-acquired through paid channels at several times the cost. The WhatsApp reminder had been sold to the board eighteen months earlier as the cheapest lever anyone had found to move that number, and it had become, in the words of one board member, "the one growth initiative nobody wants to be the one to cut."

3. The situation

The dashboard's twelve-point figure came from a simple comparison: merchants who had a valid, opted-in WhatsApp number received the reminder and renewed at 34%; merchants who could not be reached on WhatsApp, because their number was invalid, unregistered on the Business API, or they had opted out, renewed at 22%. The gap looked like the nudge's effect. Priya's data scientist, Meera Chandran, who worked out of Toronto and had joined the review after finance flagged the contract for scrutiny, pointed out the obvious hole: merchants reachable on WhatsApp were not a random slice of the borrower base. They tended to be more digitally active, checked the app more often, and had generally cleaner repayment histories — all things that predict renewal on their own, with or without a reminder. Comparing them to the unreachable group compared two different kinds of merchants, not two versions of the same merchant with and without a message.

To settle it, Meera designed a randomised holdout inside the reachable population itself: among merchants who had a valid WhatsApp number and had opted in, half were randomly assigned to receive the reminder as usual, and half were randomly withheld from it, seeing only the routine in-app renewal banner every merchant already got. Engineers Ritesh Pillai in Bengaluru and Sneha Kulkarni in Pune built the random assignment into the loan-servicing system over a single sprint, and the test ran for one full renewal cycle in June and July, covering roughly 36,000 eligible merchants.

4. The people around the table

  • Priya Nair, VP Growth, Mumbai — owns the recommendation and must defend it to the board in rupee terms, not percentages.
  • Meera Chandran, data scientist, Toronto — designed and ran the holdout; wants the decision grounded in the randomised result, not the naive dashboard number, and is wary of the sample being read as more precise than it is.
  • Devraj Oak, Head of Marketing, Mumbai — commissioned the original contract, is due to negotiate the vendor's proposed premium tier at ₹1.4 crore a year, and has a personal stake in the twelve-point figure holding up.
  • Wei Ling Tan, customer success lead, Singapore — manages the relationship with Zafraan Trading LLC and other embedded-lending partners, and worries that any visible cut to Ambar's flagship retention programme will unsettle a partner who is renewing its own contract in October.
  • Arjun Kamath, Head of Enterprise Sales, based in New Jersey to cover Ambar's push into licensing its lending API to US-based fintech resellers, who has been citing the twelve-point renewal lift in sales pitches as proof of the platform's retention tooling.

Lukas Herrmann, a product designer in Berlin who had built the WhatsApp templates being tested, had one more consideration to add: the personalisation the vendor's premium tier promised — product-specific renewal terms rendered per merchant — was exactly the kind of change that needed its own holdout before anyone assumed it would help, rather than being purchased on the strength of a demo.

5. What the numbers said

Exhibit 1 shows the naive comparison that had driven the original decision to fund the contract. Exhibit 2 shows Meera's randomised result. Exhibit 3 turns the randomised result into money.

6. The options in front of Priya

Option A: Renew at the current tier

Sign the existing ₹85 lakh contract for another year on the strength of Exhibit 3's ₹1.87 crore net gain, and commit to running the randomised holdout every quarter going forward so the number is never again taken on faith. The upside is a proven, if modest, positive return with a method the board can be walked through line by line. The cost is that Devraj's premium-tier pitch gets shelved and Arjun's sales pitch loses its headline number, which will need to be retired or re-stated more carefully.

Option B: Upgrade to the premium personalised tier

Commit ₹1.4 crore on the vendor's claim that per-merchant personalisation roughly doubles engagement, betting that the true lift clears the 2.9-point break-even shown in Exhibit 3. The upside, if the vendor is right, is a materially larger incremental gain and a stronger story for Wei Ling Tan's renewal conversation with Zafraan Trading LLC. The cost is that the claim has never been tested on Ambar's own merchants, and the last untested claim examined this closely turned out to be six times smaller than advertised.

Option C: Cancel the WhatsApp programme

Redirect the ₹85 lakh to the in-app banner team and to a lower-cost SMS fallback, on the reasoning that a 6.1% incrementality rate is thin and most of the credited renewal behaviour happens anyway. The upside is immediate savings and one less vendor dependency. The cost, visible in Exhibit 3, is walking away from a channel that the randomised test itself shows is still net positive by roughly ₹1.87 crore a year — a number Option C would have to argue is not worth the operational overhead of keeping.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What exactly is wrong with the comparison in Exhibit 1, and why does it produce a larger number than the true effect rather than a smaller one?
  2. What makes Meera's holdout in Exhibit 2 a fair test, and what would you want to check before trusting it — sample size, timing, anything else?
  3. Using Exhibit 3 alone, which of the three options is best supported by evidence today, and which is a bet rather than a decision?
  4. What specific evidence, and from whom, would need to arrive before Option B stopped being a bet?

8. A note for the learner

Incrementality measurement exists precisely for moments like this one: a dashboard number that everyone has grown comfortable citing turns out, on inspection, to compare two populations that were never alike to begin with. The naive 12-point gap in Exhibit 1 is an attribution artefact, built from a comparison of digitally active merchants against inactive ones; the randomised 1.8-point gap in Exhibit 2 is the actual, defensible effect of the message, because it is the only comparison in this case where the only systematic difference between the two groups is the treatment itself.

A well-reasoned answer does three things in order. First, it accepts the randomised number, not the naive one, as the basis for any spending decision, however much smaller and less flattering it is. Second, it prices that number out in money, as Exhibit 3 does, rather than arguing about percentage points in the abstract — a 6.1% incrementality rate sounds small until you see it is still worth ₹1.87 crore a year at the current contract price. Third, it treats an unmeasured claim, such as the premium tier's promised doubling, as a hypothesis to be tested with the same rigour, not as a reason to either fund it blindly or dismiss it outright.

The one defensible path is Option A, with a condition attached: renew at the current tier, because the randomised evidence already supports it, and use part of the saved decision-making capital to run a further matched holdout on the premium personalised templates — a subset of the existing holdout population, not the whole merchant base — before committing ₹1.4 crore to a claim that has, so far, only been made by the party selling it. This path keeps the one number the board can trust, and turns the one number nobody has tested into the next thing to test, rather than the next thing to assume.
exp20v2-ana.incrementality:
Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation · Product Analytics & Data Practice

Incrementality Measurement

Would those users have come anyway?

1. A number that felt too good

On the second Monday of March, Kavya Iyer, head of growth analytics at Chakor Grocers, a fifteen-minute grocery delivery app operating across Pune, Nashik and Nagpur, opened the marketing dashboard and saw a figure that had made her uneasy for three months running. Google's attribution model was crediting the company's Performance Max campaign with 18,000 app installs a month, at a spend of ₹40 lakh, for an attributed cost per install of ₹222 — comfortably below the ₹260 the finance team had set as the ceiling. On that number alone, the campaign looked like the best-performing channel Chakor had. The marketing head wanted to double the budget before the pre-Diwali order surge.

Kavya's discomfort was specific. Performance Max bids on branded search terms and retargets people who had already opened the app that week — exactly the users who search for "Chakor" or reopen a delivery app they use three times a week regardless of any ad. She suspected the model was mostly claiming credit for demand that already existed, not creating it. She had four weeks before the budget meeting to find out whether the ₹40 lakh was earning its keep, and the answer would decide whether Chakor doubled the spend, held it, or redirected it toward the referral programme her data scientist had been asking to fund.

2. The idea, stated plainly

Incrementality measurement is the practice of estimating how many of the outcomes credited to a channel, feature or campaign would not have happened without it — by comparing a group exposed to the thing against a comparable group that was not, rather than by tracing which ad a converting user last clicked. Attribution models, however sophisticated, only describe the path a user took before converting; they cannot tell you what that same user would have done in a world where the ad never ran, because that world is never observed. Incrementality tries to observe an approximation of that world directly, by withholding the treatment from part of the population and watching what happens.

The idea has old roots in direct-mail "matched market" tests that retailers such as Sears and later big-box chains ran through the twentieth century, holding some markets out of a mailer drop and comparing sales. It was formalised for digital marketing in the 2010s, when Google, Meta and Uber each built internal geo-experimentation platforms because their own attribution systems were increasingly gamed by last-click credit for organic, branded and retargeted traffic. The one-line version Kavya could say in the budget meeting without sounding glib: attribution tells you who touched the ad on their way to converting; incrementality tells you how many of them would have converted anyway.

3. How the test is actually built

The mechanics run in five steps, and practitioners skip the first and the last far more often than they admit. First, pick a randomisation unit large enough to contain the effect without leaking into its neighbour — for Chakor, a city, because delivery riders, warehouses and word-of-mouth mostly stay within a city's boundary, unlike a household or a device ID, which a person can carry across an untreated boundary in an afternoon. Second, split the units into a test group that keeps the campaign running and a holdout group where it is switched off, choosing the split so the two groups look alike on the outcome's recent history and not merely on population — matched on baseline order growth, not just city size.

Third, run the split for long enough that ordinary week-to-week noise in ordering behaviour is smaller than the effect you are trying to detect; this is a statistical power calculation, not a guess, and it is the step most teams skip because it takes an afternoon of work before the "real" test can start. Fourth, measure the same outcome metric in both groups over the same window — new orders per capita, not installs, because installs can be inflated by the same forces that inflate attribution. Fifth, and this is the step usually left implicit, check that the two groups tracked each other closely in the weeks before the test began; if the holdout cities were already growing slower, any post-test gap is contaminated before it starts.

Fig. 1 — Both groups grow in parallel before the test starts; the gap that opens afterward, not the level, is the estimate of interest.

4. The arithmetic, worked through

Chakor's data scientist, Rohan Mestri, ran the test across 24 cities: 18 kept Performance Max live, 6 were switched to zero paid search spend for four weeks, matched beforehand on order growth within 0.3 percentage points. Weekly order growth over the test window came out to 5.2% in the test cities and 4.1% in the holdout cities — a gap of 1.1 percentage points that the pre-period trend does not explain, since the two groups had been tracking within 0.2 points of each other for the eight weeks before.

That 1.1-point gap, divided by the 5.2% growth observed where the campaign ran, says that roughly 21% of the growth in the test cities is incremental (1.1 ÷ 5.2 = 0.212); the remaining 79% would plausibly have happened without the campaign. Applied to the attributed 18,000 monthly installs, that implies only about 3,780 installs a month (18,000 × 0.21) are actually caused by the spend. Dividing the ₹40 lakh budget by 3,780 incremental installs gives a true cost per incremental install of roughly ₹1,058 — nearly five times the ₹222 the attribution dashboard reported, and well above the ₹260 ceiling finance had set.

Attributed viewIncrementality-adjusted view
Monthly installs credited18,0003,780
Monthly spend₹40,00,000₹40,00,000
Cost per install₹222₹1,058

Rohan then re-ran the arithmetic with one input changed, because a single test window is a single data point and Kavya wanted to know how sensitive the conclusion was. If the true underlying lift had been smaller — say the holdout gap was only 0.3 points instead of 1.1, well within the range a noisier week could produce — incrementality would fall to 0.3 ÷ 5.2 = 5.8%, incremental installs to about 1,044, and true cost per install to roughly ₹3,831. The decision does not hinge on one lucky reading; it holds under a materially worse one too, which is exactly what a defensible test should show before real money moves on it.

5. What a learner has to get past the vocabulary to see

Incrementality is not a better attribution model

It is a different question entirely. Attribution answers "which touchpoint gets credit," a bookkeeping question with a mechanical answer. Incrementality answers "what would have happened without this," a causal question that requires a counterfactual, and no amount of clever multi-touch weighting can substitute for actually observing a comparable untreated group.

A holdout is only as good as its match

The entire inference rests on the test and holdout groups being alike in everything except the treatment. If the holdout cities happen to be smaller, newer to the app, or entering a different point in the local festival calendar, the gap you measure is partly that difference, not the campaign's effect. Checking pre-period parallel trends, as Fig. 1 shows, is not optional diligence; it is the test's foundation.

Geo tests assume the groups do not talk to each other

If a meaningful share of Nashik's population routinely travels to or orders through a network anchored in a test city, or if word-of-mouth crosses the city line, the holdout is contaminated and the true effect is understated, because some of the "untreated" group received a spillover effect anyway.

Short-run incrementality can miss delayed and brand effects

A four-week window catches performance-marketing style lift well but can understate a campaign's slower brand-building contribution, which shows up as improved organic search or referral volume months later, outside the measurement window entirely.

It is easily confused with a simple before-after comparison

Comparing this month's orders to last month's, with the campaign running throughout, tells you nothing about causality, because every seasonal and competitive factor moves too. Incrementality requires a live untreated comparison group in the same period, not a different period.

It cannot tell you why an effect exists, only its size

A 21% incrementality rate tells Kavya how much of the credited growth is real; it does not explain whether the real 21% comes from the ad's creative, its targeting, or simply reaching a small set of genuinely undecided users. Diagnosing the mechanism needs further, separate experimentation.

Statistical power is not optional, however inconvenient the timeline

A test run for two weeks across four cities with a metric that swings 3 points week to week on noise alone will produce a number that looks decisive and means nothing; the sample must be sized, before the test starts, to detect an effect smaller than the smallest lift that would still change the decision.

6. Where the picture changes by product type and by stage

In a consumer app like Chakor, geo holdouts work well because behaviour is local and channels are numerous enough to test one at a time without starving the business. In B2B software, where the buying unit is an account and the sales cycle runs months, the more common design is a holdout on outbound sequences or account-based marketing spend within matched account segments, with revenue recognised quarters later, which stretches the measurement window and raises the cost of getting the match wrong. In a marketplace, the complication is two-sided: a supply-side incentive can lift demand-side conversion indirectly, so an incrementality test on one side alone can misattribute an effect that actually travelled through the other side of the marketplace. An early-stage company usually cannot afford enough cities or accounts to reach statistical power and instead relies on a cruder national on/off switch, accepting a noisier answer because a wrong ₹5 lakh bet is tolerable; a large company with hundreds of geographies runs incrementality as a standing quarterly programme across every major channel, because a wrong ₹5 crore bet is not.

7. Where teams go wrong

Treating the attributed number as the incremental number

Symptom: a channel is scaled purely because its attributed CAC looks best. Underlying error: no counterfactual was ever measured. Cheapest diagnostic: a single two-week geo or user-level holdout on that one channel, even an underpowered one, usually reveals whether the attributed figure is wildly optimistic before a larger test is justified.

Letting the holdout leak

Symptom: the measured gap keeps shrinking every time the test is repeated. Underlying error: the "off" group is still being reached, often because a different team's campaign, an email list, or organic search overlaps into the same geography. Cheapest diagnostic: audit every other active channel for overlap with the holdout group before trusting the result.

Stopping the test the moment it looks significant

Symptom: a team ends a test early because the gap already looks favourable in week two. Underlying error: peeking inflates the false-positive rate; early noise regularly looks like signal. Cheapest diagnostic: pre-register the test length and the metric before launch, and hold to it regardless of what week two shows.

8. What good looks like

A team that has this right runs incrementality tests as routine infrastructure, not as a one-off investigation triggered by suspicion. At Chakor, after this episode, Rohan built a standing calendar: every paid channel above ₹10 lakh in monthly spend gets a geo holdout at least once a quarter, the pre-period match is checked automatically before any test is allowed to launch, and the marketing team is shown incrementality-adjusted CAC alongside attributed CAC on the same dashboard, so no number gets discussed in isolation. Budget conversations start from the adjusted figure by default, and attribution is used only to route creative and targeting decisions within a channel already known to be incremental.

9. What Kavya decided, and what to sit with

Kavya took the adjusted ₹1,058 cost per incremental install to the budget meeting, alongside the sensitivity check showing the conclusion held even under a much weaker assumed lift. Chakor cut Performance Max spend by 40%, redirected roughly ₹16 lakh a month into the referral programme, and agreed to run a matched geo holdout on referral incentives next quarter before scaling that too. The reasoning she gave was simple: a channel that costs five times what the dashboard claims is not obviously worth doubling, and the only way to know the true multiple was to build the counterfactual rather than trust the model that had no way to observe it.

The next thing worth learning is media-mix modelling, which extends this same causal instinct across many channels at once when running a clean holdout on each one individually becomes too slow or too expensive. Two questions worth sitting with: if every channel your company runs were incrementality-tested tomorrow, which one do you expect would survive, and which would not — and what would you actually do differently the day you found out?

Incrementality Measurement

Would those users have come anyway? A near-expert treatment of holdouts, geo tests, and the arguments the field has not settled.

1. Two decisions, two weeks apart

On 6 October 2026, four days after the quarterly close, Ananya Deshpande sat with a one-page instruction from her chief financial officer. Deshpande ran growth at Aranyaka Naturals, a Mumbai direct-to-consumer personal-care brand doing roughly ₹340 crore a year across its own site, Amazon, Nykaa and a thin but growing modern-trade presence. The instruction was to remove ₹6 crore from a ₹22 crore quarterly marketing budget before the Diwali flight locked. Her platform dashboards made the task look easy and made it impossible at the same time. Meta's attribution reported a 4.8 return on ad spend on prospecting; Google reported 6.1 on Performance Max; the branded-search campaign reported 11.2. Added together, the platforms claimed credit for 1.6 times the revenue Aranyaka had actually booked. Somebody's numbers were counting the same rupee twice, and Deshpande had to decide which ₹6 crore of spend was buying sales that would not otherwise have occurred.

Eleven days later and 980 kilometres south, Sriram Balakrishnan faced a structurally different version of the same question. Balakrishnan was director of product analytics at Samanvay Cloud, a Bengaluru company selling field-service management software to manufacturers and utilities at an average contract value of ₹18 lakh and a median sales cycle of nine months. Samanvay spent ₹6 crore a year on a field-operations community programme: regional meet-ups in Coimbatore, Pune, Vadodara and Surat, a certification track, and an annual conference. Marketing's dashboard attributed ₹41 crore of pipeline to the programme, because 38 per cent of closed-won accounts had at least one contact who had attended something. The new chief revenue officer had asked the obvious question — would those accounts have bought anyway? — and Balakrishnan had discovered, within an afternoon, that he had no clean way to answer it. Samanvay closed about 190 deals a year. There were not enough of them, and they did not close quickly enough, to detect anything but an enormous effect.

The two cases share a definition and almost nothing else. Deshpande has hundreds of thousands of weakly-connected buying units and a seven-day purchase cycle; Balakrishnan has fourteen sales territories and a nine-month one. That difference — the number of independent units divided by the time it takes the outcome to appear — decides more about which methods are available than any amount of analytical sophistication. It is the axis this page runs along.

2. The idea, and the quarrel inside it

Incrementality is the difference between the outcome that occurred and the outcome that would have occurred had the treatment not been applied: in the notation of potential outcomes, E[Y | do(T=1)] − E[Y | do(T=0)] for the population of interest. The second term is never observed for the same units in the same period, so every incrementality estimate is an argument about a plausible substitute for it. That is the whole subject. Everything else — geo splits, ghost ads, synthetic controls, Bayesian media-mix models — is machinery for constructing a credible unobserved world.

The lineage is older than digital marketing. R. A. Fisher's randomised field trials at Rothamsted in the 1920s established that randomisation, not adjustment, is what licenses a causal claim. American catalogue retailers ran matched-market mailer holdouts through the middle of the century for exactly the reason Deshpande now needs one: response rates flatter the mailer because people who buy from catalogues are people who open catalogues. Donald Rubin's potential-outcomes framework in the 1970s gave the practice its formal vocabulary. The modern digital literature arrived later and sharply: Blake, Nosko and Tadelis's 2015 eBay experiment, which switched off paid branded search across matched US markets and found the incremental return indistinguishable from zero for established users, and Lewis and Rao's paper the same year showing that even twenty-five large advertising experiments, some with millions of subjects, could not statistically distinguish a return of 0 from a return of 3. Attribution's dominance ended not because it was refuted but because Apple's App Tracking Transparency and, in India, the consent architecture of the DPDP Act made the underlying identity graph patchy enough that its errors became visible.

Four schools now argue about what to do, and it is worth stating the proposition each would sign and the one each would refuse.

Table 1 — The four positions, stated as propositions. Most practitioners hold one of these and believe the others are strawmen; they are not.
SchoolWill signWill not sign
ExperimentalistNo randomised design, no causal number; an unrandomised estimate is a prior dressed as a finding.That an estimate too imprecise to guide a budget is still better than a judgement call.
Quasi-experimentalGeo tests, synthetic control and difference-in-differences recover the effect when treatment assignment is ignorable given pre-period behaviour.That user-level randomisation is available often enough to be the default.
Bayesian media-mixA model with priors calibrated to occasional experiments allocates budget better than sparse experiments alone, because it covers every channel every week.That the model's coefficients mean anything without periodic experimental calibration.
Decision-sufficiency
(the Lewis–Rao pessimists)		For most firms the test that would settle the question is unaffordable; act on bounds, structural reasoning and cheap large cuts instead.That measurement is therefore pointless — only that precision is usually out of reach.

3. Mechanics, worked rather than named

Start with the estimand, because the commonest expert-level error is answering the wrong one. A full holdout — spend versus no spend — estimates average incrementality across the entire budget. Budget decisions are almost never about the entire budget; they are about the last rupee. Response curves are concave, so the marginal incrementality of the top ₹6 crore is typically far below the average across ₹22 crore. Deshpande's decision is a marginal question and a zero-versus-full holdout answers an average one.

Second, the randomisation unit. The unit must be large enough to contain the effect and small enough that you have many of them. Aranyaka's natural unit is the city: riders, dark-store inventory, out-of-home posters and word-of-mouth mostly respect city boundaries, while a device identifier does not survive a household sharing a phone. Samanvay's natural unit is the sales territory, of which it has fourteen — and fourteen units is a sample size, not a portfolio.

Third, and this is the step whose omission produces most of the field's disappointment, the power calculation. The minimum detectable effect of a two-group geo test is approximately MDE ≈ (zα/2 + zβ) × σ × √(1/nt + 1/nc), where σ is the standard deviation across units of the post-period outcome after removing pre-period trend. Deshpande's analysts measured σ at 7.4 per cent of mean city revenue over six-week windows. With 24 test and 12 holdout cities, at 80 per cent power and 5 per cent significance, the MDE is 2.8 × 7.4 × √(1/24 + 1/12) = 7.3 per cent of revenue in the holdout group. Aranyaka's expected true lift from the tested slice of spend is around 9 per cent. The test is detectable, barely. Samanvay's equivalent arithmetic — 7 treated and 7 control territories, pipeline variance of 31 per cent, a nine-month lag — produces an MDE of 46 per cent. No plausible programme effect is that large. Balakrishnan's honest report to his CRO was not a result but a refusal.

Table 2 — The same power formula applied to both protagonists. The number that decides whether a test is worth running is the MDE relative to the effect you would act on, not the sample size in isolation.
InputAranyaka (cities)Samanvay (territories)

Fourth, assignment and pre-period validation. Matching on population is amateur; matching on the outcome's recent trajectory is the job. Before any live test, run an A/A period — assign the groups, change nothing, and confirm the estimator returns approximately zero. Aranyaka's A/A across four pre-weeks returned a spurious "lift" of 1.9 per cent, which set the floor for how small a real effect the team could believe.

Fifth, estimation and the compliance correction. Where exposure is partial — the usual case in user-level lift tests, where only some of the treatment group ever sees an impression — the raw comparison is an intent-to-treat effect. Divide by the exposure rate to recover the effect on the treated: an ITT lift of 0.61 percentage points at 42 per cent exposure implies a treatment-on-treated effect of 1.45 points. Reporting the second number as though it applied to the whole population, which happens constantly, inflates the claim by 2.4 times.

The second-order effects are where expertise actually lives. Switching a channel off does not hold the rest of the world constant: bidding algorithms in other channels find the freed-up auction inventory cheaper and quietly absorb some of the demand, so a holdout understates loss. Platform learning phases reset when campaigns restart, so a pulsed test carries a recovery cost outside the measurement window. Retargeting pools drain slowly, so the first ten days of a holdout still carry treatment. And delayed conversion means the window must exceed the purchase-consideration lag: a six-week window on a product with a five-week median consideration period measures roughly the first sixth of the effect.

4. The conditions, stated as claims you can check

Five conditions decide whether the method applies, and each is checkable rather than a matter of taste. One: you can genuinely withhold the treatment — technically, contractually and ethically. Two: units do not interfere with each other, the assumption statisticians call SUTVA. Three: the outcome arrives inside a window you can afford to wait for. Four: the MDE sits below the effect size that would change your decision. Five: the treatment is stable while the test runs.

Against Aranyaka: one holds, two mostly holds except for a Mumbai–Thane spillover the team excludes by design, three holds comfortably, four holds only marginally, five fails if the creative refresh planned for week three goes ahead — so it is postponed. Against Samanvay: one holds for events but not for the certification track, which contractual partners are entitled to; two fails badly, because a Coimbatore plant manager who attends a meet-up tells his counterpart in Hosur; three fails outright; four fails; five fails, since two of fourteen territories change ownership mid-year.

The method is actively misleading in three situations. When a badly powered test returns no significant lift and the finding is reported as "the channel does nothing," which is the most expensive sentence in the discipline. When the treatment is a brand campaign whose returns compound over eighteen months and the window is six weeks. And when the outcome is measured on a population that is itself selected by the treatment — for instance, measuring lift on app-opens among people who opened the app.

5. Hard edges

In multi-product companies, a holdout on one line moves another: when Aranyaka suppressed hair-care ads in twelve cities, skin-care revenue rose 2.1 per cent there, because shelf attention and promotional email slots reallocated. The correctly specified outcome is therefore category revenue, not SKU revenue, and teams that own SKUs resist that specification for reasons that are budgetary rather than statistical.

In two-sided marketplaces the interference is structural. Withholding demand-side spend in six cities frees supply that migrates to the treated cities — couriers, sellers or installers reallocate — so the control group is improved by the treatment and the estimate is biased upward, sometimes by half. Geo splits at the level of whole liquidity pools, or time-based switchbacks alternating treatment on and off at the city-hour level, are the standard corrections; both cost statistical efficiency to buy validity.

In regulated categories the constraint is not statistical at all. An RBI-regulated lender cannot withhold a mandated repayment reminder to build a clean control arm; a listed-equity broker's communications are constrained by SEBI's advertising code; the DPDP Act's consent requirements make user-level treatment assignment a processing purpose that must be disclosed. The practical response is to randomise the incremental, discretionary layer — the marketing nudge on top of the compliant baseline — and to state clearly that the measured effect is incremental to that baseline, not to silence.

Hardware-plus-software products cannot randomise physical inventory. An electric-scooter company can stage a firmware feature by serial cohort or region and run the estimate on telemetry, but retail sell-through data arrives weeks late through dealers, so the effective measurement lag is a distribution lag, not a behavioural one. AI-native products face a subtler contamination: if the treatment arm's interactions feed a model that also serves the control arm, the control is being improved by the treatment continuously, and the measured gap shrinks toward zero for reasons that have nothing to do with the feature's value. Mature teams freeze the serving model or hold out the training data as well, which most teams discover only after a null result they cannot explain.

At the organisational seam, the honest description of mature practice differs from the published one. Large firms say they run rigorous holdouts; what they mostly run is a permanent 1–5 per cent global holdout for the CRM and lifecycle stack, two or three geo tests a quarter on the largest paid channels, and a Bayesian media-mix model whose priors are updated from those tests. The rest is attribution, used as a within-channel optimisation signal and not believed as a cross-channel allocation signal. The reason is political as much as technical: a holdout costs revenue that lands on one team's P&L while the knowledge benefits everyone, and no measurement programme survives long if it reports to the budget holder whose spend it is evaluating.

6. Nine distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Average is not marginal. The tell is a deck that reports a single iROAS figure and then proposes a budget increase. An expert immediately asks at which spend level that number was measured and what the curve looked like on either side. The obvious reading — "iROAS is 3.1, so more spend earns 3.1" — is wrong because the measured 3.1 averages over inframarginal spend that would have worked at any budget.

Power is usually the binding constraint. The tell is a report with a point estimate and no confidence interval. Lewis and Rao's result is not a curiosity: because sales variance dwarfs advertising effects, the sample needed to distinguish a profitable campaign from a break-even one is often larger than the firm's entire customer base. The obvious reading is that better design fixes this; it does not. Only longer windows, more units, lower-variance outcomes or accepting wider bounds do.

"Not significant" is not "zero." The tell is a summary sentence containing the word "no" and no number. An estimate of +4 per cent with a 95 per cent interval of −5 to +13 is perfectly consistent with a strongly profitable campaign. An expert reports the interval and, when the decision is to cut, asks whether the data rule out the effect size that would justify the spend — an equivalence test, not a significance test.

The holdout that is not a holdout. The tell is that spend in the holdout geography did not fall to zero when the campaign was paused, or that impressions continued for nine days after. Retargeting pools drain slowly, cross-device delivery leaks, and other campaigns expand to fill freed budget. Experts check delivery logs in the control group before they look at the outcome, and treat any residual exposure above about 2 per cent as a reason to re-run.

Branded search is the canonical trap. The tell is that branded search shows the best cost per acquisition in the account. Somebody typing "Aranyaka face wash" has already been persuaded; the paid click frequently displaces a free organic one. The obvious reading is that branded search is the most efficient channel. The eBay experiment's reading is that for established brands much of it is a toll paid on demand the brand already created — with the genuine exception of categories where a competitor bids on your name, which is exactly the condition an expert checks before generalising.

Incrementality is a property of a spend level at a moment, not of a channel. The tell is a number older than two quarters being quoted with confidence. Audiences saturate, auction competition shifts, creative fatigues, and a channel that returned 2.4 in March can return 0.9 in September with nothing changed internally. Experts date every estimate and re-test the largest lines on a cadence.

Short-run estimates are lower bounds, not point estimates. The tell is a brand campaign evaluated on a four-week window and cut. Advertising effects decay slowly and partly through channels the window cannot see — organic search volume, direct traffic, retailer reorder rates. The disciplined move is to treat the experimental result as a floor, model the remainder explicitly, and say which part of the claim is experimental and which is modelled.

New channels flatter themselves. The tell is a spectacular first test on a channel nobody has used. The first cohort is the freshest audience and the best inventory; incrementality on that channel will decline as spend scales into worse inventory. Experts discount the first read and insist on a second test at three times the spend before committing budget.

Incremental to what? The tell is a design with no articulated baseline. An email holdout that still receives an in-app banner measures the incremental value of email over the banner, not over nothing. Both numbers are legitimate; only one answers "should we cancel the email vendor," and teams routinely produce the other.

7. How the practice changes by product type and stage

For consumer products with many small units and short cycles, geo and user-level randomisation are both available and cheap; the difficulty is discipline, not feasibility. For B2B and enterprise, the unit count collapses. Samanvay's realistic options are territory-level spend-scaling over a full year, a synthetic control built from a donor pool of untreated territories, or a deliberate and unpopular under-investment in two regions to create variance the model can use. For platforms and marketplaces, interference dominates and the design question — what is a non-interfering unit — matters more than the estimator. For hardware, the lag between exposure and registered sale runs into months and the measurement window must follow the distribution chain, not the click. For AI products, the treatment mutates during the test and the control learns from the treatment, so freezing the model version is part of the design.

Where the difference is not real, it should be said plainly: the statistics are identical in every one of these settings. The power formula does not care whether the buyer is a teenager in Indore or a procurement head in Jamshedpur, and the discipline of checking pre-period parallelism applies to all of them.

Stage changes the calculus through cost rather than method. A company spending ₹40 lakh a quarter should usually not hold out; the test costs a meaningful share of the budget and the effects at that scale are large enough to see without one. A rough threshold: run the test when the annual rupees at risk in the decision exceed roughly ten times the revenue forgone by the holdout. For Aranyaka, a 12-city holdout for six weeks forgoes about ₹94 lakh of revenue against ₹24 crore a year of spend under review — a ratio of 25 to 1, and clearly worth it. For a seed-stage company the same ratio is often 2 to 1, and the honest answer is to make the decision on structural reasoning and revisit it at scale.

8. Three tests, including one that failed

Aranyaka, Meta prospecting. Thirty-six cities, twelve held out for six weeks from 14 July 2026, matched on eight weeks of per-capita revenue growth to within 0.4 points. Test-city revenue grew 8.9 per cent over the window against 5.1 per cent in holdout cities; the 3.8-point gap, applied to a ₹5.2 crore spend, produced an incremental ROAS of 1.4 against the platform's reported 4.8. Deshpande did not cut the channel — 1.4 still clears the contribution margin — but she moved ₹1.9 crore of it into the two lines that had never been tested, and she stopped quoting the platform figure in board material.

Samanvay, the test that could not be run. Balakrishnan's alternative was a spend-scaling design: three territory groups funded at 100, 60 and 20 per cent of the community budget for four quarters, with pipeline measured on a twelve-month trailing basis and the estimate fed as a prior into a Bayesian media-mix model rather than read directly. The design is weaker than a randomised holdout and he said so; it was also the only thing available that produced a number with an honest interval attached.

Panchvati Mobility, the failure. The electric two-wheeler maker ran a geo holdout across fourteen cities in early 2026 and measured a lift statistically indistinguishable from zero. Management cut digital spend by 70 per cent. Registrations fell 18 per cent over the following quarter. Two errors had compounded. Six of the eight holdout cities were also where the dealer network had opened new showrooms that quarter, so the control group received a large untreated boost that masked the ad effect. And the window was eight weeks against a median consideration-to-purchase lag, measured later from test-ride records, of 41 days — so more than half of any effect fell outside it. The recovery took two quarters: a synthetic-control re-analysis on the pre-cut data recovered a lift of roughly 6 per cent, spend was restored to 60 per cent of its old level, and the company adopted a permanent 5 per cent national holdout with a sixteen-week read, which has the useful property that it costs the same whether or not anyone is asking a question.

Table 3 — The three exercises compared. The failure is the instructive one: the design error was in the assignment and the window, both decided before any data existed.
CaseDesignResultWhat it turned on
Aranyaka36-city geo holdout, 6 weeksiROAS 1.4 vs 4.8 reportedMatched pre-trends; short purchase cycle
SamanvayTerritory spend-scaling, 4 quartersWide interval, used as priorToo few units to randomise
Panchvati14-city holdout, 8 weeksNull, then ≈6% on re-analysisConfounded control; window shorter than lag

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Most incrementality programmes fail in one of six recognisable ways, and each announces itself before the result does. Contaminated assignment announces itself as a pre-period that is not parallel, and the diagnostic question is simply whether the A/A test returned zero; caught after a budget cut, it costs a quarter of revenue and, worse, the organisation's willingness to run another test. Underpowered design announces itself as a plan with no MDE in it; the question is what effect size the test can detect, and catching it late means spending the holdout's cost to learn nothing. Windows shorter than the conversion lag announce themselves as a distribution of time-to-purchase nobody has plotted. Outcome-metric drift — measuring installs when the decision is about revenue — announces itself when the metric is the one the channel optimises toward. Result decay announces itself as an estimate being quoted a year on. And organisational capture announces itself when the analyst presenting the lift reports to the person whose budget it justifies; the diagnostic question there is who chose the window, and the cost of catching it late is that every number the team has produced becomes suspect at once.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Is the media-mix model or the experiment the system of record? The modelling camp argues that experiments cover perhaps five per cent of spend and arrive quarterly, while a well-specified Bayesian model with experiment-derived priors covers everything weekly; allocating ninety-five per cent of budget by intuition to protect the purity of the other five is not rigour. The experimental camp replies that media-mix models are fit to a handful of degrees of freedom on collinear spend series, and that their coefficients move when the modeller changes the adstock assumption. The modellers would be wrong if experimental calibration turned out not to stabilise the coefficients — which is testable, and the published evidence is thin in both directions.

Permanent holdouts or pulsed tests? The permanent-holdout position is that a standing 2–5 per cent untreated population turns measurement into infrastructure, removes the negotiation over whether to test, and captures long-run effects a pulse cannot. The pulse position is that a permanent holdout is a permanent tax whose members drift into non-comparability as the product changes around them, and that a well-timed test at decision points costs less. The first would be wrong if drift proved large; the second would be wrong if long-run effects proved to dominate short-run ones.

Can brand advertising's long-run return ever be established experimentally? The econometric tradition associated with Binet and Field holds that the effects accumulate over two to three years and that any six-week window is measuring the wrong thing; the experimentalists reply that a claim which cannot be tested on any horizon a firm can sustain is not evidence but a belief system that conveniently protects the largest budgets. Nobody has run the decisive study, because running it requires withholding brand spend from a matched region for three years, and no board has yet agreed to that.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in four visible ways. They specify the estimand before the design and the design before the data, so the question "what would have changed our decision" has an answer written down in advance. They quote intervals rather than points, and they say out loud which parts of a recommendation are experimental and which are modelled. They know when not to test — they can state the spend level below which a holdout is a waste of the budget it is evaluating — and they decline gracefully rather than producing a decorative number. And they treat the organisational design as part of the measurement design, placing the person who runs the test outside the reporting line of the person whose spend it judges, because the most reliable way to get an inconvenient result is to make it nobody's job to avoid it.

12. What each of them decided

Deshpande cut ₹6 crore by taking ₹2.4 crore from branded search, where an eight-city pause produced an iROAS she could not distinguish from 0.4, ₹2.1 crore from the untested affiliate network, and ₹1.5 crore from the top of the Performance Max budget, leaving the Diwali brand flight intact on the argument that a six-week window could not evaluate it and that cutting on an unmeasurable is not the same as cutting on a measurement. Balakrishnan told his CRO that he could not answer the question this year, proposed the spend-scaling design, and asked for the community budget to be held flat in the meantime — a recommendation to do nothing, defended on the grounds that the alternative was to act on a number that did not exist.

For discussion: First, Deshpande protected the brand flight because it could not be measured while cutting the affiliate network because it had not been measured. Is that a principled distinction or a convenient one? Second, Balakrishnan's refusal is intellectually correct and professionally risky; what would it take for "we cannot know this" to be an acceptable answer in a company with a quarterly earnings rhythm? Third, if Panchvati's permanent 5 per cent holdout had been in place two years earlier, which of the two errors it made would it have prevented, and which would it not?

13. Going deeper

  1. Attribution and its limits — the system incrementality replaces; you cannot argue against a multi-touch model until you can explain precisely what question it does answer.
  2. Quasi-experiments and causal inference — difference-in-differences, synthetic control and regression discontinuity are the toolkit for every case where randomisation is unavailable, which is most of them.
  3. Constructing a funnel — the funnel defines the outcome metric a lift test measures, and choosing the wrong stage is the most common design error.
  4. Reading drop-off — tells you where an intervention could plausibly act, which disciplines the size of effect you should expect to find.
  5. Defining activation — gives lifecycle holdouts a target worth measuring, rather than an engagement proxy the treatment trivially moves.
  6. Cohort analysis — the structure that separates a genuine lift from a composition shift in who arrived.
  7. Retention curves and the PMF signal — determines whether incremental users are worth acquiring at all, and converts a lift into a lifetime figure.
  8. Stickiness and natural frequency — sets the baseline rate of return visits, which is the counterfactual every holdout is implicitly estimating.

Product Analytics & Data Practice

Reading Retail Scan and Sell-Through Data

What do scan and sell-through data reveal that my shipments don't?

A stockroom full of good news

On the second Monday of August, Meher Anand, category analytics manager at Kadamba Foods, opened the monthly sell-in report and found exactly the number her regional sales head had been promising the leadership team: shipments of Kadamba Crunch, the company's flagship namkeen line, were up 14% over the same month last year, driven by a big pre-festive stocking order from Mannat Mart, a national supermarket chain carrying the brand in 1,200 stores. Her sales head wanted to lock in an even larger shipment for the coming quarter on the strength of that number. Before agreeing, Meher pulled the other data feed her team had spent the spring building: point-of-sale scan data from Mannat Mart itself, showing what actually left the shelf, store by store, week by week. Sell-through growth over the same month was 2%. Worse, in 9% of the stores that were supposed to be carrying Kadamba Crunch, the scan feed showed zero units sold for five or more consecutive days — a pattern that almost always means an empty shelf, not indifferent shoppers.

The gap mattered because namkeen has a shelf life of roughly five months. If Kadamba kept shipping at the sell-in rate while real consumer demand grew at a sixth of that pace, the excess would sit in Mannat Mart's stockrooms until it approached its expiry date, at which point contract terms obliged Mannat Mart to return it or demand a steep markdown allowance — a cost that would land squarely on Kadamba's margin, and on the trade relationship. If, instead, Meher dismissed the sell-in number too quickly and the stockouts turned out to be the real constraint on growth, she would be starving a genuinely growing product of the inventory it needed just as competitors moved to fill the gap on Mannat Mart's shelves. She had five days before the quarterly supply commitment had to be signed off, and the decision rested on knowing precisely what each number was actually measuring.

The idea

Sell-in is the volume a manufacturer ships and invoices to a distributor or retailer. Sell-through — also called sell-out — is the volume a retailer's point-of-sale system records as sold to the final consumer, captured the instant a cashier or self-checkout scanner reads the barcode. The two numbers answer different questions. Sell-in answers "how much did we get out of our warehouse and onto someone else's books?" Sell-through answers "how much did an actual shopper want enough to buy?" A manufacturer that only watches sell-in is, in effect, driving by looking at the fuel gauge on its own truck rather than the traffic ahead.

The practice of feeding sell-through data back upstream grew out of the retail barcode, adopted industry-wide in the United States in the mid-1970s, which made every checkout scan a data point. Retailers such as Walmart built systems through the 1990s — Retail Link chief among them — to share that scan data with suppliers directly, and research firms such as Nielsen and IRI (now merged into Circana) built businesses syndicating scan panels across thousands of stores so manufacturers without a direct retailer feed could still see the market. The underlying discipline, often called Efficient Consumer Response, was a deliberate correction to decades of manufacturers planning production and trade spending almost entirely from their own shipment ledgers. The sentence Meher could say in any meeting without sounding glib: shipments tell you what left our warehouse; scan data tells you what left the shelf, and the gap between the two is where the truth about demand and stock discipline actually lives.

How it actually works

A scan happens at checkout, when a barcode is read and matched against the retailer's product master. That transaction lands first in the store's own point-of-sale system, then rolls up nightly or weekly into the retailer's central data warehouse alongside every other store. From there it reaches the manufacturer one of three ways: a direct data-sharing feed under a vendor agreement (an EDI 852 "product activity" file or a retailer portal), a syndicated panel purchased from a firm like Nielsen or IRI that aggregates many retailers into a market view, or, for manufacturers without either, a distributor's own reported "sell-out," which is really just the distributor's sell-in to the next link in the chain and not a true consumer read at all.

Three steps that practitioners usually leave implicit are worth naming. First, the retailer's product codes must be matched, SKU by SKU, to the manufacturer's own codes — a mapping exercise that quietly breaks whenever either side repacks or relaunches a product, and a broken mapping looks exactly like a demand collapse until someone checks. Second, distribution has to be measured alongside sales: a store can be "listed" to carry an item — authorized, planogrammed, on the system — without a single unit on the shelf, and until you weight sales by how many stores actually stock the item, comparisons across chains or regions are meaningless. Third, an out-of-stock has to be inferred, not announced: because perpetual inventory systems record what the system believes is on the shelf, not what a shopper can see, the standard diagnostic is a store that is listed to carry the item yet shows zero scans for several consecutive days. That pattern is what flagged Meher's 9%.

The arithmetic, twice

Meher's team pulled four weeks of Mannat Mart data for Kadamba Crunch 150g. Kadamba had shipped 110,000 units to Mannat Mart's distribution centres for that store set over the period — the chain-specific sell-in. Mannat Mart's scan feed showed 92,000 units sold to shoppers — the sell-through. The difference, 18,000 units, was inventory quietly accumulating inside Mannat Mart's system, against a product with roughly five months of shelf life left to sell it.

Table 1 — Kadamba Crunch 150g at Mannat Mart, four weeks to 9 August

Velocity is what lets Meher compare this to any other chain or period honestly: not raw units, but units per distributing store per week, so a chain with more shelf presence isn't unfairly flattered. The next question was whether the 9% out-of-stock figure was hiding real demand — whether, if those 89 dark stores had been selling normally, the true sell-through would look a lot closer to the 110,000 units shipped. So her analyst ran it a second way: assume each of the 89 stores lost roughly one week of sales at the fleet's average velocity of 23.4 units. That is 89 × 23.4 ≈ 2,083 units of scans the stockouts likely suppressed. Add that back, and estimated true demand for the period was about 94,083 units — still barely a third of the way from 92,000 toward the 110,000 shipped. Fixing the stockouts alone would not have closed the gap. There were two problems, not one: an execution failure worth roughly 2% of shipped volume, and a genuine over-shipment worth closer to 15%.

Nuances a learner must sit with

Sell-in growth is not demand growth

A rising shipment number can mean shoppers want more, or it can mean a distributor is loading up ahead of a price increase, a sales rep is chasing a quarter-end target, or a new chain has just been added to the distribution list. None of those are wrong to do; all of them are invisible if sell-in is the only number you watch.

Coverage is never complete

Scan feeds exist only where a data-sharing agreement exists. In India, that typically means organised modern trade — chains like the one in this example — and quick-commerce platforms, whose apps generate a live, granular version of the same signal. General trade, the neighbourhood kirana stores that still carry the bulk of national FMCG volume, mostly do not scan at all; sell-through there is estimated from distributor billing, which is really sell-in one step further down the chain.

Velocity must be distribution-weighted

Comparing raw units sold across two chains without adjusting for how many stores actually stock the item rewards wide, thin distribution over strong, deep distribution, and will send a manufacturer chasing the wrong shelf.

Out-of-stock is inferred, and inference can be wrong

A zero-scan run can mean an empty shelf, or it can mean the item was delisted, moved to a different aisle location the system hasn't updated, or caught in a short administrative freeze. The diagnostic is strong, not certain, and a sudden spike deserves a store visit before it becomes a supply-chain decision.

Scan data does not explain itself

It can tell you that sell-through slowed; it cannot by itself tell you whether that's a competitor's promotion, a price increase, a bad planogram position, a weather event, or genuinely cooling demand. Explaining the number is a separate piece of work, usually requiring a store audit or a pricing and promotion overlay.

It is easy to confuse with market share

A syndicated panel's sell-through, multiplied out across its distribution, approximates a brand's share of category sales within that panel — but a raw sell-through count from one retailer's own feed is not directly comparable to a competitor's number unless both are measured on the same store set and the same weighting.

Timing lags and promotions muddy the read

Most feeds arrive several days to a week after the scan itself, and a discounted display often isn't flagged as promotional in the raw data, which can make a temporary price cut look like a permanent shift in underlying demand.

Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and scale

The concept is native to consumer packaged goods, where the barcode scan is the cleanest signal available. In B2B, there is no literal scan, but the same structural gap exists: units shipped to a reseller or systems integrator are not the same as units activated, deployed, or renewed by the end customer, and mature B2B companies track "sell-in to the channel" against "sell-through to the end account" using deal registration and partner-reported usage data for exactly the reason Meher was worried about — channel inventory building up unseen. In a marketplace or quick-commerce setting, the two numbers nearly collapse into one: a seller dashboard on a platform like a quick-commerce app shows impressions, cart adds, and stockouts in near real time, because the platform itself is both the shelf and the register. The distortion there is different — return rates and ranking algorithms replace shelf placement as the thing worth arguing about.

Scale changes who gets to see any of this. A young company rarely has the negotiating weight to secure a direct retailer data feed; it triangulates from distributor sell-out reports, informal store checks, and whatever a retail buyer is willing to share informally. A large, established manufacturer typically has EDI feeds, retailer-portal access, and purchased syndicated panels, plus a team — often called revenue growth management or shopper insights — whose entire job is reconciling exactly the gap Meher found.

Common mistakes

Celebrating the shipment number

Symptom: a strong quarter-end sell-in report while a category manager who actually visits stores sees full shelves and tired displays. The underlying error is treating an invoice as proof of consumer demand. The cheap diagnostic is simply plotting sell-in growth against scan sell-through growth for the same weeks and watching whether the lines diverge.

Trusting the fill-rate dashboard

Symptom: a national on-time, in-full metric reads near 100% while shelves are visibly empty. Fill rate measures whether the retailer's warehouse received what it ordered from the manufacturer, not whether the store shelf has stock — two entirely different checkpoints in the chain. The fix is a scan-based, store-level out-of-stock flag, not a warehouse-level shipment metric.

Comparing velocity without weighting for distribution

Symptom: a smaller chain appears to be "outperforming" a larger one on raw units sold. The error is ignoring how many stores actually carried the item. Recomputing velocity per distributing store, as in Table 1, usually reverses the conclusion.

Acting on a stale or unflagged feed

Symptom: a sudden reaction to a one-week dip that turns out to be a data lag or an untagged promotion. The fix is checking the feed's as-of date and promotional flag before any decision gets made on it.

What good looks like

A well-run version of Meher's situation has a weekly, store-level out-of-stock dashboard that flags a dark store within forty-eight hours rather than a month later; replenishment triggers set from velocity trends rather than a fixed reorder calendar; and a trade and finance function that ties incentive payouts to sell-through, not sell-in, so nobody on the sales team is quietly rewarded for building inventory someone else has to write off later. The result is not zero stockouts and zero overstock — that is unrealistic — but a business that discovers both problems in days rather than discovering them, as Kadamba nearly did, only when the markdown invoice arrives.

What Meher decided

Meher recommended holding the festive shipment increase to Mannat Mart at roughly half of what her sales head wanted, pending two weeks of joint work with the chain's supply-chain team to fix the Tier-2 stockouts, and re-based the quarter's forecast on velocity-adjusted sell-through rather than the distributor's ask. It cost her an uncomfortable conversation about a smaller near-term number, and it protected several crore of margin that a festive markdown would otherwise have consumed. The next thing worth learning is how syndicated retail and panel data extends this same logic across an entire category and every competitor in it, not just one company's own shipments — which is exactly where this topic leads next. Two questions worth sitting with: when your own company has no direct scan feed at all, what second-best signals are worth triangulating, and how far should you trust them? And how would you design a sales incentive so a team is rewarded for what a shopper actually buys, without starving the business of the cash a shipment brings in today?

Reading Retail Scan and Sell-Through Data

What do scan and sell-through data reveal that my shipments don't — and when does the shelf lie too?

1. Two desks, one week apart

On Tuesday, 4 August, Aparna Ravikumar, director of category analytics at Arunodaya Beverages, was asked to sign off a production plan for the company's 200ml cold-coffee tetra pack. Arunodaya's shipments into Ambika Superstores, a 940-store modern-trade chain, had grown 27% over the trailing quarter. The plan in front of her assumed that growth continued. Her own scan feed, delivered weekly from Ambika's vendor portal, showed consumer purchases up 9%. The 18-point gap represented roughly 340,000 units of Arunodaya product sitting somewhere in Ambika's network — in distribution centres, in back rooms, or in a facing on a chiller door that nobody had refilled. Cold coffee has a nine-month ambient shelf life and Arunodaya's supply agreement obliged it to fund markdowns on anything within sixty days of expiry. Aparna's problem was not that she doubted the scan number. It was that she could not yet say which of three stories it told: that demand was weaker than sales thought, that the product sold well wherever it was actually on a shelf and not at all where it was not, or that Ambika had pulled forward six weeks of purchasing ahead of a price revision announced in June.

A week later and 340 kilometres away, Kartik Menon, who ran channel strategy at Shravya Acoustics, faced a version of the same question with a different physical object. Shravya made wireless earbuds sold through Vidyut Retail, a 210-store electronics chain, alongside its own online store. Vidyut's scan data showed 11,400 units of Shravya's mid-tier model sold across July. Shravya's own servers showed 8,900 first-time device activations attributable to units in that serial-number range. Both numbers were accurate. Neither was the number Kartik needed. A scan says a box crossed a till; an activation says a human paired the product with a phone. The 2,500-unit wedge between them could be gift purchases not yet opened, units bought and returned, or devices activating late in a household with one shared handset — or it could be, as Kartik's counterpart in supply chain suspected, units diverted to grey-market resellers who scanned them through a friendly store to earn a channel incentive. Kartik had committed to a festive build of 140,000 units. The wedge, if supply chain was right, would change that number by a fifth.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Sell-in is the quantity a manufacturer ships and invoices to the next entity in the chain — a distributor, a retailer's distribution centre, a marketplace's fulfilment node. Sell-through, or sell-out, is the quantity that leaves the final shelf into a consumer's hands, recorded at the moment a barcode is read at a point of sale. Between the two sits retail inventory, and the relationship between all three is an accounting identity rather than a theory:

Opening retail inventory + sell-in − sell-through − shrink − returns = closing retail inventory.

Everything in the discipline follows from taking that identity seriously. If sell-in exceeds sell-through week after week, inventory is accumulating somewhere, and inventory that accumulates in front of an expiry date or a product refresh becomes a markdown, a return, or a quietly destroyed trade relationship. If sell-through exceeds sell-in, the chain is drawing down cover, and a stockout is being scheduled several weeks in advance whether or not anyone has noticed.

The practice has a datable origin. The Universal Product Code was first scanned commercially in 1974, and by the early 1980s retailers held transaction-level records no manufacturer could see. A.C. Nielsen and Information Resources Inc. — since merged into Circana — built businesses aggregating those records into syndicated panels; Walmart's Retail Link, from 1991, gave suppliers store-level scan and inventory data directly, and the Efficient Consumer Response initiative of 1992 made data sharing an industry programme rather than a favour. The intellectual justification arrived in 1997, when Hau Lee, V. Padmanabhan and Seungjin Whang formalised the bullwhip effect: demand variability amplifies as it travels upstream, because each link reacts to its neighbour's orders rather than to the end consumer. Sharing sell-through data is the standard remedy, because it lets every link plan against one signal.

Three schools argue about what follows. The shipment-primacy school holds that sell-in is the only number with legal and audited standing: revenue is recognised on transfer of control, sales compensation is paid on it, and a manufacturer that starts managing to a retailer's operational data has outsourced its own P&L to a counterparty with its own agenda. This school will sign "sell-through is a useful early warning"; it will not sign "sell-through should drive the production plan." The consumption-primacy school, native to large CPG firms and to the syndicated-data business, holds that only consumption is demand and that everything upstream is logistics: share of category, measured on scans, is the only competitive scoreboard that cannot be gamed by loading a distributor. It will sign "trade-spend ROI computed on shipments is systematically overstated"; it will not sign "a shipment shortfall is necessarily a demand problem." The availability school, which grew out of retail execution and on-shelf-availability research, holds that most of the observed gap is neither demand nor logistics but execution — product in the building and not on the shelf — and that the correct response to a sell-through shortfall is usually a store visit, not a forecast revision. It will sign "a zero-scan run is the cheapest field-audit substitute ever invented"; it will not sign "scan data measure demand," because a shelf that is empty measures nothing at all.

3. Mechanics, worked through

An expert reading of scan data proceeds in a fixed order, and the order matters more than any individual technique.

First, fix the denominators. Raw units sold are uninterpretable across chains, regions or time because the store count moves. The two working measures are distribution — what share of the market's retail volume is represented by stores carrying the item, conventionally expressed as % ACV, all-commodity volume — and velocity, units per distributing store per week. Aparna's first act was to compute both for Arunodaya at Ambika, and to do it for the twelve-week period rather than the quarter, because Ambika had opened 40 stores in May.

The table reframes the entire conversation. Sell-through grew 9% in absolute units, which sales read as growth; velocity fell 4%, which means the brand sold slightly worse in every store it was in, and the apparent growth came entirely from being in more stores. Those are different businesses with different remedies. Distribution growth is a sales achievement that can be repeated once; velocity decline is a product, price or execution problem that compounds. Meanwhile, weeks of cover — closing retail inventory divided by average weekly sell-through — more than doubled, which is the identity in section 2 asserting itself. At 4.9 weeks of cover against a nine-month shelf life, nothing is on fire; at 4.9 weeks in a chilled dairy category it would be a crisis. Cover is only meaningful against shelf life and against the buyer's own target, which for Ambika's beverage category was three weeks.

Second, separate baseline from incremental. Scan data arrive with a promotion flag — whether the item was on feature, on display, or at a temporary price reduction in that store-week. Expert practice is to estimate a baseline, the volume that would have sold without the promotion, usually from surrounding non-promoted weeks with a seasonal adjustment, and to treat the difference as incremental. Two second-order effects then become visible and both are routinely missed. Forward buying: consumers with storage capacity buy the discount, not the product, so a spike is followed by a post-promotion dip as the household pantry drains. Cannibalisation: the promoted pack size steals from the unpromoted one, so brand-level volume grows far less than the SKU-level lift suggests.

Third, detect availability, and do it statistically. The folk method — flag any listed store showing zero scans for five consecutive days — is where competent practice stops and expert practice begins. Zero sales is only evidence of an empty shelf if sales were likely to have occurred. The disciplined version models store-level daily sales as a Poisson process with rate λ, the store's own recent non-promoted rate of sale, and asks how surprising a zero run of n days would be: P(zero in n days) = e−λn. For Arunodaya's median Ambika store, λ was 2.6 units a day, so a five-day zero run has probability e−13 — about two in a million. That is a real alarm. For the slowest quintile of stores, λ was 0.22, and P = e−1.1 = 0.333. A third of perfectly healthy slow stores would raise that alarm every week.
