Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation · Product Analytics & Data Practice

Self-Serve Analytics and Metric Layers

Can everyone answer their own questions without producing five different answers?

1. A number with two faces

On the second Tuesday of March, Kabir Anand sat in the glass-walled review room on the fourth floor of Rangrez Retail's Bengaluru office, watching two slides disagree with each other. Rangrez sold sarees, kurtas and occasion wear through an app and a website to roughly 3.2 million monthly active shoppers, competing for the same wallets that Myntra, Ajio and Meesho chased. The growth team's slide said thirty-day retention for the January cohort of new users was 41 percent. The lifecycle-marketing team's slide, built from the same underlying event stream, said 53 percent. Both numbers were correctly computed from correct data. Both teams were confident. The Chief Product Officer, Sunita Iyer, needed one number in an hour, because the board wanted a decision on whether to double the performance-marketing budget behind a cohort that looked, depending on whose slide you believed, either mediocre or excellent.

Kabir had joined Rangrez eight months earlier as a senior product manager for growth, and he already knew, from three smaller versions of this same argument, that the discrepancy was not a bug in either dashboard. It was a definitions problem wearing a data problem's clothes. Growth counted a user as retained if they opened the app in the relevant window. Lifecycle marketing counted a user as retained only if they completed a checkout. Neither definition was wrong on its own terms; each simply answered a different question while using the same word, "retention," to describe it. Kabir's task that afternoon was not to arbitrate which slide was right. It was to explain to Sunita why the company had no way of stopping this from happening again next quarter, and what it would take to build one.

2. The idea, plainly

A semantic layer, sometimes called a metric layer, is a single, governed place where a company writes down what its important business terms mean in code, once, so that every tool and every person that asks "what is our retention rate" pulls the same definition and gets the same answer. It sits between the raw data warehouse — the sprawling tables of events, orders and sessions that engineers produce — and the dashboards, spreadsheets and notebooks that PMs, marketers and executives actually look at. Instead of every analyst writing their own SQL query with their own private assumptions about what counts as "active" or "retained" or "revenue," they all reference the same named metric, defined in one file that a small group owns and version-controls.

The idea has a lineage. Business-intelligence vendors were already wrestling with this in the 1990s, but the modern shape of the semantic layer traces to Looker's LookML modelling language, released around 2012, which let a company describe its business logic as code sitting on top of a warehouse rather than baked into each report. A decade later, as the "modern data stack" matured, the open-source tool dbt introduced its own metrics layer, and companies like Airbnb built internal systems — Airbnb called theirs Minerva — for exactly this purpose: one definition of a metric, consumed everywhere, instead of a thousand slightly different ones. The problem these tools were invented to solve is the one Kabir was living through: as a company's data volume and headcount both grow, the number of people who can write a query grows faster than the number of people who agree on what the query should mean.

The sentence Kabir could have said in that room, without sounding glib, is this: "Self-serve analytics only works when the metrics are defined once, centrally, and everyone downstream inherits that definition rather than re-deriving it." Self-serve is the goal — a PM should be able to answer most of their own questions without filing a ticket with the data team. The metric layer is the mechanism that makes self-serve safe rather than chaotic.

Figure 1 — Where the layer sits

3. How it actually works

Building one starts nowhere near a dashboard. It starts with a meeting Rangrez had never actually held: a room with someone from growth, someone from lifecycle marketing, someone from data engineering and a product leader, arguing out loud about what "active," "retained" and "revenue" should mean, and writing the answer down. This is the step practitioners most often skip, because it feels like a meeting rather than an engineering task, and because it requires people to give up a definition they like in favour of one the company can agree on. Kabir's own experience was that this negotiation, not the software, was the expensive part.

Once a definition exists in words, an analytics engineer encodes it as a named metric in the semantic layer: a formula, the tables and joins it depends on, the grain it applies at (per user, per order, per day), and any filters — for instance, excluding test accounts or refunded orders. That metric gets a name, "d30_retention," and a single owner responsible for changing it deliberately rather than accidentally. Crucially, the layer also handles the joins and aggregations correctly behind the scenes, so a PM pulling "d30_retention by acquisition channel" in a self-serve tool does not need to know which four tables that requires or how the app's session table changed schema last year.

The layer then exposes these metrics through whatever tools people already use — a BI product like Looker or Tableau, a notebook, or a lightweight query interface — so that asking a question becomes choosing a pre-defined metric and slicing it, not writing SQL from scratch. Governance sits underneath all of this: changes to a metric's definition go through review, get versioned, and get communicated, exactly the way a change to a payment API would. The last, and most neglected, step is retiring old dashboards and queries that predate the layer, because a company that builds a beautiful new semantic layer while leaving forty legacy spreadsheets untouched has simply added a sixth source of truth to the five it already had.

4. Working the retention dispute

Kabir asked the data engineer, Farhan, to rebuild both numbers from the same 40,000-user January cohort so the arithmetic, not the opinions, could speak. Under growth's definition — retained means the user opened the app at least once between day 23 and day 37 — 16,400 of the 40,000 users qualified: 16,400 ÷ 40,000 = 41.0 percent. Under lifecycle marketing's definition — retained means the user completed at least one paid checkout in that same window — only 21,200 users had even opened the app, and of those, 21,200 × 0.53 is roughly consistent with 21,200 users who transacted... except that was not quite what had happened: 21,200 users had opened the app, and 11,236 of them had checked out, which is 11,236 ÷ 40,000 = 28.1 percent of the whole cohort — not 53 percent at all. Marketing's slide had silently divided checkouts by app-openers rather than by the original cohort, which is a legitimate metric but a different denominator, mislabelled with the same word.

DefinitionNumeratorDenominatorResult
Growth: any app open, day 23–3716,40040,00041.0%
Marketing: checkout ÷ cohort11,23640,00028.1%
Marketing's slide as shown: checkout ÷ openers11,23621,20053.0%

Once the three columns sat next to each other, the disagreement dissolved into arithmetic. A second pass showed how fragile the picture still was: if Kabir widened the retention window by just five days, from day 23–37 to day 18–42, growth's app-open number rose to 44.6 percent purely because it captured one more weekend of casual browsing traffic around a payday, while the checkout-based number barely moved, since people who intend to buy a saree do not wait for an arbitrary window boundary. The lesson Kabir drew, and later wrote into the metric's specification, was that "retention" needed a named, singular definition — checkout-based, day 30, cohort-anchored — with app-open activity tracked as a separate, honestly named metric such as "app_revisit_rate," so that no two teams could ever again mean different things while saying the same word in front of the board.

5. What a learner must get right

A semantic layer is not a data warehouse

The warehouse stores the raw, granular truth — every event, every order row. The semantic layer stores agreements about how to summarise that truth into business terms. Confusing the two leads teams to think that buying a bigger warehouse will fix a definitions problem; it will not, because the warehouse was never disagreeing with itself.

It does not fix data quality

If the event stream misfires — duplicate app-open events, a broken checkout webhook — a semantic layer will faithfully compute a consistent, wrong number for everyone. Consistency and correctness are different properties, and self-serve tools quietly assume both once a metric looks official.

Governance is the cost, not the software

Standing up the technology is a project measured in weeks. Getting growth, marketing and finance to accept one definition of "active user" is a negotiation measured in quarters, because someone's existing report, and possibly their bonus target, is built on the definition they have to give up.

Ownership must be a named person, not a team

A metric with no accountable owner drifts: someone quietly edits the underlying query to fix an edge case, and six months later nobody can explain why the historical trend line has a step change in it.

Self-serve has a ceiling

A metric layer answers "what happened" questions reliably — funnels, cohorts, trends. It does not answer "why," and it cannot tell a PM whether a change in retention was caused by a product change or by a marketing campaign that shifted who signed up in the first place; that requires experimentation, not a better dashboard.

More metrics is not more clarity

A layer that accumulates near-duplicate metrics — "retention," "retention_v2," "retention_strict" — because no one wants to delete an old one recreates the original chaos with better tooling. Curation matters as much as construction.

Freshness has a price

Metrics computed live, on demand, cost more compute and can time out on large slices; metrics pre-aggregated overnight are cheap and fast but a day stale. Teams should know, for each metric, which trade-off they are living with, rather than assuming the number on screen is real-time.

A single number invites false confidence

Once a metric is official, people stop asking how it is built. Kabir made a habit of attaching, to every metric definition, one line explaining what it excludes — refunds, test accounts, employee purchases — precisely so the confidence the layer created was earned rather than accidental.

6. Where the shape changes

In a consumer app like Rangrez, the contested metrics are almost always about engagement and retention, because acquisition cost and lifetime value hinge on exactly the kind of ambiguous word — "active," "retained" — that started Kabir's afternoon. In a B2B product, the equivalent fights are about account-level metrics: is a seat "active" if one person on a twenty-person account logged in, or does the whole account need usage above some threshold before a renewal risk model calls it healthy? In a marketplace that has both buyers and sellers, such as Rangrez's own seller dashboard for the boutique labels that list with it, the same word can mean opposite things to each side — "growth" is good news for a seller's order volume and can simultaneously signal saturation risk for buyer choice — so a marketplace's semantic layer typically needs twinned, explicitly named metrics rather than one shared one.

Company stage matters just as much as product type. An early-stage company with fifteen people and one analyst does not need Looker's full modelling language; a shared, well-commented spreadsheet of definitions, reviewed in a weekly meeting, delivers most of the benefit at a tenth of the cost, and premature investment in tooling is itself a common mistake. A company at Rangrez's scale, with dozens of PMs and marketers each capable of running their own query, has crossed the point where informal agreement breaks down faster than people can talk it through, which is exactly the point at which a governed, code-defined layer starts paying for itself.

7. Where this goes wrong

Symptom: two dashboards disagree and nobody can say why within an hour. Underlying error: definitions live inside individual queries instead of in one governed place. Cheap diagnostic: ask each dashboard's owner to state their metric's denominator out loud; disagreements surface in under a minute.

Symptom: the data team is buried in ad-hoc ticket requests despite an expensive BI rollout. Underlying error: the tool was self-serve but the metrics behind it were never agreed, so every question still routes through the one person who remembers the exceptions. Cheap diagnostic: count how many "custom" queries were written last month that duplicate an existing named metric.

Symptom: a metric's historical trend has an unexplained jump. Underlying error: someone edited the definition without versioning or announcing it. Cheap diagnostic: check whether the metric layer keeps a change log; if it does not, this will keep happening.

Symptom: executives trust a self-serve number more than they should. Underlying error: the layer never documented what the metric excludes, so its authority outran its accuracy. Cheap diagnostic: pick any headline metric and ask whether its exclusions are written down anywhere a PM could find in thirty seconds.

8. What good looks like

Six months on, Rangrez's quarterly review looked different. When Sunita asked about thirty-day retention, one slide appeared, sourced from a single named metric, "d30_checkout_retention," with its owner's name in the footer and a one-line note on what it excluded. Kabir's team had also kept a companion metric, "app_revisit_rate," clearly labelled as a different, engagement-flavoured number, so that nobody mistook browsing for buying again. When a new analyst on the marketing team wanted to slice retention by city, she pulled the same metric through the self-serve tool in nine minutes, without filing a ticket, and got the same number Kabir would have gotten. That is the actual test of a working semantic layer: not that it looks impressive, but that two people asking the same question, independently, on the same afternoon, get the same answer without needing to talk to each other first.

9. The decision, and two questions

Kabir told Sunita, in the room, that the honest answer was 28.1 percent, not 41 or 53, and that the board's marketing-budget decision should wait one week for a rebuilt, singly-defined metric rather than be made on either of the slides in front of her. Sunita agreed, and Rangrez spent the following quarter building exactly the layer described here: agreed definitions first, code second, self-serve access last. Kabir's own next step was to study experimentation design, because he had already run into the ceiling this topic warns about — the layer could now tell him precisely what retention was, but not why it had moved, and that question belongs to a different discipline entirely.

Two questions worth sitting with: if your own team's dashboards disagree tomorrow morning, could you find the exact line of logic each one used within an hour — and who, specifically, is allowed to change what "retained" means at your company, and would you know if they just had?

Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation · Product Analytics & Data Practice

Self-Serve Analytics and Metric Layers

Everyone can answer their own questions. The question is whether the answers agree, and where the agreeing stops.

1. Two rooms, one week apart

On 4 February, Devika Rao, VP of Product at Nishkarsh Systems, a Pune company selling warehouse-execution software to large Indian retailers and 3PL operators, had to sign off on a pricing change worth roughly ₹14 crore of incremental annual recurring revenue. Nishkarsh wanted to move from per-site licensing to per-active-user pricing. The commercial model rested on one number: how many active users the installed base actually had. Sales said 41,300. The product team's own dashboard said 18,700. Finance was invoicing against 52,000 provisioned seats. Nobody had made an error. Each number was the honest output of a different sentence about what "active" meant, and none of those sentences had ever been written down.

Seven days later and 150 kilometres away, Harshad Pai, Director of Product for growth at Rozana Quick, a fifteen-minute grocery service operating in eleven Indian cities against Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart, faced the mirror image. His decision was whether to release ₹22 crore of first-quarter acquisition budget. The internal rule was simple: release the money if the sixty-day repeat rate for the December new-user cohort exceeded 48 percent. Three dashboards existed. One said 52 percent, one said 42 percent, one said 46 percent. The rule was crisp; the input was not. Harshad's real problem was that he could not tell whether he was looking at a business fact or an artefact of a denominator.

Both situations are commonly filed under data quality. Neither is. The event pipelines at both companies were healthy. What was missing at both was a governed place where the company's own vocabulary lived — and, equally important, a shared understanding of the questions that no such place can answer. This page is about building that place, about the arithmetic that tells you how badly you need it, and about the boundary where self-serve honestly stops.

2. The idea, its history, and who disagrees about it

A semantic layer is an executable, version-controlled, owned specification of a company's business vocabulary, sitting between the warehouse and every tool that reads it. It contains, for each named metric, four things that are usually left implicit: a formula, a grain (the row that the metric is one of — a user, an order, a device-day), a set of admissible dimensions with the joins that reach them, and an exclusion list. It is not a database, not a dashboard and not a data-quality system. Its single promise is that two people who ask the same question get the same answer without speaking to each other first.

The lineage is longer than the tooling suggests. The first semantic layer in commercial history is the chart of accounts: a governed list of names for money, enforced by audit, which made it possible for a Bombay mill and a Madras agency of the same firm to report comparable figures. Ralph Kimball's dimensional modelling, codified in 1996, gave data warehousing the same instinct under the name conformed dimensions — a customer table that means the same thing in the sales mart and the support mart, enforced by a bus matrix. BusinessObjects had shipped the term itself, the "universe," in the early 1990s; OLAP cubes in the late 1990s carried defined measures and hierarchies in MDX. Looker's LookML, from 2012, moved the definition into text files under version control, which is the decisive move: once a metric is code, it can be reviewed, diffed and tested like code. Between 2019 and 2022 the largest consumer platforms each built the same thing internally and wrote about it — Airbnb's Minerva, Uber's uMetric, LinkedIn's Unified Metrics Platform — and the open-source stack followed with dbt's MetricFlow and Cube. The most recent argument for the layer is not human at all: a language model writing SQL against a raw warehouse invents plausible joins, and a governed layer is the only thing that constrains it to the company's actual meaning.

Practitioners who agree on all of that history still disagree sharply about what to build. Four positions are worth stating precisely, in terms of the proposition each would sign.

The governed-layer school would sign: "A metric is production software. It has an owner, tests, a changelog and a service level, and no dashboard may compute it privately." It would not sign: "analysts should define metrics in the query that needs them." The warehouse-native school, the direct descendant of Kimball, would sign: "The fewest layers that produce one answer wins; put the logic in well-named, pre-joined marts and let the BI tool be dumb." It would not sign: "you need a headless metrics API in front of the warehouse," which it regards as a second place for logic to rot. The product-analytics school — the world of behavioural event tools — would sign: "Self-serve for product managers means cohorts and funnels defined where they work, not SQL; the warehouse is for finance." It would not sign: "the warehouse number is canonical for product decisions." The federated, or data-mesh, school would sign: "The definition belongs to the domain that generates the data; the centre supplies standards, not definitions." It would not sign: "one central team owns the definition of retention."

There is a fifth position, less organised but held by some very good practitioners, that deserves stating because it is the strongest challenge to the whole enterprise: consistency is overrated, and what matters is that a decision survives the choice of definition. That school would sign: "If the answer flips when the window moves from 28 days to 30, the defect is in the decision rule, not the metric." We will return to it in section 10, because it is not obviously wrong.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Start where the practice actually starts, which is not with tooling. Devika's team ran what they later called the vocabulary session: four people in a room for three hours, asked to produce one sentence defining "active user" for Nishkarsh. They produced five, and the five are the whole lesson.

Candidate definition of "active user"UsersARR at ₹2,400/user
Provisioned seat (what finance invoices)52,000₹12.48 cr
Any login in trailing 30 days41,300₹9.91 cr
Any login in trailing 7 days28,900₹6.94 cr
≥1 completed pick or scan task in 30 days18,700₹4.49 cr
≥5 tasks on ≥3 distinct days in 30 days11,200₹2.69 cr

Table 1. Nishkarsh Systems, January 2026. Same warehouse, same population, five defensible sentences. The spread is 4.6×.

The spread between the top and bottom rows is not noise; it is ₹9.79 crore of annual revenue, and the pricing committee had been arguing about it for six weeks without noticing that it was arguing about vocabulary. This is the first mechanical point: definitional variance usually dwarfs measurement error. Teams spend their energy on the pipeline because pipelines are tractable, while the larger number sits untouched in the language.

The second mechanical point is combinatorial, and it explains why informal agreement fails at a predictable size rather than gradually. A metric is a set of independent choices. For Rozana's repeat rate the choices were: the window length; whether the anchor is first order or first app-open; whether an order counts when placed or when delivered; whether a returned or cancelled order counts; whether the day boundary is IST midnight or UTC; and whether the denominator is the whole cohort or those who reached the second session. Five of these are binary and one has four levels, giving 25 × 4 = 128 internally consistent metrics all entitled to the name "sixty-day repeat rate."

The third mechanical step, routinely skipped, is the reconciliation anchor. Before Rozana certified its repeat-rate metric, Harshad insisted that total orders in the layer be tied monthly to the settlement file that the payment gateway produced and to the GST returns the finance team filed. The anchor does not make the metric correct, but it bounds how wrong it can silently be, and it converts a class of errors from invisible to loud. A layer without an external anchor is a closed system that will agree with itself forever.

Encoding comes fourth, and is the easy part: name, formula, grain, admissible dimensions, exclusions, owner. Then access — exposing the metric through whatever people already use. Then, last and most neglected, deprecation: removing the queries and dashboards that predate the layer. A company that builds a layer without deprecating has not reduced the number of answers; it has added one.

The quantitative case for the investment is worth doing honestly, because it is usually done dishonestly. Rozana's nine analysts handled roughly 1,400 ad-hoc requests in the prior year at a mean 2.3 hours each — about 3,220 hours, or ₹1.16 crore at a fully loaded ₹3,600 per hour. The layer cost two analytics engineers for seven months, about ₹58 lakh to build, and about ₹31 lakh a year to run. A naive business case claims 55 percent deflection and ₹64 lakh of annual saving. What actually happened is that deflection ran at 51 percent while total request volume rose 40 percent, because asking had become cheap: gross hours fell only to 2,270, a net saving of about ₹34 lakh against ₹31 lakh of cost. On cost alone the project roughly broke even. Its return came from somewhere else entirely — from the ₹22 crore decision that was, as the next section shows, on the wrong side of the threshold.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

The conditions can be stated as claims that can be checked in an afternoon. Claim one: the number of people who can write a query exceeds the number who can be kept in agreement by conversation. True at Rozana, where sixty-odd people had warehouse access; true at Nishkarsh, where only nine did but they sat in three cities and two functions. Claim two: the same word appears in more than one function's targets. "Active user" at Nishkarsh sat in sales compensation, finance invoicing and product planning simultaneously — the strongest possible signal. Claim three: decisions of material size are threshold decisions on the metric. Rozana's ₹22 crore rule is exactly this; Nishkarsh's pricing model is worse, because the metric is not an input to the decision but the thing being sold.

Where the idea actively misleads is less often discussed. If the underlying event data is wrong, a semantic layer converts a scattered, self-correcting error into a uniform, authoritative one; discrepancy between dashboards is an immune response, and suppressing it before fixing the pipeline removes the only signal the company had. If the company is genuinely pre-product-market-fit, definitional stability is a cost rather than a benefit, because the right definition of activation is changing monthly and governance will lock in a guess. And where a regulator supplies a definition — an RBI provisioning convention, an IRDAI claim ratio — collapsing the regulatory number and the product number into one certified metric is not consistency, it is a category error: the company genuinely has two correct answers and its layer must carry both with lineage rather than choose.

5. Hard edges

In multi-product companies the difficulty is never the individual metric; it is the roll-up nobody owns. Rozana ran groceries, a pharmacy vertical and a seller-facing dashboard. Company-level "monthly actives" belonged to no product team, so it was computed by whoever prepared the board deck, and it deduplicated across products in a way that was never written down. In two-sided businesses the same word is genuinely two metrics: order growth is unambiguously good for a Rozana seller and simultaneously a saturation signal for buyer choice, so a marketplace's layer needs twinned, explicitly named metrics rather than one shared one.

Hardware plus software is the hardest technically. Tvisha Energy, a Chennai maker of connected rooftop-solar inverters, has devices that go offline for days and then backfill telemetry with original timestamps. Yesterday's "active devices" is therefore not a fact but an estimate that keeps rising for a week; a layer that reports it as final is confidently wrong. The mature handling is to publish the metric with an explicit maturity window and to mark any figure inside that window as provisional. AI-native products add a stranger problem. At Nazariya AI, a Bengaluru support-automation company, the headline metric is resolution rate, and resolution is judged by a model. The definition therefore contains a model version, and an upgrade silently moves the metric. Nazariya's answer — pin the judge model inside the metric definition and re-score a fixed holdout on every change — is the correct one and is still rare.

At the organisational seams, the recurring fights are predictable: finance books on accrual and product on event timestamp, so revenue never matches; marketing owns attribution windows that product does not see; sales defines "the customer" at a parent account that product's schema has as fourteen unrelated tenants. What mature companies say they do is certify everything. What they actually do is tier: roughly ten to thirty tier-one metrics that appear in planning and board packs, reviewed quarterly and change-controlled; a middle tier owned by teams; and a large, ungoverned exploratory tier that everyone quietly relies on and that the catalogue pretends is temporary.

6. Eight things experts see that competent practitioners miss

Consistency is not correctness, and the layer hides the difference. A metric everyone shares is a metric nobody reconciles, because the social function of disagreement — noticing — has been designed away. The expert's tell is a metric with a suspiciously clean history: if a number has never been restated in three years, it has never been checked against anything outside the system. The obvious reading, that stability signals quality, is backwards; stability that tight usually signals a closed loop.

Almost every metric dispute is a denominator dispute. Teams rarely disagree about how many users did something; they disagree about what the something is divided by. The tell is two people quoting different rates while agreeing on the count. Experts therefore ask for the denominator first, and they distrust any metric whose name does not encode it — "repeat rate" is a bad name, "60-day repeat rate per acquired cohort" is a usable one.

Time is the hardest dimension, and the first question is whose midnight. Event time versus ingest time, IST versus UTC, week starting Monday versus Sunday, late-arriving events: each shifts daily actives by one to four percent, and the shifts are correlated with exactly the behaviour being measured, because a payday or a festival moves both traffic and latency. The tell is a metric that looks fine at monthly grain and jitters at daily grain. The naive reading blames the pipeline; the expert reads it as a grain and boundary specification that was never written.

Certification changes behaviour before it changes accuracy. The moment a metric becomes official, it becomes a target, and the incentive to shape it moves upstream into the definition meeting. The tell is a cluster of requests to certify new metrics in the six weeks before annual planning. This is not cynicism about colleagues; it is a structural consequence of governance, and the standard mitigation — freezing tier-one definitions outside a fixed change window — exists precisely because good people respond to incentives.

Self-serve changes the shape of the data team's queue rather than emptying it. Requests shift from "please run this" to "why does this differ from that," which take longer and require more seniority. The tell is flat ticket count with rising average ticket length. The naive conclusion is that self-serve failed; the expert's reading is that it worked and surfaced a governance debt that was previously hidden inside the queue.

The catalogue's health is measured by deletion, not addition. Every layer accumulates near-duplicates because deleting someone's metric requires a conversation and creating one does not. The tell is three metrics whose definitions differ only in an exclusion clause, all still live. A healthy catalogue shrinks at least once a year, and the strongest single governance rule in practice is that no new tier-one metric is admitted without naming one to retire.

Non-additive metrics break silently across slices. Distinct counts and ratios cannot be summed. Rozana's distinct buyers by city summed to 1.38 crore while the company-level distinct count was 1.11 crore, because two million people ordered in more than one city. The tell is a total row that does not equal the sum of its rows and that nobody has queried. The layer must therefore know each metric's grain and refuse illegal aggregations — this is a correctness feature dressed as a performance feature.

The ceiling of self-serve is causal, not technical. A layer answers what happened with high reliability and says nothing about why. When Rozana's repeat rate rose four points in March, the layer could not distinguish a product improvement from a change in acquisition mix that brought in better-intentioned users. The tell is dashboards being used to win arguments rather than to notice things. Past this line the honest instruments are experiments and quasi-experiments, and an expert says so instead of slicing further.

7. How the shape changes by product and stage

In consumer products the contested words are engagement words, and the stakes are acquisition budgets. In B2B the contest moves up a level of aggregation: the fight is not what a user did but what an account is, and whether a twenty-seat account with one active user is healthy. Nishkarsh's entire problem is this. In platforms and marketplaces the requirement is twinned definitions, as above. In hardware the requirement is a maturity window and a device-versus-account distinction. In AI products the requirement is that metric definitions carry model versions and that cost per unit of usage — which can vary a hundredfold between two queries — becomes a first-class dimension rather than a finance footnote.

Where the difference is not real, it is worth saying plainly: the governance mechanics are the same everywhere. Ownership, versioning, an external anchor and deprecation do not vary by industry, and a team that believes its domain is too special for them is usually avoiding the meeting rather than facing a genuine constraint.

Stage matters more than sector. Below roughly twenty employees, a commented spreadsheet of nine definitions reviewed weekly delivers most of the value; building a modelled layer at that stage is a common and expensive mistake, because the definitions are still being discovered. The transition point is not a headcount but a condition: the first time two people independently produce different answers to the same question in the same week. Above a few hundred people the problem inverts — the layer exists, the governance exists, and the binding constraint becomes curation and the courage to delete.

8. Three worked cases

Nishkarsh, and the account-level definition. Devika did not pick one of the five rows in Table 1. She split them: billable_seat (52,000) for invoicing, engaged_user (≥1 task in 30 days; 18,700) for product health, and a new account-level metric, account_utilisation, the ratio of engaged users to provisioned seats, which came out at 36 percent. That third number was the one that mattered commercially: at 36 percent utilisation, per-active-user pricing would have cut revenue, not raised it. The pricing change was redesigned as a floor-plus-usage model, and the redesign was worth more than the original proposal.

Rozana, and the threshold that was already crossed. Harshad's three dashboards resolved to a single definition — orders counted at delivery, returns excluded, cohort denominator, IST boundary — and the December cohort came out at 42 percent against a 48 percent rule. Figure 2 shows why the other numbers existed.

The ₹22 crore was held back. Six weeks later, cohort analysis showed the December intake had been dominated by a heavily discounted festival offer whose users did not return at price. The layer did not produce that insight; it produced the honest number that made someone go looking.

Tvisha Energy, where the layer failed. Tvisha built a textbook semantic layer in 2025 and certified active_devices as tier one. For nine months every dashboard, board pack and warranty forecast agreed — and every one was wrong by eleven to fourteen percent, because offline inverters backfilled telemetry after the daily job ran and the metric was computed on a one-day maturity window. Consistency had made the error invisible; before the layer, three teams had disagreed, and the disagreement had been the clue. The failure surfaced only when a service contract renewal used the number and the field team said it did not match their van schedules. Recovery took four months: a seven-day maturity window with provisional flagging, a monthly reconciliation against shipment and activation records held outside the warehouse, and a restated two-year history. The restatement cost about ₹2.3 crore in revised warranty provisioning. The lesson Tvisha wrote into its own runbook was that no metric may be certified tier one until it has an external anchor, because a layer without one is an echo chamber with version control.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Failure modeEarly warningDiagnostic question
Uniform wrongnessMetric never restatedWhat outside source does it tie to?
Shadow layer in spreadsheetsRising CSV exportsWhat did the export do that the tool could not?
Metric sprawlNear-duplicate names liveWhat was retired last quarter?
Silent definition driftStep change in a trendIs there a changelog with owners?
Premature governanceCertified metrics unusedWhich decision used this last?
Authority outrunning accuracyExclusions undocumentedWhat does this number leave out?

Table 2. Each diagnostic is answerable in under a minute by the metric's owner. If it is not, that is itself the finding.

The cost of catching these late scales with how load-bearing the metric has become. A sprawl problem caught in the first year costs a cleanup sprint. The same problem caught after the metric has entered sales compensation, an investor deck and a customer-facing service level costs a restatement, and restatements are expensive less for the arithmetic than for the credibility.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The first live disagreement is central versus federated ownership. The centralist evidence is strong: Airbnb and Uber both published that a single certified definition ended years of recurring disputes, and the counterfactual — thousands of private definitions — is observable in any large company. The federated case is equally grounded: central teams become bottlenecks, and a definition written by people who do not operate the domain drifts from the domain's reality. This would be settled if someone could show that central ownership does not slow the creation of new metrics; nobody has, and the practical compromise, central for tier one and federated below, is a truce rather than a resolution.

The second is whether the layer should be headless. The warehouse-native school's strongest claim is that a metrics API is a second place for logic to live, and two places for logic is the original disease; materialised marts with disciplined naming achieve the same consistency with less machinery. The headless school's strongest claim is that marts cannot express ratios and distinct counts safely across arbitrary slices, which is a correctness argument, not an elegance one. Each would be wrong if the other's failure mode turned out to be rare, and both failure modes are common.

The third, and the one product managers should take most seriously, is the robustness school's challenge: that the effort belongs in making decisions insensitive to definitional choice rather than in certifying one choice. Its evidence is that most governance programmes produce agreement without producing better decisions. Figure 2 is the counter-evidence: Rozana's rule genuinely flipped on the choice, and no amount of robustness engineering makes a threshold rule indifferent to its input. The honest position is that both are right about different decisions, and that nobody has a principled test for telling in advance which kind you are facing.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this builds the layer and announces it. Someone who has internalised it does four things differently. They ask for the denominator and the day boundary before they look at the chart, which takes eleven seconds and catches most disputes. They insist that every tier-one metric tie to something outside the data system — a settlement file, a GST return, a shipment record — because they have seen a consistent company be uniformly wrong. They treat the catalogue as something to prune rather than to grow, and they can name what they retired last quarter. And they say "this is where the dashboard stops" out loud, and reach for an experiment, rather than slicing a descriptive metric six ways in the hope that causation will fall out of it.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Devika shipped three metrics instead of one, and redesigned the pricing model around the utilisation figure that the vocabulary session had exposed. Harshad held the ₹22 crore, took a difficult meeting with the CMO, and spent the following quarter building a layer whose first certified metric carried a written note on what it excluded. Neither outcome was the one either of them expected in the first week of February, and in both cases the value came from the definition work rather than from the software.

One: Pick the number your company's last large decision turned on. How many independent definitional choices sit inside it, and would the decision have been different under a different admissible combination? Two: Which of your tier-one metrics ties to something outside your own data system, and when was that tie last checked? Three: Who is allowed to change what "active" means at your company, what would that change cost to reverse — and would you find out from a changelog or from a customer?

13. Going deeper

  1. Metric definitions and data quality — the layer inherits whatever the definitions and pipelines give it; this is the prerequisite it cannot compensate for.
  2. Data platforms as products — treating the layer as a product with users and a roadmap is what keeps it curated rather than abandoned.
  3. Constructing a funnel — funnels are where grain and denominator errors show up first and most expensively.
  4. Reading drop-off — the skill that turns a consistent funnel into a decision rather than a description.
  5. Defining activation (the aha moment) — the hardest definition to certify early, and the one most damaged by premature governance.
  6. Cohort analysis — the technique that revealed why Rozana's December intake did not repeat.
  7. Retention curves and the PMF signal — where definitional choices change the shape of the curve, not just its level.
  8. Stickiness and natural frequency — the check that stops a team from measuring weekly behaviour with a daily metric.

The Two Delinquency Numbers

Tarazu Systems, Bengaluru · a decision due by Friday

1. Friday, six days away

On the morning of 12 November, Rhea Vashisht, VP of Product at Tarazu Systems, opened her laptop in the company's Indiranagar office to find two emails that could not both be true. One, from the risk team in Mumbai, reported that 7.0 percent of the loans issued during the October Diwali sale season were thirty-day delinquent. The other, from collections in Bengaluru, reported 4.5 percent for the identical cohort. Both numbers would be read aloud in the board meeting on Friday, where Tarazu's Series C round was meant to close, and both would be read again the following week by risk officers at a Dubai-headquartered digital bank deciding whether to license Tarazu's underwriting engine for its own market. Rhea had four working days to find out which number, if either, was the truth — and to make sure the company never again walked into a room carrying two answers to the same question.

2. Tarazu Systems

Founded in 2019 and headquartered in Bengaluru with a second office in Mumbai, Tarazu Systems was a Reserve Bank of India–registered non-banking finance company offering short-tenure personal loans and checkout-time BNPL financing, embedded inside partner e-commerce and quick-commerce apps rather than sold directly. It competed for the same borrowers as KreditBee, MoneyTap, Navi and CASHe, and watched Bajaj Finserv's consumer-lending arm the way a smaller boat watches a larger one. By November, Tarazu had disbursed a cumulative loan book of roughly ₹340 crore across 480 employees, with engineering split between Bengaluru and Pune and a small underwriting-model team that worked remotely out of Toronto. The business model depended on two things simultaneously: partners trusting Tarazu's risk numbers enough to keep embedding its financing widget at checkout, and investors trusting the same numbers enough to keep funding growth. Both trusts were now, briefly, standing on the same disputed statistic.

3. What had actually happened

During the Diwali sale window in October, Tarazu had disbursed loans to 60,000 borrowers through partner checkouts, averaging ₹20,000 each, for a cohort total of ₹120 crore — an unusually large single cohort, built for an unusually large seasonal spike. Six weeks later, two teams had each computed how much of that cohort had gone thirty-plus days delinquent, using data drawn from the same warehouse tables, and arrived at answers nearly sixty percent apart. Risk, in Mumbai, counted a loan as delinquent if it had ever been thirty-plus days overdue at any point during the month — the "ever-30" convention regulators expect for provisioning purposes — and found 4,200 of the 60,000 loans qualified: 7.0 percent. Collections, in Bengaluru, counted delinquency as the rupee value still overdue on the last day of the month, as a share of the rupee value disbursed, and found ₹5.4 crore overdue against ₹120 crore disbursed: 4.5 percent. Both were legitimate ways to ask "how bad is this cohort." Neither team knew, until Rhea forced the comparison onto one page, that the other was answering a related but different question and calling it the same name.

4. The people in the room, and out of it

Karan Oberoi, Head of Risk & Underwriting, Mumbai, wanted the ever-30, count-based number reported without softening, because it matched the convention Tarazu's auditors and the RBI's provisioning norms expected; understating delinquency, in his view, was the one mistake the company could not survive a regulatory inspection over. Elena Petrova, lead data scientist, working remotely from Toronto, argued that neither raw number meant much on its own, since a cohort only six weeks old had not finished "maturing," and she wanted a vintage-adjusted projection instead — technically the most defensible answer, but the hardest one to explain in a board meeting. Farhan Qureshi, Head of Sales & Partnerships, based in New Jersey to be near Tarazu's US-facing investor conversations, wanted one clean, favourable-reading number by Friday, worried that visible internal disagreement would itself spook a Series C round led by a Singapore-based growth fund. Mei Lin, Customer Success Lead in Singapore, managed the Dubai partner relationship directly and was already fielding pointed questions from the partner's own risk desk, who had noticed the discrepancy in a data extract before Tarazu had finished discussing it internally.

5. Options before Rhea

Option A — Report the regulatory number, plainly

Adopt Karan's ever-30, count-based 7.0 percent as the single official figure for Friday's board meeting and for the Dubai partner, with a short note on methodology. This is the number Tarazu's auditors already expect and the one closest to how the RBI thinks about provisioning. The cost is narrative: 7.0 percent reads worse than 4.5 percent in a fundraising deck, and Farhan believed it could unsettle the Singapore fund's partners days before signing.

Option B — Report the friendlier number now, reconcile later

Present collections' value-based 4.5 percent on Friday, since it is not fabricated, only differently defined, and commit internally to reconciling the two metrics afterward. This protects the week's two deals but risks a second, more damaging conversation later, if the Dubai bank's own risk team — already alert to the discrepancy — recomputes the count-based figure themselves and asks why Tarazu did not lead with it.

Option C — Disclose both, commit to one metric going forward

Present both numbers to the board and the partner with full methodology, explain why they diverge, and commit to a single governed "thirty-day delinquency" definition, owned by a named team, within thirty days. This is the slowest option to deliver full confidence and requires Rhea to admit, in the room, that Tarazu's own dashboards had disagreed — a harder sentence to say than either single number.

6. Questions for discussion

  • Why did two internally consistent, correctly computed numbers describe the same cohort so differently — and whose fault, if anyone's, was that?
  • How should Rhea weigh the RBI-facing convention Karan wants against the fundraising narrative Farhan wants, given that both audiences will eventually see the same underlying data?
  • What does Mei Lin's position in Singapore, fielding the Dubai partner's questions before Bengaluru had even resolved the internal debate, tell Rhea about how fast an unowned metric can travel outside the company?
  • Which of the three options best serves Tarazu a year from now, rather than only this Friday — and what would have to be true about the semantic layer Tarazu builds afterward for that option to hold up?

7. A note for the learner

This case is a self-serve analytics problem wearing a credit-risk costume. The learning objective behind it is narrow and practical: a semantic layer lets everyone answer their own questions consistently, and knowing where self-serve stops means knowing that a single number, however official-looking, is only as trustworthy as the definition sitting underneath it. Tarazu's two teams were not careless; they had simply never been forced to agree, in writing, on what "delinquent" meant before both of them shipped a dashboard that used the word. That is precisely the condition a metric layer exists to prevent — not by making the arithmetic cleverer, but by making the definition singular and owned before anyone builds on top of it.

A well-reasoned answer here does not chase the most comfortable number; it asks which definition survives contact with the audience that has the least patience for nuance and the most power to hurt Tarazu if it turns out to be wrong. That audience is the regulator, not the investor, because a fundraising conversation can absorb an honest, well-explained 7.0 percent, while a provisioning shortfall discovered later by an RBI inspector cannot be talked back down. The defensible path, then, leans on Option A, but only in its fullest form: report the ever-30 count-based number as the official figure for both the board and the Dubai partner, explain in one paragraph why collections' value-based figure differs and what it is separately useful for, and use the same meeting to announce that a single, jointly-owned "delinquency" metric will exist in the semantic layer within thirty days, with Karan's team as its named owner. This does not make the week comfortable. It does make Tarazu the party that found the discrepancy and explained it, rather than the party that got caught by it — and it leaves behind exactly one definition of delinquency, not two, for the quarter after this one.
